en: I pay homage to Caṇḍikā and the Moon-crested Lord, who, like the rising of the world, expand both heaven and liberation, and who remove the disease of worldly existence.

The accomplishment of mercury (rasa), together with the oils, roots, and fruits of the metals, secondary minerals, and base metals—accompanied by empirical proof—is declared to be unattainable [by ordinary means]. Rā 1.1.2.
For the fame and profit of physicians, for the welfare of the diseased,
for the curiosity of disputants, and for the bodily perfection of the elderly.
This scripture, consisting of five sections, which brings about various wonders for the sake of the mantrasiddhi of ministers and bestows benefit upon practitioners, [is here presented].
In the section on tastes for physicians, in the section on mercury for the diseased, in the section on debate for disputants, and in the section on elixirs for the elderly; Rrā_1,1.5.
And for the ministers, the accomplishment of the elixir (rasasiddhi) arises from the Mantra-khaṇḍa;
there is no doubt at all for those who have examined each respective section.
When killed, it destroys old age and death; when liquefied, it is the slayer of disease;
and when bound, it bestows the power of moving through the sky—what else is more compassionate than mercury?
Because it destroys old age, death, poverty, and disease,
it removes all ailments even as it moves within the body, like a swoon.
Who would not serve that charioteer who, while himself bound, can bewilder his enemies; who, though dead, can bring others back to life;
and who, while swooning, can awaken others?
Through the service of the essence (rasa), there shall arise long life, wealth, health, digestive fire, intelligence, great strength, beauty, youth, and charm.
One should kill the mercury by means of sulphur and cause it to coagulate;
once bound, it undergoes liquefaction through the two qualities of essence (sattva). Thus is the threefold movement of mercury.
The rasa devoid of defects is Brahmā; when swooned, it is Janārdana;
when killed, it takes the form of Rudra; and when bound, it is Maheśvara himself.
O Goddess, the piercing agent is the body and the metal, while the mercury is Sadāśiva;
by the mere sight of the king of rasas, one dispels even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
O Goddess, by touching it one destroys the sin of killing a cow; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, how much more so by eating it—that the supreme state is attained!
Because it requires only a small amount, because it avoids the occurrence of aversion,
and because it bestows health quickly, *rasa* is superior to medicinal drugs.
As was previously stated by Śambhu in the *Rasakhaṇḍa* and the *Rasāyana*, as well as in the *Dīpikā* and the *Rasamaṅgala*, for the purpose of venerating mercury: [1.1.16]
That which was spoken by Nāgārjuna for the benefit of those afflicted by disease, and that which was taught by Carpaṭi Siddha at Svargavaidya Kāpālika; Rrā 1.1.17.
That which has been stated in the various treatises on rasa, in the *saṃhitās*, and in the *āgamas*, as well as in the *Vāgbhaṭa-tantra* and the ocean of physicians, the *Suśruta*.
Having observed what was said by many other perfected beings (siddhas), whatever therein might be impossible to accomplish or whatever medicine might be difficult to obtain— [he taught all that].
Having abandoned all of that, the essential core has been extracted:
in some scriptures there is no ritual action, and in others there is no enumeration of stages.
In some cases there is no knowledge of dosage or proper application, nor is there any traditional transmission;
therefore, success is not found therein, whether in the field of alchemy (rasa) or rejuvenation (rasāyana).
Since I have exerted effort in medicine, debate, and practical application,
whatever has been learned from the mouths of my gurus and whatever has been personally experienced by me—
all that is now being made manifest for the benefit of the world. (Rājamārtaṇḍa 1.1.22)

The illustrious King of Sūtas bestows a resplendent, eternal body that brings joy to his own people and is as steadfast for men as a mother; since there is no other destroyer of diseases that cause the destruction of the body, one should first perform the preparation of the body through the Sūta with constant great festivals.

May this King of Sūtas, who is expert in helping others, protect the world—he who directly bestows inexhaustible [merit] upon men on earth; who, having assumed a physical form, destroys the intense delusion of those afflicted by disease; and who, having attained that state practiced by the lords of gods and asuras, leads bound beings to their respective destinies.
What exists elsewhere exists here; what exists here does not exist anywhere else.
This *Rasaratnākara* has been composed by Nityanātha;
therefore, one should diligently perform the supreme purification of mercury (*rasasaṃskāra*). (Rrā 1.1.25)
And a physician who is skilled in practice but ignorant of the meaning of the medical treatises should be known as Yama himself, assuming the form of death for mortals.
The great defects of mercury are:
nāga, vaṅga, mala, vahnī, astability, viṣa, giri, and asahyāgni; these great defects residing in pārada are prohibited.
From Gaṇḍa comes the birth of swellings on the breasts; from Vaṅga, leprosy; from Mala, pain;
from Vahni, a burning sensation; from Bīja, the destruction of offspring; and from Añcala, death due to poison.
Indeed, from the defect of unbearable fire, there arises a bursting of the mountain and delusion;
when the mercury (*sūta*) is free from defects, then it removes death and old age. (Rā 1.1.29) [The qualities of faultless mercury]
Even this nectar, when possessed of defects, is poison in its very essence;
therefore, for the sake of purifying the defects, the purification of mercury is prescribed.
The juice should be extracted under an auspicious constellation, measuring one hundred palas,
or fifty, or twenty-five, or twelve, or even just one.
One must not perform the reduction of mercury; rather, one should perform the supreme refinement of mercury and the worship for the refinement of mercury with the Aghora mantra.
To those who are non-terrible, to those who are terrible, to those who are more terrible than the most terrible—
to all of them, to every single one in their Rudra-forms, let there be salutation unto you.
Having perceived the universe as essence-less, afflicted by disease, and pervaded by intense suffering,
[he sought] the method of the King of Alchemists— the ocean of compassion and treasury of all virtues.
Having examined the treatises on the *sūta* with a concentrated mind for the sake of accomplishing the desired goals of living beings,
let the lords of the *bhogins*, together with the lords of the *saras*, of vast intellect, listen attentively to what is spoken by me:
as long as the *sūta* is neither pure, nor dead, nor in a state of stupor, it cannot be bound by fragrance.

As long as the diamond has not been killed, nor the sky slain, nor the waters brought forth— remaining pure— and as long as all metals such as gold and even poison have not been rendered inert, and oil has not been made to fall [into fire],
how can a physician be considered accomplished and worthy of praise within the circle of those who enjoy wealth?
{The Elimination of the Eight Faults} Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the elimination of the eight faults:
by means of sixteen parts of the powder of *iṣṭakāraja* (brick-born) mixed with mercury.
One should grind it for one day in a heated mortar with the juice extracted from jambīra fruits;
the mortar may be made of iron, or else of stone or rock.
One should wash the mercury with *kāñjika* (fermented rice water) for the pacification of the defect of lead;
one should destroy the defect of tin with the powder of *viśālā* and *aṅkola*.
Rājavṛkṣa destroys impurities; Citraka destroys [impurities] born of fire; with black dhattūra one overcomes fickleness; and with the three myrobalans (triphalā), there is the destruction of poison.
The three pungents destroy *giri*, and *trikaṇṭaka* destroys unbearable fire;
there, the powder should be mixed with *kanyā*, each added in a one-sixteenth part according to the respective humor (*doṣa*).
Having placed the mercury, filtered through fine cloth,
into a mortar, one should diligently rub it with each [ingredient] in the proper sequence for seven nights, day by day.
Having extracted it, the wise one should wash it in a clay vessel with warm sour gruel;
thus freed from all defects and divested of the seven coverings.
This pure mercury is born and is fit for medical application.
{Purification of Mercury} Having ignited a fire of goat dung and chaff, one should cast [the mercury] upon the ground.
One should indeed place a stone vessel upon that and grind the mercury as prescribed therein.
Having added *śrīkhaṇḍa*, *devadāru*, and *kākatuṇḍī* with the juices of *jayā*,
and having added the juices of *karkoṭī*, *mūṣalī*, and *kanyā*,
one should grind it for one day in a *pātanāyantra* and then employ it once purified.
One should grind mercury for one day with the powder of a virgin and a night-blooming flower;
by precipitating it in a *pātanāyantra*, the mercury becomes perfectly purified.
{Purification of Mercury Derived from Cinnabar}:
One should grind cinnabar for one *yāma* with the juices of *pāribhadra*, or else with the juices of *jambīra* fruits; it should then be subjected to sublimation (*pātana*) in a *pātālayantra*.
One should yoke that *sūtra* to the yoga, freed from the seven coverings (*kañcuka*).
Thus are the purifications proclaimed; one may perform them in whichever single manner one desires.
{Medicinal plants for the killing of pure mercury} Now I shall describe these root-herbs for the killing of pure mercury:
*brahmadaṇḍī*, *meghanādā*, *citraka*, *tṛṇa*, and *mustikā*.
Vajravallī, balā, śuṇṭhī, kaṭutumbī, ardhacandrikā, viṣamuṣṭi, arka, lākṣā, gokṣura, and kākatuṇḍikā.
Kanyā, caṇḍālinīkanda, sarpākṣī, sarapuṅkhikā, vastā, raktāgranirguṇḍī, lajjālī, and devadālikā.
Jātī, jayantī, vārāhī, bhūkadamba,
kuraṇṭaka, koṣātakī, nīrakaṇā, lāṅgalī, and sahadevikā.
Cakramarda, amṛtākanda, kākamācī, ravipriyā, viṣṇukrāntā, hastiśuṇḍī, the latex of snuhī, bhṛṅgarāja, and paṭu; // Rrā_1.2.19 //
Thus have these medicinal roots been described, which are to be employed for the sake of subduing mercury;
they should be administered either collectively or individually, numbering eighteen in total.
{The preparation of mercury ash}: One should grind red-rooted plantain (*raktamūlikā*) in the urine of a cow that has not yet calved.
Mercury (*sūta*), purified with its juices and combined with an equal amount of sulfur, [should be processed].
One should grind it continuously for four watches in a heated mortar;
then one should cast that mass into the machine within a great crucible of thirty *ghaṭṭas*.
Thus, having repeatedly ground, rubbed, and dropped it through ten layers,
one should extract it again, grind it once more, and place it within a diamond crucible (vajramūṣā).
One should cook it ten times in a crucible called *bhūdharapuṭa* until it reaches the state of ash;
then, having repeatedly rubbed it with various liquid juices, this *vajrasūtaka* is perfected.
Mercury killed with medicinal roots, even if devoid of the process of digestion (*jāraṇa*), will certainly not permeate the body or the metal; yet it will surely be a remover of diseases.
One should grind mercury with double the amount of sulphur oil for one day,
or else with [the juices] derived from *sarpākṣī*, *viṣṇukrāntā*, and *bhṛṅgarāja*.
One should macerate it for three days with juices in thirty large *haṭṭa* crucibles;
thus, having been cooked eight times in this manner, the mercury will certainly be reduced to ash.
{The Preparation of Mercury Ash (3)}:
Having ground mercury with the water from the roots of white *Aṅkoṭa* for three days, one should roast it in a crucible within a *bhūdhara* furnace; thus it will attain the state of ash.
One should grind devadālī and harikrāntā with the juice of āranāla;
with that, one should perform sevenfold blowing upon the arisen mercury.
One should place that mercury in an iron pan, repeatedly adding the four liquids,
and cook it over a fire on a hearth until it becomes ash resembling the color of dawn.
{Mercury-killing (4)}:
One should thoroughly process white sugar and asafoetida with milks derived from the *udumbara* tree seven times with effort, grinding them again and again. Rrā_1.2.31.
Having added a decoction made from the five parts of the *udumbara* wood in a sixteenfold proportion,
one should then grind *hiṅgu* and mercury (the lord of the essence of tin) with that.
Having cast [the mercury] into a crucible and sealed it within a *bhūdhara*-named *puṭa*, one should cook it;
thus the mercury dies eight times, and asafoetida should be added in each *puṭa*.
{Mercury-killing (5)} One should grind the seeds of *apāmārga* as well as those of *eraṇḍa*;
that powder should be added to the mercury and confined within the crucible itself.
Having sealed it in a small crucible, one should cook it with four [substances] until it reaches the state of ash; [this is] the killing of mercury.
Indeed, [it is done] in the bulb arising from the bitter gourd (*kaṭutumbī*), within its interior, and in the milk of a woman.
The mercury dies in seven ways; one should cause it to sweat over a fire of cow dung.
Having ground it with the water of *aṅkola* roots, one should rub it in a mortar. (7) [This is the killing of mercury. *Rasārṇava*, 1.2.36.
One should combine mercury with sulfur and restrain it at the end of the day;
one should then roast it in a *bhūdhara* (earth) furnace and extract it at the end of the day.

{8} For the killing of mercury: one should grind equal parts of *dhānyābhra* and mercury with the juices of the "killers" (*māraka*) for one day. With that paste, one should smear a wick upon a cloth.
Having repeatedly smeared that wick with oils derived from castor seeds,
and having ignited it, one should cause the clarified butter in the vessel to be drawn down as it falls.
That black ash should then be ground again with *triyāmaka* for one day; it should undoubtedly be cooked in the apparatus known as the *kacchapa*.
The dead mercury becomes active immediately; one should employ it in various formulations.
(9) For the killing of mercury: two palas of purified mercury and half that amount of purified sulfur.
One should grind [the substance] continuously for one day with the juices of *māraka* plants;
then, having bound it in a *bhūdhara* (earth-holding) apparatus, one should kill it by means of *puṭa* (roasting) for one day.
In the *vajramūṣā* crucible, there are two parts of burnt chaff, one part of anthill earth,
one part of iron dross, and one part of white stone.
One should grind a certain substance equal in weight to human hair with goat’s milk;
having thoroughly rubbed it for two *yāmas*, one should use it to form a sealed crucible (*mūṣāndhasaṃpuṭa*).
Having dried it, then smeared it with those pastes, and having sealed it completely,
this is called the *vajramūṣā* (thunderbolt crucible), which effectively kills mercury.
The colors of the ash-elixir (bhasmasūta) are fourfold: white, yellow, red, and black;
among these, each subsequent one is superior in its characteristics.
{Digestion preceding killing} Now, therefore, the killing of the seed preceded by digestion is explained:
"He who would kill the mercury (sūtaka) while it is undigested and not yet a seed [would fail]. Rrā_1,3.1 //
O Maheśvarī, that wicked man who harms me is a slayer of a Brahmin;
therefore, with every effort, one should cause the mercury to die once it has been heated.
{The preparation of the mercury's face}:
Having placed cow-dung on the ground and then a baked crucible upon it, one should pour oil extracted from bitter *kaṭutumby* into its center and then cast the mercury therein. (Rasārṇava 1.3.3)
One should then add the juice of *kākamācī* and an equal amount of oil;
having added sulphur the size of a grain of rice, one should seal that [mixture].
Upon its back, fire should be applied, or a full crucible of fire;
once the oil is known to have cooled to the temperature of one's own limbs and is digested, one should add sulfur.
Having repeatedly added the juice of *kākamācī* into the fire, one should cause it to digest;
and here, having placed cow-dung beneath the crucible, one should apply a downward-flowing fire.

Having processed the sulphur six times [with mercury], the mouth of the mercury itself will thus be formed. One should then repeatedly rub that mercury with waters derived from jambīra fruits. (This is the procedure for killing mercury, preceded by the digestion of mercury that has been "mouthed").
Then, one should place thirty-two parts, followed by sixteen parts of pure gold leaf, into the molten metals along with the previously mentioned sixty-four parts.
Having ground it with peacock bile and mustard oils,
one should smear gold and then cast the mercury into it for one *yāma* with the juices of *jambīra* fruits.
One should grind that [substance] as before and cook it in a crucible with the juice of *jambīra* fruits;
one should fill it, seal it, apply fire with care, and cause [the mercury] to digest.
And with every morsel, that [substance] should be thoroughly rubbed with the juices of *jambīra* fruits;
[one may use] root-herbs and salt as a fragrance in the absence of bile and oil.
Having ground [the ingredients] with the juice of *jambīra*, one should smear the gold leaf;
in this manner, the digestion (*jāraṇā*) should be performed, and thereafter one should kill the mercury (*sūta*).
Alternatively, one may kill mouthless mercury by means of a *viḍa* mixture.
I shall now describe the method for preparing the *viḍa*; let the best of physicians accomplish it.
One should macerate conch powder in the milky sap of the sun-plant (*ravikṣīra*) for one day in the heat of the sun;
likewise, one should macerate *dhūmasāra* for one day in the juices of *jambīra* fruit.
One should boil *suvarcala* with goat’s urine for four watches,
and one should boil *kaṇṭakārī* with human urine for one day.
Sajjikṣāra, tintiḍīka, kāśīśa,
and śilājatu should be processed separately for four yāmas with the juices extracted from jambīra fruits.
One should [process] the seed of *jayapāla* deprived of its skin with the juices of radishes for one day;
likewise, rock salt (*saindhava*), borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*), and *guñjā* with the juice of the root of *śigru* for one day.
All of this should be ground together in equal parts with the juices of *jambīra* fruits;
one should carefully preserve that ball, for this is the "Vāḍavānala" *viḍa*.
With this, one should grind the mercury (*sūta*), which it then devours in a heated mortar (*taptakhalvaka*).

{The method for killing mercury and other substances by means of *viḍa*}: One should digest gold, mica, all metals, and whatever else is desired; one should kill them by the previously mentioned method, and the process of killing is described here. Rrā_1,3.19.
Having uprooted a gourd plant along with its roots, one should grind it well with cow urine;
with that liquid, one should rub the mercury for one day inside a crucible made of *kāntaloha*.
Having smeared it, the restraining agents should be applied above and below according to that sequence;
one should cook it on the stove for one day with a mild fire, and it will become calcined.
{Mercury-killing (2)} Having ground cow’s ghee, sulfur, and mercury, one should form a pill;
having placed it between the leaves of a *kumārī* plant, one should wrap it with thread.
Having enclosed that [substance] within a *kānta* crucible, one should cook it with three small crucibles;
then, when blown [with a bellows], it becomes ash, and in an *andhamūṣā* crucible, it certainly reaches complete consumption.
(3) For the killing of mercury: having taken ripe fruits of the *śāka* tree, one should purify them;
one should grind them with the milk of a goat and smear [the resulting paste] upon the crucible.

Having filled the interior of a cow that has recently calved and whose afterbirth has already emerged with powder, one should seal the mercury (sūtaka) within it; when heated, it shall be reduced to ashes.
{The killing of mercury (4):} *karkoṭakī*, *kākamācī*, *kañcukī*, *kaṭutumbikā*,
*kākajaṅghā*, *kākatuṇḍī*, *kākinī*, and *kākamañjarī*.
Having ground these [ingredients] in a *vajramūṣā* crucible and applied a coating with them, one should place the mercury inside;
it should then be rubbed for one day with those very juices extracted from fresh [herbs].
Then, having sealed it in an earthen crucible, one should cook it eight times again and again;
having smeared those [crucibles] with a *liptamūṣā* and sealed them, when heated, the mercury becomes dead (*mṛta*).
The mercury should be thoroughly rubbed for four *yāmas* with binding agents (*niyāmaka*) and *pārada-māraṇa* [reagents];
then it should be cooked slowly over a mild fire with double the amount of sulphur oil (*gandhataila*).
One should seal that very substance in an iron crucible as long as it remains solid;
having ground harītakī with water, one should prepare a crucible with iron dross.
Having prepared it and placed [the substance] in the middle, one should again seal it in a casket;
then, having removed the shape of a śrāvaka from its top, one should pour in molten lead.
One should blow with the *kaṭhina* [bellows] until the nāga has become fluid;
however, one should not blow again until it returns to its solid state.
Thus, when blown repeatedly for three nights, the mercury dies;
therefore, I shall now describe the binding herbs used for the process of killing the mercury.
Sarpākṣī, Kṣīriṇī, Vandhyā, Matsyākṣī, Śarapuṅkhikā,
Kākajaṅghā, Śikhiśikhā, Brahmadaṇḍī, and Ākhuparṇikā.
Varṣābhū, kañcukī, mūrvā, padmaka, utpala,
ciñcikā, śatāvarī, vajralatā, vajrakandā, and triparṇikā.
Maṇḍūkaparṇī, pāṭalī, citraka, grīṣmasundara, kākamācī, mahārāṣṭrī, haridrā, and tilakarṇikā.
White arka, śigru, dhattūra, mṛga, dūrvā grass, harītakī,
guḍūcī, mūṣalī, puṅkhā, bhṛṅgarāja, and red citraka.
Tagara, śūraṇa, muṇḍī, mayañkā, and potakokila;
rock salt, white varṣābhū, sea salt, asafoetida, and honey.
Viṣṇukāntā, somavallī, vraṇaghnī, yakṣalocana, vyāghrapādī, haṃsapadī, vṛścikālī, and kuraṇṭaka.
The *svayambhūkusuma*, the *kuñcī*, the *hastiśuṇḍī*, the *indravāruṇī*,
and even the seeds of the sun (*ahaskara*)— these are the regulators in all cases.
These [mantras], whether combined as a whole or used individually, amounting to eighteen in total, should indeed be bestowed;
one should employ these for the killing, fainting, and binding of mercury.
{The procedure for the digestion and killing of mercury}: Having ground the previously mentioned *niyāmikās* with the urine of cows that have not yet calved,
one should rub the mercury (*sūta*) with those liquids according to the sequence previously described.
Thus has digestion (jāraṇa) been declared; now the killing (māraṇa) is fully described.
Once the mercury has been killed, the examination of the mercury-ash (rasabhasma) must be performed exactly as stated.
When the fire below has been heated by the chaff-fire and remains without being extinguished, then one should know it to be ash; one should observe this for a watch (yāma) in the hearth.
One should employ mercury killed by medicinal roots in all formulations;
once processed (*jārita*), this mercury removes old age, poverty, and disease.
One should apply [this] everywhere, having bound it for the sake of destroying disease while in a state of *mūrcchita*.
{Mūrchana} Now, therefore, the procedure for the mūrchana (coagulation) of pure mercury is described: one should grind the mercury with meghanāda, vacā, hiṅgu, and śūraṇa.
Having ground that ball until it is thoroughly pulverized, one should wrap its exterior with asafoetida;
then, placed within a salt-vessel, one should cook it for one day over a fierce fire.
Having mounted it so that it is fixed upright, one should bind it firmly with a cloth;
having applied an equal amount of sulphur above and below, one should cook it in a mild fire.
When the odor has been digested, it should be added again in equal amounts six times;
once the sulfur has been digested sixfold, the mercury becomes "mūrchita" (coagulated) and becomes a destroyer of diseases.
Take equal parts of sulphur, the essence of honey (madhusāra), and purified mercury;
cook them together in a mortar for one watch (yāma) and place the mixture in a glass vessel.
Having sealed it for twelve watches, one should cook it in a sand-pan (vālukāyantra);
when it has cooled to the temperature of its own body, one should break it open and discard the sulphur from above.
Having taken the mercury situated below, one should employ it for all diseases.
[Mercury formulation:
One should take purified mercury, twice the amount of sulphur, and half the amount of mercury of rock salt (*saindhava*).
One should grind it with the juices of white jayantī for three days;
having formed a ball and dried it thoroughly, one should place it in a crucible and seal it.
Having dried it, one should blow upon it slightly and, once well-heated, cast it into water;
then, having extracted the juice from that, it should be saturated with the juice of *trikaṇṭaka*.
One should employ [this] in all diseases, or one should heat it in a *bhūdhara* [furnace] or cook it;
half a part of mercury and one part of sulfur should be ground together with ghee to form a pill (*golaka*).
Having prepared it, one should bind it in a cloth and cook it in a swinging apparatus (*dolāyantra*);
it should be kept for one watch (*yāma*) inside cow urine and for three days in human urine.
One should dry it again by wrapping it firmly in a cloth and binding it;
once dried, having sealed it in a crucible, one should then cook it with a fire of husks.
Having reversed the upper portion to the lower and the lower portion to the upper,
one should apply sudation for three days by means of such alternating movements.
Afterwards, having extracted that Sūtra which carries the yoga and removes all affliction, [one should proceed].
{Mercury::
formulation} The excrement of a newborn infant, the seed of the *pālāśa* tree, the blood of a *caṇḍālī*, mercury, a quarter-part of mercury, and borax; Rrā_1,4.15.
One should rub that ball with the juices of *jayantī* for one day;
then, having ground it with *sahadevī*, one should coat a copper crucible with it.
Having placed the globule in the middle of that, one should gently steam it for two watches;
then, having removed it from the midst of the sand-vessel (vālukāyantra), once again—
One should apply an external ointment of *citraka*, *sahadevī*, and sulphur;
then, having bound it in a cloth pouch and coated it with clay, one should let it dry.
Having sealed it in a blind crucible and heated it, one should take out the casket;
this great mercury, which carries the medicinal application, removes diseases when reduced to a fine powder.
The *sampuṭa* [mudrā] should be equal to the *sūta* [mercury] through the ritual procedure seen in the scriptures.
Having ground mercury together with sulphur and *sūtaka* for one day using the juices of *dhattūra*,
it should be heated in a sealed crucible (*andhamūṣā*) for one day; thus, it becomes liquefied in the *bhūdhara* furnace.
Having prepared a crucible six finger-breadths deep, well-baked, made of clay, and firm,
one should then plaster the interior of the crucible with roots and many leaves.
Having cast the *sūtaka* into the middle of that, one should fill the crucible with those liquids;
having sealed it with salted apparatuses, one should cook it in a furnace over a blazing fire.
At the end of seven days, having extracted [the mercury] to the size of a barley grain, it removes fever.
One should grind together equal parts of ferrous sulfate (kāśīśa), rock salt (saindhava), and mercury (sūta) until they are thoroughly mixed.
One part of this kāśīśa should be given with full-blown tūrikā;
one should add it little by little into the mortar and cause it to coagulate for three watches of the night.
Each [dose] should be one hundred niṣkas, neither less nor more;
one should cook it for a day with a fierce fire using a *sthālī-sampuṭa* apparatus.
Then, one should bring the mercury, which has become solidified upon the hearth after being attached to the upper part;
it should be processed with the juices of *kuraṇṭaka* and the mercury should be rubbed in the sun.
One should rub it with the leaves of the *latākarañja* for one day using the tip of the thumb; once it is properly rendered unconscious (*mūrchita*), it may be employed against all diseases.
Now, this is the procedure for pure mercury that has been liquefied and solidified:
one part aged ghee equal to the mercury, and one part sulphur equal to both.
It should be rubbed for a day with the milky sap of the sun-plant (ravikṣīra), then blinded and placed in a crucible;
by means of this *puṭapāka* treatment, the mercury becomes perfected as the "Golden-Womb" (*hairaṇyagarbhaka*) elixir.

Having taken one unripe *vaikrānta* pill bound with mercury from a tuber produced by the bitter *tuṃbī* plant or from the *kṣīrakanda* of the *vandhyā* plant, one should then place it inside that [tuber].
Take ten *niṣkas* of pure mercury and one *niṣka* of pure sulfur;
adding the sulfur little by little, one should grind it upon a stone.
When the mass has formed after just one watch (yāma), one should place the juice into the bulb;
having applied half a niṣka each of ash and vaikrānta above and below it.
Then, having sealed the opening with the pith of a *kanda* root and firmly plastered it all over with clay to the thickness of one finger-breadth, one should let the globule dry completely.
One should cook it in the *bhūdhara* apparatus; then, having extracted it, one should cook it again, turning it over in this manner so that the upper part goes to the bottom.
One should gradually move it upward and cook it externally with pairs of stones;
then, once it has split, it should be collected, having become bound like a pomegranate.
This is known as "bound vaikrānta," and one should employ it in all diseases.
Alternatively, having bound the sulphur (gandhaka) in a cloth together with mercury bound by sulphur (gandhabaddhapārada), or with the powder of sulphur-seats (gandhapīṭhī),
one should place equal amounts of them inside a firm iron crucible and then seal it.
One should seal it in an earthen crucible until the sulphur is digested;
in this manner, it should be applied again and again until the sulphur has become sixfold [in weight].
Thus, mercury bound with sulphur becomes the remover of all diseases. [The crucible for mercury bound with sulphur:
the crucible should be as wide as a *jambīra* fruit and sixteen finger-breadths in length.
It should be made uncooked and very firm, placed within a vessel filled with sand.
One-third part of sand should be attached [to the crucible], and one-quarter part should remain outside;
then, one *pala* of powdered fragrant substance should be placed inside the crucible.
Then, one should add an equal amount of pure mercury and subsequently one pala of gandhaka;
having carefully covered the crucible with a lid, one should place the vessel upon the furnace.
One should cook it over a mild fire until it reaches the state of being smokeless;
once the fragrant smoke has vanished, it should be filled with the juices of *kākamācī*.
When the liquid has been digested, it should be filled again with the juices of betel leaves;
once those have been digested, one should fill it with the juices of thorn-apple (dhustūra) and cook it once more.

One should cook that [substance] until its odor is worn away; then, having repeatedly added the juice of *kākamācī* and other plants, one should likewise cook it in the sequence beginning with *dhustūra*.
Having pierced the crucible and taken up the mercury which removes old age and disease, one should employ this mercury—
bound with sulfur— in all cases among those substances that act as vehicles for the yoga.
When mercury, having abandoned its dense volatility, becomes like collyrium,
it should then be known as "mūrchita" (coagulated), even though it may occasionally assume various colors.
Endowed with sweetness and dignity, resembling the sun in brilliance—
when he stands in the midst of fire, that is the characteristic of the tree.
Victorious is that king of elixirs, which removes the fear of death, is a treasury of all virtues, and acts as a sovereign for the body;
it brings about the destruction of wrinkles and grey hair, increases virility, and even renders one firm in the company of beloved women through its use.
Thus, these sūtas— whether killed, swooning, bound, or arrived—
each may become a *yogavāha* (a carrier of union) and should be employed in their respective combinations.
For the sake of attaining the perfection of the body, it is "killed" (mārita); for the destruction of disease, it is "fainted" (mūrchita).
In some diseases, the mercury-ash (rasabhasma) is used for the sake of the body, while in others, it is used in its "fainted" state.
One should employ the bound [mercury] with the ritual prescribed in the scriptures;
one should preserve the processed mercury in a tooth, a horn, or a bamboo tube.
Mercury destroys worms and skin diseases; it is strengthening, promotes longevity, and bestows vision.
Through its consumption, it cures all diseases, improves the appetite, and is heavy and astringent.

A hundred million qualities are produced in diamond; a thousand in meteoric iron; one hundred in gold; eighty in silver; half of that (forty) in ruby; sixty-four in steel; and half of that (thirty-two) in copper.

That medical treatment which is performed by means of juices and the like is proclaimed as "divine" (daivī) by the wise; that which is prepared with mantras and roots and the like is "human" (mānuṣī); and that which is performed with surgical instruments and the like is "demonic" (rākṣasī). Rrā 1.4.54.
{Names of the secondary minerals}: sulfur, *vajravaikrānta*, *vajrābhra*,
*tālaka*, realgar, *kharpara*, *śikhituttha*, *vimalā*, and gold pyrite.
Kāsīsa, kāntapāṣāṇa, varāṭī, hiṅgula,
kaṅkuṣṭha, śaṅkha, bhūnāga, ṭaṅkaṇa, and śilājatu.
These secondary minerals (uparasa) are to be purified, calcined, and sometimes melted by means of a *puṭa*.
Unripe *gandha* causes severe leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), fever, vertigo, and diseases of the bile (*pitta*).
It destroys beauty, happiness, and the power of vigor; therefore, it should be applied according to the purified rules.
{Purification of Sulphur}:
Having placed milk mixed with clarified butter in a vessel, one should seal its mouth with cloth;
then, having scattered powdered sulphur on top of it, one should seal it with a flux.
Having placed the vessel on the ground, a light packet should be applied above it;
then, once the mercury has been liquefied in milk, one should employ the pure substance in medicinal formulations.
{Purification of Sulfur (2)} Alternatively, one should smear a cloth seven times with the milks of the *arka* and *snuhī* plants;
then, having ground the sulfur with fresh butter, one should coat the cloth with it.
Having taken that [substance] from a place ignited by fire, it should indeed be held with its opening facing downwards;
the oil will fall into a vessel below and should be collected and employed in yogic practices.
Pure sulfur removes diseases such as leprosy, death, fever, and others.
The fire-maker is greatly hot and increases virility.
Vajra combined with the tuber of *vyāghrī*,
when cooked in a *dolāyantra* for seven days in a decoction of *kaudrava* or *kaulattha*, becomes pure.
Heat that [mercury] twenty-one times and sprinkle it with donkey urine;
having ground the orpiment sixfold, one should cast the vajra into that globule.

Blown with horse urine and sprinkled according to the previously mentioned procedures, that *vajra* is reduced to ashes; like a thunderbolt, it makes the body [of the enemy] as if struck by a *vajra*.
Having thoroughly ground the hair from between the horns of a *ūrṇāśṛṅga* [goat], one should place the *vajra* in the center of its mass;
or else, having placed it in the mass, one should apply three layers of *vajravallī* to its juice.
For this one called Vajra, death itself will surely occur; of this there is no doubt.
Impure diamond destroys longevity and causes suffering as well as leprosy.
There is also paleness and heaviness; therefore, one should cause it to be purified.
White, red, yellow, and black are the castes of the twice-born and so forth; these are the families of the Vajra.
In the practice of alchemy (rasāyana), the Brahmin becomes white and a bestower of spiritual accomplishments (siddhi).
A red *kṣatriya* conquers death and removes wrinkles, gray hair, and disease; a yellow *vaiśya* acts as a liquefier and brings firmness to the body.
The black variety of *śūdra* destroys diseases and bestows stability of youth;
one should identify these as male, female, or neuter by their characteristics.
Those which are circular, complete with facets, radiant, large in size,
free from lines and spots, are declared to be male diamonds.

Those [lines] joined with lines and dots, forming hexagons, are known as women. (Examination of the Female Vajra) Those [lines] joined with lines and dots, forming hexagons, are known as neuter. (Examination of the Neuter Vajra)
Those that are triangular, long, and dependent [on others] should be known as neuter.
Each preceding one of these men is praised as being more powerful than the next;
these Vajra women bestow physical luster and grant enjoyments.
But those who are neuter have little virility, are lustful, and are devoid of strength;
a woman should be given to women, and likewise a eunuch to a eunuch.
In all matters and at all times, men who are more powerful should be employed by everyone.
Having taken the auspicious *vajra*, one should place it inside the bulb of a tigress;
having smeared it with buffalo dung, one should cook it over a fire of dried cow-dung.
At night, during each of the four watches, or at the end of the night, one should sprinkle those [seeds] with horse urine; after seven nights, they become pure.
Meghanādā, śamī, śyāmā, śṛṅgī, that which arises from madana, kulattha, vetasa, agastya, and sindhuvāraka— these are for purification.
These [herbs] should be boiled with water; the diamond (vajra) placed inside a jambīra fruit should be cooked in a dolāyantra for three days. In this way, the diamond becomes purified.
One should cook the *vajra* placed inside the root-bulb of *vyāghrī* in a decoction of *kulattha* and *kodrava* using a *dolāyantra*; after seven days, it attains purification.
For the purification of *vajra*:

one should cook a *vyāghrī* root containing a *vajra* that has been smeared with clay inside a sealed crucible (*puṭa*). After twenty-four hours, having extracted it, one should sprinkle it with horse urine.
Or one may sprinkle it with *vajrī* milk; thus it becomes pure and one should kill [the substance].
Furthermore, the slaying of the *vajras* belonging to the brahmin caste and others is described:
the *aśvattha*, *badarī*, *jhiṇṭī*, honey, and the bone of a crab.

Having ground an equal amount of snuhī milk, one should place the *vajra* (diamond) within that globule; having sealed it, one should cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire, and the diamond will become dead (reduced to powder).
Having ground together karavīra, meṣaśṛṅga, badara, and udumbara,
along with an amount equal to the milky sap of the arka plant, one may kill a king just as one kills a brahmin.
One should grind together *balā*, *atibalā*, fragrant substances, and tortoise shell;
with these, or with the milk of the *vāruṇī* plant, even a Vaiśya shall die just like a Brāhmaṇa.
Having ground together suraṇa,
garlic, conch-shell,
and realgar in equal parts with the milky sap of the banyan tree inside a crucible, one effects the "killing" of a Śūdra, as prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa.
By means of those respective medicinal applications, women among them die;
and the death of the four types of neuter beings occurs simultaneously with those same medicines.
Having ground the root together with two-year-old cotton fibers and lovely-smelling flowers using breast milk from a woman, and having blown [the resulting mixture] into the fire, it becomes dead.
Having ground together the horn of a ram, the bone of a snake, the shell of a tortoise, and *amlavetasa*—
each equal in measure to an elephant’s tusk— with the milk of a *vajrī*, one should form a pill (*golaka*).
Having fashioned a vajra from that [substance] and placed it within [the victim], one kills [them] by means of blowing [into it].
As for the three-year-old nāga and the barren woman, there is also the root of cotton.
Having ground [the ingredients] and placed the *vajra* in their midst, one should prepare a crucible and seal it.
And that [substance] dies by means of seven applications in the gajapuṭa furnace.
A vajra that has been empowered with the blood of bedbugs, dried in the heat seven times, and combined with realgar ground together with it, [accomplishes the rite of] slaying.
Having smeared it with [the paste] and wrapped it with jujube leaves, one should cook it in a crucible;
having smeared it again and cooked it again, it dies even after being processed seven times.
One should repeatedly visualize a vajra cast into the pearl-oyster of the great river;
[this is done] for one day with two, one, or half a *snuhī*, *arka*, *unmatta*, and *kanyā* [leaves].
One should wrap it outside with the flesh of a black crab and a paste of *bhūnāga* clay;
when properly heated, it attains the state of ash.
When a vajra is wrapped with the roots of the red lotus (*raktotpala*) and the buds of the *meghanāda* plant,
and then heated while in a massed state, it is completely reduced to ashes.
Diamond bestows longevity, strength, beauty, and physical well-being.
When consumed, it destroys diseases, and when dead [in the alchemical process], it is undoubtedly a diamond;
{purification of vaikrānta} vaikrānta, whether blue or red, should be purified like a diamond.
The *vaikrānta* [mineral] should be heated repeatedly twenty-one times and sprinkled with horse urine each time it is heated.
Then, one should place it into a five-part globule of *uttaravāruṇī* and, having sealed it in a crucible (*mūṣāpuṭa*), heat it; then, having removed it, [place it] back into the globule.
Having cast it [into the crucible] and sealed it, one should heat it in this manner seven times until it reaches the state of ash.
Once the *vaikrānta*— which serves as a substitute for *vajra*— has been reduced to ash, one should employ that powdered *vaikrānta* in place of *vajra*.
Impure mica destroys longevity and increases wind and phlegm.
One should cut off the unstruck body, which produces weak digestion and worms.
Black, yellow, white, and red [minerals] are to be employed in alchemical elixirs (*rasāyana*).
There are four types: *pināka*, *dardura*, *nāga*, and *vajra*.
The three beginning with the *pināka* should be avoided; one should carefully collect the *vajra*.
When cast into fire, the *pināka* emits a mass of flakes.
Eating it out of ignorance bestows great leprosy; for the *dardura* [poison],
when placed in fire, produces the sound of a frog.
The *nāga* that has entered the fire emits the sound of hissing;
when it is constantly located within the body, it causes the disease of fistula-in-ano.
Vajrābhra, when placed in fire, undergoes no transformation whatsoever;
therefore, vajrābhra should be employed as it conquers disease, old age, and death.
One should heat vajra-abhraka in fire and then quench it in milk.
Having recognized that the leaf is split, one should apply the juices of *meghanāda* and *amlaya*.
The wise person should cause that grain-cloud (dhānyābhra) to be processed for eight watches (yāmas).
{The production of dhānyābhra}
Alternatively, two parts of abhra and one ṭaṅka [of mercury] should be combined with water.
Having ground it finely, one should let it sit in a vessel for two days;
then, having tied it along with grains in a cloth, one should mash it together with *kāñjika*.
That which has been strained below, subtle and pure, becomes *dhānyābhraka*.
Having ground *dhānyābhraka* for one day with the juices of *punarnavā*, *meghanāda*, and *niścandra*,
one should cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire; then again with *ciñcā* and *sūraṇa*.
Having ground it with the juices derived from *musta*, one should apply three separate *puṭa* treatments;
likewise, having wrapped it in *markaṭa* leaves, it should be placed inside a *sampuṭa* of *moca*.
For indeed, the cloud (abhra) becomes moonless (niścandra) when applied to the defects;
having cooked it with cow’s ghee and decoctions of triphalā, one should cook it as before. (Rājanighaṇṭu 1.6.13)
One should cook it with twenty-five layers of the juice of *kāsamardī*;
it should be given three layers [of fuel], and one should rub it with milk in each layer.
Indeed, the cloud-like mineral (abhraka) becomes moonless (*niścandra*), destroying old age, death, and disease.
For the "killing" (*māraṇa*) of grain-like mica (*dhānyābhraka*), take one part of it and two parts of borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*).
Having ground it and sealed it in a blind crucible (andhamūṣā), one should cook it with a fierce fire;
once cooled naturally, one should employ the powder for all diseases.
Rice-processed mica (dhānyābhraka) ground with acid, heated in a closed crucible (puṭa), and sprinkled with acid;
having ground that again, one should hold it in a mortar and saturate it with sour *āranālaka* juice.
Heated repeatedly with *āranāla* (sour gruel), it should be cooked and purified again and again;
or it should be cooked twenty times, repeatedly, either in a crucible (*puṭa*) or by blowing.
Having heated it repeatedly, one should throw it into milk, grind it, and then dry it again;
having heated it in milk, one should cook it in a *puṭapāka* vessel and sprinkle it with heated milk.
In this manner, having dried and ground it twenty-one times, one should bake it in a *puṭa* vessel;
having ground it again, one should cook it in a pot, stirring with an iron ladle.
Then, one should cook it in milk while submerged in milk, repeatedly;
thus one should cook it for seven days, placing it in the *puṭa* during the day and [removing it] at night.
Tandulī, vajravallī, tālamūlī, punarnavā, cāṅgerī,
and marica, together with the milk of balā.
And with these one should grind the mica for three days at a time;
having remained in a heated crucible, one should then do so again and again with each [substance] individually.
Having ground it again and rubbed it in a crucible, it becomes dead (mṛta), resembling collyrium in appearance.
To purified *dhānyābhraka* (grain-sulphide of iron), one should add one-tenth part of black pepper;
it should be ground with the group of acidic substances (*amlavarga*) and then macerated in acid for three days.
Once it is dry, one should strongly heat that [substance] in a crucible using charcoal from the *khadira* tree;
then, having turned the vessel upside down, one should sprinkle it with sour gruel (*amlaka*).

Having ground that abhra with the roots of agastya, śigru, and varṣābhū, along with the juices produced from their leaves— or else with the juice of other sour liquids— one should sprinkle [the powder] with it.
Abhra (mica) should be ground with sugar, honey, clarified butter, cow’s milk, curd, and sour [liquids],
then ground with the juices of *matsyākṣī* and *karavīrā*, and cooked three times.
Then, in Gajapura, the moonless mica (niścandra-abhraka) is to be cooked;
the grain-mica (dhānyābhraka) should be ground with juices, namely the juices of *matsyākṣī* and *tulasī*.
One should grind these for a day with the roots of *kokilākṣa*, *kumārī*, white *dūrvā*, *vyāghrī*, tuber, and *punarnavā*.
Having ground it repeatedly seven times with the substances known as *kuñjara*, one should cook it again;
likewise, it should be cooked after being ground seven times with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*).
In this way, it becomes moonless; one should apply it in all diseases.
Equal parts of *dhānyābhra* (rice-iron) and *ṭaṅkaṇa* (borax), having been ground for one day with cow’s urine, *tulasī* leaves,
*vākucī*, and small amounts of *sūraṇa* (mountain sorrel), should be cooked in a *puṭa* (sealed crucible).

Afterwards, it should be rubbed with the juices of *jayantī* three times, and then subjected to four *gajapuṭa* roastings; thus, it becomes free of its metallic luster (*niścandra*) and conquers all diseases.
Having repeatedly ground purified mica with the milk of the sun-plant (*ravikṣīra*) or with the juice of the sun-plant's root,
one should cook it in a *puṭa* vessel seven times; thus it will certainly die [i.e., be reduced to ash].
One should place dehusked mica with acidic rice-husks and sour liquids in the sun for a day;
after grinding it for one watch (yāma), it should be formed into four pills, sealed, and cooked in a *gajapuṭa* fire.
In this manner, having placed it in the midst of cow’s milk, one should set it aside, grind it, and cook it in a *puṭa*;
likewise, having placed it in cotton-water, one should grind it and cook it in a *puṭa*.
Then, with non-acidic cotton and cow's milk, one should repeatedly perform heating,
cooking, rubbing, and sealing (puṭa) in this successive order.
Thus, when the twentieth fold is reached, death occurs for certain.
Regarding the immortalization of all killed mercury and mica: listen to the method for the immortalization of all killed micas.
Taking sixteen palas of the decoction produced from the three myrobalans (triphalā), Rrā_1,6.40.
Eight *pala* of cow urine and ten *pala* of dead mica,
having combined these, one should cook them in an iron vessel over a gentle fire.

Once the liquid has been digested, one should take the entire [preparation] and employ it against all diseases; for indeed, even without a post-digestive vehicle (anupāna), mica (abhraka) removes old age, death, and disease.
Or one should administer it with appropriate after-drinks (anupāna) to instantly alleviate various diseases;
furthermore, processed mica (mṛtābhraka) removes diseases, old age, and death in many ways.
When practiced, it increases the firmness of the body and augments beauty and vitality.
Impure haritāla (orpiment) destroys longevity and causes cough, wind disorders, and urinary disease.
It causes burning, swelling, and contraction of the limbs; therefore, one should purify it.
{Purification of Haritāla}:
Having reduced *tālaka* into pieces and adding one-tenth part of *ṭaṅkaṇa*,
it should be washed with the juices of *jambīra* fruits and then washed again with *kāñjika*.
Having bound it with fourfold layers of cloth, one should cook it in a swinging apparatus (*dolāyantra*) for one day,
combined with *cāranāla* and the juices of pumpkin (*kuṣmāṇḍa*) for one day.
One should cook talaka (antimony) for one *yāma* in sesame oil and for one *yāma* in the decoction of *triphalā*;
it should be processed three times in this manner, having been ground with urine and *kāñjika*.
Having enclosed it in a *puṭa* and ground it with its own fruits, one should cook it ten times;
thus processed twelve times, it should be employed in medicinal formulations once purified.
For the purification of *haritāla*:
one should cook *tālaka* bound in a cloth pouch for seven days in *kāñjika* using a *dolāyantra*, and then for one *yāma* in the juices of *kuṣmāṇḍa*.
One should cook it for one watch (yāma) in sesame oil and for one watch in the decoction of triphalā;
thus, having been cooked in the apparatus for four watches, the tālaka is purified.
Haritāla (tālaka), when purified, removes diseases; it wards off leprosy, death, and fever.
When purified, it is cold in potency and increases the wind (vāyu).
Impure realgar (manaḥśilā) causes urinary calculi and heart disease.
When purified, it removes all ailments, including weak digestion and the retention of waste.
Manaḥśilā should be boiled for three days in goat’s urine using a *dolāyantra* (swinging apparatus). For the sake of purification,
it should be soaked seven times in those same goat’s bile juices while exposed to the heat of the sun.
Realgar should be purified by being boiled for one day in a *dolāyantra* (swing-oven) with the red juices of *jayantī*, *bhṛṅgarāja*, and *agastya*,
and for one watch (*yāma*) in goat’s urine.
One should wash with fermented rice-water and apply it in all diseases.
One should cook *rasaka* for seven days with human urine and cow urine using a *dolāyantra*; once it is thoroughly purified, one should employ it in medicinal formulations.
For the purification of tuttha, one should grind it with the excrement of a cat and a pigeon in a mortar;
then one should add borax in a tenth part and cook it over a gentle fire.
A packet with curd and a packet with honey should be given for the purification of *tuttha*.
Vimalā is to be purified in three ways; combined with the juice of plantain (rambhā),
one should grind it with sour vetasa, fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla), and the urine of a ewe.
In a swinging apparatus (*dolāyantra*), this purification for four watches is most excellent;
[it is performed] with the juices of *karkaṭī*, *meṣaśṛṅgī*, and *jambīra*. (Rā 1.7.17)
One should meditate in intense sunlight; then Vimalā certainly becomes purified.
Impure honey causes weak digestion, loss of strength, obstruction of wounds, and pain in the eyes.
If impure, the *mākṣika* [mercury] brings about death; of this there is no doubt.
To purify *mākṣika* (pyrite),
one should boil it with human urine, the liquid of *kodrava* grains, *vetasa*, the group of sour substances (*amlavarga*),
potassium carbonate (*ṭaṅkaṇa*), and the three pungents (*kaṭutrika*).

It should be cooked for one day in a dolāyantra (swinging vessel) placed inside a *sūraṇa* (mountain ginger) root, and then cooked for one day with the juices of plantain; having removed it from there, one should grind it with clarified butter.
One should cook it in a *puṭa* with castor oil for purification.
For the purification of honey (*mākṣika*):
three parts of honey and one part of rock salt.
Alternatively, one should cook it in an iron vessel with the juices of *mātuluṅga* or the juices derived from *jambīra*,
until the vessel becomes beautifully red.
Copper-colored lead ore becomes purified;
one should rub *mākṣika* with the resin of *agastya* flowers and the root of *śigru*. (Mākṣika purification) Rā 1.7.24.
One should cook *mākṣika* with the juices of *pāṣāṇabhedinī* and the aforementioned [substances];
then, one should roast that pill in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*) using twenty *upalas* of weight.
Having ground it again, one should then enclose it in six *puṭas*; thus it becomes purified.
For the purification of *mākṣika* (pyrite):
having ground *meghanāda* and *pāṣāṇabhedī*, one should place the *mākṣika* in small pieces into the middle of that mass.
Having bound that ball in a cloth, one should cook it for one day in a *dolāyantra* in a decoction of *kulattha* beans.
This [method] is to be employed for the killing of pure metals in their appropriate place.
{Honey:: Examination::
Good Quality} When broken, it resembles gold within, while its external luster is black.
That which is known as *bṛhadvarṇa* is called the best kind of honey.
Like a drop of oil on water, it pervades limb after limb;
yet none of the bodily constituents (dhātus), such as the *prabala* and others, can function without purification.
Since they bring about the pacification of diseases, purification by means of them shall now be described.
{coral::
killing} One should saturate corals with the milk of a woman; then, having placed them inside a crucible, sealed it, and applied a lid on top, one should coat it.
By applying a strong fire for two *praharas*, the coral is killed. Rrā_1,7.31.
The wise one should boil one *droṇa* of horse gram (*kulattha*) with one *droṇa* of water;
when that decoction is reduced to one-quarter, eight *maṇas* of mica (*śilā*) [should be added].
Having dried pearl powder for three days in the sun, sprinkling it repeatedly with a decoction, one should take that powder and saturate it with rainwater.
Having been powdered, it should be processed in the sun for three days; [the enemy] shall meet with death.
One should purify *śilājatu* for one day as previously described, using conch shell and blue vitriol; likewise,
one should purify bitumen (*jatu*) with cow’s urine, decoctions of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*.
One should rub *śilājatu* in an iron vessel for a day; this is the purification of *śilājatu*.
As for *darada*: it should be processed with ewe’s milk and the group of acidic substances (*amlavarga*).
By practicing this diligently seven times, it certainly attains purification.
{Purification of the minor metals (*uparasa*):} *sūryāvarta*, *vajrakanda*, *kadalī*, and *devadālikā*.
Śigru, kośātakī, vandhyā, kākamācī, and vāyasī—
using the juice of these alone, combined with the three alkalis and salts.
One should diligently process sauvīra, kāntapāṣāṇa, pure bhūnāga, and clay with the group of acidic substances for one day.
Conch, blue antimony, and all other metallic ores should be processed separately according to the prescribed method; thus they attain purity day by day.
Thereafter, the wise one should place them in a swinging apparatus (*dolāyantra*) with those very juices for one day;
they are purified, of this there is no doubt, for these are the most excellent among all.
They release beings who are agitated; this is considered the common [form] of the mantra.
{:: Sattvapātana} Guggulu, ṭaṅkaṇa, lac, marrow, and again sarjarasa;
wool, guñjā, kṣetramīna, and the bones of a rabbit.
Jaggery, honey, clarified butter, oil-cake, and blue vitriol should be ground with goat’s urine;
all these, along with *dhānyābhra*, *bhūnāga*, and clay, should be taken in equal proportions.
One should mix those which are like "beloved stones" (kāntapāṣāṇa) and the various hard secondary minerals (kaṭhinyuparasas),
and cook them with buffalo products, beginning with curd and ending with cow-dung.
One should firmly knead [the ingredients] and form them into pills weighing one karṣa;
then, having dried them, one should heat them intensely in a crucible furnace using charcoal that has been smoldering for a long time.
By blowing [the breath] just three times, the stainless *sattva* descends;
it liberates even those beings who are incurable—what need is there to mention [those made of] clay?
Having combined lac, clarified butter, sesame seeds, drumstick tree, borax, salt,
and jaggery with half as much yellow orpiment (*haritāla*), one should seal the crucible with a hole (*chidramūṣā*).
When placed in a crucible using the *pātālayantra* [underground apparatus], the essence certainly falls down.
{??} Cumin, sorrel, sour chickpeas, citron, sour vetiver, tamarind, orange, and lime— this is known as the sour group (*amlavarga*).
Having powdered *tālaka* (haritāla), one should then saturate it with goat’s milk.
Then, having ground the root three times over and mixed it [with the previous substances],
one should form a pill, dry it, and extract the essence as before.
{Haritāla:: Extraction of Essence} One should grind *tālaka* with milks or with *sarpākṣī* or radishes;
having sealed the *chidramūṣā* as before, one should cause the essence to be extracted.
The essence of realgar is to be extracted just like that of palmyra;
by means of those same medicinal herbs and an equal amount of borax, when blown in the furnace, the fourth essence is obtained.
Mākṣika [sulphur] should be processed with cow's milk, *tuttha*-milk,
and castor oil; having been ground for one day, it should be formed into pills.
When the essence is being blown out like a cloud, this is the correct procedure for its dissolution:
jayantī, the powder of triphalā, turmeric, jaggery, and ṭaṅkaṇa. (The extraction of the essence of *mākṣika*).
Having ground this together with one-quarter part of ṭaṅkaṇa (borax), one should smear the crucible;
having joined it into a sealed vessel (*sampuṭa*), one should dry it in the hot sun.
The substance to be grasped is in the netherworld machine (*pātālayantra*), and it is heated by means of a *puṭa* [furnace].
Gold, silver, copper, lead, tin, magnetite, and iron;
these are the eight types of metal ending with *muṇḍa*. Bell-metal, brass, and bronze are the three types of alloys.
Metals such as upalauha are declared to include maṇḍūra and the dross of iron;
these twelve types are to be purified, calcined, and melted by means of *puṭa* and other processes.
In oil, buttermilk, cow’s urine, sour gruel, and horse-gram decoction— having been processed sequentially in these and likewise heated in each liquid seven times— {the metal is purified}. Rrā_1,8.3.
This purification of gold and other metal leaves has been proclaimed. [For the killing of mercury:
One-fourth part of dead mercury, ground with some acid, [is to be applied to gold].
Having smeared it on a leaf, one should cook it in a *puṭa* [furnace]; thus it certainly dies [is killed].
Such is the method for killing all pure metals.
Impure gold destroys happiness, virility, and strength, and causes various diseases.
Impure gold and mercury must therefore be purified before they are subjected to the process of killing.
The five earths:
anthill earth, soot, red ochre, and brick-dust, [placed] in a crucible for the purification of gold.
These and other five types of earth [should be used] with citrons and fermented rice-gruel.
Having ground it, one should apply it as a paste to an excellent gold leaf; it is purified by means of a *puṭa* [roasting].
One should then saturate the five earths (*pañcamṛttikā*) with the acid of *mātuluṅga* for three days.
Even rock salt or the dust of the earth purifies gold as before.
Gold and silver are killed by *nāgas*; copper by *tāpyas* and *gandha*; lead by *śilā*;
tin by *tāla*; and the three types of iron are killed by the milk of a woman and *hiṅgula*.
Mākṣika and lead powder, ground with the juice of *arka* leaves,
cause a gold leaf to die [i.e., become fixed] in a mere instant by means of a *puṭa* (roasting) process.
Having added half as much mercury to gold, one should carefully prepare a paste;
by adding lead powder above and below and subjecting it to heating in a closed crucible (puṭana), it certainly dies [is killed]. Rrā_1,8.12.
Naga-powder and mica soaked in the milk of the *vajrī* plant:
having smeared these along with a paste of gold, [the gold] dies [i.e., is fixed] from the crucible.
Having ground a dead *nāga* with the milky sap of *snuhī* or some kind of acid,
one should smear it onto a gold leaf, seal it, and cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire.
Having taken eight parts of tin (mṛnnāga) and grinding it with acidic liquids,
one should bind it together with the aforementioned tin and cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire.
Thus, being cooked again and again, it certainly dies eight times;
[one should treat] mercury equal in quantity to pure sulfur, honey, and great acids.
The gold is killed by means of eight coatings according to the procedure previously described.
One should then place an equal amount of pure mercury and gold together in a mortar and form them into a ball.
Having placed an equal amount of sulphur (gandhaka) below and having sealed everything, one should apply thirty vanopalas; in this manner, fourteen such puṭas should be administered.
Ash is produced that is free of residue; fragrance should be added in each crucible.
For gold, one should take double the amount of mercury and grind it with sour gruel for one *yāma*. (Rasārṇava 1.8.19)
Having ground honey below and above [the crucible] in a crucible equal in weight to the gold,
one should rub the gold on its surface, and then rub the gold-honey mixture on top of that.
One should take an equal amount of gold and an equal amount of its back-side paste (gandha);
having ground them six times and placed them inside, one should seal the crucible and heat it strongly.
One should take five parts of that ash, which is naturally cool and fit for consumption,
and employ one part each of borax and white glass.
The triad [of mercury, sulfur, and mica], mixed with honey and clarified butter and formed into a ball,
should be placed one part of *dhānyābhraka* (grain-sulfur) below and above it.
Having sealed it, one should heat it intensely in a crucible for two *ghaṭikās*;
it becomes an indestructible ash (*niruttha-bhasma*), which one should employ in various medicinal formulations.
Take one part of pure *mākṣika* (sulphur), one part of *avoṭa-mākṣika*,
and three parts of mercury; having added these three together, one should grind them with acid.
One should then cook that ball in a *pātālayantra* for three watches;
in this way, the gold dies, becoming *niruttha*—of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, having smeared gold leaves with *rājavṛkṣa*, *bhallātaka*,
and *iṣṭakāṇa* (borax), and having enclosed them, one should cook them in a *gajapuṭa*.
Having ground it again with those liquids, it is killed by being subjected to seven puṭas;
starting with one *tola* of gold, [one should add] one *māṣa* of purified lead.
Having smeared that powder with pure fragrant honey,
one should grind it with an acid for one watch (yāma), seal it, and cook it in a mild puṭa.
Furthermore, the fragrance should be applied repeatedly; it dies after ten applications.
{Gold:: dead:: medicinal properties}
And gold is cool, bitter, unctuous, cold, and heavy.
It produces intelligence, knowledge, and memory; it is an elixir that destroys poison.
Impure silver destroys longevity, semen, and strength, and it causes the onset of disease.
The impure is the nectar (amṛta) and the pure is the one to be killed; therefore, it should be understood by the wise.
Silver, melted with *nāga* and *ṭaṅkaṇa*, attains purity;
[this is] the killing of silver.
One should likewise grind honey and sulfur with the milk of the *arka* plant.
A silver leaf smeared with that [substance] is certainly killed by means of a *puṭa* [firing]. Silver, when immersed three times in *jyotiṣmatī* oil, becomes [pure].
One should grind copper with the milks of the *snuk* plant and smear it upon silver leaves;
having sealed them, one should cook them in a *gajapuṭa* fire and then grind them again with the previously mentioned substances.
Having smeared silver leaves with equal parts of *bhūdhātrī*, honey, long pepper (*pippalī*), rock salt, and sour gruel,
one should seal them and cook them in seven *puṭas*.
Having ground it again and again with liquid substances, it is killed; of this there is no doubt.
[This is the *niruttha* killing of silver.
With three parts of silver leaf, one part of pure *mākṣika* [is used].
One should grind silver leaves with the juices of *jambīra* fruits and smear them [with the paste];
having dried and sealed it, one should cook it with thirty pieces of wild stone (*vanyopala*).
In this manner, by means of fourteen layers, [the silver] certainly dies without residue.
For a silver leaf, one part of dead lead is used for every four parts [of silver].
Alternatively, having coated it with a paste of *gandhatāla* ground with *jambīra*,
one should seal it within three crucibles and cook it with twenty-five pieces of flint stone (*vanopala*).
There is no doubt that it dies; sulphur should be added in every crucible.
Having made mercury and sulphur equal in measure, [one should add] the root of *kākatuṇḍa*.
One should massage it with buffalo milk, grind it, and wash it with water;
then, having placed it inside a ball of turmeric, one should cast that ball into horse dung.
Having cast that into [the crucible] for twenty-one days, one should extract that sphere again;
having ground it, the silver leaves should be smeared with some kind of acid.
With twenty *puṭas*, ash is produced; there is no doubt about this.
One should then mix the *tālaka* with the ash ground in acidic liquid (*amlapiṣṭa*) and [subject it to] *puṭas*.
By means of that procedure, it arises as the remover of all diseases.
Impure copper destroys longevity, diminishes luster, and depletes all bodily constituents.
It causes delusion, fainting, dizziness, and disheveled hair, as well as various diseases, leprosy, and piercing pains.
Having smeared a copper leaf with the milky sap of *snuhī* and *arka*, salt, and sour gruel (*kāñjika*),
one should heat it and repeatedly sprinkle it with the juice of *nirguṇḍī*.
By applying a plaster made from chalk and salt ground with buttermilk and sour gruel, and by pouring it over copper, one attains the state of being purified twelve times. Rā 1.8.48.
Having smeared a copper leaf with that [substance],
one should repeatedly quench it while it is hot six times with a paste of *nirguṇḍī* and sour gruel for the sake of purification.
One should boil a copper leaf with cow urine for one *yāma* over a steady fire;
it is purified, of this there is no doubt. Now, the process of killing [the metal] is described.
One should smear a leaf that has been perforated with thorns with a paste of copper-colored fragrance ground with acid; having prepared it thus, one should cook it in a *puṭa*.
Having extracted [the mercury], one should grind it and add sulfur equal to one-fourth its weight;
then, one should mix it with *jambīra* fruits, fermented rice-gruel (*āranāla*), or the juices of *mṛgadūrvā*.
Having ground it repeatedly in that same manner, one should cook it with fragrant substances in four *puṭas*;
then, having ground it with the juice of *mātuluṅga*, one should administer one *puṭa*.
By this very procedure, copper ash will certainly be produced.
One should grind mercury, which is double the amount of the copper, with the acid of *jambīra* fruit.
In this same manner, with white sugar, it becomes dead after three *puṭas*.
For the killing of copper:
[use] *pāṣāṇabhedin*, *matsyākṣī* juice, and double the amount of sulphur.
One should smear a leaf of copper, seal it, and cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire;
having burnt it again with one-seventh part [of the reagent], one should grind it with liquid extracts.

In this way, after seven layers [of processing], the copper ash will certainly be cooked. For mercury and cinnabar of copper should be ground with the acid juice of *jambīra* fruit. (Rājaratnākara 1.8.57)
First, having placed a leaf of dhattūra inside a crucible,
one should sprinkle powdered sulphur equal in weight to that [leaf] upon its surface.
Upon that surface, one should place an equal amount of rubbed copper and sulphur;
having covered it with a *dhustūra* leaf and sealed it, one should cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire.
When that powder has cooled to the temperature of one's own body, it certainly turns into ash.
One should then wash the copper leaf with a little fragrance and acid.
One should smear a copper leaf with that expressed oil;
subsequently, it is killed by being enclosed in a *puṭa* with the fragrant substance—of this there is no doubt.
Then, having ground copper with twice its amount of sulphur and an acidic liquid,
the wise one should add it below by half its portion, mixed with ground acidic substances.
Having sealed that mass inside the interior of a vessel, one should cook it on the stove for one watch (yāma) with intense heat;
it will certainly be reduced to ashes.
Take one part of mercury and two parts of sulfur; having processed them for one watch (yāma) and thoroughly rubbed them together,
place a copper leaf equal in weight to those two inside the interior of a crucible.
One should place ashes at the side of the salt-mechanism situated correctly;
one should cook it on the hearth for four watches (yāmas) upon the back of a vessel containing cow-dung.
Water should be given again and again until the coolness of one's own limbs is diminished;
one dies, there is no doubt in this—this should be applied in all diseases.
Regarding the various methods for the killing (and purification) of copper: for the sake of purification, take five parts of copper,
one part of white glass, and five parts of one part of ṭaṅkaṇa (borax).
Having combined one part of copper leaf with [the mercury] in a crucible,
placing it above and sealing it, one should take it once it has been heated and has become thoroughly cooled.
Copper that is free from defects shall become a remover of all diseases.
Alternatively, one should grind killed copper with a single acid.
Having placed that ball inside a suraṇa root and sealed it from above, one should coat it;
once dried, one should cook it in a gajapuṭa fire, and it will become a remover of all defects.
It never causes vomiting, dizziness, or purgation.
{Copper (in its killed state):
medicinal properties}
Copper is sharp, hot, sweet, astringent, cooling, and laxative.

It is an elixir (rasāyana) that destroys disorders of phlegm (kapha), bile (pitta), and wasting (kṣaya), as well as jaundice and skin diseases; it also eliminates chronic abdominal pain (pariṇāma-śūla), hemorrhoids, and weak digestion.
Tin and lead,
when not properly processed,
cause leprosy and abdominal tumors.
It is said that [these] cause urinary disorders, jaundice, abdominal dropsy, wind-disorders, phlegm-disorders, and death.
One should apply a paste of powdered *nirguṇḍī* root mixed with the milk of *mārka*;
once that lead-leaf has dried, one should melt it and pour [the liquid] over it.
Then one should cause the leaf to be placed in the midst of *nirguṇḍī* juice;
having smeared it, it should be processed and sprinkled again seven times for the sake of purification.
Lead, turmeric, seeds of *tumbaru*, *kokilākṣa*, *kuṭhārikā*,
*gaurīphala*, *amlīkā*, *caṇḍī*, *kṣudrā*, *brāhmī*, and cumin; Rrā 1.8.76.
One should saturate a single portion of ash with *vajrī* milk according to its availability;
within that, one should purify the *nāga* by sprinkling it seven times.
{Lead:: Killing::
Niruttha} Having cast the ash of the bark of the *aśvattha* and *ciñcā* trees along with one-fourth part of lead into a cauldron, one should cook it in a vessel while stirring it with an iron ladle.
When this has become ash,
one should grind that ash with an equal amount of realgar using jambīra fruits or sour gruel, seal it, and cook it in a *puṭa*.

Having ground it again once it has cooled to the temperature of one's own body, with twenty parts of *śilāmlaka*, [one should apply] six such roastings (*puṭapāka*); thus even lead (*nāga*) becomes completely purified (*nirutthita*).
Alternatively, one should place nāga leaves smeared with powder in a pan and cook them over a fierce fire for one *yāma*; then that ash [should be processed] with the juices of *citraka*.
One should roast it in an iron vessel, stirring with Arjuna sticks,
for a period of up to sixteen *yāmas*, adding liquid again and again.
One should crush the substance to be boiled with a pestle, extract it with the juices of *citraka*, form it into a ball,
seal it, and then perform a light firing (*māraṇa*) using the six-pot method (*ṣaṭpuṭa*).
For the purpose of killing (*māraṇa*),
one should roast [the substance] firmly with the ashes of *ciñcā*, *akṣa*, sugar cane, *bhallātaka*, *balā*, *vajralatā*, *apāmārga*, *arjuna*, and *aśvattha*. Rrā_1.8.84.
If an iron vessel is placed for seven days in ashes of equal weight along with *daṇḍapalāśa* alone, it dissolves; of this there is no doubt.
Having ground *agasti* and *bhūnāga*, one should smear a vessel and let it dry thoroughly;
one should then melt [the ingredients] in that vessel for one *yāma* and cast them into a sturdy vessel.
One should rub [the substance] in the alkaline solution of *vāsā* and *ciṭī*, or on a *vāsā* leaf;
having cooked it on the stove for one *yāma*, one should remove it and mix it together.
That powder, combined with mica (śilā), sulphate of iron (tāpya), and the alkali of vāsaka,
should be cooked in twenty-one puṭas along with an equal amount of the previously mentioned nāga.
Having applied two layers with the alkali of *ciñciṭā* together with the juice of *vāsā*, the mercury—
shining like the color of vermilion— dies, performing all its functions.
One should take equal parts of realgar and honey;
having ground them with *arka* leaves, one should kill (i.e., dissolve) the lead plates.
Lead, when calcined into ashes, becomes bitter and sweet in its medicinal properties.
By constant practice, it brings about longevity, renown, and an increase in vigor.
Having smeared tin leaves with a paste made of honey, yellow orpiment, and the fresh juice of *palāśa*, one should kill [the metal] (reduce it to ash).
One should purify tin with *nāgavacchā* in the same manner as with *aśvattha* and *ciñcā*;
then, that ash and an equal amount of yellow orpiment (*haritāla*) should be mixed with some kind of acid.
Alternatively, having formed a ball with juices derived from *palāśa*, one should seal it in a crucible;
then, having extracted it, one should grind it together with *tāla* in a quantity equal to one-tenth [of the original].
Having stirred it with the previously mentioned juices and sealed it, one should cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire;
having cooked it thus in twenty *puṭas*, it becomes dead, reduced to ashes.
One should smear the leaves of the tin plant with tin-mercury (sūta) using tin as a flux;
having gathered them from the *ciñcā* tree, they should be covered at the ends with rice grains.
Having ground those [ingredients], one should smear lead leaves within that mass;
with the powders of *śirīṣa* and turmeric, along with *kumārī*, it becomes an auspicious pill (*golaka*).
A leaf of tin coated with *sūta* and smeared inside a ball (*golaka*),
having been sealed and cooked in a *gajapuṭa* fire, becomes dead according to the previously mentioned number.
Having ground *akṣa* and *bhallātaka* with water, one should smear them [on the target].
Then, having placed them inside a mortar of sesame husks and sealed it, one should cook them in a *puṭa*.
In the substance called *gaja*, ash is produced consisting of forty parts of tin.
(Tin: dead;
medicinal properties)
Tin, which is slightly bitter and salty, cures anemia and conquers worms and urinary disorders.
A small amount of *lekhina* brass removes all diseases of the body.
Impure iron is not nectar; it causes the loss of life and brings about disease.
It causes pain in the heart, thirst, and numbness; therefore, one should kill it when it is pure.
{Examination of Kāntaloha}:
In whichever vessel a drop of oil, when cast, does not spread;
and in which asafoetida spreads its own fragrance, and the nimbu fruit its bitterness.
When heated, it becomes burnt and does not flatten upon the ground;
that iron which is thus lovely is said to be as described by the characteristics, and nothing else.
The paste of *nimba* that has been kept overnight becomes pleasant, very soft, bright, golden-hued, darkening to the eyes, and effective against worms; it is therefore sweet-tasting.
That which is melted with silver is most excellent and beautiful;
it removes all diseases and is supreme in curing all forms of leprosy.
Coated with the blood of a rabbit or a goat and heated over the fire three times, iron—
from *kāntaloha* down to *muṇḍaloha*— is the supreme remedy for all diseases.
Take eight parts of water for every one part of triphalā; with this water, take sixteen *palas* of triphalā.
When that decoction is reduced to one-fourth, add five leaf-pieces of iron.
Having heated the leaves, one should sprinkle them seven times;
in this way, the impurity arising from the mountain [ore] and from iron is dissolved.
