Iron powder, which is of three kinds, should be cooked with six times its quantity of cow urine;
it should then be washed in fermented rice gruel and dried, whereby it attains purity.
Raktamālā, haṃsapāda, gojihvā, triphalā,
amṛtā, gopālī, tumburu, and dantī— these, ground together with equal parts cow’s urine, [are used for the purification of iron].
In this process, one should heat an iron leaf repeatedly twenty-one times and quench it in the range from *kānta* to *muṇḍa* iron, for the removal of all defects.
Among all the pharmaceutical preparations of medicinal herbs, the preparation of iron is praised;
therefore, one should diligently refine iron first of all.
For iron weighing more than five palas up to thirteen palas,
the mantra is first recited, and then the ritual to be performed is described as follows.
One should grind five *pala* of cinnabar with breast milk;
with that, one should coat iron leaves weighing five *pala*.
Having sealed it in a *gajapuṭa* fire-vessel, one should cook it again with the decoctions of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), or with *jambīra* fruits or *āranāla* vinegar;
indeed, [one should add] vermilion (*hiṅgula*) in a twentieth part [of the total].
Having ground and enclosed the metal, one should likewise cook it again;
thus, by forty *puṭas*, one treats *kānta*, *tīkṣṇa*, and *muṇḍaka* iron.
Having repeatedly applied vermilion (*hiṅgula*) to *trālasanda*, one dies;
likewise, the bark of the *arjuna* tree, ground with extremely red *kāñjika* vinegar, [effects death]. (Rājaratnākara 1.9.16)
Into the middle of that, one should place iron powder in a bell-metal vessel;
it should be infused for one day in the heat, being filled repeatedly with the liquids.
One should kill iron in three ways using *arjuna* or *sāranāla*; one should stir together iron powder with the juice of *dantī* leaves.
One should macerate it for one day in the heat, adding liquid again and again;
having sealed it at night, one should cook it with *puṭa* applications and macerate it with these liquids.
In this manner, one should perform [the rite] for eight days; indeed, iron dies in three ways. One should fashion the three types of metal leaves so that they resemble the leaf of the *ciñcā* tree.
One should place it in a clay vessel and heat it in the sun, filling it repeatedly with the juice of *dantī* leaves until the iron indeed glows red-hot.
One should kill [the iron] with intense heat and reduce it to powder;
then one should employ *kānta* iron, *tīkṣṇa* iron, and likewise powdered *muṇḍa* iron, along with the juices of *matsyākṣaja*.
It should be processed in the sun for three days, with the juices of *citraka* for two days,
with the juices of *trikaṇṭaka* for three days, and with the juices of *sahadevī* for three days.
One should saturate [the powder] for three days each with cow urine and a decoction of triphalā;
then, after grinding it with dhātakī, one should apply the *puṭapāka* treatment in successive stages.
Having thus sealed it with the *gajapuṭa* fire, one should employ the killed [iron] in medicinal formulations;
one should rub iron powder with the juices extracted from *kuraṇṭaka* leaves.
Having ground it with the juices of *trikaṇṭaka*, *vandhyā*, *bhṛṅgī*, and *punarnavā* for one day in the intense heat of the sun,
one should grind it again for one day with cow's urine.
Triphalā should be boiled with cow’s urine;
one should then saturate [the powder] with that decoction for twenty-one days with diligence, and thereafter grind it for one day.
Having sealed it in a *gajapuṭa* vessel, one should grind it with a decoction;
it should be ground during the day and subjected to the *puṭa* process at night for twenty-one days.
Indeed, within twenty-one days, the three types of iron—
mākṣika and śilājatu— are killed by means of acids, turmeric, and black pepper.
Having ground it, one should rub the iron leaf;
heating it repeatedly, one should pour [the liquid] over it seven times with a decoction of triphalā, and then wash it again with water.
One should pound it with an iron rod and grind it with a decoction of triphalā;
one-sixteenth part of the iron's weight of mākṣika and śilā should be added.
Having stirred it with sour gruel and sealed it within an elephant-hide crucible, one should cook it;
thus the ash of *kānta*, *tīkṣṇa*, and other types of *muṇḍaka* becomes "niruttha" (non-residual).
Having smeared [the iron] with the marrow of *tinduka* fruit and placed it in the intense heat of the sun,
one should keep it in a bell-metal vessel; in a single day, it will certainly undergo the *puṭa* process.
One should apply the plaster again and again, coating it until the end of the day;
combined with a decoction of the three myrobalans (triphalā), it becomes dead [calcined] in a single day.
One should stir iron powder in a vessel made of iron or a metal bowl using an iron ladle,
and cook it for one day in a decoction of triphalā. (Rasārṇava 1.9.35)
Having ground that bolus with the decoction of the three myrobalans (triphalā) and sealed it in a crucible, one should cook it;
one should cook it for a day and night in a windless place inside a crucible using a sixteenth part [of the ingredients].
In this manner, one should prepare the *sthālīpāka* in three ways within the inner compartments;
[the ingredients are] *bhṛṅgī*, *drāva*, *tālamūlī*, and the root of *hastikarṇa*.

Having ground [the ingredients] in a decoction of śatāvarī, vidārī, and mūla, as well as triphalā, it should be cooked in a pot as before; the paste should then be subjected to three puṭapāka treatments.
Then, [one should bathe] with the waters of punarnavā, or with decoctions of the ten roots (daśamūla),
or with decoctions of bṛhatī, or with the juice of bījapūra.
Likewise, having ground the seeds of *brahma* either in a decoction of *aśigru*, or with cow’s milk—
using one or the other— one should cook it in the aforementioned crucible containing the embryo.
One should then process it with the liquid itself for exactly one *yāma* at the end of each *puṭa*;
having thus ground it with each [ingredient] in sequence, one should process it with the *puṭas*.
There is no doubt that it dies; [the metals] Kānta, Tīkṣṇa, and Muṇḍaka—all this iron, once dead, should be smelted with the five friends (*mitrapañcaka*).
If it should thus become non-revivable, it should be used as a water-crossing (*vāritara*).
One should place honey, clarified butter, dead iron, and silver together in a crucible;
having sealed it with clay, one should take out the silver, which will have returned to its original weight.
Then one should know that iron is "dead"; one should kill it again so that it becomes "immortal."
One should grind equal parts of dead sulphur and dead iron together in a mortar for one day with the juice of *kanyākā*, then seal it and cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire.
In this manner, this [process] should be performed for all metals so that they do not rise again.
Having prepared pure mercury and sulfur in two parts as a collyrium (kajjalī) in a mortar,
one should grind an equal amount of iron powder with the juice of *kanyākā* (datura).
Having extracted that globule from two *yāmas* [of processing] and placed it in a copper vessel, one should cover it with castor leaves; within half a *yāma*, it will become hot.
One should place it in a heap of grain and later, at the end of three days, extract it;
having ground it and strained it through a cloth, it will immediately become water-clear.
The beloved [substance], the sharp, the shaven, and the non-arising become "dead" (mṛta);
one should thus kill gold and the other metals by reducing them to powder, just like iron.
This is known as the Siddhayoga, which has come directly from the Siddhas;
beginning with iron and including mercury, it is like food itself, removing all diseases and fevers.
Combined with the juice of triphalā, one should employ it in all diseases.
Dead metals become subjugated;
indeed, through proper application, they destroy all diseases.
This is achieved through the perfection of firm yoga resulting from repeated practice.
They effect the destruction of illness, death, and old age.
When eight parts of the water remain, one should add five palas of the three myrobalans (triphalā).
The ghee should be equal in quantity to the decoction, and the powder should be equal to the quantity of iron filings.
One should cook it in a copper vessel, stirring with an iron ladle;
one should cook it over a mild fire until the sulfur is fully digested.
Śivā, equal to iron, should be applied; one should extract it only when well-cooked.
This is known as the "carrier of yoga" (yogavāha), and dead iron is the great nectar (mahāmṛta).
In this manner, the procedure for soft iron, hard iron, and even wrought iron is prescribed;
[this is] the process of immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*).
One pala of iron ash cooked in one kuḍava of jaggery.
Regarding diseases, one should apply that [medicine] in the measure of a *kola* and administer it according to the appropriate method;
one should cook clarified butter with an equal amount of dead iron in an iron vessel.
Once it has been digested, one should take ghee and administer it with the *yogavāha* [herbs].
"Oṃ, obeisance to the one for eating with nectar. By means of this mantra, one should consume iron.
[The medicinal properties of dead iron:]

Iron (lauha) bestows longevity, virility, and strength; it cures anemia, urinary disorders, and skin diseases such as leprosy; it removes deranged wind associated with undigested matter (āmavāta), and destroys wrinkles and graying hair.
One should grind the three alkalis and the five salts seven times with sour gruel;
then one should smear leaves of bell-metal, iron, and brass with sesame paste.
Having sealed it in a *gajapuṭa* furnace, one should cook it; it attains purification, not otherwise.
One should kill them as one does copper, and having done so, employ them everywhere.
Bell-metal (kāṃsya) is astringent, hot, light, dry, and bitter;
it destroys diseases caused by phlegm and bile, and increases the strength of the heart, the body, and the lifespan.
Bell-metal (rītikā) is dry, slightly bitter and salty, laxative, purifying, a destroyer of all diseases, and increases strength, virility, and longevity. (Rājanighaṇṭu 1.9.64)
One should smelt the iron dross in a small charcoal fire and repeatedly sprinkle it with cow’s urine and with *akṣa* leaves seven times over and over again.
This is declared to be maṇḍūra; one should employ it when pure and finely ground.
Muṇḍa is a hundred times more potent than kiṭṭa, and tīkṣṇa is more than a hundred times more potent than muṇḍa.
Magnetite (kānta) produces a hundred-thousandfold greater benefit than iron-sulphide (tīkṣṇa) through its consumption;
therefore, magnetite, which supremely wards off old age and death, should always be utilized.
I shall describe the extraction of oils, whether by solar heating or by fire;
the oil that is to be obtained by means of a mechanical apparatus should be employed in medicinal formulations.
One should have the powder of *dhattūra* seeds filtered through a cloth;
having smeared a bell-metal vessel with it, one should keep it in the intense heat of the sun.
One should cause the oil— well-heated and strained through a cloth— to be poured out and collect it;
[the oils] of the drumstick tree (*śigru*), lotus seeds, and *mārkava* seeds.
One should take the oil of each [plant] separately, like that of the *dhattūra*;
just as the *dhattūra* oil is extracted from its decoction while heated in the sun.
Likewise, oils should be collected everywhere along with other medicinal substances;
there may also be the oil of *aṅkoṭa* together with the entire plant of *kākatuṇḍī*.
Oil prepared with vākucī, devadālī, and the root of karkoṭī, along with a decoction of apāmārga, serves as a remedy for snake venom.
Oil derived from *jaipāla* seeds should be prepared with the decoction of *mūlaka* and *kumārī*;
one should likewise obtain *vākucī* oil using the decoction of *raktamārga*.
Oil prepared with the decoction of *Indravāruṇī* becomes [an ointment] for *āragvadha*;
one should likewise extract oil from the decoction arising from *Kākatuṇḍī* and *Apāmārga*.
One should mix the seeds of the bitter gourd (*kaṭutumbī*) with cow dung; once dried,
one should grind them together with grain husks in a mortar.
Then, having removed the husks from that [semen] and powdered it, one should grind it with the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja* in the sun;
when pressed, the oil should be collected.
One should cause the seeds of *kṛṣṇā* and *kākatuṇḍī* to be made into powders;
having combined these with the powder of *kāntapāṣāṇa*, one should seal [the mixture].
Having cooked [the seeds] contained in a heap of grain and extracted the oil,
one should saturate the powder of *pāṣāṇabījaka* with the juice of *dhātrī* fruits.
Then, after one day, the oil should be extracted from the apparatus.
One should then macerate the fruits of *guñjā* and *karañja* in human urine.
Then, one should smear a bronze vessel with [the paste] seven times in the heat;
having removed it, one should hold it in the heat so that the oil falls out under pressure.
Having ground the powder of *jyotiṣmatī* with the juice of *vardhamāna*, one should saturate it; then,
one should extract the oil from the seeds of *jyotiṣmatī* in the sun.
One should prepare a powder of *putrajīva* seeds and a powder born from *agastya* seeds according to the method for mangoes; from these, the oils should be extracted separately.
The powder of *bilva* seeds should be infused with coconut water for one day; then, having extracted the oil using an oil-press, one should employ it.
One should gently rub the seeds of *aṅkola* after removing their husks;
then, having ground them in a bronze vessel, one should apply it as a paste like chickpea flour.
One should apply a small amount of borax powder to its surface and hold it in the intense heat of the sun; one should then collect the oil from its mouth.
Having ground *keśataila* together with an equal amount of *śamī* powder, one should place it inside a vessel with a hole;
one should position the vessel so that it stands over [another] vessel below the hole and cause the hair to enter through the hole.
One should sprinkle the substance with water and cause it to be held beneath a crevice;
then, having placed hair in its center, one should slowly insert the lid over it from above.
At that moment, this oil from hair and sesame becomes the form of Śrava;
one should take the juice of unripe *bhānu* leaves and saturate [the substance] with it.
Whether all the seed-powders mentioned or those not mentioned are used individually,
the oil released in the sun will undoubtedly cure both curable and incurable ailments.
In the same manner, one should extract the oil from all seeds using a decoction of *uttaravāruṇī*, and cause it to be absorbed in the intense heat of the sun.
Having dried and ground many times the seeds, kernels, and flesh of all [plants],
one should extract the oil from all those seeds using a *pātālayantra* (subterranean press).
Oil is extracted from all types of wood, such as bamboo and others, using a coconut shell;
oil is extracted from seeds such as chaff-grain and others using a seed-crushing machine.
One should cause him to grasp all the seed-syllables and employ him in the yogic practices.
Vatsanābha poison is sweet, digestive, and overcomes phlegm and wind;
when properly compounded, it pacifies the three humors and becomes like nectar.
It is nourishing for strength and vigor, equal to a hundred submarine fires;
indeed, it is the sovereign power in the treatment of *sannipāta*.
That which is harvested at the end of the ripening of its fruit— fresh, unctuous, dense, heavy, non-spreading, a destroyer of poison, and dried by wind and sun— is [the best].
One should wear it smeared with red mustard oil on a cloth;
or else, one may take whatever poison is available combined with cow urine.
Dried for three days in the sun, it becomes a preserver of virility;
mercury, mica, iron, and poison, when processed (mṛta), possess equal potency.
Therefore, poison should be employed in a yoga-conducting formulation for the purpose of *rasāyana*;
and those measures are indeed eight, six, or four [units].
Three measures are declared: superior, inferior, and middling;
these should be administered in all diseases to one who eats ghee and eats wholesome food.
It should be given to a man who consumes milk, who practices *rasāyana*, and is free from anger, excessive bile, impotence, and pulmonary consumption (*rājayakṣman*). (Rājanighaṇṭu 1.10.35)

Poison is not administered in the royal palace to those emaciated by hunger, thirst, fatigue, labor, or travel, nor to those suffering from consumption, nor to pregnant women, children, or the elderly.
Neither should it be given nor should it be consumed at any time during a breach of agreement;
however, the preceptor may consume it in order to inspire confidence in the disciple.
One should rub [the ground] with this mantra and not place it down;
one should say "Amṛta"—this is the sequence. Oṃ, homage to the accomplished gurus.
Homage to the supreme gurus! Homage to the gurus higher than the highest! Homage to the gurus who abide in the supreme!
The vegetable poisons are *saktuka*, *mustaka*, *śṛṅgī*, *vālaka*, that which is called *sarṣapa*,
*vatsanābha*, *kūrma*, and *śvetaśṛṅgī* as the eighth.
Thus, one should employ these eight in yoga, while avoiding the poisons beginning with kālakūṭa:
*kālakūṭa*, *meṣaśṛṅgī*, *hālāhala*, and *dardura*.
Karkaṭa, markaṭa, granthi, hāridra, raktaśṛṅgaka,
and keśava as the tenth— these should be avoided by the best of physicians.
One should employ roasted barley flour and other such substances for all diseases and as an elixir (*rasāyana*);
having carefully considered this poison and the four castes, it should be administered by the best of physicians.
The Brahmin preserves youth; the King protects it upon this earth; the Vaiśya is indeed skilled in its nourishment; and the Śūdra is capable of destroying leprosy.
Therefore, a physician who is excellent, skillful, and knowledgeable in that [science] should cultivate and apply it; thus, O best of kings, poison on earth becomes the conqueror of death.
Whether white or tawny, sweet-smelling or even saline, a cow with hairy limbs belongs to the Brahmin caste; one that is red belongs to the Kṣatriya caste.
The Vaiśya caste is seen as yellowish or somewhat sweet;
the Śūdra's is greyish-black; and these are observed by the best of physicians.
One should contemplate placing poison even into a vessel filled with milk;
when it assumes that color, then one should declare its origin.
White, red, yellow, and black— thus is the fourfold determination of caste to be known for the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
If a physician should gradually recognize that poison thrown into milk becomes white,
red, yellow, black, and even hot, [he may know it as such].
Poison is neutralized by grinding it with tuttha and ṭaṅkaṇa;
among poisons known as mobile (jaṅgama), that originating from snakes is beneficial [as an antidote].
This alone is the most excellent [remedy], which instantly destroys the three humors;
it immediately acts as a digestive stimulant, equal to a hundred submarine fires.
His power lies in counteracting the humors; for he is indeed the source of power.
Poison derived from a snake, as it is obtained, combined with cow urine and dried for three days in the sun, shall become a sustainer of virility when administered.
When one eats in excess, one should then drink borax,
or else *rajanī*, *meghanādā*, or *sarpākṣī* combined with clarified butter.
Or one should lick powdered *arjunatvac* with honey and ghee;
or drink the marrow of *putrajīvaka*, or the two types of *nimba*.
Thus the procedure for poison has been declared; now I shall describe its application:
poison, the three pungents (trikaṭuka), musta, turmeric, and nimba leaves.
With *viḍaṅga* as the eighth [ingredient], an equal amount of each should be powdered with goat's urine;
the resulting pills, the size of chickpeas, are known as *jayā*, which acts as a vehicle for other medicinal properties.
Poison, *pāṭhā*, *aśvagandhā*, *balā*, *tālīsa* leaf, black pepper, and long pepper— these, along with neem, should be taken in equal parts with goat's urine.
The pill should be prepared as before; this pill is a "carrier" (yogavāhikā) [of the medicine].
It cures sleepiness, lethargy, exhaustion, burning sensations, frothy secretions, and horripilation.
Mobile poison (jaṅgamaviṣa) causes emaciation as well as diarrhea,
whereas stationary poison (sthāvaraviṣa) causes fever, hiccup, sensitivity of the teeth, and throat obstruction.
Poison causes swelling, indigestion, dyspnea, and fainting;
when the practitioner does not recognize it, he should administer the treatment after consuming the poison himself.
Taking up that very poison, he sinks as if into the ocean;
therefore, the king should protect himself with great effort from the physician who treats for poison.
First, having slightly roasted it in a fire-pan and rendered it non-poisonous with the mantra to be described, one should collect it.
Having infused the bile in lime juice three times, washed it, and dried it thoroughly, one should collect it. [Thus ends the section on the origin of *śilājatu*.]
When heated by the sun, the mineral ores of the mountains—such as gold and others—ooze out;
that exudation which resembles lac, is soft, and has the appearance of clay, is called *śilājatu*.
Śilājatu is free from defects, slightly astringent, and pungent in its post-digestive effect;
it is neither excessively hot nor cold, and its origin is from four minerals.
Śilājatu derived from gold, silver, copper, or even iron is excellent in its medicinal properties.
That which is sweet and bitter, and resembles the color of the Japā flower;
That which is exuded from gold is bitter in its post-digestive effect and cold in potency.
Silver is pungent, white, cold, sweet, and its post-digestive transformation is sweet.
That which comes from copper has the luster of a peacock's neck; it is sharp, hot, and pungent when digested.
And that which resembles guggulu, being bitter and endowed with saltiness, [is derived from iron].
Bitter in its post-digestive effect (*vipāka*) and cold in potency, that iron is the most excellent of all;
it has the smell of cow’s urine and is suitable for all ritual actions among all [metals].
Among the applications of elixirs (rasāyana), the last one is distinguished;
it is indicated respectively for vāta-pitta, pitta-śleṣman, and for all three [doṣas] together.
Those minerals produced from gold and other metals are especially praised;
*śilājatu* turns to dross in fire like iron, yet it burns without smoke when placed in water.
That which is placed on the tip of a blade of grass and so forth is best; it trickles down like a thread.
For the purpose of removing defects such as the fangs of gadflies, insects, or medicinal poisons, one should fumigate a ram's horn with birch bark.

Regarding the decoction: one part of the substance to be boiled, equal in measure to the *śilājatu*, should be mixed with four parts of water and processed until one-fourth remains; this is one method.
Vāgbhaṭa, however, states that by the gift of eightfold water, when eight parts remain, the procedure for both cases is as before.

One should place *bhadraśilājatu* into a decoction of *triphalā*, *daśamūla*, and hot water, or simply in hot water; once it has settled and the supernatant has become clear, everything should be taken like the leaf of a lotus.
Then, having applied the meditative infusion (bhāvanā) according to the procedure described for the *śivāguḍikā* and having purified it, one should infuse it with the *sālasāra* group as follows:
"Two *sāla* trees, two *karañjas*, *khadira*, the two types of *candana*, *gardabhāṇḍa*, *arjuna*, the two types of *lodhra*, and *dhava* and *asanā*. (Rājanighaṇṭu 1.10.69)
Śirīṣa, aguru, kālīya, pūga, pūtika, karkaṭa,
and the sālasāra group— this collection also removes diseases caused by phlegm.
It destroys urinary disorders, tumors, hemorrhoids, skin diseases, leprosy, and the ailments of jaundice;
it should be dried in the heat of the sun during the day and soaked every night.
The quantity of liquid that, having become one with the substance, causes it to reach a state of moisture—
this is the measure prescribed by physicians for the procedure of medicinal saturation (*bhāvanā*).
One should boil an equal amount of the substance until the decoction remains at one-eighth;
with that decoction, one should dry the fresh substance in strong sunlight until it is equal [in weight] to the original material.
One should take burnt diamond, place it in fire, and blow it until melted; then, having extinguished it seven times with the juice of *nirguṇḍī* and washed it, one should collect it.
They are born in the Vāmaruka region during the summer, afflicted by the heat of the sun;
in the cool season and the winter, they emit the resin of guggulu in five ways.

One [variety] is golden-hued, another is like buffalo-antimony (mahiṣākṣa), another resembles a ruby (padmarāga), some have the luster of a bumblebee, and others possess the brilliance of a white water-lily; these should be collected according to rule and then examined.
In a blazing fire they go to dissolution; in lukewarm water they become moistened, being equal to milk.

One should accept those that are auspicious and avoid those that have been present for a long time, which are clearly visible on the body and have a color resembling that of a foul-smelling skull-cup.
Guggulu is sweet in taste, astringent, bitter, and pungent; it is sharp in its potency and pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka).
It is aphrodisiac, extremely clear in purifying the channels, sharp, expansive, and laxative.
It bestows longevity, grants the celestial voice (*svarada*), pacifies the three *doṣas*, and produces wisdom, memory, and splendor;
it is auspicious, destroys evil, generates fire, and furthermore purifies the heart and throat.
Regarding the purification of *guggulu*:

having added *guggulu* to a warm, strained decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūla*), stirred it, and filtered it through cloth, one should dry it in the intense heat of the sun, add clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and then form it into a mass.
One should soak the navel of a conch shell with sour liquid seven times;
having discarded the impurities and so forth during the fierce [process], one should wash it and take hold of it.
Having placed a cowrie shell in the auspicious juice of buttermilk, cāṅgerī, and jambīra,
one should saturate it until it no longer appears white.
Afterward, having extracted it, one should take the cowrie shell that has attained purity.
Taking earth-born water and even a pearl that has been left overnight,
one should discard its impurities and the like, wash it, and then cause it to be taken up.
Victorious is that king of elixirs, which removes the fear of death, is a treasury of all virtues, and serves as the overseer for the longevity of the body;
when practiced, it destroys wrinkles and grey hair, increases virility, and even enables one to maintain a steady union with women.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the most auspicious accomplishment of the body (*dehasiddhi*),
through the attainment of which all accomplishments arise for human beings.
There is nothing desired in the three worlds that exists apart from the body;
therefore, with every effort, let exertion be applied toward it.
On an auspicious lunar mansion and day, having performed emesis and purgation,
one should then [use] the liquid produced from the stalks of the *ketakī* for the sake of special purification.
One should drink one *kuḍava* each of these for three days to remove the disorder of *loṇa*:
*viḍaṅga*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, and *ketakī* combined with *stanasa*.
Boiled for three days and drunk, it is the supreme remedy for disorders caused by acidity.
Śyāmā, fire (citraka), viḍaṅga, the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), triphalā, and vṛṣa—[these are used in the preparation].
Saindhava salt, devadāru, and mustā— each of these taken in equal parts and licked with ghee in a dose of one karṣa for seven days conquers all disorders.
Thus, with his body purified, he should worship the deity, the guru, the maiden, and the circle of yoginīs; thereafter, he should prepare the elixir (*rasāyana*).
For the practice of *rasāyana*,
one should remain in a windless underground chamber or a similar place, free from external thoughts,
having conquered the senses and subdued anger, and subsisting on milk and *śāli* rice.
He may eat rice cooked sixty times, barley-gruel, wheat, mung-bean soup,
the meat of wild animals, or simply milk alone.
One should eat food with strength, avoiding vegetables and salt;
one should perform an oil massage with whey and bathe with pleasantly warm water.
One should constantly consort with a Kākinī woman who is well-suited to oneself and in the prime of youth;
for when the lord of essences (rasendra) is being consumed, a man becomes blinded by passion.
For in the absence of sexual union, his vital essence (rasa) becomes undigested;
from that indigestion arise trembling, burning sensations, pain, hiccups, fainting, fever, and restlessness.
Indeed, cough, dyspnea, loss of appetite, vomiting, vertigo, and delusion arise;
therefore, one should consort with a beautiful woman and avoid an unattractive one.
Anointing with pungent oil, sour gruel, wine, and curd;
*kaliṅga*, *kāravallī*, sour oil, and eggplant and black mustard.

One should avoid the wood-apple (*bilva*), the umbrella-plant (*chatrāka*), eggplant (*vārtāka*), split bamboo shoots (*vidala*), the *kākamācī* creeper, radish (*mūlaka*), garlic (*laśuna*), and anything that is pungent, cold, or hot.
One should avoid staying awake at night, sleeping during the day, and sexual intercourse; one should also renounce quarreling, agitation, anxiety, and grief.
From its suppression, there may arise piercing pain, drowsiness, lethargy, fever, and restlessness;
for their pacification, one should drink the fruit of the *karkaṭī* with water for three days.
One should lick a powder of ginger and rock salt with the acidic juices of citron;
or, for its pacification, one should drink sauvarcala salt with the urine of cows.
One should boil vandhyākarkoṭakī, puṅkhā, and pātālagaruḍī with eight times the amount of water; when reduced to one-eighth, it should be mixed with rock salt.
One should drink for three days that which destroys all disorders, as spoken by Śiva;
or else the root of the *kāravallī* plant, or rock salt, with the urine of cows.
One should drink one karṣa for three days; it conquers all disorders.
This has been prescribed for those who consume meat broth but indulge in unwholesome habits.
One should indeed perform this very same procedure in the practice of alchemy (rasāyana);
for nectar, when conjoined with the proper rite, is life-giving, but devoid of the rite, it is poison.
One should consume the four types of nutmeg (*cāturjātaka*), camphor, *kaṅkola*, and *kaṭukī* fruit, combined with betel leaf; this is beneficial for the transference of the vital essence (*rasa*).
Now, the correct method for the initial killing of mercury shall be explained here—
either that of mercury which has been "faced" (*samukha*) or that which has been "perfumed" by the face (*vāsanāmukhita*).
Then, one should gradually digest gold in equal parts as before;
having added an equal amount of sulfur to that [gold] along with the juices of divine herbs, [one should proceed].
One should grind it in a mortar for three days,
then seal it in a crucible and heat it in a fire of dried cow-dung for a day and night, or for three nights in a fire of chaff.
One should grind the sweated [substance] again with seeds produced from divine herbs in equal measure in a mortar for four watches (yāmas), and then heat it while enclosed in a *vajramūṣā* crucible.
That indeed becomes *bhasmasūta* (ash-mercury), which is to be employed in all elixirs (*rasāyana*).
One should grind purified mercury and an equal amount of gold with acidic liquids for one *yāma*.

Having washed [the vessel], one should cause a paste to be applied; half a part of this paste is pure sulphur, half of that sulphur is borax, and an amount of turmeric equal to the total [of these] is added.
All of that should be ground together with *strīpuṣpa* and the juice of plantain;
having formed it into a ball at the end of the day, one should cook it in a sand-bath (*vālukāyantra*).
Having extracted that indeed with a mild fire over the course of a day, one should grind it into powder;
having added an equal portion of sulfur to the powder, one should cook it in a *garbhayantra* for three days.
By means of the fire of chaff, through its lightness, the mercury is reduced to ashes;
there should be three parts of pure mercury and one part of copper powder.
One should rub it with acidic liquids for one day, wash it, and then obtain the paste; one should likewise prepare the washed essence of *mākṣika* in an amount equal to the paste.
All of that should be rubbed for three days with the juice of *cakramarda* leaves;
then that ball, placed inside a crucible apparatus (*garbhayantra*), should be heated for three days with a fire of chaff.
One should cook pure mercury, iron essence, and gold in equal parts in a fire of dried cow-dung for day and night, or until it reaches the state of ashes.
Having added an equal amount of *viḍa* salt, it should be ground with the juice of plantain for one day;
then it should be ground for two days with an equal amount of the seeds of divine medicinal herbs.
One should cook that which has entered the womb-machine in a crucible as before;
it should be four finger-breadths in length and three finger-breadths in width.
Having fashioned a clay casket, one should cause it to be dried in the shade;
it should consist of twenty parts of salt and one part of guggulu resin.

Then, having ground everything with water, one should smear the interior of a hollowed-out vessel with that [mixture] and confine the mercury within it; this becomes a *garbhayantra* (womb-contrivance).
One should grind pure, stainless mercury with an equal amount of *nirguṇḍī* juice for three days, and then place it inside a glass flask.

In the absence of a glass flask (kācakūpī), one should seal it within a pair of earthenware bowls and cook it in a sand-bath apparatus (vālukāyantra) for four watches; thus it becomes dead [sublimated].
One part of purified essence washed from honey-bees' wax,
one part of pure sulfur, and an equal amount of purified mercury— these should be macerated for a day with the juice of *nirguṇḍī*.
All that, having been crushed into a ball and sealed within a *vajramūṣā* crucible, should be cooked for one day in a *vālukāyantra*; it will become dead [mercury] of a red color.
An equal amount of sulphur should be added above and below pure mercury;
furthermore, the juice of *kākamācī* should be placed inside a sealed crucible (*pakvamūṣā*).

Having added four times the amount of the two [substances] and covered it, one should cook it slowly over a gradual fire in a sand-vessel (vālukāyantra) for four watches; it will then be reduced to ash.

One should grind purified mercury with an equal amount of sulphur using the milky juice of either *snuhī* or *hemavallī* for one day; then, having placed it inside a *garbhayantra*, one should subject it to heating in a *puṭa*.
As before, by means of the sequential application of yoga, one should join the deceased [mercury] with the yogas;
[one should take] equal parts of pure mercury, guñjā, lac, wool, honey, and ṭaṅkaṇa.
One should grind all of that for one day with the juices of *bhṛṅga*;
sealed in a *vajramūṣā* crucible and heated, it dies [as a powder], resembling the moon.
Alternatively, one may use the juices of *kīṭamāriṇī*, or the juices of *ajamodā*,
or the juices of *ahimārī*, or else the juices of white *aṅkola*.
One should grind purified mercury with an equal amount of sulphur for three days,
having sealed it within a clay crucible, in a fire of dried cow-dung cakes day and night.
Or else, one should cook it for three days with a fire of husks; thus it certainly dies.
Pure mercury, dead diamond, and [other ingredients] in equal parts [should be placed] in a heated mortar.
One should grind [the substance] with the juices of *haṃsapādī* for three days, then extract it;
and one should coat the *vajramūṣā* crucible with the seeds of divine medicinal herbs.
There, having sealed the previous liquid and cooked it for three days with a fire of husks,
one should extract it and take an equal amount of purified mercury.
Having combined [the ingredients] and ground them firmly for three days with the juices of *haṃsapādī*, one should cook that ball as before; it becomes beautifully transformed into a dead [metal].

The killing (*māraṇa*) of the eight metals, beginning with *vajra* and *abhra*, as described in the section on mercury (*rasakhaṇḍa*), or in the section on the primary [metals] (*vādikhaṇḍa*), should be understood in the same way in the section on alchemy (*rasāyana*).

Thus, when the excellent mercury has died and become supremely transmuted (*paramāmūta*), those who constantly serve it will find that it suddenly makes their bodies eternally most beautiful and capable of sporting with celestial nymphs.

By those who know the Dharma, by those devoted to Śiva, by the gods, by kings, and by great adepts, the body must be constantly protected with the truly divine elixir until the end of the aeon; for from that, liberation arises within an infinite accumulation of merit. Therefore, I shall describe that most wonderful [elixir], which bestows happiness and grants sovereignty to the wise.
First, one should consume mica that has been killed and turned into nectar,
one *niṣka* at a time for one month, for the purpose of making the body a fit field [for the elixir].
Since mercury is a field for the essence [of immortality], one should therefore prepare an elixir;
for if it is not made into a field, mercury, though nectar, turns into poison.
How could there be the attainment of fruit for him, just as [there is none] for a good seed in saline soil?
One should prepare equal parts of the ashes of diamond and mercury.
All the gold mixed with dead mercury should be ground for a period of days;
having sealed that mass with the juices of *haṃsapādī*, one should subject it to *puṭapāka* (cupping).
Having ground it again with the milky sap of *arka*, one should cook it likewise in a *gajapuṭa* fire.
One should consume it starting from the size of a mustard seed and gradually increase the dose until it reaches a *māṣa*.
This Vajrapañjara elixir is indeed a refuge for practitioners;
it consists of citraka, fresh ginger, rock salt, immortality (asafoetida), black pepper, and suvarcala.
All [substances] should always be consumed in equal proportions; this is beneficial for the process of transference (*krāmaṇa*).
By employing this for six months, one may live as long as the moon and stars endure.
Free from wrinkles and grey hair, possessing a divine body and great strength,
one should prepare dead vajra as a twelfth part of dead mercury.
Equal parts of *mṛta-kānta* (dead magnetite) and *mṛtābhra* (dead mica)— the latter being equal to the former—
should all be ground with the juices of *bhṛṅgarāja* and processed by maceration for three days.
For three days, one should then lick a *māṣa* measure [of the powder] with the juices of *gokṣuraka* and honey;
this elixir, named Vajreśvara, makes the bodies of men as hard as adamant.
By consuming it for four months, one destroys old age and indeed lives for a day of Brahmā.
One should powder the five parts of *bhṛṅgarāja* in equal measure with *triphalā*.
One *pala* should be licked with honey; it is the supreme promoter of vitality in the *rasa*.
Furthermore, there is the purified ash of *vajra*, mercury, iron, mica, and gold, as well as pure *mākṣika*.
One should grind it firmly for seven equal days with the juices of divine herbs;
then, having sealed it, one should cook it again for three days while placed in a vālukāyantra.
Having extracted [the essence], it should be processed for three days with the juices of *bhṛṅga* and *sarpākṣī*.
One should lick a single *māṣa* dose with honey and clarified butter; this is the *vajradhārā-rasa*.
By practicing this for six months, a man becomes equal to Rudra;
freed from wrinkles and grey hair, he possesses the speed of the wind and great strength.
Equal parts of *punarnavā*, *bhṛṅga*, sesame, and *vājigandhā* should be combined with an amount of sugar equal to the total; this powder should be consumed in a dose of one *pala*.
Gold, mercury, and magnetite—all these, once reduced to powder, should be made equal in quantity.
One should then saturate them with the juice of the roots of *śatāvarī* for three days.
Having processed it for three days with decoctions of triphalā and for three days with the juice of bhṛṅga,
one should consume the Bhairava mercury, mixed with honey and ghee.
Taking one *māṣa* at a time, one may live for as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure,
by consuming the root-powder of *śatāvarī* combined with the milk of a black goat.
One should drink each of these in a dose of one *pala*, following them in sequence; this is supremely beneficial.
Equal parts of mercury-ash (*rasabhasma*), sulfur (*gandha*), bitumen (*śilājatu*), and *amlavetasa* [should be taken].
One should grind all of this for one *yāma* and lick it mixed with honey and clarified butter;
taking one *niṣka* each for the duration of a year, this is the great elixir known as *Śilāvīra*.
One quickly destroys old age and shall live for three hundred years;
one should drink half a pala of *musalī* powder with the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*.
Alternatively, the purifier (krāmaka) should be used as an after-drink with the juices of *dhātrī* fruits;
or, purified mercury should be rubbed with the juices of *meghanāda* for three days.
One should prepare a powder consisting of equal parts of viḍaṅga, the two types of niśā (dāruharidrā and haridrā), and vyoṣa;
the root of āragvadha, however, should be twice the amount of this powder.
Having added twice as much clarified butter and four times as much honey to the powder,
one should place everything into the previous liquid and cook it over a gentle fire while stirring.
The Ocean of Nectar should consume that pill one karṣa at a time;
by doing so for just one year, he destroys old age and shall live for three hundred years.
One should drink one karṣa of vākucī powder with the juice of dhātrī fruits.
One should thoroughly rub together purified mercury and twice its amount of purified sulphur. Rā 2.28.
One should repeatedly place it in a mortar for twenty-one days using the juice of fresh *muṇḍī* leaves;
then, one should enclose an equal amount of purified copper within a crucible and seal it.
One should wrap it with a piece of cloth and coat the exterior with diamond-clay;
having dried it thoroughly, one should indeed cook it properly in a "gaja-puṭa" (elephant-oven).
Having extracted and powdered it, one should macerate it for three days with the juices of *devadālī*,
and then separately for three days each with the juices of *bhaṅgī* and *punarnavā*.
Having added an equal amount of powdered *nāgara* (ginger) mixed with honey and clarified butter,
one should regularly consume two *māṣa* measures of it daily for a period of up to one year.
This supreme elixir, Udayāditya, removes old age and death;
it consists of equal parts of powdered punarnavā, devadālī, and bhṛṅga.
One should lick one *karṣa* of this with honey and clarified butter; it is the supreme *krāmaṇa*.
Equal parts of mercury, mica, magnetite, and steel are to be killed [by calcination].
One should macerate [the powder] for three days in the juice of *bhṛṅga* and *dhātrī* fruits in the shade;
then, having combined all the ingredients in equal parts with sugar, honey, and ghee, one should seal it in a vessel.
Having remained for a month on a heap of grain, one should then consume three niṣkas of [the powder] equally,
and drink one karṣa of milk following a dose of triphalā.
If one eats ginger and long pepper at night for one year, one becomes immortal;
the hero shall live for the duration of a day of Brahmā, for he is the mercury known as Gaganeshvara.
One should grind the mercury (śuddharasa) and the fragrance (gandha) in equal parts with banyan (vaṭa) milk for three days;
then one should cook it in an earthen vessel over a fire of banyan wood for five hours (yāma).
Repeatedly throwing in the milk of the *vaṭa* tree, one should stir it with that very wood;
having removed it, it should be infused for three days with the juice of *devadālī* leaves.
During the hot season, however, one should always consume one *guñjā* along with a betel leaf,
increasing it daily by one *guñjā* until it reaches sixteen *guñjās*.

One should lick one karṣa of the powder made from *uttaravāruṇī*, *vākucī*, and *devadālī* with honey and clarified butter; this is indeed a promoter of sexual vigor (*krāmaka*) when taken without any other after-drink.
Within a single year it destroys old age, and one shall live for three hundred years;
this elixir named Vaṭeśvara makes the bodies of men as firm as adamant.
One should always lick one *karṣa* each of dead mercury, purified sulfur, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and *guggulu*, all mixed with *vātāri-taila*.
Within six months he destroys old age and lives for three days of Brahmā;
by his urine and feces, copper becomes gold.
One should drink at night the testicle of a goat, cooked in cow's milk and mixed with sugar;
this is the "Lord of Mountains" (Acaleśvara) elixir.
Equal parts of mercury, vajra, gold-oxide (svarṇakānta), and processed iron filings,
along with purified mākṣika and sulphur, [should all be combined] with the juices of jambīra fruits.
One should grind it in a mortar for seven days, then place that ball in a sealed vessel and roast it in a *bhūdhara* furnace for one day; this is known as the supreme *siddharasa*.
One *māṣa* [weight] should be licked with honey for a year; it removes death and old age.
The man becomes perfected, possessing a divine body and the prowess of Viṣṇu.
One should always drink the root of white *punarnavā* ground with milk,
or one should eat it together with sugar as a potent aphrodisiac of supreme flavor.
One should mix purified sulphur in double the quantity of dead mercury;
having ground it for one day with the juices of *kanyā*, one should seal it away.
One should cook one *niṣka* of [the powder] with honey for one day and then lick it with honey;
this elixir named Gandhāmṛtarasa will conquer death within a year.
One should powder the *bhṛṅgarāja* plant together with its roots after it has been dried in the shade;
the powder of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) should be equal to that, and sugar should be equal to the total amount of the other ingredients.
Having combined them, one should consume one *pala* each without a vehicle;
equal parts of mercury and mica, and an amount of sulfur equal to the sum of those two.
One should rub all of that with juices of *bhṛṅga* for seven days, and then,
having impregnated it six times with *aṅkuli* oils, one should consume it.
This *kālakaṇṭaka* elixir should be taken for one year in a dose of one *māṣa*;
after grinding the leaves of the *karañja* tree, one should drink them with cow's milk as a follow-up.
A man liberated from old age and death may live for a day of Brahmā;
[the elixir consists of] mercury killed by sulfur, mica, magnetite, poison, pyrite, and bitumen.
One should always lick three *guñjā* seeds mixed with equal parts honey and ghee;
after six months, this destroys old age, and the man shall live for the duration of a day of Brahmā.
One should take the powder of the root of *aśvagandhā* equal in measure to seven parts of ghee;
one should add eight parts of jaggery and one part of *pippalī* to it.
And with a mild fire, one should consume all that as a consolidated mass weighing one pala;
for this is the "traverser" (*krāmaka*) of Amṛteśa, for the sake of accomplishing the King of Mercury (*rasarāja*).
One should add three parts of purified sulfur to one part of purified mercury,
and then one should throw in a powder of iron *parpaṭikā* equal in weight to the mercury.
All of that should be rubbed with the milky sap of *snuhī* and *arka* for three days;
once dried and placed in a sealed vessel, it should be cooked in a fire of dried cow dung day and night.
Then, having added borax and glass and sealed [the crucible], one should heat it strongly;
one should consume one *guñjā* of this great mercury, the hero of elixirs, with honey.
By drinking the powder of the root of *musalī* with the juice of *guñjā* leaves for one year, one destroys old age and may live as long as the moon and stars endure.
Alternatively, one *karṣa* of that [mercury] indeed becomes a supreme transmuter when combined with goat's urine;
likewise, mercury and sulfur in equal proportions should be processed for a day with the juices of *kākamācī*.
One should cook the ground and blinded [substance] in a fire of dried cow dung day and night;
having ground it for a day with the juices of divine medicinal leaves, one should blind it again.
Therefore, having extracted from that [ore] an equal amount of dead gold (hāṭaka) and combined it with clarified butter,
one should consume one māṣa of this electuary for the duration of a year.
The mercury of Kāñcāyana truly destroys old age and death quickly;
it should be processed with the juices of *kākamācī* and a powder derived from *dhātrī* fruits.
One should eat one *karṣa* with honey; it is a supreme promoter of virility.
Mortar mercury, mica, and sulfur, in equal parts, [should be processed] for a period of seven days.
Having ground it with the juices of the roots of *śigru*, one should place that ball inside a vessel,
seal it, and cook it for a period of one day over a gentle fire using the wood of vegetables.
One should always lick *niṣka* of *ghṛta* known as *parānanda-rasa*;
for one day, one should properly cook *kuṣṭha* with decoctions of *triphalā*.
Having dried and powdered that [substance], one should lick one *karṣa* with honey and clarified butter;
by practicing this for a year, one may live as long as the moon and stars endure.
Equal parts of processed mercury and processed mica, and an amount of processed iron equal to those two;
one part of purified sulfur should be infused with these for seven days.
All of that should be processed separately with the decoctions of triphalā, and with the juices of bhṛṅga, śigru, and citraka,
seven times each in succession.
One should powder it again after having impregnated it seven times with decoctions of *kaṭukī*;
then, one should mix this powder with an equal amount of *kaṇā* powder and an equal amount of old jaggery.
If one consumes all these combined as a single *niṣka* for the duration of a year,
it is the mercury named Mahākāla, which strikes fear into old age and death.
One should eat the petals of the *tilaka* and *koraṇṭa* flowers with jaggery;
thereafter, the iron tablet will become equal to dead mercury.
Three times the amount of sulphur relative to the mercury, having been ground for that day with the juices of all divine herbs, and then sealed and heated, the mercury becomes bound.
Having added one-fourth part of dead gold (mṛtasvarṇa) to that, it should be ground for one watch (yāma) with the juices of fire-catalyst (vahni) and fresh ginger (ārdraka);
then it should be powdered together with trikaṭu (vyoṣa), cumin (jīraka), and rock salt (saindhava).
One should consume an equal amount of the previous elixir along with one *niṣka* of gold at a time;
this "gold-leaf" elixir quickly destroys old age and death.
One should have licorice (yaṣṭi) equal in weight to aśvagandhā soaked for a day in the juice of āmalaka fruits;
one should then cause [the patient] to lick one pala of this with honey—this is a supreme aphrodisiac.
Gold, star-iron (tārā), and sun-stone (arkakānta), or else steel (tīkṣṇa) that has been killed [by mercury] in equal parts;
and black cloud-essence (kṛṣṇābhrasattva) and vitriol (mākṣika), each equal to the gold.
All that [impurity] should be blinded and smelted;
then one should add an equal amount of dead mercury and a quarter-part of dead diamond (vajra) to that *khoṭa*.
One should grind everything with the juices of citron in a heated mortar for one day; then, having sealed it, one should heat it in a *bhūdhara* [furnace] for a day.
Having extracted an equal amount of sulfur and enclosed it, one should heat it quickly;
one should always consume that powder, the size of a black gram, with honey and clarified butter.
This elixir named Śrīkaṇṭha bestows the power of moving through the air;
by its practice for one year, one may live even until the end of a kalpa.
From his urine and feces, all metals turn into gold;
one should cause [the patient] to drink one *pala* of sulfur with milk as a digestive aid (*krāmaka*).
One part of pure copper, twelve parts of pure mercury,
and three parts of the essence of *bhūnāga*— one should combine these portions together.
All of this should be ground for one day in a heated mortar with the juices of *jambīra* fruits;
then, having placed all of that in a *kacchapa* apparatus, [one should add] sulfur right there.
Having ground [the mercury] with an equal amount of *kāsamarda* juice and enclosed it, one should cook it in a *puṭa* until it is digested;
in this manner, the sulfur becomes sixfold.

One should digest it by means of the sequential method, then extract it and grind it for one watch (yāma) with juices from *jambīra* fruits; thereafter, the mica becomes free of its lunar spots (*niścandra*).
One should cause equal parts of *amlavetasa* to be ground and added to the liquid;
and sixteen parts each of *caṇakāmla* and *tālaka* should be added to the heated mortar (*taptakhalva*).
Having added green vitriol (kāsīsa) in a tenth part [of the total], one should grind it for the duration of a day;
then, having placed all of that in a sealed crucible (pakvamūṣā), one should bind it with a cloth.
One should cook it for three days over a mild fire in a *dolāyantra* (swinging apparatus) using *sāranāla*;
having removed it, one should wash it with warm *kāñjika* if it has not yet been digested.
If it is undigested, one should cook it in the vessel called *kacchapa* together with *viḍa* salt;
in this manner, the *gagana* (mica) should be digested again and again until it is equal in weight to the mercury.
Having applied sixty-four parts of his gold leaf smeared with peacock bile, one should place it in a mortar and grind it thoroughly.
One should cause it to sweat in the apparatus as before, and once it is digested, one should add gold;
in this manner, gold amounting to a sixteenth part of the mercury should indeed be consumed by it.
Then, one should grind aged mercury with sixteen parts of gold-like *vajra* (thunderbolt), combined with *tāla*, *kāsīsa*, and *jambīra*; and thereafter, it should be rubbed together.
Then, one should grind that mercury for three days with the juices of divine medicinal herbs;
having sealed it in a *vajramūṣā* crucible, it should be heated until bound, and then it should be powdered again.
One should consume a dose the size of a *guñjā* seed together with honey and sugar;
this mercury, once bound as a *khecarī*, shall conquer death within six months.
Free from wrinkles and grey hair, and endowed with great strength and prowess,
one should [take] the three fruits of *nīlamuṇḍī* along with the juices of *bhṛṅgarāja* for seven days.
One should cultivate [the practice] with honey and ghee; thereafter, one should lick a dose of one karṣa.
One should take purified mercury and twice as much sulfur, and grind them into a collyrium-like paste using a mortar and pestle.
Equal parts of *kāntaloha* powder, *tīkṣṇaloha*, or even *muṇḍaloha*,
all combined together, should be ground in a mortar with the juices of *kanyākā*.
Having formed a ball for one day, one should place it in a copper vessel; covered with castor leaves, it will reach a state of extreme heat within half a watch (yāmārdha).
One should place it in a heap of grain and retrieve it at the end of two days;
[one should also use] kanyā, bhṛṅgī, kākamācī, muṇḍī, nirguṇḍī, and citraka.
The juices of *koraṇṭaka*, *vākucī*, *brāhmī*, *sahadevī*, *punarnavā*,
*śālmalī*, *vijayā*, and *dhūrta* should each be used separately.
It should be processed seven times with each of the seven groups of decoctions derived from the three fruits (triphalā);
then, having been processed, the powder of nutmeg (jātīphala) and clove (lavaṅga) should be prepared.
One should powder together equal parts of the nine ingredients—trikaṭu, triphalā, and elā.
This powder, along with an equal amount of the previously mentioned powder, should be taken in a dose of one karṣa with honey.
One should constantly lick it for one year to pacify old age and death;
this is the "Agnirasa" itself, which has come from the mouths of the perfected ones (siddhas).
One should lick half a *pala* of the powder of sesame and *aśvagandhā* with honey.
[The following are the herbs: *nirguṇḍī*, *nīlikā*, *vajrī*, *brahmadaṇḍī*, and *tridaṇḍikā*.
Śatapuṣpā, mudgaparṇī, śvetārka, vānarī, jayā, peṭārī,
kṛṣṇadhattūra, vijayā, and kṣīrakandaka.
These substances, either collectively or individually, should be rubbed for three days with pure mercury in a heated mortar; that paste is then placed in a milk-tuber (kṣīrakandaka).
Alternatively, having sealed it in a *vajra* bulb and again with clay mixed with its marrow,
one should seal that bulb in a *vajramūṣā* crucible and cook it in a mild fire-packing (*laghupuṭa*).
The mercury should be rubbed and cooked again in this manner seven times in succession; this is the preparation known as *Kakṣapuṭa*, which one should lick in a dose of one *guñjā* with honey.
He shall live for a single day of Brahmā, free from wrinkles and grey hair;
within one year, there is no doubt, the man shall become a body of rasa.
One should consume one pala of the powder of *bhallātaka* seeds along with *hayagandhā*, *amṛtā*, and clarified butter; this is an excellent and most beneficial purgative.
Dead mercury, mica, diamond, magnetite, silver, copper, gold, and iron—each taken in equal parts—and an amount of sulfur equal to the total of all these; Rrā_2.2.116.
One should rub everything with *pālāśa* oil for seven days;
this is called the *mahāśaktirasas*, which one should always eat as a *māṣa* dose with honey.
Within six months he destroys old age and lives for three days of Brahmā;
after one year, he undoubtedly lives for seven kalpas.
One who possesses the force of will becomes a great adept equal to the Supreme Power;
by his urine and feces, copper becomes gold.
Oil produced from *pālāśa* seeds, eight *palas* in weight, should be licked with honey;
indeed, it serves as an aphrodisiac when taken as an after-drink, as has been clearly explained according to its full potency.
One pala of killed *vaikrānta*—either red or black—and one pala of gold powder, along with two palas of pure mercury; Rrā_2.2.121.
One should grind all of that for a day with the urine of a young girl and goat's urine.
[The ingredients are: *śarapuṅkhā*, *meṣaśṛṅgī*, *sarpākṣī*, and *kaṭutumbikā*.
One should grind these with the juices of *indravāruṇikā* for three days;
having sealed that mass in a *garbhayantra*, one should cook it for three days.
Having extracted it with its lightness by means of a fire of chaff, one should grind it;
then, having impregnated it seven times with juices of *bhṛṅgarāja*, one should grind it again.
One should mix the powder of Triphalā, Tryūṣaṇa, honey, and ghee in equal proportions;
one should always consume it in single-māṣa doses. This elixir is called Nāṭakeśvara.
Within a year, he will utterly destroy all diseases, old age, and death;
possessing divine splendor and a massive body, he shall live as long as the moon and stars endure.
One should drink two *niṣkas* of the powdered inner bark of the *brahmavṛkṣa*, dried in the shade, along with buttermilk; this is a most auspicious and supreme aphrodisiac.
Pure white vaikrānta should be processed for seven days in the sun, ground with amlavetasa; by that means, it attains liquefaction.
Having ground this liquefied, pure mercury together with honey for three days in equal proportions, one should have it licked in the measure of a māṣa; after one month, the man becomes a child.
After one year, this "Bālasundara" elixir becomes equal to Brahman;
thereafter, one should lick one karṣa of vākucī seeds with honey and clarified butter.
Four *palas* of pure mercury and one *pala* of dead gold [are to be processed] for three days with the juices of *palāśa* buds and their oils.
One should rub purified sulfur equal in weight to the gold in a heated mortar;
one should cast it into that [gold] and grind it with the previously mentioned substances for one day.
One should eat a pill the size of a *māṣa* bean; by doing so for years, one becomes a conqueror of death.
This hero’s elixir, "Brahma’s Cage," enables one to live for the duration of a day of Brahmā.
One should take equal parts of the powdered seeds arising from *vānarī* and *kākātuṇḍī*,
and macerate them for three days with the juice of the leaves and bark of *śālmalī*.
Then, having impregnated it with the juices of *bhṛṅgarāja* for three days, one should powder it;
one should consume one *karṣa* of this, together with an equal amount of old jaggery.
On red ground, however, one should cause earth-snakes to be caught and examine them;
if blood flows out when they are cut, one should diligently take possession of them.
One should cook those [ingredients] together with equal amounts of black-colored cow-ghee in an iron vessel, stirring them until they take on the color of vermilion.
All that is reduced to ashes, and dead mercury is equal to that;
mixed with honey, one should increase the dose by half a *guñjā* at a time.
Thereafter, one should always consume *guñjā* for a period of one year;
this elixir named *śivāmṛtarasa* removes old age and death for men.
It bestows a lifespan equal to a day of Brahmā; thereafter, one should drink the water of Śiva.
Thus, having seen by me those whose bodies were perfected through various means of power using auspicious, divine elixirs— the very essence of essences—
and having propitiated them and gathered the entirety of their core teachings from the scriptures as well, this has been proclaimed for the benefit of kings, the learned, and the high-minded.

The divine medicinal pill and elixir do not succeed if devoid of the process of transmutation (*krāmaṇa*). Therefore, let that which brings about swift success be employed; indeed, the appropriate adjunct (*anupāna*) for this purpose must be used here.
Kākatumbī, kākamācī, nirguṇḍī, kumārikā, gojihvā, rock salt (saindhava), guñjā, and fresh ginger— each taken in equal measure.
Having ground these together, one should smear the crucible up to the height of all the fingers;
[using] mercury, the essence of *vyoma*, magnetite, steel, and *muṇḍaka* iron.
Having powdered all these ingredients— including equal parts of iron filings and mercury—
one should grind them together for one day with the juices of *jambīra* fruits and place the mixture into a crucible.
Having covered it and smeared it with a paste, one should seal it and let it dry;
having cooked it in a *puṭa* in a fire of dried cow-dung for a day and night, one should then extract it.
Then, having cast [the substance] back into the smeared crucible and sealed it, one should perform the *puṭa* firing;
in this manner, one should cook it in ten smeared crucibles.
A supreme, divine pill that restores the dead to life is produced;
when it is held in the mouth, on the head, at the throat, in the ear, or in the hand.
When properly wrapped in gold, it is supreme for firmly stabilizing youth;
it destroys wrinkles, gray hair, the fire of time, and the fear of death.
Without a doubt, after only one year, he shall live for three hundred years;
he should always drink one pure pala of [the powder] with cow's milk.
By means of this after-drink (anupāna), however, the essence (rasa) enters the body—
namely, mercury (pārada), kānta-iron, muṇḍa-iron, and the essence of mica (abhrasattva)— all in their proper form.
One should grind the essence of mercury and all the *vajras* together with juices produced from *jambīra* for seven days; having made them equal in measure, one should extract a pill.
Having ground together nirguṇḍī, rock salt, honey, gojihvā, and kākatuṇḍikā,
one should apply the paste all over the pill to a thickness of one finger-breadth.
Having sealed it in a vajra-muṣā crucible, one should cook it for one yāma in a bhūdhara furnace;
having smeared it and sealed it again, it should be cooked in this manner for just a fortnight.
One should smear the crucible with a well-ground paste made from *yavaciñcā*, *palāśa*, *rājī*, and cotton seeds; then, place the previously prepared ball inside it.
Having added borax and white glass and having sealed the back,
one should heat it with khadira charcoal until it becomes liquefied.
Then one should place it in a crucible smeared with cow-dung ash;
one should add an equal amount of gold and, blowing repeatedly, cause it to be conquered [by the mercury].

Once the gold has been digested, one should extract it and grind it in a heated mortar with the juices of divine herbs for three days; then, having placed it in a sealed crucible (vajramūṣā), one should heat it in a furnace.
A divine pill arises, supreme by name Vajreśvarī;
when held in the mouth, it truly destroys old age and death within a year.
It causes the paralysis of weapons and certainly bestows the lifespan of Brahmā;
having taken sahadevī on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one should grind it into a fine powder.
One should consume one *karṣa* [of the powder] with clarified butter;
it is beneficial when followed by the sequential consumption of *meghanāda* that is not reddish and likewise *pāṣāṇabheda*.
Having ground [the ingredients] together with breast milk, one should smear the crucible with that;
[using] one part of dead-vajra (mṛtavajra) and sixteen parts of gold powder.
Having cast [the mercury] into it and then suppressed it, one should blow firmly for the duration of a watch (yāma).
Then, having extracted it, one should place pure mercury equal in quantity into a mortar.
One should grind it with the juices of fresh ginger until it forms a ball;
then, having taken the root of *caṇḍālī*, one should grind it well with breast milk.
Having smeared the *golaka* with this, one should seal it in a *vajramūṣā* crucible;
after heating it in a *gajapuṭa*, the pill known as Vajrasundarī is to be extracted.
If one holds [the powder] in the mouth for one year, one may live for three days of Brahmā;
one should daily drink one *pala* of the powdered bark of the *brahmavṛkṣa* with milk.
Indeed, this *krāmaṇa* (the process of transmutation) serves as an after-drink for the practitioner, bestowing supreme accomplishment;
for copper smeared with the impurities arising from that [process] is indeed purified by smelting.
Divine gold is produced; this is the truth spoken by Śaṅkara.
When the mercury (rasendra) is facing [the crucible], the gold becomes equal [in quality] as before.

One should cause it to digest by means of a *viḍa* mixture; then, having ground it for three days with divine herbs and cow urine, one should blow [the crucible] while it is sealed within a *vajramūṣā*.
Having extracted it, one should hold the *guṭikā* named *Hemasundarī* in the mouth;
thereafter, one should lick half a *pala* of sulfur with twice as much clarified butter.
In one year it destroys old age; one may live as long as the moon and stars endure.
[This applies to] pure mercury, killed diamond, the essence of the sky (mica), along with gold.
One should grind all the ingredients of the sour group (amlavarga) together for three days;
having made that into a firm ball, one should then dry it in the shade.
Having ground together equal parts of seeds of *brahmakārpāsa*, black mustard, *yavaciñcikā*,
and *vandhyā*, one should smear the previously prepared ball with it.
Having sealed it in a *gajapuṭa* fire, one should cook it; then, having extracted it, one should apply a coating.
Having sealed it again in a crucible (*mūṣā*), one should heat it intensely; this pill is the *vajrakhecarī*.
When held in the mouth for years, it destroys death;
likewise, one *pala* of powdered *bhūtāravaṭa* mixed with sugar [is effective].
One should consume [the powder] for the purpose of transference; thus the man attains the lifespan of Brahmā.
[This is done] with the juices of the leaves of *kārpāsī*, *kākamācī*, and *kanyā*.
Pure mercury should be rubbed for one day and washed with acidic liquids; then it should be extracted.
Four *niṣkas* of that mercury and half a *niṣka* of copper powder [should be used].
One should grind together three-quarters of a niṣka of mercury, one-quarter of gold,
and an equal amount of powdered iron filings, all thoroughly processed with acidic liquids.
At the end of the day, having formed a ball, one should place it inside a citron;
one should cook it for three days in a *sāranālaka* using a *dolakayantra*.
Having extracted it, one should hold the pill in the mouth; it is called Vyomasundarī.
Within a single year it destroys old age, and the man shall live for the duration of a Brahma-day.
Having stirred the powder of *citramūla* with honey in a vessel of *kāntaloha*, one should consume one *karṣa*; this is beneficial for the purpose of transference (*krāmaṇa*).
One *niṣka* of gold leaf and three *niṣkas* of pure mercury should be rubbed together for the duration of a day with the juices extracted from *jambīra* and *śarapuṅkhā*.
One should bind that ball in a cloth and cook it in a *dolāyantra* (swinging apparatus) filled with cow’s milk for a day and night; thus the pill becomes Hāṭakeśvarī.
When worn in the mouth, it destroys old age and death;
after merely one year, there is no doubt that a man shall live for ten thousand years.

For one day, one should lick one *pala* of powdered *triphalā* that has been processed with decoctions of *khadira* seeds and mixed with honey and ghee; this promotes the upward movement [of the semen].
Three pure niṣkas of mercury and one niṣka of copper powder should be ground in a mortar for a full day with the sour juice of tamarind fruit and buttermilk.

One should bind that ball with cloths and cook it for one day in a *dolāyantra* (swinging apparatus) filled with buttermilk and tamarind juice; thus it becomes a pill possessing the luster of the sun.
If one holds oil produced from *pālāśa* seeds, measuring one *karṣa*, with cow’s milk in the mouth for one year, that person shall become equal to the sun.
Indeed, this elixir as a post-drink (anupāna) is a supreme remover of old age and death;
it consists of one part gold, one part kānta iron, five parts silver, and two parts mercury.
One-third part shall be *vyomasattva* (mica) and six parts shall be copper powder; all of this, made into a fine paste, should be processed in a heated mortar for three days.
One should rub it with the group of sour substances (amla-varga) in a *dolāyantra* over *kāñjika*;
that ball should be cooked for three days, resulting in the pill known as *surasundarī*.
When held in the mouth, it destroys death and old age after a year;
one should then drink one *karṣa* of the root of the *bhūtāravaṭa* tree with milk.

Gold, silver, copper, and human skull, along with tin, lead, and the essence of mica— all these should be made into an equal powder, and an amount equal to one part of that powder of the powder should consist of processed diamond (mṛtavajra).
One should grind pure mercury equal in quantity to all [the other ingredients] with the juices of all divine herbs for one day, and then heat it in a sealed *vajramūṣā* crucible.
This pill, Vajratuṇḍā by name, when held in the mouth,
is said to destroy old age, death, and the multitude of weapons within a year.
The great hero with a vajra-body shall live for three hundred years;
one should take the natural juice of a virgin and stir it together with molasses.
One *pala* of the powder for walking [on water] is always to be taken as a linctus with a liquid after-drink;
one part of gold powder and three parts of purified mercury [are to be combined].

One part of powdered *vajra* (diamond) should all be processed for the duration of a day in a heated mortar with the juices extracted from milk-tubers (*kṣīrakanda*) and those arising from *devadālī*.
One should grind the powder of *kāntaloha* and indeed add an amount equal to the diamond (*vajra*);
having sealed it in a diamond-crucible (*vajramūṣā*) and smelted it, there arises the pill known as *Kāmasundarī*.
When worn in the mouth, it destroys death and old age after one year.
Three *niṣkas* of *brahmatela* and two *palas* of cow's milk [are required].
One should drink this mixture as an after-potion, and the man becomes possessed of a lifespan of a hundred thousand years.
When the mercury has been liquefied in an iron vessel, one should add mercury equal to one-fourth the amount of the sulphur (gandha).
One should stir it slightly with a wooden stick and remove it from the fire after a short while;
[the ingredients are] śatāvarī, kṣīrakanda, vajravallī, and indravāruṇī.
Pāṭhā, punarnavā, ciñcā, lāṅgalī, and suradālikā—
one should grind [the substance] for three days with the juices of these, filtered through cloth.
In that vessel, having formed pills from [the substance] dried in the shade using an iron hammer,
one should place them inside an iron casket and seal the joint firmly with clay and salt.
One should heat it over charcoal of khadira wood until it becomes bright red;
then, repeatedly digging into its center, one should extract that liquid essence once more.
Combined with glass and borax, it should be sealed in a crucible and heated;
this perfected Gāndhārī pill, when always held in the mouth for a year, [achieves its purpose].
One should administer one *karṣa* of oil from the seeds of the *kākatuṇḍī* as a nasal drop (*nasya*);
with a digestive stimulant as an after-drink (*anupāna*), one shall live for a thousand years.
Having made a kajjalī by grinding purified mercury with an equal amount of sulphur,
one should seal it within a copper crucible, firmly closing it with salt and clay.
One should cook the dried substance for one watch (three hours) in a bhasmayantra using the flame of a lamp.
Having extracted that which is attached to the upper part of the crucible, one should then grind it;
combined with an equal amount of mercury, one should cook it in a crucible as before.
Having extracted [the essence], one should combine it with an equal amount of mercury, rub it together, and cook it;
in this manner, one should repeat the process seven times with mercury and ṭaṅkaṇa.
One should add equal amounts [of the ingredients] to that [substance] and triturate it for an entire day;
having placed it in a *vajramūṣā* crucible and sealed it, when heated by a blowpipe, the mercury becomes a solid *khoṭa*.
This is indeed the Mārtaṇḍī pill; he who keeps it in his mouth for one year shall be freed from wrinkles and grey hair, and live as long as the moon and stars endure.
One should daily drink one *pala* of oil produced from *palāśa* seeds mixed with an equal amount of milk as a transmuting agent (*krāmaṇa*); at that very moment, one becomes unconscious.
One should pour cow's milk drop by drop into its mouth;
once it has awakened, milk and food shall be the most beneficial for its nourishment.
Through his urine and feces, copper becomes gold;
possessing the speed of the wind, the great adept perceives the earth as full of holes.
One should grind mercury and realgar in equal parts with the juices of *kākamācī* and *amṛtā* for one day; having formed a ball, one should dry it thoroughly.
One should place [the mercury] in a vajra-musha crucible, cover it with iron leaflets, seal the joint, and heat it intensely; thus the mercury becomes bound as a solid bolus (khoṭa).
Having administered the iron-foil (*lohaparpaṭaka*), it should be heated again in that same manner three times;
this pill, the Mistress of the Stars (*tārakeśvarī*), should be held in the mouth for one year.
One should drink one karṣa of vākucī seeds followed by cow's milk;
likewise, dead *vyomasattva*, *vajra*, gold, silver, copper, and *muṇḍaka*.
Having purified sharp and beautiful *tālaka* (orpiment), one should mix it;
all these should be made into a fine powder, and pure mercury equal in weight to the entire portion of the powder should be added.

Having been rubbed for three days with the group of sour substances (amlavarga) and placed in a sealed crucible, one should heat it; this pill is known as Vidyāvāgīśvarī and remains effective for the duration of a year.
For one in whose mouth it resides, neither old age nor death exists;
one should always drink one *karṣa* of *jyotiṣmatī* oil for the purpose of transference.
One becomes wise and a master of speech, and may live as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure—
by means of kāntapāṣāṇa, mākṣika, ṭaṅkaṇa, and the shell of a crab.
Snuhi, arka-milk, and bhūnāga—all these should be taken in equal parts.
This should be ground with breast milk for one day, and with that mixture, one should coat the crucible.
Into the midst of that, having thrown equal parts of molten mercury and diamond ash,
one should seal it and cook it in a "gaja" (elephant) type crucible for the duration of one watch (yāma).
Then, having thrown it into a smeared crucible and sealed it, one should heat it vigorously;
this should be done again and again until the *vajrasūta* (diamond-mercury) is thoroughly fused.
Then, an equal amount of glass (kāca) mixed with ṭaṅkaṇa should be added to that very [substance];
in this manner, one should blow the furnace repeatedly, adding an equal amount for every hundred crucibles.
This mercury, a mass of brilliance, becomes like the sun;
this "diamond-tipped" pill, when held in the mouth, destroys death.
Within just one year, without a doubt, that man shall become equal to Rudra;
by his urine and feces, gold shall be produced as before.
One should consume one karṣa of the five ingredients— borax, crab shells, wool, and bitumen— with honey and ghee while weeping.
Having ground together the impurity arising from the ears and eyes of a buffalo along with breast milk of a woman,
one should place the essence of mica (*abhrasattva*) smeared with that mixture into a crucible and blow upon it.
One should cast mercury, equal in quantity to the *sattva*, there as before;
having added the juice of divine medicinal herbs, one should heat it right there.
When combined with glass and borax as before, it becomes bound;
when blown in a crucible a hundred times, this mercury becomes a mass of radiant light.
If one wears this pill in the mouth for one year, that person becomes equal to Śiva;
this *gaganeśvarī* pill brings about freedom from old age and death.
One should drink one niṣka of oil extracted from bilva seeds;
thereby, fire arises in the stomach, and one should drink milk again and again.
The direct recollection of past births, poetic genius, the retention of what has been heard, the power of moving through the sky, and invisibility arise; of this there is no doubt.
