Agnimantha, Vajravallī, Sūraṇa, Vanaśūraṇa, and Citraka— with the juices of these, purified mercury should be processed for the duration of a day.
One should grind that mercury, weighing one *pala*,
along with one *pala* each of *tāla* and *vaṅga*, and all of these together with *amlavetasa* in a heated mortar (*taptakhalva*).
One should grind it for one day, then form it again into a ball;
having prepared a snake-shaped crucible (nāgamūṣā) weighing four palas, one should place that [ball] inside it.
One should seal it within a crucible of pure copper weighing four palas;
having sealed it in an earthen crucible, one should then roast it with wild lotuses (*āraṇyotpala*).
When it has reached the measure of two hundred [units] and has become cool to the touch of one's own body,
one should extract it all and grind it for three days with the juices of divine medicinal herbs.
One should prepare pills weighing four niṣkas and then dry them;
having sealed each one individually in a vajra-mūṣā crucible, one should blow it with a fierce fire.
Indeed, this pill of bliss, when placed in the mouth, destroys death;
for a year there is no doubt, one shall live for three days of Brahmā.
One should daily drink one niṣka of oil extracted from *vātāri* seeds with cow's milk for the purpose of *krāmaṇa*; this is the supreme means for achieving swift success.

Mercury, equal in measure to diamond-ash, should be ground with the juices of *haṃsapādī* for three days; then, having smeared it inside a crucible using the "pair" (*dvaṃdva*) method and sealed it, one should roast it in a fire-pit (*puṭa*).
Then, having extracted the eastern portion of that [substance] known as Bhūdhara day and night,
one should add mercury (pārada) and, using the juices of Haṃsapādī, process it for three days.
Having ground it in a crucible smeared with *dvandva* [salts] and sealed (*andhita*), one should blow it in the furnace;
that residue (*khoṭa*) should then be purified by blowing, through the application of glass and *ṭaṅkaṇa*.
As long as it possesses the luster of a star, it should be heated again and again;
then that essence, along with *vyomasattva* and gold, [should be mixed] in equal parts.
Then, having brought [the ingredients] together, one should prepare a pill to be placed within the mouth;
known as Vajrakhecarī, it destroys death for the duration of a year.
A man shall become free from wrinkles and grey hair and possess a divine body;
he should drink one *karṣa* of powdered *nirguṇḍī* and *muni* with clarified butter as an after-drink.
One should melt equal parts of mercury and sulfur as a powder, enclosed within a vajra-mūṣā crucible, and blow it [with a bellows];
then, one should grind that resulting *khoṭa* (residue) powder with sulfur and sour gruel.
Having sealed it properly in a crucible, one should cook it; then, having extracted it, one should grind it.
Following the same sequence as before, one should roast it fourteen times.
One should color gold that has been alloyed with *vajra* using this very [substance];
while blowing [the fire] within the crucible, one should thus add equal amounts seven times.
That powder of the calx should be processed with women's menses for a number of days;
one should then grind all that, equal in amount to quicksilver, for one watch (yāma).
One should wrap it in birch bark, bind it with cloth, and cook it for three days in a *dolāyantra* using the juice of *sāra* wood; once prepared, one should extract the resulting ball (*gola*).
With the paste of the balls made from these— gāndhārī, jīvantī, lāṅgalī, and indravāruṇī— one should envelop the previously prepared sphere.
Having blinded it for a day, one should cook it in the *bhūdhara* [furnace] and then extract it;
having plastered it again, it should be cooked once more, continuing this until fourteen days have passed.
A divine pill is produced, likewise named Ratneśvarī;
by keeping it in the mouth for just one year, a man becomes equal to Nandin.
He shall live for thousands of years, possessing divine luster and great strength,
as long as that [mantra] remains in his mouth for twelve years.
Through contact with his perspiration, the eight metals and gold are produced;
there is no doubt in this, for this is the truth spoken by the Lord.
One should lick the powder of the five ingredients with honey and ghee, followed by that derived from *rudantī*.
Then, well-powdered gold, the essence of black mica, silver, and copper [should be consumed].
One should blow [the crucible] while it is sealed in a crucible smeared with *dvandva* [mercury and sulfur] in equal parts;
that resulting *khoṭa* consists of four parts, and one part of dead diamond (*mṛtavajra*).
Take one part each of honey-iron (mākṣika) and sharp magnetite (tīkṣṇakānta), finely powdered;
having smeared a crucible with the entire mixture in pairs, close it and heat it in a closed furnace (andhramūṣā).
That powder should be made into a fine dust, and one part of this powder should be mixed with one part of molten mercury;
it should then be rubbed for three days in a heated mortar with the juices of divine medicinal plants.
Then, having sealed it within a *bhūdhara* (earth-mold), one should cook it and extract it after a day and night;
having added an equal amount of liquefied mercury again, it should be rubbed and likewise subjected to *puṭa* firing.
Having thus added the molten mercury seven times, each portion being equal, one should grind it and cook it in a *puṭa*; thus it becomes "dead mercury" (*bhasmasūtaka*).
Having added sulphur equal in weight to the ash-mercury and having sealed it, one should heat it strongly;
a divine pill arises, renowned as the "Divyakhecarī."
If one holds it in the mouth for one year, one shall live for a thousand kalpas;
by smearing all metals with his urine and feces, [the same result follows].
Divine gold is produced at the time of the Samāvarta rite; of this there is no doubt.
One should always drink two *pala* of *bhṛṅgarāja* juice thereafter.

Or, one should always lick the previously mentioned ash-mercury in a dose of one *guñjā*, mixed with honey and clarified butter; after one year, the man attains a lifespan of a hundred thousand years.
Free from wrinkles and grey hair, possessing great strength and prowess,
one should cause gold and the essence of vaikrānta, combined together, to be digested within the mercury.
It should remain in equal portions; then, one should circulate it by that very means.
When bound by the equal [state], it arises; one should always hold that in the mouth.
By practicing this for a year, one conquers old age, time, and untimely death;
thereafter, one should drink a decoction made from the petals of the *kumārī* plant mixed with sugar.
This [preparation], bound with gold and vaikrānta, bestows the lifespan of Brahmā upon men.
One should thoroughly rub pure mercury with an equal portion of the essence of vaikrānta.
Having smeared that ball with the juices of divine medicinal herbs for a day,
one should indeed seal it within a diamond crucible filled with salt.
One should dry the joint in the shade for three days using the heat of chaff-fire,
or one should steam it in a fire of dried cow-dung for a day and night, and then remove it.
Having smeared that ball with lac and likewise enclosed it, one should heat it thoroughly until it is dried in the shade; it will certainly attain firmness of bond.
If one holds this Vaikrānta pill in the mouth for one year, one shall live for three days of Brahmā;
indeed, this pill bestows the fruits of all desires.
One should lick one *karṣa* of powdered *triphalā* with honey and clarified butter;
likewise, one should make a fine powder of diamond (*vajra*) that has been alloyed with gold.
O Guhyasūti, this should be placed in the crucible with one part below and one part above;
having diligently sealed the joint to the extent of a quarter-measure, one should let it dry thoroughly.
Having extracted [the substance] from that which is called Bhūdharā,
one should cook it for a day and then grind it for a full day in a heated mortar with the juices of divine medicinal fruits.
Then, having sealed it within a crucible, one should cook it for a day using small *puṭa* (herbivorous) seals;
having extracted it, one should again crush it in that same manner and seal it for three days.
One should gently fume it with a fire of chaff while turning it over from top to bottom;
thus this "ash-mercury" is produced, which one should employ in all formulations.
One part of quicksilver, one part of the aforementioned ash,
and one part of pure lead— grind all of these together with acid juice.
The mercury, having been placed in a blind crucible (andhamūṣā) and heated, becomes a *khoṭa*;
one should heat it in an open crucible (*prakaṭamūṣā*) until the destruction of the *nāga* [impurity] occurs.
Having liquefied this mercury by means of the method for melting the ore,
one should place it in a tortoise-shaped apparatus (kacchapa-yantre) after adding a flux (viḍa) in a tenth part [of the mercury's weight].
One should digest all metals, beginning with gold, in their proper sequence, each six times [the weight of the mercury]; thereafter, one should digest the pair of diamonds.
Once [the base metal] has become threefold [in weight], one should then gradually digest the gems,
each melted separately, in a quantity three times that amount.
Then, having extracted [the substance] from the apparatus and ground it for a day with the juices of divine herbs, one should seal it and heat it intensely; thus an auspicious pill is produced.
One should worship her with the mantras of Aṅkuśī; she is indeed named Divyakhecarī.
For he in whose mouth she resides shall become equal to Bhairava.
Possessing divine splendor and a massive body, he travels by means of the power of moving through the sky;
wherever he desires, right there he sports with women and other companions.
He remains for as long as the end of the great eon (mahākalpa), of this there is no doubt;
by his urine and feces, copper becomes gold.
One should daily consume three *pala* of powdered *palāśa* flowers, black sesame seeds, and sugar; this is beneficial for the process of *krāmaṇa*.
One should add an equal amount of the powder of a horse's hoof to the secret extract;
for three days, one should thoroughly grind all of that with the acidic juice of *mātuluṅga*.

Having added mercury equal in weight to the dead *vajra*, one should then grind it for a day with acidic liquids in a heated mortar; having formed that into a ball and placed it in a closed crucible, one should subject it to *puṭa* firing.
Having placed one part of the aforementioned mercury into the *bhūdhara* apparatus for one day,
it should be thoroughly rubbed with the juice of *mātuluṅga* for a day.
Then, having sealed it as before, one should cook it again and mercury should be added once more;
it should be rubbed and cooked just as previously, and one should do this seven times.
By repeatedly adding the liquid, the mercury thus becomes a "dead" (bhasma) state;
it may then be employed in all formulations and shall become the destroyer of old age and death.
One part of powdered nāga, one part of the aforementioned ash,
and one part of quicksilver— one should form a pill (khoṭa) as previously described.
In the same way, when the serpent has been incinerated, one should again cause the liquefied substance to be digested;
as before, up to the point where the metals and gems are digested, once it is fully digested, it remains bound within the mouth [of the mercury].
The pill named Pracaṇḍakhecarī grants movement through the sky;
by means of it, O Hero, one obtains as before a fruit that is exceedingly difficult to attain.
One should drink one *karṣa* of the powder of *nirguṇḍī* root with buttermilk;
then, a sixteenth part (*kalāṃśa*) of purified mercury and dead *vajra* should be administered.
Having ground all of that with the group of acidic substances (amlavarga) in a heated mortar for three days,
one should then apply a coating of it in equal proportions.
The leaves of the ripened seed should again be wrapped with solar petals;
having thus sealed them, one should bury them within the interior of a hearth.
Having covered it, one should ignite a wood fire there for three days;
then, having extracted it, one should seal it within a crucible smeared with a pair [of substances].
One should cook it in a *puṭa* over a fire of dried cow-dung for a day and night, then remove it;
once the mercury has been treated with the *vāsana*, one should add an equal amount of this [substance].
One should grind it with sour juice for one *yāma*; once formed into a ball, one should take it out, place it inside a *jambīra* fruit, tie it in a cloth, and cook it for three days.
In a swinging apparatus (*dolāyantra*) within the essence-liquid (*sāranāla*), an auspicious pill is produced;
known by the name Kaṅkālakhecarī, when held in the mouth, it destroys death.
He who wears it for one year shall live for a day of Brahmā;
thereafter, he should lick a karṣa of equal parts of sulphur and guggulu with clarified butter.
Having sealed together equal parts of the essence of black mica, magnetite, copper pyrite, gold, steel, and powdered *sauvīra* salt, one should heat it strongly in a closed crucible.
That powder from the crucible should be made into a fine dust equal in weight to the liquefied mercury;
one should then grind all of this together with acid, along with half as much killed *vajra* (diamond).
Having sealed it in a heated mortar for one day, one should cook it in an earthen vessel (bhūdhara);
after twenty-four hours, having extracted it, [one adds] an equal amount of the previously mentioned flux (sūtaka).
Having added [the ingredients] and rubbed everything for a day with the juices of divine medicinal herbs,
one should again cook the liquefied mercury equally with [the herbs] in a crucible as before.
Having added [the ingredients] and kneaded them, one should cook them again; thus, seven times over.
Having added an amount of fragrance equal to this ash, one should strongly blow upon it until it becomes blind (i.e., solidified).
A divine pill is produced, supreme and the destroyer of Time;
for him in whose mouth this resides, what can Time do?
By practicing this for six years, one may live for a thousand kalpas;
by the mere sweat of that body, all metals turn into gold.

They are born; there is no doubt in this. One should drink the purifying water of Śiva (śivāmbu) along with the equal parts of gold, silver, sun-stone (arkakānta), and sharp iron powder (tīkṣṇacūrṇa).
One should blow upon the sealed crucible smeared with the mixture of the two [substances];
having reduced that residue to powder, it should be consecrated as before.
One should cause it to be digested within the mercury face-to-face until it has increased fivefold in sequence;
then, one should indeed grind it for three days with the juices of divine herbs.
When heated in an andhamūṣā crucible, it becomes an auspicious pill;
known by the name Pañcānanā, it should be held in the mouth for the duration of a year.
Free from wrinkles and graying hair, one may live as long as the moon, sun, and stars,
by taking the *hastikarṇī* plant with its roots, powdered and combined with honey and clarified butter.
Having sealed it in a smooth vessel, one should place it in a heap of grain;
after three weeks have passed, one should extract it and consume one *pala* as an after-meal tonic.

However, regarding the various methods of binding mercury that were proclaimed in the section on supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), I shall here describe the procedure for piercing the body (*dehavedha*) by means of that very [mercury]. Rrā_2,3.183 //
With those various sovereign elixirs (rasarāja), having been separately processed and bound,
one should fashion a divine pill the size of a jujube fruit.
This pill, which bestows fruits corresponding to one's own merit, should be held in the mouth for one year;
it possesses a potency of a hundredfold penetration and grants men the lifespan of a Yuga.
The pill that pierces a thousand [leaves] protects for eight kalpas;
however, that which pierces a hundred thousand bestows strength equal to Viṣṇu.
That [piercing] which occurs at ten lakhs is the bestower of the state of Rudra;
that which effects piercing at ten million (koṭi) brings about lordship for men.
The *vedhikā* [elixir] pierces ten crores [of atoms] and bestows the state known as Sadāśiva; that pill which pierces a hundred million (*arbuda*) bestows the state of Śrīkaṇṭha.
The pill that pierces the conch-shell bestows the state of perfect existence;
but that which is perfected as the "smoke-piercer" grants the station of power.
That [initiation] which effects penetration by touch bestows the state of the Supreme Power (parāśakti),
while that which effects penetration by sound belongs to one for whom it takes a year's duration.
Abiding in the mouth, he indeed becomes perfected and shall eternally attain the eternal state;
moving according to his own will, possessing a vajra-body, he cannot be pierced even by vajra-strikes.
From his urine and feces, all metals and gold are produced through contact with his sweat and even from the touch of his body.
Following all the aforementioned yogas, one should regularly consume half a *pala* of pure sulfur; this is beneficial for the transference of the mercury (*rasasaṃkrāmaṇa*).
O Kālī, O Mahākālī, you who feast upon flesh and blood,
O Goddess with a red and black face, grant me the accomplishment of the elixir!
With this perfected mantra, "svāhā," one should worship the wheel of energies (śakticakra),
Kālikā, Bhairava, the Siddhas, the Kumārī, and the accomplished mercury (rasa).
Then one should employ the divine elixir (*rasāyana*) and attain perfection;
one should hold the pill in the mouth and always recite the aforementioned mantra.
Through the application of the mantra of mercury (rasamantra), one shall swiftly attain accomplishment;
that which was described in the Manthānabhairava as the gradual attainment of accomplishment through mercury [is here surpassed].
For that purpose, one should accomplish the five principles and the sixth, the individual soul (jīva);
having united with Kākinī during her period of menstruation, one should collect [the essence].
The wise know that sky to be the seed of passion (rajas) situated within that womb;
it is called the wind of immediate excrement for the son born of Kākinī.
Fire is the flower of Kākinī, and water is the blood of her son;
the entire body of the son of Kākinī is said to be the earth element.
The vitality arising from the body of one who consumes mercury is called *jīva*;
each of these, when combined with one *karṣa* of mercury, effects a penetration of ten million (*koṭivedha*).
Having prepared it, one should preserve it; once broken, it should be well-ground and formed into a ball, rising to the height of a man and half that in width.
One should have a copper vessel made, thick up to six finger-breadths,
so that it may be held firmly upon the back of the four-faced box.
One should mix cow’s ghee and human oil in equal proportions;
having filled that cauldron with it, one should then worship the *Siddhacakra*.
One should satisfy the maiden, the guru, the deity, and the fire, as well as Bhairava together with Bhairavī, with an offering of meat; one should also worship the Kṣetrapāla.
There, one should perform blowing slowly and gradually in the four directions using four curved tubes joined with charcoal from the *khadira* tree.
When it has been thoroughly heated, freed from froth, and becomes smokeless,
[one perceives] the moon, the sun, the planets, the constellations, the deities, and the worlds.
Having paid homage to the Guru and the God, one should cast the body there;
one should know that it is well-cooked when the earthly essence has been cast away.
One should blow [upon] this very [substance] with effort until it reaches the state of a paste;
one should then pour the liquid called the water-element (*aptattva*) into it, and that [paste] will indeed become blood.
By casting the mercury joined with air, it becomes white in color;
by casting the mercury joined with fire, it shall become solidified.
Then one should pour mercury that has been united with space into it;
once it has been stirred, it becomes gold-colored, and one should pour [the resulting substance] back into that [mercury].
Then one should utter the divine *rasa* joined with *jīva*,
and having produced a great roar there, conjoined with three *huṃ* syllables.
Then the Siddha arises in the forenoon like the sun,
possessing divine splendor, a massive body, and great strength and prowess.
The strength of nine thousand elephants shall be surpassed by his;
possessing a body of adamant, he lives—this is the truth, the truth spoken by Śiva.
Of those whose limbs are worn out by old age, of the blind, the lame, and those afflicted with leprosy;
of those who have lost their speech, the dull-witted, the eunuchs, the hunchbacked, and those with bodies ravaged by skin diseases.
If this is so for those afflicted by many diseases, who are deluded, insane, or like piśāca-demons,
how much more so for kings who possess pure bodies and indulge in sensual pleasures?
It bestows divine accomplishments upon heroes and practitioners;
therefore, he who is the most heroic here is Bhairava—of this there is no doubt.
One shall become a perfected being with a vajra-body, wise and possessing a divine form;
and there shall be a celestial mansion, half a yojana in extent, filled with apsarases.
There is no doubt that he comes before that perfected one;
having ascended there, he sports in the world of Rudra like Bhairava himself.
Freed from hunger and thirst, he does not perish even at the destruction of the world;
enjoying all objects of pleasure, he becomes dear to the yogins.
Accomplishing his desires, the great hero becomes composed of eternal bliss.

Having observed all [methods] and experienced them, among the elixirs (*rasāyana*), those applications of pills (*guṭikā*) are declared to be the most excellent, easy to accomplish, and bringing supreme auspiciousness for men, in order to constantly achieve the perfect success of making the body firm.
Lead, mercury, sulphur, iron, and copper, when killed and rendered into the supreme nectar,
as well as even a single desired group of medicinal roots, when consumed, quickly grant the perfection of the body.
Take sixteen palas each of mercury purified with mica, sulfur, *bhṛṅga*, *viḍaṅga*, and the seeds of *bilva* (excluding the bark).
Thirty palas each of the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), thirty palas of ghee, thirty palas of honey,
and ten palas of citramūla— one should thoroughly mix all these into a powder.
Twenty-four hundred palas of the three myrobalans (triphalā) should be boiled with eight times as much water, until one-eighth remains.
One should infuse the decoction with that [powder] for one month, previously stirred in an iron vessel; one should always drink half a *pala* of it during the intense heat of the sun.
If one drinks [the medicine] with milk at the time of going to bed for a year, it removes death and old age;
the child will have firm joints and live as long as the moon, sun, and stars.
One should cast black mica, heated by fire and possessing the color of fire, into milk; it is a divine great elixir that gratifies hundreds of women.
Then, having torn the leaf, one should carefully cast it into the middle of the water,
along with thirty palas of black pepper and five palas [of another substance].
One should throw the powder into that [liquid] and remove it at the end of three days;
one should grind all of that until very fine and bind it with a white cloth.
One should place [the vessel] in a swing-contrivance over a jar filled with water during the heat;
when the water has dried up, one should add more water until it has reached [the desired level].
Then the wise one should discard that cloth along with the mica, preserving the water;
thereafter, he should reduce that water containing the mica to one-thirtieth its original volume.
Having stirred one *pala* of white rice with one part of that [mixture], one should cook it in thirty *palas* of cow's milk; then, once it has cooled, [one should proceed].
The practitioner should daily consume [this preparation] combined with two palas each of honey and clarified butter, and one niṣka each of black pepper; for a month, it removes death and old age.
His hair, teeth, and nails indeed fall out and grow back again;
he becomes one perfected with a vajra-body, possessing the speed of the wind and great strength.
This "Amṛtābhraka" formulation was proclaimed by Śambhu in ancient times:
dead mica, purified sulfur, and long pepper—all in equal parts—with ghee.
One should eat one *karṣa* daily for a year; it removes death and old age.
[The recipe consists of] the leaves of *koraṇṭaka*, mercury, mica, and sulfur in equal parts.
All of that should be infused with the juices of *nīlikā* for seven days in the sun;
one should drink one karṣa of it with milk for a year, which removes death and old age.
One *karṣa* of purified mica (*mṛtābhraka*), one *pala* of cow’s milk,
and fresh *sarpākṣī* with its roots and leaves, along with sulfur, should be ground together.
Having combined them all, one should drink [the elixir]; by doing so for one year, one conquers old age.
Possessing a vajra-body and the power of flight, one shall live for three days of Brahmā.
One should combine powdered dead mica, magnetite, the three myrobalans, and *māgadhī* in equal parts,
along with an amount of *badarī* powder equal to the mica.
One should always consume half a *pala* of white sugar combined with honey and clarified butter;
by doing so for a year, one destroys old age and death, and one's lifespan shall equal a day of Brahmā.
*Amṛtakrīḍe viṣṇusaṃvaraṇi svāhā*. By means of this mantra, all preparations of mica (*abhraka*) should be consecrated and then consumed.
[Likewise,] mercury, magnetite, black sesame seeds, and the powder of jujube fruit.
One should prepare all these together with an equal amount of powdered *kākatuṇḍī* seeds.
It should be impregnated for three days with the juices of *śālmalī* and *mallikā* leaves;
having been impregnated for three days with the juices of *bhṛṅgarāja*, it should be dried again.
Having added an equal amount of jaggery to that, one should make pills weighing one karṣa each;
these "weepers" (rudantī) should always be drunk with rising fluids, milk, honey, and ghee.
By using this for one year, one destroys old age and death; this is the truth, there is no doubt.
One should powder together equal parts of black sesame seeds, the three myrobalans (triphalā), and the ashes of a deceased beloved.
One should drink half a *pala* of this mixture—stirred with the juices of *śālmalī* and *ketakī* in a beautiful vessel and kept overnight—at dawn; it destroys death.
It destroys old age after one year; one shall live for three days of Brahmā.
[One should take] the ash of *kāntaloha*, the powder of *kaṇā* (long pepper), and the exudate of *nimba*.

One should lick a mixture of equal parts of the three myrobalans (triphalā) combined with half a pala each of honey and clarified butter, daily for eight months; such a person shall live for the duration of a day of Brahmā.
Having boiled pieces of kuṣṭha in an equal quantity of triphalā decoction,
and having dried and powdered them, one should then add an equal amount of iron (kānta) and mercury (mṛta).

One should lick one karṣa of the powder of *koraṇṭa* leaves mixed with honey and clarified butter for a year; this removes death and old age. [Likewise,] iron ash, sesame seeds, and jaggery [may be used]. (Rasārṇava 2.4.30)
Half a pala of that [mercury] is an equal amount of edible [substance]; for a year, it removes death and old age.
[One should mix] an equal amount of iron ash and sulphur with oils derived from *jyotiṣmatī*.
By weighing himself against four niṣkas daily, a man attains the lifespan of Brahmā;
within a year, he certainly becomes equal to Bṛhaspati in speech.
Three parts of dead mercury (mṛtatīkṣṇa) and eight parts of pure sulphur should all be processed for twenty-one days in the heat with the juices of *kanyā* flowers.
One should drink one karṣa of that with cow’s milk; one will live for three days of Brahmā.
After merely one year, there is no doubt, one will possess divine luster and great strength.
One should lick pure stone (śilājatu) equal in weight to dead mercury, mixed with honey and clarified butter;
by taking one niṣka at a time for one year, one shall live for three days of Brahmā.
One should drink three niṣkas of either dead iron (mṛtatīkṣṇa), muṇḍa, or kānta iron with warm milk; this causes the stabilization of the vital age of men.
By practicing this for two years, one shall live as long as the moon and stars endure;
[one should take] the powder of *dhātrī* with *śivāmbu* in a vessel consisting entirely of *kānta* iron.
Having smeared one *pala* at night and rising in the morning, one should consume it;
freed from wrinkles and grey hair, one shall conquer death within a year.
One should smear the interior of a vessel made of kāntaloha with one pala each of triphalā and honey;
having left it there for a day and night, it should be drunk daily with the water of Śiva (cow’s urine).
After one year, it destroys death and old age; one shall live for three hundred years.

Oṃ haḥ amṛte amṛtaśakti amṛtagandhopajīvi niṣpannaṃ candrāmṛtam ājñāpitaṃ kuru kuru svāhā he he haṃ haḥ gaṃ. This is the mantra for consuming the fragrant substances and the metals. Following all metallic formulations, there should be the drinking of milk; one should taste the sweet juice of musta (cyperus rotundus) extracted by the teeth. Rrā 2.4.40.
One should eat their roots to pacify the bad taste in the mouth;
however, when the digestive tract is bound and the digestive fire is blazing, one should always drink warm milk.
When there is constipation, one should avoid bathing, massage, and pungent or hot substances;
one should constantly and repeatedly consume betel leaf together with camphor.

When the medicine has been properly digested and the digestive fire is stimulated, one who is hungry should drink boiled milk; thereafter, food should be consumed during the iron-based elixir therapy (*lauharasāyana*).

One should lick one karṣa of the well-powdered five parts of the Brahma-tree (Brahmavṛkṣa), dried in the shade, mixed with honey and clarified butter; by doing so for one year, one shall conquer old age.
Possessing divine luster and great strength, he shall live for a thousand years;
one should cause the flowers of the Brahma-tree to be dried in the shade.
Having combined thirty palas of that powder with twenty-four palas of ghee, one should place it in a vessel, seal it, and bury it in a heap of grain.
Having prepared it and extracted it after one month, one should divide it into fourteen portions;
one should eat one portion daily from a beautiful vessel.
One should practice in this manner for three months, and the person shall become one with a vajra-body;
by means of his urine and feces, copper turns into gold.
The seeds of the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree, ground into powder and mixed with clarified butter,
should be placed inside grain as before and retrieved after one month.
If one should always eat it, even a single *pala* at a time, for a year, one will conquer death;
freed from wrinkles and grey hair, one shall live for three days of Brahmā.
One should drink two palas of oil produced from the seed of *brahmabīja* mixed with an equal amount of cow's milk;
this causes fainting, and one should sprinkle water on the person's face.
On the fifth lunar day, one should offer milk-rice; within a month, the man becomes a possessor of knowledge.
On the second [fifth], he becomes equal to Śukra, and on the third, he becomes like a diamond.

In the fourth month, one becomes capable of hearing from afar; in the fifth, one gains the power of moving through the sky; and in the sixth month, one becomes a creator oneself, possessing prowess equal to Śiva.
By practicing this for one year, one may live until the end of a great kalpa;
one should cut down a very thick Brahma-tree from its upper portion.
The area below should be protected for a distance of three cubits;
a cavity is made at its top, which is to be filled with ripe dhātrī fruits and then sealed with wood.
One should wrap the entire object with *kuśa* grass and then plaster it with clay and cow dung;
having wrapped it with a piece of cloth, one should then smear it again with clay and cow dung.
Once dried, one should apply the *gajapuṭa* method, surrounding it with wild blue lotuses;
then, having removed the fruits while they are still moist, one should let them cool naturally.
One should cast those very [seeds] into a vessel mixed with honey and clarified butter;
staying within an underground chamber, subsisting on milk, one may eat them as desired and conquer old age.
Within two months, he certainly perceives the earth as having holes;
he shall live for the duration of a day of Brahmā, casting off his skin like a serpent.
One should daily consume one *karṣa* of the powdered five parts of the white *pālāśa* tree together with honey; after a month, this removes death and old age.
Within just one year, he becomes a perfected Siddha with the lifespan of Brahmā; of this there is no doubt.
He should always consume that seed one by one with goat’s ghee.
By rubbing the body with ashes for a month, one conquers death and old age;
that man shall live for the duration of a day of Brahmā, his body becoming divine.
Whatever other yogas exist, and whatever qualities are found in the red Brahmavr̥kṣa tree, those very same qualities shall indeed belong to the practitioner in the white Pālāśa tree as well.
"Make [this] nectar, make [this] nectar; homage to Amṛtamālinī!
By means of this mantra, all yogas should be consumed after being consecrated seven times.
This should be done during the bright fortnight, on the full moon day, or under the asterisms of Puṣya or Śravaṇa.
Or else, having performed worship under the asterism Revatī, one should extract the five parts of Muṇḍī.
That powder, dried in the shade, should be taken in a dose of one *karṣa* with cow's milk;
by doing so for one year, it destroys old age, and one shall live for three hundred years.
By means of his urine and feces, copper attains the state of gold;
that powder, when licked with clarified butter, likewise produces marvelous strength.
Oṃ, salutation to the one arisen from nectar; make [this] nectar, make it, svāhā! Oṃ hrāṃ saḥ.
This is the mantra for consuming the medicinal herb.
Then, one should powder the five parts of *devadālī*, dried in the shade.
One should lick a karṣa measure [of this] with honey and clarified butter; within a year, one shall conquer death and old age.
A man shall live for a thousand kalpas and become equal to Rudra;
one karṣa of that powder should be drunk daily with the water of Śiva.
Success arises as before within a year; there is no doubt about this.
That powder consists of equal parts *vākucī*, *vahni* (citraka), *sarpākṣī*, and *bhṛṅgarāja*.
One should daily drink one karṣa of this powder with auspicious water;
after a year, it destroys death and old age, and one perceives the earth as having no hidden flaws.
A person should daily drink the juices of *punarnavā* and *devadālī*,
or one *pala* of *devadālī* and *sarpākṣī* with the water of *śivā*.
One should drink [it] as before; success will be achieved within a year—of this there is no doubt.
One should drink one *karṣa* of *devadālī* and *nirguṇḍī* with the water of Śiva (*śivāmbu*);
in one year it destroys old age, and one shall live as long as the moon and stars endure.
Oṃ amṛtagaṇa rudragaṇāmbhaḥ svāhā! This is the mantra for taking [the water]. Namo bhagavate rudrāya huṃ phaṭ svāhā!
This is the mantra for binding the topknot of the practitioner:
*oṃ cara ra ra*. This is the mantra for consumption.
Under the Puṣya asterism, one should take the root of the white Arka plant and dry it in the shade;
then, one should drink one karṣa of its powder mixed with two palas of cow’s milk.
By drinking the juice of white *arka* leaves mixed with an equal amount of the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*, one destroys old age after six months and may live for three days of Brahmā.
Having combined [the ingredients] and dried them in the sun, one should cook the powder with four times as much milk over a gentle fire until it reaches the consistency of a bolus.
One karṣa of that should be licked with ghee; after a year, the result will be as previously described.
Oṃ āṃ haṃ vāsaramāline svāhā. This is the mantra for consumption.
On the thirteenth day of the moon, one should take the leaf of the *hastikarṇa* plant.
One should drink one pala of that powder, dried in the shade, with cow's milk.
By using the five parts of the *hastikarṇa* plant, dried in the shade and powdered, for one year, a man destroys old age and may live for a Brahma-day.
One should drink a quantity of one *karṣa* daily for one month with water,
followed by fermented rice-gruel (*āranāla*), then buttermilk, curd, milk, ghee, and honey.
Each one should be practiced in succession for one month to remove old age;
possessing a vajra-body and great strength, one shall live for one and a half Brahma-days.
Oṃ, I seize the poison of pride within the sight, svāhā!
This is the mantra for seizing the elephant-ear [herb].
Oṃ, for those born from the Amṛtakuṭī [vessel], make it nectar, make it nectar, svāhā!
One should worship with this:
*Oṃ amṛtodbhavāya amṛtaṃ kuru kuru nityaṃ namo namaḥ*. This is the mantra for consumption. *Rājatarangiṇī* 2.4.81.
One should powder the five parts of *rudantī* that have been dried in the shade;
to half that amount, add the powder of *musali*, and to half that amount of *musali*, add the three fruits (*phalatraya*).
One should cause the oil extracted from *kataka* roots to settle in a *pātālayantra* or a *garbhayantra*;
then, one should wash that oil with water.
Alternatively, having washed it with coconut water, one should gradually lick the aforementioned powder mixed with five parts of oil.

One should perform the increase starting from one *karṣa* up to the end of a *pala*; then, one should increase it in this manner for a year, whereby one destroys old age, and one's lifespan becomes equal to a day of Brahmā.
This is indeed known as the Siddhayoga, which bestows a vajra-body upon men;
one should collect the bark from the root of nirguṇḍī at dawn on a Sunday coinciding with the Puṣya asterism.
Having powdered the shade-dried [substance], one should always drink one karṣa with one pala of goat urine;
after six months, one becomes immortal.
By practicing this for only one year, a man becomes equal to Śiva.
That powder, stirred with milk, honey, and clarified butter, should be placed in a smooth vessel.
Having sealed it, one should cast it into a heap of grain;
after a month, having extracted it, one should consume two palas of it for a year, and thus live as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure.
One should lick half a *pala* of that powder with clarified butter, and the result will be as described before.
That powder consists of *triphalā*, *muṇḍī*, *bhṛṅgī*, *nimba*, and *guḍūcī*.
One should lick one *pala* of their equal powder with honey and clarified butter;
after a year, it destroys death and old age, and one shall live for three days of Brahmā.
One should cook the juice extracted from *nirguṇḍī* leaves in a vessel over a gentle fire;
when it has reached the consistency of jaggery, it should be drunk to induce vomiting and purgation.
Worms emerge from his mouth, nose, eyes, and ears;
he destroys diseases such as pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣmā) within seven days;
after three months, he overcomes old age and shall live for three hundred years.
"Oṃ, salutation to Māyā-Gaṇapati, the lord of the earth, Kubera; svāhā!"—this is the mantra for consumption.
Bhallātaka, abhayā, vīrā, the fruit of kākatuṇḍī, vacā, lāṅgalī, nimba leaves, and sahadevī—in equal parts each. (Rāmāyaṇa 2.4.94)
From these, one should diligently extract the oil using the *pātālayantra* (subterranean press).
One should drink half a *pala* of that oil combined with the root of *nīlikā*.
It destroys gray hair within a year; a day of Brahmā constitutes the lifespan [of this practice].
When half a niṣka of oil is used as a nasal drop, the same result as previously described shall be attained.
One *prastha* of black cumin seeds and an equal amount of *bhṛṅgarāja* juice should be taken,
along with half a *prastha* each of licorice and blue lotus.
One should cook one *prastha* of sesame seeds with oil until everything is cooked together;
that which remains as oil should be taken and used for nasal administration (*nasya*).
One should administer nasal drops with *aṅkolla* oil to ward off death and old age;
by using half a *niṣka* or one *niṣka* [of the oil], one shall live for three hundred years.
Having ground the fruit of *kākamācī*, one should drink one *karṣa* with water;
after a year, it destroys graying hair, and one's lifespan shall become equal to the day of Brahmā.
Equal parts of powdered guḍūcī, musalī, muṇḍī, nirguṇḍī, śatāvarī, and vijayā, combined with sugar, honey, and clarified butter; Rrā_2.4.101.
One should eat two karṣas daily; after one year, one will conquer graying hair.
As stated by Gorakṣanātha, such a person shall live for three Brahma-days.

On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, having wrapped a tree of the *śunaka-śālmali* with black threads while reciting the Aghora mantra, one should offer a black goat as a sacrificial oblation at night.
Having offered the Aghora mantra there, one should recite it up to eight thousand times;
then, one should take the root bark of that [tree], dry it in the shade, and grind it into powder.
If one always eats one pala of this with honey and clarified butter for the duration of a year,
that person shall be freed from wrinkles and graying hair and live for the length of a day of Brahmā.
Having gathered its flowers, one should always cook them with cow's milk;
one should drink the milk, excluding the flowers, for a month, which removes death and old age.
One should cook a single fruit of that tree with cow's milk;
having removed the fruit, the wise man should drink the milk, and in this manner he should continue drinking only milk.
By practicing for four months, a person shall become one with a vajra-body;
possessing great strength and the speed of the wind, he shall live until the end of the kalpa.
Through his urine and excrement, copper becomes gold.
[The herbs] *kākamācī*, *bhṛṅgarāja*, *sarpākṣī*, and *sahadevikā* [are used for this].
Devadālī with its roots, the seeds of nimba and vākucī,
the fruits of kākatuṇḍī, and the roots of brahmī and aśvagandhā.
Take equal parts of the leaves of *nīlakoraṇṭa* and *triphalā*,
and having made them into a powder, one should macerate it for seven days with the juices of *kanyā*.
One should dry it in the shade and prepare it combined with sugar, honey, and clarified butter.
By eating two *karṣas* of this daily for one year, one conquers old age;
possessing a great body and great strength, one shall live as long as the moon, sun, and stars.

Oṃ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ saḥ saḥ saḥ, O immortal one, O showerer of nectar, O reviver by nectar, O bestower of all desires, the Blessed Lord Somarāja commands: svāhā! This is the mantra for consumption. One should take equal parts of triphalā, vākucī seeds, pippalī, and aśvagandhā, grind them into a powder, and lick one pala of it with honey and clarified butter.
After one year, it destroys death and old age; one shall live for three days of Brahmā.
Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ saḥ svāhā. With this mantra, one should consume it.
In the applications of the *mūlikā* rituals, one should eat a single *guñjā* seed of dead mercury combined with its counter-agent; the result shall be a hundredfold.
By the power of the lord of mercury (rasendra), one shall swiftly attain perfection.
The mantra-practitioner, wearing the bone-seal (asthimudrā), should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times at a cremation ground;
this destroys great fear, grants accomplishment (siddhi), and bestows the elixir of life (rasāyana).
By merely consuming it, one shall live as long as the moon and stars;
invincible to gods and daityas alike, one may even shake the mountains.
Oṃ hrīṃ mahābhayerum!

On an auspicious day such as the morning of the Puṣya asterism or under the influence of the Sun, one should collect the fruits, leaves, flowers, roots, petals, or juices of the divine medicinal plants according to the ritual procedures for mantra-worship.

For the sake of accomplishment, one who observes celibacy should consume the entirety of these fresh substances; milk-rice or water-rice is the beneficial diet, and all other food should be avoided. Rrā 2.4.117.

I shall describe the application of *udvartana*, which removes grey hair for men, brings great beauty, provides comfort, and dyes the hair; it is suitable for the elderly, easy to accomplish, and proven through many methods as a well-established path of experience.
One should grind equal parts of mercury and sulfur with breast milk,
along with *viṣṇukrāntā*, *meghanādā*, *sarpākṣī*, and *munimuṇḍikā*.
One should grind these with their juices in a mortar for a day and then extract them;
one part each of barley powder and sesame seeds, equal to the weight of the juice, [should be added].
One should cast [the ingredients] into that, mixing everything with ghee and honey, and preserve it;
by means of this, an ointment for rubbing on the body effectively destroys wrinkles and graying hair.
After one year, one shall possess a divine body and live for a thousand years;
[this is achieved by using] equal parts of the root of Vajrakāpālinī and mercury.
One should rub [the body] with auspicious water for three days; the result from this massage is as described previously.
Take blue lotuses together with their roots and mercury in equal parts.
One should grind it in a mortar for seven days with one's own *aśivā* water;
by rubbing the body with that very [mixture], the same result as before is produced.
Having added an equal portion of the root of *brahmadaṇḍī* to mercury,
one should grind it for seven days with its own urine.
With this one should rub the body; the result arises as before.
Sulphur should be infused with mustard oil in the heat for the duration of a day.
One should always eat half of that dose; it makes the bodies of men divine.
After one year, the body becomes like gold and free from wrinkles.
He who daily licks one *karṣa* of *kuṣṭha* powder mixed with honey and clarified butter will,
after a year, possess a divine body, fragrant like the *śatapuṣpa* flower.
One should prepare an equal mixture of the powder of magnetite (kāntapāṣāṇa) combined with oil, honey, and clarified butter, along with the fruit of the kākatuṇḍī plant. Rrā 2.5.12.
Having sealed it in a vessel, one should leave it for a month within a heap of grain and then remove it;
with this one should smear the head and indeed administer it as a nasal drop (nasya). Rrā 2.5.13.
After three days, the hair becomes as dark as a bee and remains so for half a year.
One pala of powdered *nāga* and two palas of powdered conch shell [should be used].
One niṣka of powdered pathyā should be ground entirely over the course of a day;
having bathed first with care, one should apply it to the head together with sour curd.
One should massage [the head] for half a ghaṭikā, wrap it with castor leaves,
and after wrapping the head with a cloth, one should perform the morning bath.
Having thus diligently prepared this for three days, one should dye the hair with the five ingredients: nīlikā, bhṛṅgarāja, triphalā, and iron powder.
Having made everything equal and ground it finely with urine, one should rub it for half a day; with that paste, the coloring of the hair is achieved as before.
The seeds of *guñjā*, excluding the husk, along with *kuṣṭha*, *elā*, and *devadāru*,
should be powdered in equal parts and infused for one day with the juices derived from *bhṛṅgarāja*.
One should cook all these ingredients in oil possessing four times the quantity of liquid, using a gentle fire;
by means of that massage, the hair becomes colored like a bumblebee.
Equal amounts of burnt elephant tusk and *rasāñjana* should be mixed together;
having ground them with goat’s milk, applying this as an ointment results in the darkening of the hair.
One should place triphalā, iron powder, black earth, the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*,
and the juice of sugarcane in a vessel and seal it for one month.
By applying that ointment, one shall dye the hair for a period of five months;
having ground iron dross, hibiscus flowers, and myrobalan fruits in equal parts.
If applied for three days by him, the hair becomes like a bumblebee;
[one should prepare] a prastha of *bhṛṅgarāja* juice and oil produced from black sesame.
One should grind all these together with an equal amount of the juice of *nīlikā* for one watch (three hours);
its application should be made for three days, and it will result in the coloring of the hair.
Equal parts of vermilion powder and soap, these two mixed together and ground with water, should be applied as a paste; it causes the hair to turn black instantly.
One should grind together *śatapuṣpā*, *kākamācī*, black sesame seeds,
and yellow pigment (*rocanā*) for one day in an iron vessel with the water of Śiva.
One should apply this ointment for three days, and it will result in the coloring of the hair.
[The powder consists of] *sarjī*, *yavakṣāra*, and *siddhārtha*, together with *kāñjika*.
One should grind it with the juices of *nāgapuṣpa*; from the application of that ointment, there will be coloring.
[Also, one may use] indigo leaves, green vitriol (*kāsīsa*), the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*, and curd.
Having ground iron powder with equal parts, that ointment is for the coloring of the hair;
[another formulation consists of] the powder of vermilion, charcoal, combined with the bulb of the plantain tree.
Having rubbed it in an iron vessel with an iron pestle using the juices of *jambīra* for one day, it should then be applied as a paste; this will result in the coloring of the hair.
One should crush the leaves of the *kuraṇṭaka* plant with *nāgamuṣṭī*;
by applying that ointment for three days, the coloring of the hair is achieved.
Mango stone, the three myrobalans, *bhṛṅgī*, *priyaṅgu*, citron, turmeric, indigo, lotus stalks, lead, and iron— all these should be powdered.
One should macerate an equal amount of the paste in neem oil within a vessel made of *kāntaloha* for exactly one month; then, by applying it as an ointment, coloring occurs.
Take equal parts of *kākamācī* seeds and black sesame seeds;
having extracted that oil in a press, it should be used as an ointment for the nose (*nasya*) to dye the hair black.
Cow’s ghee, *bhṛṅgarāja* juice, and *drāva*, together with *mayūraśikhā*, should be cooked over a gentle fire; from this, an errhine (*nasya*) for dyeing the hair is prepared.

One should administer a nasal drop (*nasya*) consisting of one *karṣa* each of the juice of the hibiscus flower (*japāpuṣpa*) and honey; within seven days it will dye the hair. This is the procedure for all nasal applications.
One should grind equal parts of triphalā and iron powder with water,
along with an equal amount of oil and the juice of bhṛṅgarāja.
One should cook it until only oil remains, then seal it in a greased vessel;
having buried it in the ground for one month, one should smear the head with that [oil].
Having wrapped it with the leaves of *kāravallī*, one should then bind it with a cloth;
staying in a windless place and subsisting on a milk diet, one should wash it with water decocted from the three myrobalans (*triphalā*).
In this manner, one should perform the application [of the ointment] constantly for seven days;
it is known as the "staining of the skull," which lasts for as long as one lives—of this there is no doubt.
The seeds of *kākatuṇḍī* combined with the seeds of *siryālī*—
this powder should be infused for four days with the juices of *nirguṇḍī*.

Then, having extracted oil from the juice of hibiscus flowers (*japāpuṣpa*) using a subterranean apparatus (*pātālayantraka*), the hair becomes dyed by anointing it with that [oil]. (Rāma-rakṣā 2.5.43)
One should wrap [the area] with castor leaves and, in a windless place, consume a diet of milk;
after seven days have passed, one should perform a bath with fermented rice-gruel (kāñjika) every day.
For as long as one lives, there is no doubt that the hair will become like bees;
[this is achieved by using] *bhṛṅgarāja*, *kācamācī*, and *jalamaṇḍavī* in equal parts.
Having ground it together and made it into a cake, one should cook it in oil;
once cooked, one should grind it again with oils, and this ointment will be for the coloring of the hair.
By following the sequence as before, that fruit will be attained within seven days.
At night, one should smear the three fruits upon a vessel made of magnetite.
One should smear the hair with the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja* in the morning;
by doing this for three weeks, the same result as before is produced.
One should throw black cumin into the horn of a buffalo and blind it;
having cast it into the mud in front of a house, one should retrieve it after six months.
That [substance] quickly becomes black; one should place one *karṣa* of it upon the head and wrap it with the previously mentioned method, whereby the coloring of the skull occurs.
One will undoubtedly remain as dark as black bees or collyrium for the rest of one's life;
[this is achieved by using] indigo leaves, *bhṛṅgarāja*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and black iron.
The seeds of Madana, the flower of Koraṇṭaka, the bark-powder of Arjuna, and the mud from the roots of the Nalinī lotus; Rrā_2,5.52.
One should throw all [the ingredients] equally into a vessel made of iron and seal it;
after one fortnight, one should take the paste out from the vessel and place it on the ground.
One should add oil four times the amount of the paste, and liquid four times the amount of the oil—
consisting of *bhṛṅga* and the three myrobalans— and cook it until only the oil remains.
When the test is performed for one fortnight and the crane becomes black in color, then it is accomplished; one should place [the substance] in an iron vessel.
One should maintain that [oil] for one month, and thereafter apply it to the hair;
it will remain for six months, appearing like a swarm of bees.
With a firm staff made from the wood of the vāsā, palāśa, ciñcā, or aśvattha tree,
one should move the serpent contained within the vessel until it becomes unconscious.
Taking one *pala* of that [iron], two *palas* of iron powder,
three *palas* of powdered *triphalā*, and the rind of pomegranate fruit;
One pala of the dried powder and an equal amount of *kāñjika* should all be cooked slightly in a vessel; once it has cooled somewhat, one should pour it into an iron container.
Having added the juice extracted from *bhṛṅgarāja* and *kurṇṭa*, one should expose it to the sun;
for three weeks, with diligence, the juice should be applied again and again.
Then one should protect it; from that ointment, the coloring of the hair occurs.
In the case of both the aforementioned and unmentioned ointments, one should wrap [the head] with castor leaves.
Anointing the head at night and bathing during the day—this method is highly recommended.
One should soak *abhayā* fruits in *vajrī* milk for seven days;
by applying an ointment of oil mixed with their powder, the hair indeed becomes white.
Indeed, the hair and all the body hairs become the color of a conch shell;
one should then soak sesame seeds in white ones for seven days with vajra-milk.
Having taken oil from them, by anointing with it, they indeed become white.
Furthermore, one should take the powder of *gaurī* and *āmalaka* seven times with *vajrī* milk.
By applying that ointment, the hair becomes white.
One should apply vermilion and white crystal together with water as an ointment.
Indeed, by applying that ointment, the body hairs become perfectly white.
One should macerate powdered *māgadhī* for one month with the milk of a *vajrī*.
The following is the supreme method for whitening men, horses, and elephants:
*indragopa*, *tailinī*, *tālaka*, and the two types of *rajanī*.
One should macerate an equal portion of powdered realgar with the milk of *snuk* for three days,
and then [further] for three days in the hot sun with the milks of the *arka* plant.
Then, one should saturate it for seven days with juices extracted from *kūṣmāṇḍa* fruits;
thereafter, having placed it inside the womb of a *kūṣmāṇḍa*, one should extract it after one month.
One should smear all the body hairs and the hair of the head with oil for three days;
by wrapping them with leaves of the *arka* plant, they become white in color.
When the bath has been performed and the hair is dry, at night one should apply an ointment and wrap [the head] with the aforementioned leaves;
then, in the morning, one should perform a bath with curd and sesame seeds, and in this same manner, the application of the ointment should be continued for three days.

For those who possess women skilled in dalliance, attached with passion, bold, devoted to love, fawn-eyed, and moon-faced— for them I shall describe the abundant increase of virility that grants the pleasure of desire; even a hundred such intoxicated, perfected, and steadfast men can satisfy them.
The ashes of vajra, gold, copper, mercury, mica, and iron should be ground in ascending order,
all with the juices of a virgin and the juices of *śālmali* for three days.
Having sealed that [flask], one should cook it for three days in sand inside a glass jar;
then, one should process that paste with decoctions of *musalī* combined with the milks of *vajra* and *arka*.
One should grind it for one day in a mortar, seal it, and roast it in a *bhūdhara* furnace;
after removing it after three hours (*yāma*), one should pulverize it with sugar, black pepper, and the three aromatics (*trijātaka*).
Then, having mixed equal parts of *māgadhī*, *musālī*, *yaṣṭī*, and the seeds of *vānarī* together, one should always consume one *māṣa* of this mixture.
One should administer half a *pala* of this powder with sugar, clarified butter, and cow’s milk;
by doing so, one does not lose control while sporting with a thousand women.
Through its use, the body becomes firm; this elixir is known as Makaradhvaja.
One should grind pure mercury and an equal amount of sulfur for one watch (yāma) with the juice of red lotus petals;
then, one should again add an additional half-amount of sulfur to that mixture.
Having ground half a part of mercury with the aforementioned juices for one day,
and having added sulphur again in the same manner, one should grind it for another day and then seal it within a glass flask.
Having cooked it for one day in a sand-bath (vālukāyantra) and removed it,
one should grind it into a powder and saturate it with a decoction of *bhūkuṣmāṇḍī* for seven days.
In the shade, one should always consume one *niṣka* of that [mercury] equalized with white [sugar];
likewise, *śaṇa* root with its seeds, *musallī*, and sugar in equal parts.
One should always drink half a *pala* of cow's milk at night;
this elixir, known as Madanodaya, increases virility infinitely.
One should grind mercury purified [as described] with an equal amount of sulfur, using the juices of *badarī* and *citraka*,
along with the juices of *aṅkola*, for three days in a heated mortar (*taptakhalva*).
One should place it upon a ball of fresh beef meat and sew it shut;
then, one should slowly cook that ball in an iron vessel with sesame oil.
As long as the meat remains red in color, one should extract the essence (sūta);
it should then be processed for three days with decoctions of *musali* and combined with sugar.
One should eat one *niṣka* of this "Lord of Intoxication" elixir daily;
furthermore, one should drink one *pala* of powdered *vidārī* root with milk and clarified butter.
One may constantly enjoy a hundred women, yet by abandoning them, one falls into blindness.
One should grind together equal parts of mercury, gold, and mica that has been killed [by processing], for three days.
One should roast that ball, having sealed it, with decoctions of *musalī* and *triphalā*, with infusions of *vājigandhā*, and with juices extracted from the root of the plantain (*kadalī*).
Having extracted [the substance] for just one day in a crucible (bhūdhara), one should then grind it;
having likewise sealed it with the aforementioned fluxes for one day, one should cook it in a *puṭa*.
It should be kneaded again and cooked again; thus one should cook it in eight layers with the resin produced from the *śālmali* tree, together with an equal amount of sugar.
One should eat two niṣkas of this daily; it will cause one to attract hundreds of women.
Afterwards, one should drink half a pala of *markaṭī* seeds with cow’s milk.
One should perform a full-body massage with *yava* grains and the juices of the *śālmalī* tree;
this elixir, known as Kāmakalā, bestows great virility upon men.
Three parts of dead mercury and one part of dead gold [are to be processed] for a day with juices from the root of the plantain tree and juices from the silk-cotton tree.
It should be rubbed with cow's milk for a day and cooked for a single moment in ghee;
into that mixture, one should add sugar, grapes, āmalakī, plantain fruit, and honey.
Having added cow’s milk, *musalī*, black gram, and the seeds of *kokilākṣa*—
each four times the quantity of mercury— one should grind them with the juices of *śālmalī*.
All of that becomes the essence of Kāmadeva for one day;
one should always consume a quantity of exactly one niṣka, and afterwards drink cow’s milk.
In sexual intercourse, he shall possess a firm penis and cause the wombs of women to melt;
with the first menstrual blood of women, he should rub the *bhasmasūtaka* [mercurial preparation].
Equal parts of dead copper, silver, and sulfur, combined with sugar, honey, and clarified butter, should be consumed for one day; having taken a *niṣka* of this, one should drink milk.
The elixir known as *ratikāmarasa* is beneficial for the pleasure of amorous women;
it consists of the root of the female monkey (*vānarī*), wheat (*godhūma*), and the seeds of *kokilākṣa*.
One should cook all these ingredients—māṣa beans mixed with sugarcane juice—in ghee;
from that same preparation, one should make *vaṭaka* balls and eat two of them every day.
This accomplished beverage, when consumed, will delight even a hundred women.
Take an equal amount of pure mercury and sulfur, and for three days [process them] with the juices of white water lilies.
Having crushed and blinded it, one should cook it raw in a sand-vessel (vālukayantra),
then saturate it for one day with the juice of red Agastya and combine it with sugar.
One should always consume a measure of one niṣka of this juice, which increases virility;
it consists of a goat's testicle cooked in milk and combined with sesame and white sugar.
One may eat as much as desired and enjoy a hundred women;
[the preparation consists of] two pure *pala*s each of mercury and auspicious sulfur.
One *karṣa* of purified gold, one *pala* of purified copper,
and four *niṣkas* of silver ash— all these should be processed with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) for one day.
Having ground it and sealed it, one should cook it in a *bhūdharayantra* for one day and then extract it;
having crushed it with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), one should eat a pill the size of a jujube fruit.
Known as Anaṅgasundarī, she enjoys a hundred women;
[this is achieved by] the powder of the root of the śālmali tree mixed with honey and sugar.
One should consume one *pala* [of the preparation] and afterwards drink milk with sugar;
pure mercury should be rubbed with the juices of *śālmali* for one fortnight.
One should rub pure fragrant substances with their respective juices separately for three weeks;
then these two, taken in equal parts, should again be rubbed with clarified butter for four yāmas.
One should bind that ball in a cloth and cook it with clarified butter for two watches (six hours);
thereafter, one should rub it with the juices of the *śālmalī* tree for three days.
One should place it inside a glass flask within a sand-bath apparatus and cook it;
one should drop the juice of *śālmali* into the interior of the flask for the duration of a day.

by consuming their leaves, one becomes immortal at that very moment.

Likewise, there is an elephant-stone (*hastiśilā*) there; one should dig to the south of it for a depth of one cubit (*hastamātra*), and there one will see [a mark] shaped like the fruit of the *jambū* tree.
The stone there is said to be perceptible by touch with effort;
it is known by the name Hastiśiras, and that very stone is called Hastiśilā.
One yojana to the south of that place stands the famous Chāyāchattra, which is the form of Śiva as declared by Śiva.
That field is circular and measures one hundred cubits;
no one can see him as he goes beneath it.
The perfected one becomes equal to Rudra and sports throughout the three worlds;
or else, he may accomplish from afar that which is known as the eightfold supernatural power (*aṣṭasiddhi*).
One should grind together mica, gold, and mercury, increasing the quantity of each in successive order;
then, one should carefully encase that globule with the three metals in their proper sequence.
Having tied that cloth to another garment, one should fasten it firmly to the top of a bamboo pole;
having consecrated it with the Kālī mantra, one should place it within a parasol made of shadows.
In a single moment, that tip of the bamboo becomes a pill;
the practitioner should place it in his mouth, for it bestows the power of moving through the sky.
Likewise, having bound realgar and iron sulfate within a bamboo tube, one should insert it;
he whose eyes are anointed with these two beholds the treasure buried in the earth.
Having tied the sword to a bamboo pole and consecrated it with the previously mentioned mantra, one should hold that sword in the hand; thus, one shall become a conqueror of the three worlds.
Having tied a piece of yellow orpiment (gorocanā) in a cloth, one should place it inside a bamboo tube;
by applying a forehead mark (tilaka) with that very substance, one bewilders the entire world upon seeing it.
Having cast mineral collyrium and soot right there as before,
one whose eyes are anointed with that cannot be seen even by the gods.
Having cast off the sandals by that yoga, one should wear them on one's feet;
then, wherever one desires, one goes there at that very moment.
In the same way, having thrown a red cloth there and wrapped himself in it, the practitioner becomes invisible; however, when the cloth is removed, he is seen again.
Having made a ball of mercury mixed with gold and mica, one should place it at the tip of a bamboo stalk;
when empowered by mantra, that becomes a substance capable of transmuting by mere touch.
At the western gate of Śrīśaila is the one named Brahmeśvareśvara;
they say that his liṅga is called Sparśa, and Durgā is likewise present right there.
As for the ninth step in the river, it stands in such a manner at the gateway of the deity; one should behold it as having the color of mung beans.
To the southwest of Brahmeśvara is situated a grove of tamarind trees;
in that grove stands a pool, and there resides Caṇḍikā.
Standing on one leg beneath a *ciñcā* tree, one should pluck a leaf from that tree;
having tied it in a cloth, one should cast it into the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and perform a bath there.
At the conclusion of the bath, a bundle (poṭalī) should be taken; all those [fish] become fish.
One should cook them with their wood, discarding the throat, the tail, and the head.
Having assigned one portion to the deity, the second shall belong to the guest;
having eaten the third portion, the practitioner becomes momentarily unconscious.
At that very moment, he becomes a perfected one (siddha) and perceives the earth as having openings;
he attains freedom from old age and death, and cannot be harmed even by the gods.
To the northern part of Alampura, there shall be a village named Bhīmapāduka;
one should dig the earth for a distance of one cubit at the side of that village.
Those touches which are to be grasped are curved like serpents;
she who is the deity renowned as Yogeśvarī resides in Alampura.
Indeed, in front of the Goddess is a delightful cave;
one should dig the earth there, and stones resembling frogs should be taken along with cat excrement.
Having mixed [the ingredients], one should cast it into tin; that tin will attain the state of silver.
A wise person should consume those stones along with honey and clarified butter.
At the northern gate of Śrīśaila, there is a deity named Maheśa;
a *bhramarāmra* tree stands there, and its fruits are indeed ripe.
One should cause [the vessel] to burst; then bees, together with their life-force, emerge.
Having recognized this sign, one should abandon those bees.
One should cook the fruits with milk and drink as much milk as desired;
by that, a slight fainting may occur, and upon regaining consciousness, one should drink again.
If one practices in this way for three weeks, that person will possess a vajra-body;
freed from wrinkles and gray hair, they shall live as long as the moon and stars.
A man shall become a knower of all speech and possess the speed of the wind.
By means of that very single mango fruit from which the bees have been removed,
one thousand sprouts of the *palavaṅga* tree will certainly be liquefied and then solidified.
"By casting [the seed], one attains longevity; this is the truth spoken by the Lord.
Having pierced that fruit and then extracted the bee from it..."
Having placed one karṣa of pure mercury and an equal amount of black mica into that [vessel],
and having sealed its mouth, one should smear it with a mixture of clay and cow dung.
Once dried in the shade, one should cook it for one watch (three hours) with decoctions derived from mangoes;
the pills, which are naturally cool, should be taken while still within the fruit.

When placed in the mouth, it grants the power of flight (khecarī) and invisibility; when of great potency, one becomes equal to Bṛhaspati through its decoction and may live as long as the moon and stars endure.
One should pierce silver, copper, or mercury with a ten-millionth part [of the essence];
then, as before, one should cast black mica and pure mercury into that result.
Likewise, one should coat it with clay, cow dung, and wild lotuses, and then enclose it in a crucible;
once it has become naturally cool, its essence should be extracted along with honey and ghee.
By always consuming a mere *guñjā* [of this], a man becomes a youth after one month;
as a hero endowed with the strength of nine elephants, he shall live for a day of Brahmā.
He exists, world-renowned and worthy of worship with the fivefold offerings,
by means of the mantra *oṃ huṃ phaṭ* through the practitioners who are free from conceptual construction.
Having gazed toward the western quarter, one shall instantly behold divine celestial chariots in the sky; thereby, a great conviction arises.
Then, in the western direction, the wise one should go and cross a river;
there a cave is seen, and he should enter it facing west.
One should travel alone and free from conceptual construction for three yojanas;
there, a plantain grove extending five yojanas in width will be seen.
In its center is an exceedingly vast lake filled with water;
in the middle of that [lake] is a lion-throne resembling pure crystal.
Upon seeing him, one should prostrate on the ground like a staff and recite the mantra:
*oṃ hrīṃ vidyāvāgīśvarādhipataye hrīṃ oṃ svāhā*.
Having performed the ritual bath with diligence, one should subsequently recite it one hundred thousand times.
Having eaten as much as desired of bulbs, roots, fruits, and so forth, [one should proceed].
Then, above the lion-throne, the Supreme Lord is seen, resembling pure crystal, possessing four arms and three eyes.
By means of hymns, mantras, and prostrations, bowing down again and again, he indeed grants whatever boon the practitioner desires; of this there is no doubt.
There are one hundred abodes there, as well as one hundred and nine wells;
there are that same number of groves and forests known as Nandana.
Likewise, there are nine hundred ponds in the grove of plantain trees;
there are as many openings to the caves, and just as many *kalpa* trees.
Right there, a yakṣiṇī named Maukalī stood manifest;
she said, "Give me food if you desire what you wish for."
Then, O Supreme Goddess, one should tell him: "I shall give [you food]";
the wise man should cause milk-rice or fruit-food to be offered before him.
She said: "Hold this son of mine for a moment against your chest;
when you do not release him onto the ground, then the eightfold supernatural powers will be yours."
"I shall give it to you, of this there is no doubt—either at the end of the meal or when it has been discarded;
however, I perform the withdrawal [of the breath] once it is released, therefore protect it with great effort."
In this manner, the heroic practitioner should act; he shall attain accomplishment and go toward the northern direction to that lake, which is half a *yojana* away.
There is a divine forest there called Nandana, filled with flowers;
by the mere scent of those flowers, hunger and thirst no longer exist.
Alternatively, one should eat a single fruit from that tree as desired;
by merely eating it, a person shall possess a vajra-body.
The lake should go toward the southern direction for a quarter of a yojana;
there, the Nandana grove is seen, filled with pomegranate trees.
The perfected one (siddha) should eat that fruit and live for a thousand yugas;
he should then go half a krośa toward the eastern direction of that lake.
There, in the dark Nandana grove filled with dhātrī fruits, one should eat those fruits; thus one shall live for three hundred kalpas.
One should go one yojana to the western part of that lake;
there, the Nandana grove is seen, filled with bilva fruits.
The hero who consumes that fruit shall live as long as the moon, sun, and stars;
in the delightful Nandana grove, there shall be a linga of blue color.
One should enter through the northern gate; there, a nāga of great strength is seen, fierce, with seven hoods, and extremely terrifying.
One should perform a salutation to him and utter "hruṃ hruṃ"; one should then lift [the mantra] up.
Then he speaks these words: "I grant you invisibility."
Go to the western gate; there dwells a divine maiden.
O great hero, the practitioner should go there while reciting the mantra.
When she is pleased, she will give the necklace, yet she does not grant entrance;
one should wear that necklace upon the neck, and one will become Vāgīśvara in person.
Then one should go to the southern gate, where there is a terrifying being with disheveled hair, crooked eyes, a mace in hand, and clad in the directions as his garment.
Having seen the blue-colored Kṣetrapāla, one should recite the mantra:
*ha hā he he haṃ hruṃ* and ending with *phaṭ huṃ svāhā*.
By the recitation of this mantra, Kṣetrapāla becomes pleased;
he bestows the siddhi of the Khecarī, but never [grants] entrance.
Then, on the eastern side, there is a door where Gaṇeśvara is seen; the practitioner should indeed worship him and then enter.
A divine bow and a captivating linga are seen there;
one should worship Śiva with the mantra consisting of the syllable "ra" alone, and not otherwise.
Then, having fasted for a day and night, one should perform recitation there;
Rudra becomes manifest and grants a boon as desired.
Such are the supernatural powers (*siddhis*) found in the Kadalī forest;
there, at the entrance, the opening to Padmāvatī’s subterranean chamber is inscribed with letters.
One *yojana* to the east of the lake stands [the city];
having performed *vamana* (emesis) and *recana* (purgation), the practitioner should enter there.
When he has gone as far as a hundred *dhanvantaras*, the hero shall see a drum there; having seen it, Padmāvatī shall then play it correctly.
Having arrived, he bestows the nectar of immortality, by drinking which one becomes immortal;
therefore, he indeed entreats him: "Come to my abode."
Accept five hundred divine maidens as your retinue;
I shall become your wife for as long as Brahmā lives.
At its end, we shall go to the supreme abode; of this there is no doubt.
The deity Kadambeshvara is located in the south-eastern direction.
There is a Kadambaka tree situated at the edge of that eastern pond;
having gathered its leaves, one should smear them with pungent oil.
The wise one should cook them with the oils of those tree seeds or with their wood;
all those fish will then appear, and he should place them in a copper vessel.
Excluding the neck, tail, and head, one should consume [the meat] with honey and clarified butter;
at that very moment, one becomes a perfected being, equal to Rudra and possessed of great strength.
And the tree that stands at the site of the river at Kuṇḍaleśvara—by means of the sequential application as before, accomplishment shall be attained; there is no doubt in this matter.
To the north of the deity Kapoteśvara stands Puṣpagiri;
one should diligently perform its circumambulation three times.
Then, by ascending to the head [of that image], a man shall attain the power of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*).
To its northeast direction stands the door of Chelikā.
One should enter there facing north for the distance of three bows;
stones shaped like mice are found there, and one should collect them.
Having ground that same [substance] with buttermilk, one should drink it alone;
one will attain a state of swoon and, becoming perfected, shall rise up in an instant and live for three days of Brahmā.
That very [substance] shall effect the transmutation by touch of all metals;
having fasted for a day and night, one shall attain perfection before the deity.
To the south of the deity Kapoteśvara are two deities;
in the space between them, one should dig down to the depth of a hip, where there will be objects resembling gorocanā.
Having taken those stones, one should grind them with honey and clarified butter;
by drinking that, a mortal becomes long-lived for an eon—of this there is no doubt.
To the northwest of the deity Kapoteśvara, one should dig a pit measuring one cubit;
there will be stones resembling pigeons that pierce upon touch.
Having performed the propitiation of the deity, one should cause another to stand [there];
at the northeast of the god Mallikārjuna is the Bhṛgupātana [tīrtha].
There exists a sacrificial pit situated near that;
from it, one should take earth, mix it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and heat it with embers of the Khadira wood.
Then, one should pour [the liquid] over the iron, which becomes like a blue lotus;
having heated it thoroughly, one should sprinkle it with honey and ghee seven times, again and again.
A man who wears that ball in his mouth becomes equal to Viṣṇu;
[it is located] in the district of Krośodadhipāṭaka, in the eastern part of Bhṛgupāta.
In front of it is the famous mountain named Acchataila;
to its west is the entrance to a cave, and within it is a distance of five dhanus.
