But upon entering, a pool is seen whose liquid has the luster of lac juice; having collected it in a gourd vessel, that [liquid] shall possess the power of piercing through ten million [atoms].
{Sparśavedha:
A rock near a temple} To the east of the deity Mallikārjuna, there is one world-renowned.
There exists a wall belonging to Candragupta, and there is a palace there as well.
To its east stands a shrine, and to the east of that shrine is a great stone;
it is known as Mudgavarṇā, and it possesses the power to pierce through by touch.
There is a famous elephant named Gaja; having mounted it with a concentrated mind, one should pluck a blade of grass from its back, and all of that shall turn into gold.
On the northern side of the elephant, one should dig the earth to the depth of a knee;
there are those [substances] shaped like jambu fruits which are "piercers by touch."
Alternatively, one should dig beneath an elephant until reaching knee-deep;
therefrom, one obtains the supreme perfected triangular pill, which has the power to pierce a target at a distance of one hundred thousand [yojanas].
To the northwest of Śrīśaila is situated the Devahrada Tīrtha;
there, in that pool, are stones the color of mung beans which possess the power of touch-transmission.
In that regard, the supreme *liṅga* resembling a tortoise brings about the piercing of touch;
having performed worship on the full moon of the month of Kṛttikā, one should accomplish [the rite].
Two *gavyūtis* from there is the place known by the name Nīlavana;
there the *liṅga* is blue in color, and the water is likewise.
There are stones resembling horses, clouds, and crows that possess the power of penetration by touch;
they are found inside the temple of the gods; one should dig them out from a depth of one knee's length and take them away.
To the southwest of Śrīśaila resides the goddess named Guṇḍiprabhā;
from her summit, earth from a pit should be taken—yellow in color—and one should burn it with sacrificial vessels.
From that, gold of shimmering form emerges without a doubt;
and right there, bees shall appear as before, bestowing their fruit.
Likewise, at the auspicious and vast holy site named Tambīpura,
which is renowned as "Ever-Fruitful," the wise practitioner should perform the rite as before.
The place named Mahānandeśvara is to the southwest of Śrīśaila;
one should go to its northeastern side by way of the royal road.
The deity named Kālavarṇeśvara has a preeminent sacrificial pit;
in its center, there exists a mercury resembling an indragopaka insect.
The seven molten metals become gold by sprinkling [them] with that [water].
To the northeast of Śrīśaila, there shall be the deity Turaleśvara.
To its north is the most famous and excellent Umā mountain;
upon its summit stand beautiful *darbha* grasses with the luster of tridents.
Having dug down to the depth of a hip-breadth beneath that [spot], one should take blue earth;
one should bake it with wood from the Akṣa tree and offer a portion to the deity.
One should assign a portion to the guest and likewise a portion to the fire;
one should consume the portion for oneself, and such a man shall live for ten thousand kalpas.
There, near Ileśvara, is the famous Koṭīśvara;
merely by touching a flower placed before it, one becomes empowered by touch.
And Acaleśa, the supreme bestower of the piercing of touch, is located there at that very spot;
it is found one yojana to the south of Leśa.
There is a beautiful golden stone named Amareśvaradeva;
upon its surface, one should place either beef or mahāmāṃsa.
Having been kindled with *badarī* wood, at dawn that cloth fragment of the women, permeated by their menstrual blood, appears like gold.
One should stir that [substance] with a stone and preserve it in a gourd vessel;
by the mere touch of it, iron becomes gold.
In Śrīśaila, here and there, stones exist in the form of lumps;
one should always consume one karṣa of their powder mixed with an equal amount of triphalā.
Indeed, after half a month, it destroys old age, and one shall live as long as the moon and stars endure.
To the southwest of the king of mountains (Gandhamādana) is the lord Paṭāhakarṇa.
And in the north-eastern direction of that [site], at a distance of twenty-five bow-lengths, there is a stone slab two cubits high; one should dig two cubits deep there.
One should take thirty stones resembling the hollows of ears of grain;
having heated them until they are the color of fire, one should sprinkle them with the juices of *kūṣmāṇḍa* plants.
From the midst of that [curd], one should take the butter as a portion for the deity;
one portion should be for the guest, and the wise man should consume one portion himself.
He may fall into a swoon by day or night, yet the man awakens;
such a hero shall live for ten thousand years, free from wrinkles and grey hair.
The second stairway of that deity is one that effects transmutation through touch;
moreover, by the side of that deity, there are stones that are white and yellow.
Without doubt, one should collect all the earth from every touch;
to the east of that deity, there shall be a well not very far away.
In the midst of that are stones resembling frogs that pierce by touch;
to the north of that deity is the famous Liṅga Mountain.
And on its northern side there shall be a river flowing toward the east;
on the western portion of that river is a linga of tawny color.
There, a pool filled with mountain waters shall be a piercer [of the vital points] in an instant;
it is located two yojanas to the south of Maheśa, at the site of Caṇḍikā.
She is renowned as the goddess Piṇḍādevī; to her northwest stands a well, in the middle of which there are stones the color of mung beans.
Likewise, all those that are beneficial and bright are penetrators by touch;
here, the method of penetration for all of them is prescribed through contact.
If it is coarse, one should grind it finely and have a crucible made from it;
within that, one should cause the eight metals to be melted together.
All that becomes gold; in this way one may act as desired, even if [the substance] is minute, wherever the eight molten metals are found.
One should cast all of that into the center, and it shall all become gold.
To the northwest of Mallikārjuna stands the holy site (tīrtha) known as Sarveśvara.
Half a yojana away from there, on the southern side along the waterway, one sees the place called Ḍāṅgarika; there, upon its summit, [is found].
Black *dhātrī* fruits are found; one should eat them as desired for seven days, and that person will become one with a vajra-body.
Freed from wrinkles and grey hair, one shall live for three hundred kalpas;
and to the south of that is the great mountain Kākali.
There stands a plantain pillar; the practitioner should enter there and go for half a krośa, where a pool of mercury is seen.
Having taken an alābu vessel, the mercury will become "piercing ten million" (koṭivedhī);
in that forest there is a peacock made of blue-colored stone.
At the tip of his mouth, there is a twelve-finger-long blue vessel;
by casting a dry bamboo stalk into its center, it becomes new in an instant.
On that day, leaves, fruits, and flowers grow [on the plant], and not otherwise.
Having thrown one *prastha* of mercury into it, one should then remove the water.
One should indeed drink that [substance] equal to honey; at that very moment one becomes unconscious, but after a Muhūrta one regains the kingdom and shall live for a thousand Yugas.
On the southeast side of the mountain resides Guṭikāsiddhakeśvara;
one should dig five cubits into the ground in front of him.
There are stones shaped like jujube fruits that grant the power of flight; having taken even one of these, those who travel through the sky should hold it in their mouth.
On Śrīśaila, the procedure for all the yogas previously mentioned is now declared:
having first performed the ritual placement of the mantra (mantranyāsa), one should subsequently recite it one hundred thousand times.
By that means, indeed, one will swiftly attain various accomplishments (siddhis).
One should invoke the deity of the sacred field (kṣetradevatā);
there, the deity, having become manifest in a dream, bestows a boon.

Thus, the practice for the attainment of Śrī Giri should be performed by those devoted to the mantra, who are exceedingly steadfast, who are devotees and practitioners of that [path], who are intent on the worship of Śambhu, who daily observe the rules of worship, who are dedicated to *japa*, and who have mastered the traditional scriptures (*āmnāya*). Otherwise, alas, it will certainly become fruitless and result in nothing but affliction.

May He—the Lord of the Nameless, who created the groups of ether, consciousness, self, wind, fire, water, and earth; the aspects of Sadasiva, Vidya, Shiva, Shakti, and Bhairava; the five-faced Shrikantha;
Ishvara, Rudra, Vishnu, Brahma, and the gods; and the hosts of moon, sun, and stars—protect this entire world of moving and unmoving beings.

The best of elixirs produces excellent gold; through sound, touch, and smoke, it pierces [the body] in that very instant. It removes sins and, according to the number of repetitions—whether by the hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, billions, or lakhs—it grants, by means of the proper method, the power of flight and the imperishable state of Śiva. Homage to that Supreme One!
Having bowed to the goddess Śrī Pārvatī, Bhairava, and the lineage of Siddhas,
I shall expound the *Rasaratnākara*, which brings auspiciousness to both the body and metals.
The names of mercury (rasa) are: Śivabīja, Sūtarāja, Pārada, and Rasendraka; these are the names of mercury, as well as others, O Śivā.
It bestows the supreme perfection of the state of Śiva upon practitioners;
it is declared to be the seed-syllable of Śiva, the granter of all accomplishments.
Because he was produced from Paraśiva, he is called Sūta; and because he impels [the soul], he is so designated.
Since he grants the further shore of saṃsāra, he is known as Pārada.
Metals become liquid through excellent treatment, and even bodies [become so];
therefore, it is renowned as Rasendra (the Lord of Tastes), and it is known as Rasa because of its fluidity.
In all the treatises on alchemy, the divine mercury and elixir were indicated by Śambhu in the past; yet, because they were merely indicated, they were not understood.
The Siddhas obtained [this knowledge] from the mouth of Śiva; their success comes from its practice.
The lineage of transmission and the reasoning [behind it] were concealed by them within their own scriptures.
I too received it from his mouth and accomplished it in many ways thereafter,
having thoroughly examined all the treatises on alchemy in their proper sequence.
For the benefit of practitioners, it is now being revealed;
for without the sequence there is no scripture, and without the scripture there is no sequence.

Having understood the scripture endowed with its proper sequence, he who practices it becomes a possessor of accomplishment (*siddhi*). An *ācārya* is one who possesses knowledge, is skillful, and is an expert in the science of mercury (*rasa-śāstra*).
Accomplished in mantra, a great hero, immovable and devoted to Śiva,
always steadfast as a devotee of the Goddess, he is intent upon the sacrifice to the deity.
One who knows the specific details of all traditions, who is skilled in the work of alchemy,
and who is endowed with such characteristics shall be a teacher of the science of mercury.
The disciples were devoted to their guru, possessed of good conduct, truthful, firm in their vows, free from laziness, knowers of their own duty, and always observers of the commands.
Free from deceit and envy, initiated into the traditional practices of their lineage,
they are supreme practitioners, tranquil, and devoted to the propitiation of the mantra.
Disciples endowed with such characteristics as these shall be for the sake of attaining the *rasa*;
likewise, attendants and companions who are diligent are all like disciples, yet superior to them.
Those of noble birth and devoted to their master should be employed in the work of mercury (*rasakarma*);
those who are atheists, of wicked conduct, swindlers, or violators of the guru’s bed [must be excluded].
Those who desire to acquire knowledge through theft, force, or deceit—
none of their gems, mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth, will ever succeed.
If they act out of delusion, they destroy their own wealth;
there is no happiness for them in this world, nor likewise in the next world.
Therefore, just as the Guru is satisfied solely by the power of devotion,
so too must that [devotion] be cultivated by the disciple for the sake of attaining the realization of the science of aesthetic essence (rasavidyā).
Having obtained the boon through the union of hand and head,
one should practice it well in a delightful kingdom of Dharma, in a region free from affliction, [at] the Rasa-shala.
In that auspicious and prosperous city, inhabited by Umā and Maheśvara,
the wise one should perform the practice of the king of essences (rasarāja).
In an exceedingly beautiful grove, adorned with four gates,
a very spacious and delightful hall should be constructed there.
Equipped with proper windows and adorned with divine paintings,
a *rasamaṇḍapa* should be constructed nearby on level, elongated ground. Rrā 3.1.25.
It was well-protected, adorned with wide door-leaves and bolts,
enriched with banners, umbrellas, and canopies, and hung with garlands of flowers.
Resounding with the sounds of kettledrums, lutes, bells, and horns,
the ground there should be made level, very firm, and like a mirror.
In the center of that, a beautiful altar endowed with the proper characteristics should be constructed.
[Therein should be placed] three *niṣkas* of mercury-linga and nine *niṣkas* of gold leaf.
One should grind it with sour juice for one *yāma* and fashion a *liṅga* from it;
then, placed in a *jambīra* fruit within a *dolāyantra*, one should cook it in *sāranāla* for a day.
One should worship that Liṅga there with most auspicious offerings;
the fruit which results from the perfect worship of ten billion Liṅgas [is obtained here].
The fruit of that becomes multiplied ten millionfold by worshipping the *rasaliṅga*;
even thousands of killings of Brahmins and millions of killings of cows [are thus expiated].
They go to dissolution at that very moment from the sight of the *rasaliṅga*;
liberation is attained through its touch—this is the truth spoken by Śiva.
One should worship [the deity] with speech, with *māyā*, or with the glorious *Ghora*, the king of mantras.
He has eighteen arms, is white in color, possesses five faces, and has three eyes.
One should meditate upon the blue-throated Lord mounted upon a corpse as a *rasaliṅga*;
in his lap is the Great Goddess, with one face and four arms.

One should contemplate her as having the appearance of molten gold, wearing yellow garments, and holding a rosary and a goad in her right hands, and a noose and the gesture of fearlessness in her left hands.
Vāṅmāyā, Śrī, Kāmarājaśakti, Bīja, Rasā, and Aṅkuśā;
preceded by "Namaḥ" to these twelve, this is the Kāmavidyā Rasāṅkuśā.
With these, one should worship the Goddess with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and so forth;
one should worship Nandin, Bhṛṅgin, and Mahākāla according to the sequence starting from the eastern direction.
One should worship with name-mantras beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*;
in this manner, daily worship should be performed there for the sake of attaining mastery over mercury (*rasasiddhi*).

The initiation by means of mercury (*rasadīkṣā*) has been taught by Śiva; it should indeed be bestowed upon the practitioner by a teacher who is joyful in spirit, according to the prescribed procedure.
At an auspicious moment, under a favorable constellation, and endowed with the strength of the moon and stars,
he should prepare a water-pot filled with water and joined with gold, gems, and fruits.
One should place [the vessel] before the mercury-liṅga, which has been wrapped in a divine cloth,
and worship it with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, incense, lamps, and food offerings.
At the conclusion of the worship, one should perform the fire-oblation (havana) in a well-characterized yoni-shaped sacrificial pit,
using sesame seeds, clarified butter, milk-rice, and flowers— each offered one hundred and eight times individually.

At the conclusion of the fire-offering (homa), one should bring the disciple— endowed with the power of Kākinī and devoted to the perfection of mercury (rasasiddhi)— by means of the Aghora mantra and the Rasāṅkuśī mudrā.
The Kākinī is she whose hair is curly, who is dark-complexioned and lotus-eyed;
she is beautiful, youthful, variegated, possessed of broad hips, and auspicious.
Her teeth were closely set, she was bent by the weight of her full breasts,
she was soft in her kisses, embraces, and touch, and she spoke gently.
Adorned with a vulva resembling a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree,
that woman who bears flowers during the dark fortnight is known as a *kākinī*.
In the practice of binding mercury and in the preparation of elixirs, a *kākiṇī* (a young woman) is supreme;
in her absence, however, any beautiful young woman will do.
To her, for three weeks, one *karṣa* of sulphur mixed with ghee should be given every morning; she will then become equal to a *kākinī*.
{Rasadīkṣā (continued)} Thus, that best of gurus, endowed with power, should initiate him;
he should consecrate him, who has been well-bathed, with the pure waters of the ritual jars.
The true guru should bestow the Aghora-Aṅkuśī Vidyā upon the disciple;
then, according to his capacity, the disciple should offer a teacher’s fee (gurudakṣiṇā).
Then, by the command of the Guru, one should recite each mantra separately one hundred thousand times;
one should perform oblations in a triangular fire-pit measuring one cubit, using a tenth part [of the recitations].
Having worshipped the lotus mandala, which is square and beautifully adorned with four doors,
having offered jasmine flowers smeared with the three sweets at the conclusion of the full oblation, and having performed the worship of the maiden,
one should then enter the auspicious hall, which has been well-smeared and contains a beautiful altar.
There, upon the altar, one should properly draw a two-cubit hexagonal mandala with vermilion, and outside of that, an eight-petaled lotus.
One should place a lotus that is square and adorned with four doors;
upon its pericarp, one should indeed set a mortar made of iron and marked with gold lines.
In the center of that, one should worship the king of mercury (rasarāja) in a quantity of exactly one hundred palas,
or fifty, or twenty-five, as if it were a mercury-liṅga.
One should worship these six— diamond, vaikrānta, diamond-stone, magnet-stone, borax, and bhūnāga— as the śaktis upon the six petals.
The secondary minerals (uparasas) are known to be sulphur, talc, green vitriol, realgar, orpiment, antimony, mica, magnetite, and red ochre. Rrā 3.1.57.
These secondary essences (uparasa) are to be worshipped in the eight petals, proceeding in order from the east to the northeast.
[The primary essences (mahārasa):]
Rasaka, vimalā, tāpya, capalā, tuttha, and añjana.
Cinnabar and sasyaka—these are known as the great minerals (mahārasa);
one should worship them on the tips of the petals, starting from the east and ending in the northeast.
At the eastern gate are gold and silver; at the southern, copper and lead;
at the western, tin and magnetite; and at the northern, steel and mica.
One should worship all of this, including the goad, with the Aghora mantra.
[The equipment of the alchemist:
vit, kāñjika, yantras, alkali, clay, and salt. (Rrā 3.1.61)
The furnace, the crucible, the blowpipe, chaff, charcoal, sand, and stones;
the bellows, the tongs, the single slab, the mortar, and also the pestle.
The tools of a goldsmith, all types of scales, and various vessels made of clay, wood, copper, iron, and so forth; Rāvaṇa 3.1.63.
One should worship the divine medicinal herbs, the various groups, the coloring agents,
and the unctuous substances outside the entrance with the root mantra.
The five-syllable mantra is *vāṃ*, *māyāṃ*, *heṃ*, then *kṣmeṃ* and *kṣmaḥ*.
With this root mantra, one should worship Bhairava there.
Then one should proclaim the names of all the *rasasiddhas*:
Vyālācārya, Candrasena, Subuddhi, and Naravāhana.
Nāgārjuna, Ratnaghoṣa, Surānanda, Yaśodhara,
Indradyumna, Māṇḍavya, Carpaṭi, and Śūrasenaka.
Vāḍaba, Nāgabuddhi, Khaṇḍa, Kāpālika, Hara, Kāmalin, Tāttvika, Śambhu, Loka, Lampaṭa, and Śārada.
Bāṇāsura, Muniśreṣṭha, Govinda, Kapila, and Bali—
all these were lords of the earth, masters of the elixir, and possessed of great strength.
They always move through all the worlds, free from old age and death;
numbering twenty-seven, they are the bestowers of the attainment of the elixir.
They are to be saluted and worshipped with diligence; thereafter, one should prepare the elixir (*rasāyana*), gladden the twice-born and the gods, and satisfy one's chosen deity.
One should satisfy and worship with devotion the Kumārīs, Yoginīs, Yogins, Māyikas, and Sādhakas, according to one's own capacity.
Thus, one should perform the festival of the essence (rasotsava), endowed with all necessary requisites,
for the sake of pacifying all obstacles and bestowing the fruit of all desired goals.
Otherwise, if that deluded soul, devoid of a guru, desires to perform the practice of the *sūta* without the sequence of mantra-initiation, [he shall fail].
One does not attain success even through hundreds of millions of efforts;
therefore, with every exertion, one should perform the rites prescribed in the scriptures.

Those who possess correct means of accomplishment, who are diligent, endowed with a guru, adorned by the king’s command, skilled in various arts, devoted to mercury (*rasa*), wealthy, sought after by people, expert in the work of measuring, apparatus, and proper cooking, and proficient in all medicinal herbs—for them alone, through the power of the ritual procedure, does the glorious mercury (*pārada*) succeed; not otherwise.

Through devotion, through daily inquiry into the scriptures, through the observance of the rules of worship, through immersion in the bliss of one's own Self, through acts for the welfare of others, through the concealment of one's deeds,

through constant service to the true Guru, through spiritual experience, and through the cultivation of the true state of being as the Son, one's own rays will clearly manifest by the power of the boon from the True Tradition.

The various groups [of substances], beginning with mercury (rasa) and ending with iron (loha), are declared to be beneficial for purification, killing, and in some cases, for saturation (bhāvanā). Rājanighaṇṭu 3.2.2.

If no specific limb is mentioned, the root [ingredient] should be used; if none is specified for all limbs, it should be liquid. In the preparation of medicinal juices (*rasa*), when no measure is stated, the measure should be understood as equal.
{The Alkali Section} One should burn sesame, apāmārga, plantain, citraka, ginger, radish, śigru, mokṣa, and palāśa— all together within a sealed crucible.
Having stirred it with water and bound it with cloths, one should take the water from below;
then, that water should be purified and cooked in a clay vessel over a fire.
That which remains after the liquid has been extracted is to be taken; this is known as tree-alkali.
(The White Group, the White Class)
Powdered substances, the elbow-joint, conch-shells, mother-of-pearl, and cowries constitute the white category.
The group of feces (*viḍvarga*) consists of the excrement of pigeons, blue jays, vultures, peacocks, and roosters.
The group of acids (*amlavarga*).
Cāṅgerī, sour chickpeas (caṇakāmla), mātuluṅga, and amlavetasa; // Rrā_3.2.7 //
Ciñcā, nāraṅga, and jambīra are known as the group of sour substances;
the five salts consist of sāmudra, saindhava, kāca, cullikā, and suvarcala.
The five salts consist of this [set]:
the three alkalies (trikṣāra), sajji-kṣāra, yavakṣāra, and ṭaṅkaṇa as the third.
This is known as the "Tri-kṣāra" (the three alkalis) derived from goats, horses, buffaloes, and cows;
the group of urines includes those of women, ewes, donkeys, camels, and elephants.
The five friends (*mitrapañcaka*):
honey, clarified butter, borax, *guñjā*, and jaggery constitute the five friends.
[This concludes] the section on bile (*pittavarga*).
Human, horse, peacock, cow, and fish bile constitute the group of bile (pitta).
The group of fats (*vasāvarga*) is considered to consist of the fats of fish, snakes, humans, rams, and peacocks.
The group of bloods (*raktavarga*).
Madder, saffron, lac, pomegranate, and red sandalwood;
Bandhūka and karavīra constitute this red group.
[The yellow group consists of] kusumbha, kiṃśuka, rātri, pataṅga, and madayantikā.
This yellow group has indeed been described; now hear the collection of divine medicinal herbs (*divyauṣadhigaṇa*):
*ajakarṇī*, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *rudantī*, and *kākatuṇḍikā*.
Haṃsapādī, vyāghranakhī, cāṇḍālī, kṣīrakandaka, vandhyākarkoṭakī, rambhā, gojihvā, and kokilākṣaka.
Śākavṛkṣa, Hemavallī, Pātālagaruḍī, Śamī, Kaṭutumbī, Vajralatā, Sūraṇa, and Vanasūraṇa.
Meṣaśṛṅgī, cakramarda, jalakumbhī, śatāvarī, guñjā,
kośātakī, nīlī, ākhukarṇī, and triparṇikā.
Kukkuṭī, kṛṣṇatulasī, puṅkhā, śvetāparājitā,
garuḍī, lāṅgalī, brāhmī, cāṅgerī, and padmacāriṇī.
Having taken the auspicious *vajra* for purification, one should place it inside the bulb of a tigress;
having smeared it with buffalo dung, one should cook it in a crucible over the fire of a balance-scale.
Having extracted it after a day and night, one should sprinkle it with horse urine;
then, having placed it again in a *vyāghrī* bulb, one should place it inside a *vajra* bulb.
One should sprinkle it with horse urine, and roast it (*puṭayet*), sprinkling it as before.
In this way, after seven days, the vajra will become pure; there is no doubt about this.
{The purification of the vajra (2):} A decoction of *kulattha* and *kodrava*, horse urine, and the milky sap of *snuhī*.
Having cast it into that vessel, one should place the *pavi* (pestle) containing the *vyāghrī* root into it;
having extracted it from the *dolāyantra* (swinging apparatus), one should cast it back again day and night.
Having placed *vyāghrī* root among the great roots, one should cook it in a "gaja-puṭa" (elephant-seal) vessel.
Once cooked, one should sprinkle it with the juice of *kāñcanī*; thus it attains purification.
(Vajra-purification, 3)
Ākhukarṇī, meghanāda, priyaṅgu, meṣaśṛṅgikā,
amlavetasa, nirguṇḍī, kulattha, kodrava, and śamī.
The Sage should prepare an auspicious decoction with horse urine;
having placed the *vajra* in either *jambīra* or *sūraṇa*, one should cook it for a day.
Through the previous decoction in a swinging vessel (dolā), it attains purification; not otherwise.
Having smeared purified *vajra* with the blood of bedbugs (*matkuṇa*), one should then blow upon it.
One should repeatedly cast it, red-hot as fire, into the urine of a donkey;
having been smeared and heated in that same manner, one should perform this twenty-one times.
Having ground talaka with bedbugs, one should place it into that *gola*;
having sealed the crucible and heated it until solidified, one should then cast it into horse urine.
Having extracted [the powder] again in that same manner seven times, one would die.
{Vajramāraṇam (3)} [The ingredients are:
*meṣaśṛṅgī*, snake-bone, tortoise-shell, and *śilājatu*.
Sulphur, loadstone, *munipuṣpa*, and *satālaka*,
the three alkalis, the five salts, *meṣaśṛṅgī*, and *indravāruṇī*.
Vajravallī, mūṣakarṇī, and the buds of badarī;
the excrement of a rat, breast milk, the latex of snuhī and arka, and bedbugs.
The five-limbed *śarapuṅkhā*, the ichor of a female elephant, [the blood] of a man and a deer, the seed of *peṭārī*, a woman’s menses, the excrement of a pigeon, and realgar; Rrā 3.2.31.
The flowers of vākucī, the five parts (pañcāṅga) of nimba,
the five parts of the dhātrī tree, gorambhā, and goat’s urine.
One should mix haṃsapādī, vajrakanda, the fruit of bṛhatī, sūraṇa, gojihvā, karkaṭa-māṃsa, and the group of urines.
This [substance], whether taken as a whole or individually, well-compacted according to its availability,
one should place into that lump along with a vajra, enclosed in a blind crucible (andhamūṣā), and subject it to heating in a closed crucible (puṭa).
Having ground *kulattha* and *kodrava* and stirred them with horse urine,
one should pour that mixture over a crucible that has been heated and removed from the *puṭa*.
In this manner, one should perform it again and again for twenty-one times,
having first taken the *vajratāla* mixed with the crushed body of a bedbug.
Having placed [the substance] into a globule and sealed the crucible, one should blow it in a fierce fire;
thus it should be smelted seven times and sprinkled with horse urine.
By this sequential method, death occurs with certainty;
one should grind that dead substance in a mortar—this is declared as the perfected yoga (siddhayoga).
The mouth of mercury (bhrāmaka) should be heated with peṭārī seeds, ṭaṅkaṇa,
the alkali of uttaravāruṇī, sulphur, realgar, and śamī.
Having extracted [the substance] situated in the crucible with a single charge, one should rub it;
then, having sealed it as before with the aforementioned fluxes, one should cook it in the same manner.
It should be rubbed again and cooked again ten times as before;
when it is dropped into a *pātana* (sublimation) apparatus, the mercury will become perfectly purified.
Having added sulfur equal to one-tenth part of the mercury, one should grind it with juices from *jambīra* fruits for one watch (*yāma*) and then subject it to sublimation in a *pātanayantra*.
It should be rubbed again and dropped again seven times for purification;
{the purification of mercury} or alternatively, mercury should be rubbed in a heated mortar (taptakhalva) for the duration of a day.
One should cause it to fall using the powder of *kumārī* and *rajanī* in a falling apparatus (*pātanayantra*).
One should grind [the mercury] again with kanyā, agni, and triphalā, and then cause it to fall [into the crucible].
Having ground it again, one should cause it to fall again, seven times for the sake of purification.
Thus, one should perform this sevenfold process; then the mercury will become perfectly pure.
The mardana (rubbing) of all mercury is performed by grinding it in a heated mortar.
It is especially praised for purification, extraction, and digestion, as well as for coagulation,
killing, and binding.
One should place three things— [a heated] mortar, goat dung, and chaff fire— into a pit in the ground;
the mortar situated upon them becomes what is known as a "heated mortar" (taptakhalva).
An iron mortar is recommended, and the grinding tool should likewise be made of iron;
in its absence, stone-made ones are suitable for both the mortar and the grinding tool.
Alternatively, one should cause mercury to be extracted from cinnabar; that is described as follows:
[it is processed] with cow urine, buffalo urine, sesame oil, and fermented rice-gruel.
Cinnabar should be cooked for seven days in an iron vessel over a gradual fire;
one should stir it with an iron rod, repeatedly adding liquid.
Having taken that excellent substance, one should saturate it with peacock bile;
at the end of the day, one should cause it to fall into a *pātanā* apparatus by means of a fierce fire.
Freed from the seven coverings, this is known as pure mercury (śuddhasūtaka).
One should grind it again with *kanyā* and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) and cause it to fall [into the crucible];
in this manner one should perform it seven times, whereby the mercury will become perfectly purified.
For mercury extracted from cinnabar (*hiṅgulākṛṣṭa*): one should grind cinnabar with some kind of acid in a mortar for one day;
at the end of the day, one should cause it to fall using a sublimation apparatus (*pātanāyantra*) and then extract it.
Without even the eightfold karma, this Sūtra accomplishes all tasks.
This wonderful and supreme method for purifying mercury, which accomplishes all goals, has been proclaimed;
it grants abundant success through even a few ritual procedures and is indeed highly recommended for the transmutation of bodies and metals.
The six groups of eight, the eighth group, and the [final] eighth are to be purified and processed as previously described;
having been previously explained starting from diamond and ending with iron, that shall now be taught for the accomplishment of the best of elixirs.
White, red, yellow, and black are the types of Vajras corresponding to the twice-born castes and so forth;
one should identify them by their characteristics as male, female, or neuter.
Those which are circular, complete with their ridges, radiant, and very large,
are declared to be male; they are devoid of lines and spots.
Those [stones] endowed with lines and dots and having six corners are known as female (*strī*).
[Now follows] the examination of the neuter (*napuṃsaka*):
That which is triangular and has the form of a leaf is long; that which is [triangular] is neuter.
Among all [beings], men are the best; they are the piercers and the binders of mercury.
For the sake of attaining the perfection of the body, women are the vajras, while the neuter is the *krāmaka*.
Divine medicinal herbs: ajāmārī, kākamācī, devadālī, indravāruṇī,
kākajaṅghā, śikhiśikhā, sarpākṣī, and nāgavallikā.
Mīnākṣī, kṛṣṇadhattūra, balā, nāgavallī,
jayā, muṇḍī, mahābalā, pūgī, the three types of citraka, and niśā.
Mūrvā, kāñcanana, kanyā, peṭārī, sūryavartaka, viṣṇukrāntā, kāravallī, vākucī, and sinduvārikā.
Svarṇapuṣpī, khaṇḍajārī, mañjiṣṭhā, pīluka,
vacā, snuhī, raktasnuhī, bilva, kārpāsa, kaṅguṇī, and ghanā.
Palāśa, aṅkola, vijayā, meghanāda, arka, sarṣapa,
brahmadaṇḍī, mahārāṣṭrī, and white and red punarnavā.
Udumbara, somalatā, kumbhī, puṣkaramūlaka,
tilaparṇī, kṛṣṇajīrā, vṛścikālī, and kālikā.
Karavīra, agnidamanī, bṛhatī, bhūmipāṭalī, yavaciñcī, candralatā, markaṭī, and vanarājaka. (Rājanighaṇṭu 3.3.12)
Badarī, lajjarī, lākṣā, caṇā, vartulapatraka,
apāmārga, bhūkadambo, viṣamuṣṭi, and ekavīraka.
Gorambhā, kadalī, jātī, musalī, sahadevikā,
eraṇḍa, saindhava, pathyā, śuṇṭhī, and maṇḍūkaparṇikā.
Marūvaka, asafoetida, vāla, lakṣmaṇā, hastimūlikā, all the milk-exuding trees, and likewise various kinds of poison; Rrā_3,3.15.
The group of divine medicinal herbs is renowned for the preparation of the king of elixirs (rasarāja);
one should employ them either individually or collectively, according to what is available.
{The Chapter on Poisons} Through various forest-born substances possessing intense odors, tastes, and tactile qualities,
by means of rubbing and sweating, mercury is killed and also bound. Rrā 3.3.17.
Raktaśṛṅgī, kālakūṭa, hāridra, saktūka, and likewise mauṣṭika constitute the group of poisons; the preparation of the crucible (mūṣā) is now described.
{The production of the vajramūṣā}
Husk, cloth, and mud in equal parts, with a quarter-part of brick and a quarter-part of stone,
should be processed for a day with the juices of *vajravallī*.
One should grind [the ingredients] and fashion a crucible called *vajramūṣā*, which binds mercury;
it is made from anthill clay, charcoal, and old iron dross. (Vajramūṣā 2)
This white stone and all these [other ingredients] should be ground together in equal proportions;
likewise, burnt husks equal to the whole [mixture] should be combined with water and rubbed thoroughly.
One should fashion a crucible-casket and seal the joint with that very [substance];
this Vajramūṣā is of great power and accomplishes all tasks.
{Vajramūṣā (3)}:
Charcoal that has been burnt, husks that have been burnt, and anthill earth that has been burnt;
the excrement of elephants and horses that has been burnt until it has turned black.
The leaves of *pāṣāṇabhedin* and black earth in equal parts should be ground with the juices of *vajravallī* for one day, or else thoroughly dried.
With that [clay], one should fashion a crucible (*koṣṭha*), a curved tube (*vaṅkanāla*), and a diamond-crucible (*vajramūṣā*).
A diamond-crucible is described as being circular and shaped like a cow’s udder.

That same [vowel], when provided with a *chidra* (breath-pause) and deepened in the middle, is suitable for *sāraṇā* (intonation), and is beneficial for fainting, killing, binding, and the union of couples. (Rrā 3.3.25)
Manifested in the shape of a small bowl, it is beneficial for the sowing of seeds.
[For the *vajra* of killing:
Equal parts of mercury and *dhānyābhraka* (grain-sulphur) should be processed for one day with the juices of *punarnavā*.
Having ground it in a heated mortar, one should cook it enclosed within a *vajramūṣā* crucible.
Ciñcā seed, meṣaśṛṅgī, female menses, and amlavetasa;
the five parts of śarapuṅkhā, rabbit teeth, and śilājatu.

This entire collection, or each part individually, should be finely powdered according to availability and then rubbed with the milks of *snuhī*, *arka*, *unmatta*, and *vāruṇī*, as well as with breast milk.
One should cast the vajra into that crucible, seal the crucible, and heat it strongly;
[using] guḍūcī, rock salt, asafoetida, musta, and uttaravāruṇī.
Having ground it with decoctions of *kaulatthaka* beans, one should pour it into that molten liquid;
then, having placed that *vajra* in a crucible as before and sealed it, one should blow upon it in that manner.
One should perform the sprinkling twenty-one times;
then, by means of the combination of palmyra and bedbugs, one should blow [upon it] seven more times.
One should sprinkle that *vajra* with horse urine; thus it certainly dies.
{Vajra:: killing} Taking the root of cotton that has grown for three years, one should grind it. Rrā_3,3.32.
Alternatively, one should grind it with the juice of a three-year-old *nāgavallī* plant;
then, having placed the *vajra* within that ball and sealed it, one should cook it in a *gajapuṭa*.
Thus, when cooked in seven layers, it becomes dead with each individual layer. {The killing of vajra (6):} The ashes of tāla, kāsīsa, saurāṣṭra, and apāmārga— Rrā_3,3.34.
Having ground *vajra* that has been well-heated, one should throw it into a decoction of *kaulatthaka* beans twenty-one times; it dies, of this there is no doubt.
One should grind amlavetasa together with the ash of vaikrānta;
one should place the vajra into that ball and heat it in a closed crucible (*andhamūṣā*).
One should sprinkle it with horse urine and then throw it back into the previous crucible;
having sealed it, it is blown with a blowpipe and sprinkled again—thus one should perform this twenty-one times.
One dies; there is no doubt about this—this should be employed in all rites.
{Vajramāraṇam (8)} A "mouth" [of mercury] produced from magnetite (*kāntapāṣāṇa*) [is treated] with the milky juice of *uttarāvāruṇī*.
Having ground it for a moment, one should place that vajra into a globule and then cook it in human oil or fragrant oil; it is killed, of this there is no doubt.
(9) {Vajra-māraṇa}:
One should grind earth-born nāga or sulphur with breast milk;
one should cook the vajra in that ball [of paste] in the aforementioned oil, and it will become dead. Rrā_3,3.40 //
(10) For the killing of diamond (*vajramāraṇa*):
having ground *vimalā* with the milky sap of *snuhī*, one should place it into a globule.
Having sealed the diamond within that crucible, once it is dry, one should blow upon it with a fierce fire.
One should place a diamond into the urine of a heated horse and extract it;
this process should be performed seven times, and then the tālaka and matkuṇa [substances] are added.
Having formed a ball and cast it into that [liquid], and having sealed it with a vajra-mūṣā crucible, it should be heated as before and sprinkled seven times; thus it becomes dead (melted).
{Vajramāraṇa (11)}:
Having cast a vajra into the blood of bedbugs and smeared it, one should place it in the sun.
It should be smeared when dry and dried again, continuing this for up to seven days.
One should repeatedly sprinkle that vajra with the juices of *viṣṇukrāntā* and *peṭakāri*; when heated again and again, after a hundred such cycles, it becomes dead (melted).
(12) {Vajramāraṇa}:
Sulfur should be ground into powder and infused seven times with women’s menstrual blood;
then, having stirred it again with female menses, one should thoroughly heat the vajra within it.
One should thus sprinkle and heat it twenty-one times until it becomes dead;
{this is the softening of the vajra}.
Having placed the vajra inside a citron and sealed it, one should smear the exterior with clay.
One should cook it in a *puṭa* vessel, and having removed it, one should likewise cook it with *śatapuṭa* flowers.
Smeared with the juices of *nāgavallī* and wrapped in its own leaf,
that vajra, held between the knees for one watch (three hours), will attain softness.
{The Vajra-rice, which makes the vajra soft} (2):

One should place the vajra in the center of the living being who carries the mother; or else, one should cook it for a day in a *dolāyantra* situated within the belly of a *jambīra* fruit. Rrā_3,3.49.

Having extracted [the mercury] after one day and night in a decoction of *kulattha* and *kodrava*, or in a decoction of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), one should then place it again into a *jambīra* fruit.
Or, having cast it into the life-force of the *mātṛvāhaka*, and having cooked it as before, it should be cast in again and cooked again;
at the end of three days, one should extract it.
One should collect the sprouts of the Badarī, Vaṭa, and Nimba trees;
having ground them into a paste, one should place the previously heated diamond into that ball.
Having wrapped that ball with *aśvattha* leaves, one should place it between the knees or wear it under the arm for a day; [the penis] will certainly become soft.
{Making the Vajra Soft} (3):
One should grind mercury and fine powder of *tīkṣṇa* with sour liquid for a day;
one should place the vajra inside that ball and wrap it on the outside with thread. Rrā 3.3.54.
Wrapped in the juices of betel leaves and placed upon a heap of grain,
at the end of a month it should be extracted and smeared with the juices of betel leaves;
wrapped in those leaves and kept between the knees, it will attain softness.
{Making the Vajra Soft} (4):
Either an iron-stone vajra, or a powder made from magnetite. Rrā 3.3.56.
One should grind it together with its mercury for one day using sour substances;
then one should place the diamond inside that ball, using [a paste] derived from neem, cotton, and jujube.
Then, having wrapped it with leaves of ground [substances] and betel-leaf,
and having encased it so that it rests between the knees, it will attain softness at the end of the day.
{Varjamṛdūkaraṇam (5)}:
One should cast an iron nail into the interior of an *eraṇḍa* tree or into its fruit;
after extracting it after exactly one month, [one should place it] between the knees as before.
Vajra becomes soft at the end of the day; there is no doubt about this.
{The Softening of Vajra (6)} One should wrap the vajra in the flesh of a partridge and place it in the mouth. Rrā_3,3.60.
One should wrap the mouth of an extremely large frog with thread,
bury it in the ground to a depth of one cubit, and after a month, dig it up.
Having enclosed it within a frog-seal (maṇḍūkasaṃpuṭa), one should cook it properly in a "gaja-puṭa" (elephant-seal);
that vajra, situated in the aforementioned sphere, remains for a day between the knees.
One should directly perform the slaying of Vajraudana and subsequently apply it;
however, for all other Vajraudanas, the method of slaying shall be as previously described.
{The purification of vaikrānta}:
with the three alkalis, the five salts, fat, urine, sour gruel, kodrava grain, fish bile, oil, ghee, horse gram (kulattha), and sour rice-water. Rājanighaṇṭu 3.3.64.
One should cook *vaikrānta* stone, which has the color of a tiger and consists of seven layers, inside a *dolaka* apparatus for seven days; it will certainly attain purification.
{The Purification of Secondary Metals}: Immersed in the juice of *jambīra* fruits, one should keep [the substances] in the sun for a day;
thus *ṭaṅkaṇa*, conch shell, cowrie, antimony, and red ochre are purified.
One should employ purified green vitriol (kāsīsa) and antimony (bhūkhaga) in medicinal formulations.
{Purification of Sulphur (1)} One *yāma* of sulphur should be ground with the juices of *nimba* and *ajagandha*,
or else with the juices of *śṛṅgī* and *dhattūra*, or with the juices of *tilaparṇī*.
Taking that, one should cook it for a moment in an iron vessel together with an equal amount of clarified butter.
One should quickly melt that [sulfur] with a mild fire and cast it into goat's milk;
one should perform this process seven times, and thus the sulfur attains purity.
{Purification of Sulphur (2):} Place karanja and castor oil, along with goat’s milk, in a vessel.
Having cast [the powder] into its mouth and blocked it with a clean cloth,
the wise one should saturate the sulphur with the juices of *dhūrta* for one day and then dry it.
One should place that powder upon a cloth inside the previously mentioned vessel, cover it with a shallow bowl, and apply a mild *puṭapāka* (sealed heating) to its back.
Having quickly taken up the fragrance, it should be processed with juices produced from the *dhattūra*;
likewise, it should be melted and processed again, and then melted once more thereafter.
Having taken [the powder], it should be soaked seven times in fish gall at the heat of the sun;
thereafter, one should grind it together with the powder of *kośātakī* seeds.
One should soak it with juices derived from bees for seven days in the intense heat of the sun;
then, having washed it with water and dried it, one should heat it for a moment over a mild fire.
Then, having melted it in an iron vessel smeared with ghee, one should quench it;
when placed within the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*, it becomes perfectly purified.
{Gandhataila}:
Now, the extraction of oil from purified *gandha* is described.
[Take] *amlaparṇī*, *devadālī*, pomegranate, and citron. Rā_3.3.76.
Or one should take orange juice as available for a single dose;
then, add borax mixed with liquid in a quarter-part proportion relative to the fragrance.
Sulphur should be processed with these two three times in the heat;
[the ingredients are] dhattūra, tulasī, kṛṣṇā, garlic, and devadālikā.
The root of the *śigru*, *kākamācī*, camphor, *śaṅkhapuṣpikā*, black agallochum, musk, and *vandhyākarkoṭakī* in equal parts; Rrā 3.3.79.
Having ground [the ingredients] with the juice of *mātuluṅga*, one should throw them into castor oil;
with this, one should impregnate the previously mentioned sulfur contained in an iron vessel.
When processed three times, it becomes equal to honey and is freed from its odor;
this shall be known as sulphur oil (gandhakataila), which one should employ in various medicinal formulations.
{Purification of Haritāla (1):} Talc,
having been cooked for one day in a dolāyantra with powdered *āranāla*, should then be ground into a powder and saturated with the juices of *kūṣmāṇḍa* gourds.
To achieve complete purification, the mineral should be dried, ground, and processed again one hundred times.
{The Purification of Haritāla (Orpiment):} Having reduced tālaka into small granules, one should add a quarter-part of ṭaṅkaṇa (borax) to the tāla.
One should wash it twice with juices of *jambīra* fruits and likewise with fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*).
Once dried, it should be tied in a cloth bundle and boiled in fermented rice-gruel mixed with powder.
Likewise, if it is cooked for two days in a dolakayantra with juices derived from *kūṣmāṇḍa* (pumpkin gourd), the mineral *tāla* attains purity; one may employ it everywhere.
Vimalaśuddhi: Pure,
gold-colored,
or refined lead made into small pieces should be placed in a paste of *punarnavā* and steamed in water containing *kaulattha* beans.
Alternatively, combined with rock salt and smeared with *bījapūra*, it should be placed in a cloth pouch and steamed for one day in a *dolāyantra*; it will certainly attain purification.
{Purification of Rasaka}:
One should soak *rasaka* with the menstrual blood and urine of a woman during her courses for one day;
by grinding it with those same substances for one day, it attains purity.
The purification of the secondary metals (*uparasa*) is performed with *punarnavā*, *meghanāda*, *kapittha*, *jambīra*, *tinduka*,
*agasti* flowers, *kumuda*, *yava*, *ciñcā*, and *amlavetasa*.
With *yava*, *sūraṇa*, *bhūdhātrī*, *māṇḍūkī*, and *karavīraka*;
with *kāravallī*, *kṣīrakanda*, red lotus (*raktotpala*), and groves of *śamī* trees.
With *meṣaśṛṅgī*, camel fat, *śakravāruṇī*, and *ṭaṅkaṇa*;
with oil, fish fat, *vyoṣa*, and these liquids along with *kāñjika*— Rā_3.3.91.

One should cook the mineral ores such as mica-leaf and other minor minerals for three days in a swinging vessel (dolāyantra), using either all these [substances] together or individually, for the sake of purification.
The secondary minerals (*uparasa*) for purification are:
*sūryāvarta*, *vajrakanda*, plantain (*kadalī*), *devadālikā*,
*śigru*, *kośātakī*, *vandhyā*, *kākamācī*, and *vālukam*.
One should saturate the three alkalis and the five pungents with the single juice of these [plants], along with the group of sour substances, under intense heat for the duration of a day.
This [mixture] should be used as a paste to smear abhraka, vajra, mākṣika,
vaikrānta, sasyaka, tāla, kāntapāṣāṇa, and añjana.

One should cook *vimalā*, *śilā*, *tuttha*, and other secondary minerals (*uparasas*) in a swinging vessel (*dolāyantra*) with *sāranāla* and the previously mentioned paste; by means of a fierce fire for a single day, they indeed attain purification.
{The Preparation of Grain-like Abhraka}: Having made pure abhraka into split leaves and bound them in a strong cloth filled with rice, one should macerate it in the juice of *sāra* within a vessel.
When it comes out by itself with both hands, one should discard that liquid once it has reached the state of being slightly sour; having dried it for a day, it becomes *dhānyābhraka*.
This moonless *abhraka* (mica) processed with grain should be ground with the milk of the sun (*bhānu*) for the duration of a day;
having formed it into a cake and wrapped it in the leaves of the sun (*bhānu*), one should cook it in a *puṭa* vessel.
Thus, it should be cooked ten times in this manner, being saturated repeatedly with milk;
thereafter, it should be rubbed with a decoction of *vaṭa* roots and cooked in ten *puṭa* applications.
Having been rubbed with buffalo milk mixed with ghee, it should be subjected to three *puṭa* cycles;
thus the mica (*abhra*) becomes "moonless" (*niścandra*) and may be employed in alchemical elixirs (*rasāyana*).
Punarnavā and other well-known medicinal herbs are indeed prescribed for the purification of mica-ash.
One should cook *dhānyābhraka* in a closed crucible (*puṭa*) for three days using those same [substances];
by the sequential method as before, it is killed after five *puṭas*.
The purification of metals [is performed] in oil, buttermilk, cow urine, sour gruel, the milk of the sun-plant (arka),
in the decoction of horse gram (kulattha), and likewise in the juice of citrons (jambīra).
Having heated them repeatedly, one should sprinkle each leaf seven times;
thus, leaves made of gold and other metals will certainly attain purity.
Lead and tin, having been melted, should likewise be cooked for the sake of purification;
so too [should] bronze and copper.
The three alkalis and the five salts [should be processed] seven times with the acid juice of the *jambīra* fruit.
Having smeared it with that paste, one should heat it in intense sunlight;
for the purification of bell-metal, brass, and copper sheets, one should cook them in a *gajapuṭa* fire.
One should cook lead in an iron vessel until it becomes liquefied;
stirring it with a palāśa stick, one should remove it once it has been reduced to ashes.
Having thrown a stone equal in weight to the ash into that [liquid] and ground it with some kind of acid for one *yāma*, one should seal it and cook it in a *gajapuṭa*.
Having ground it again once it has cooled to the touch of one's own body, combined with realgar (śilā) in a twentieth part,
and having sealed it with an acid for one *yāma*, one should cook it as before.
Thus, cooked by sixty *puṭas*, the serpent-mercury becomes dead (*mṛta*).
Five palas of cinnabar, ground with a woman's breast milk, [is used for] the killing of iron.
One should smear five *palas* of iron plates with that [substance],
seal them, and cook them in a *gajapuṭa* fire, again using a decoction of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*).

Having ground the metal with jambīra fruits or āranāla sour gruel, along with one-twentieth part of cinnabar, and having enclosed it, one should roast it in a puṭa; in this manner, it should be cooked again and again.
By means of exactly forty cycles, the sharp, magnetic, and "shaven" (muṇḍaka) iron is killed; there is no doubt about this, provided that the cinnabar is applied again and again.
When tin has been melted in an iron vessel, one should add realgar (tālaka) amounting to a quarter part;
stirring it with an ashvattha stick, one should collect the resulting ash. Rrā_3.3.115.

One should grind that ash together with an equal amount of yellow orpiment and an acidic liquid, or else with the juice of *palāśa* leaves; then, at the end of one *yāma*, it should be removed and subjected to *puṭapāka*.
Having extracted [the essence] with a tenth part, one should grind it together with *tāla*;
having sealed it for one *yāma* with the previous fluxes, one should cook it in a *gajapuṭa*.
Thus, after forty *puṭas*, the vanadium (vaṅga) becomes dead.
A copper leaf that has been pierced through the neck [should be treated] with equal parts of sulphur.
Then, having smeared it with sour-gruel paste and sealed it, one should cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire;
having removed it, one should powder it and add sulfur equal to one-fourth part of that.
Having ground [the ingredients] with jambīra or āranāla and having enclosed [the substance], one should again apply the puṭapāka;
thus one should cook it with four puṭas, providing the medicinal fragrance at each puṭa.
In this manner, one should administer a single *puṭa* with the juices of *mātuluṅga*;
five *puṭas* should be given with white sugar, and it becomes deadened (*mṛta*).
Having smeared a silver leaf with an equal amount of honey ground with sour gruel,
having enclosed it and cooked it in a *puṭa*, one should remove it and grind it into powder.
Take equal parts of *kaṇā*, *ākṣika*, rock salt (*sindhūttha*), and *bhūdhātrī*; this mixture, with portions equal to the previous powder, should be rubbed with an acidic liquid.
Having sealed it in a *gajapuṭa* furnace, one should cook it; with those same ingredients, one should rub and then seal it again.
Thus, cooked through seven such *puṭas*, the silver attains the state of ash.
Having ground a dead nāga with the milky sap of *snuhī* or some kind of acid,
one should smear gold leaves with that [mixture] in equal proportions.
Having sealed it in a *gajapuṭa* and cooked it, one should extract it and grind it into a powder;
with this, one should coat the mercury that has been thus killed with an eighth part [of the powder].
One should rub it for one *yāma* with acidic substances, seal it, and cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire;
thus, after being cooked in eight *puṭas*, the gold becomes dead (*mṛta*). (The killing of brass/bronze)
The supreme killing should be performed at a distance with a loud sound, like copper.

Through various supreme yogas, joined with established methods seen on the path of experience, the purification and killing of mercury, mica, sulfur, and the sky [space]—specifically regarding all metals—are here declared for the benefit and prosperity of the commentators. (Rrā 3.3.128)

Through various well-established methods such as the sublimation of sulphur, which are proven by other systems, appropriate, auspicious, renowned, and belonging to authentic traditions, that method of making gold—
which is easy to obtain through the coloring of silver— has been observed; out of a longing to protect virtuous people, it is now set forth in truth.
Ten *niṣkas* of purified mercury and one *niṣka* of purified sulfur—
these should be added little by little into the mortar, being ground slowly and steadily with the pestle.
From grinding, a paste is produced; this is the paste of sulfur (or, the paste of gold). Three parts of purified mercury and one part of purified gold [are taken].
One should grind it with sour juice for one *yāma*; this is known as the "Gold-Paste" (*svarṇapiṣṭikā*).
One should enclose the "Sulphur-Paste" (*gandhapiṣṭi*) on the outside with an equal amount of the Gold-Paste.
One should wrap it tightly with cloth inside a crucible made of the metal called *sūta*,
place it within a medicinal packet (*poṭalī*), and add sulfur equal in weight to the entire mixture.
Having cast [the ingredients] in, one should seal the joint and block it with clay and salt;
having cooked it in the crucible called Bhūdhara, once it is digested, one should again add the fragrance.
When the sulphur has been digested six times its weight, one should gradually remove the cloth;
having added an equal amount of sulphur again and again, it should be digested very slowly.
One must not allow it to be completely exhausted, for through negligence the *sūtaka* may escape;
thus, when it has been processed a hundredfold, one should extract the paste from the apparatus.
Having enclosed [the substance] equal to that [silver] within a crucible of gold,
one should seal it and wrap the exterior with glass ground with the juice of *kumārī* to a thickness of one finger-breadth.
Then, it should be wrapped with borax and salt-clay,
and subsequently smeared with oil from the fingers and dried in the heat of the sun.
When the substance to be smelted is placed in a crucible furnace and heated with a steady fire in a blowpipe,
that resulting *khoṭa* becomes divine, resembling the reddish hue of vermilion.
By that [process], a hundredth part of the piercing of the star-like [substance] in its molten state should be applied;
thus gold is produced, which is declared to be the "Siddhayoga."
Regarding *gandhapiṣṭi*: purified sulfur should be powdered and infused seven times with liquid gold,
and likewise with the menstrual blood (*rajas*) of women, while being dried in the sun.
One *karṣa* of that fragrance, stirred with human bile,
and one *pala* of purified mercury, should be placed in a shallow dish in the sun.
Having sprinkled the volatile fragrance upon its back, one should rub it with the thumb;
a divine paste is produced that bestows the fruits of all desires.
One should purify the pure sulphur seven times with the juice of *tilaparṇī* using a fragrant paste;
one should then grind it and dry it repeatedly in the shade.
One should place one *pala* of pure mercury into a crucible,
and then cast in a pellet of pure gold weighing one *niṣka*.
One should place that crucible containing the previously mentioned sulfur in a sand-bath apparatus (vālukāyantra),
adding it bit by bit, and cook it over a gentle fire on a stove.
When one-quarter part of sulfur has been digested [in the mercury], "sulfur-paste" (gandhapiṣṭikā) is produced;
this sulfur-paste is to be taken separately, without the gold pellet.
The fragrant powder should be processed in the shade by saturating the sulphur a hundred times with the juice of *markaṭī*; then,
while it is warm, one should place mercury in an earthen pan and add a small amount of sulphur.

When the odor has subsided, one should again add liquid combined with the juice of *markaṭī*; as much liquid as is required for the sulfur should be added gradually until the sulfur is fully dissolved.
A divine paste is produced that grants the fruits of all desires.
{Gandhapiṣṭi}:
One should wash finely powdered sulphur three times with *kāñjika* (sour gruel).
Camphor should be processed separately three times with the juices of the *jambīra* fruit and seven times with the juice of *haṃsapādī*,
and [further] with the juices of white mountain *karṇikā*.
After exposing it to the sun for three sessions, one should then begin the process of digestion (*jāraṇa*);
one should smear the interior of the apparatus with camphor measuring two *guñjās*.
One should cause that scent, processed within its interior, to be given at a price of one and a half niṣkas;
likewise, one pala of pure mercury and an amount of camphor equal to the former [should be added].
Then, one should offer incense in the same manner as before, and subsequently provide [the following]:
one should grind the root of the *karṇikā* from a white mountain with cow’s urine.
Having coated it with that paste and sealed it with a shallow dish, one should cook it in a *nalikā* apparatus; at the end of the day, one should extract it.
Furthermore, camphor and other ingredients should be added, and likewise processed for a period of days;
by doing so repeatedly in this manner, a fragrant paste (gandhapiṣṭikā) is produced.
One *pala* of mercury and one *karṣa* of purified sulfur, along with a fragrant powder,
should be soaked in the juice of *devadālī* using the hands and fingers within a smooth mortar.
One should rub it in the intense heat of the sun until a fragrant paste (*gandhapiṣṭikā*) is produced. [The proportions are: one *pala* of purified mercury and half a *karṣa* of purified sulfur.
Having placed [the substance] in a copper mortar, one should apply a mild fire beneath it;
by rubbing it with the thumb of the hand for one watch (yāma), it becomes a paste.
For the immobilization [of a woman] by means of a fragrant paste (*gandhapiṣṭi*):
one should grind the seeds of bitter *kośātakī* and the root-tuber of *cāṇḍālī* with breast milk and apply it as a fragrant paste.
One should deposit it in the sūraṇa tuber, or likewise in the interior of the kṣīrakanda,
or in the vandhyākarkoṭakī, the vajrakanda, or the kuḍuhuñjikā.
Having blocked the opening of the bulb with marrow, one should smear the bulb with clay and cook it in a *bhūdhara* (earth) apparatus over a fire of dried cow-dung for the duration of a day.
By turning it upside down, so that the bulbous root is not burnt, one should then extract the paste; it will certainly become solidified.
Now, its digestion (jāraṇā) should be performed within a crucible known as "the breast" (stanākhye), which has been solidified with fragrant pastes (gandhapiṣṭi).
Having placed it, one should cause the fragrance to be digested equally and equally within the *bhūdhara* [crucible].
When the fragrance has been digested, it should be added again, and the substance should be processed in the apparatus as before;
in this manner, it should be digested a hundredfold, and once digested, one should extract it from the apparatus.
The coloring of all types of *gandhapiṣṭi* occurs through the process of *jāraṇā*.
To perform the *māraṇa* of *gandhapiṣṭi*,
one should grind the paste with the juices of the collection of divine medicinal herbs in a mortar.
At the end of the day, having fashioned a ball from seeds produced by a divine host, [one should proceed].
One should smear the vajra-mūṣā crucible and place the ball inside it;
one should cook it for one day in the earth-oven (bhūdharayantra), turning it over from top to bottom.
Having extracted it again and crushed it as before with the previous liquors,
one should indeed perform the *puṭa* process in this manner ten times, repeatedly.
{Gandhapiṣṭi: Transmutation: Silver = Gold}
There is no doubt that [the subject] dies by means of this fragrant paste;
thereafter, one should again grind one *pala* of the dead body's paste with the juice of *vāsaka*.
Having smeared eight palas of nāgapatra with the paste of that [plant],
one should dry it in the shade and place it within a ball made from vāsā leaves.
Having enclosed that bolus within a casket, one should roast it with wild blue lotuses;
then, having extracted it, one ounce of powdered mercury should be added once again.
One should grind that ball with the juices of *vāsā* for a day, then wrap it again with a paste made from *vāsā* leaves,
seal it, and cook it in a *gajapuṭa*.
One should repeat this process again and again until the nāga becomes red in color; then, taking one *pala* of that nāga, one should macerate it for one watch (*yāma*) in the juices of the *vāsaka*.
One should smear eight *palas* of copper leaf with that [substance] and cook it for one day in a *pācanāyantra*; it will certainly be killed [rendered inert].
By means of that very sixteenth part, one should cause the piercing of the silver;
that silver becomes gold, possessing a luster equal to Jāmbūnada.
By means of any fragrant paste, without the processes of *stambhana* (fixing) and *jāraṇa* (digestion),
through the application of the previously mentioned sequence, it becomes divine gold.

The ash of the bark of the *arjuna* tree and the ash of *vāsā* in equal parts should be ground together with the juice of *gṛhakanyā* for one day; one should then apply it [to the crucible]. (Rājanighaṇṭu 3.4.49)
Having sealed the *nāgapatra* that is to be pierced through the throat within a small crucible, one should cook it;
then, having extracted it, one should grind it for one *yāma* with the previous juices along with its ashes.
Having sealed it in a *gajapuṭa* and cooked it, one should remove it once it has cooled to the temperature of its own body;
in this manner, it should be cooked for a hundred *puṭas*, and the resulting ash should be rubbed with liquid extracts.
One should smear the leaf-cups with honey using that very [substance],
seal them, cook them in a *gajapuṭa*, smear them again, and cook them in a *puṭa* once more.
In this manner, one should perform the piercing three times, whereby the lead attains the state of gold;
when the lead is melted in an iron vessel, an equal amount of powdered *rasaka* [is added]. (Rājanighaṇṭu 3.4.53)
Having cast it into a furnace, one should cook it for one watch (yāma), stirring it with a handful of stones;
at the end of the watch, powdered vermilion equal in weight to the mercury should be added.
One should grind it very finely and firmly with a stone fist,
and then cook it over a fierce fire for twenty-one days.
Silver that has the luster of saffron is produced; one should pierce it with that very [substance] by a sixty-fourth part, and it becomes divine gold.
One should melt lead in an iron pan and cast into it one-quarter part [of the mixture];
then, one should rub it with the alkali of the bark of *ciñcā* and *aśvattha* using an iron ladle.
At the end of that watch, having extracted it, one should grind it with *vajrī* milk for a full day in a mortar;
then, having removed it, one should seal it inside an earthen vessel.
Then, having cooked it for four watches at night over a fierce fire on the hearth,
one should take it out and grind it in a mortar with *vajrī* milk for the duration of a day.
It should be cooked at night and rubbed during the day for a period of exactly six months.
One must protect it so that neither water nor dust falls upon it.
When a thousandth part has been held in place and applied to the target, excellent gold is produced.

mercury, tin, copper, glass, white [substance], and human hair.
One should grind each of these five pala-measures separately.

furthermore, eight niṣkas each of sulphur, calamine, bell-metal, and honey-ore (mākṣika) should be added.
Twenty niṣkas of the essence of soot should be ground with the juices of jambīra fruits for the duration of this day; then, in portions of one karṣa each, they should be made into pills.
In a crucible furnace, one should blow with force until it is reduced to copper;
then, blowing repeatedly, one should add six times that amount of lead to the copper.
One should pierce the eight-syllable [mantra] with that very thirty-sixth part;
it will then become ten syllables—there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Now, for another type of copper purified with lead,
one should perform a soaking fifty times using the juice of *nirguṇḍī* alone.
One should perform the washing seven times with the juice of *kuṣmāṇḍa* itself,
and seven times with buttermilk mixed with *niśā*.
In this way, the molten copper should be washed until it becomes free from blackness (*kālikā*).
In this [alloy], copper shall constitute three parts, while gold shall consist of exactly five parts.

Divine gold is produced as previously described by Nāgārjuna;
[it is] a refinement of two color-stages.
Having ignited *aṅkolla* wood, [one should use] powdered wild stone.
One should throw the powder of *aṅkola* seeds onto a burning piece of wood;
having taken those embers once they have become cool, one should blow upon them again.
Having thrown the powder of *aṅkola* seeds onto it, one should bind it with a cloth;
with its smoke, one should fumigate gold leaves so that they turn ten colors.
Having melted it, one should throw it again into oil derived from the *putrajīva* tree;
when thus thrown twice, the two colors increase.

For the benefit of all the world, I have truly taught this instruction on the one-tenth part of the fourth house for the sake of gain, by means of very simple methods and easily accomplished yogas, through a few ritual procedures and many specific details.
Having extracted the essence from a collection of various red and bright yellow flowers,
one should quickly dissolve purified mercury into that [essence] one hundred times;
thereafter, the dyeing and piercing of copper for the sake of the Moon and Sun should be performed according to the prescribed rite.
All of that is now being explained by my own intellect, based upon the Guru and the scriptures.
That mercury-paste (gandhapiṣṭī) which has been solidified but is devoid of the digestion of sulfur (gandhajāraṇa) is [known as] *raktapārada*.
Indeed, one sixteenth part of that is a single portion of the "dead vajra" (mṛtavajra).
Having ground [the mercury] for three days with the juices of *devadālī* and *śaṅkhapuṣpī*,
one should cook it in a *kacchapa* apparatus and then extract it after a single *puṭa*.
One should grind it for one *yāma* with those same juices used by the predecessors and then seal it as before;
