One should cook it for one day in a *pātanā* apparatus over a mild fire;
it should be ground again and cooked again until it no longer rises upward.
When it remains in the lower apparatus (*adhoyantra*), then it becomes vermilion-mercury (*raktapārada*).
One part of vermilion-mercury and two parts of the essence of black mica—{lead =) gold}. Rā 3.6.6.
One part of ṭaṅkaṇa should be ground with all [the other ingredients] for the duration of one day;
having enclosed that mass with the milks of the *vajrī*, one should cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire.
It should be rubbed again and boiled again in this manner for fourteen cycles;
when the piercing with the naga [mercury] is given in the proportion of one-sixteenth, gold is produced.

From the juices of *śāka*, *kiṃśuka*, and *koraṇṭa* flowers, combined with *kaṅguṇī* oil, there arises [an ointment] rich in divine form, the most excellent ornament of the gods— [lead, that is,] gold.
One should rub the powder of nāga for one day and cook it within a sealed crucible (*saṃpuṭa*);
having rubbed it thoroughly with the *gajapuṭa* method, it should be cooked again and again.
Through forty cycles, the divine gold is perfected;
[the ingredients are] *rasaka*, saffron, copper sulfate, and the dung of a young calf.
Equal parts of yellow mica and poison should be ground for a day with the juice of *mātuluṅga*;
dried in the shade, it should then be made into a paste with honey.
Having smeared the leaves of the *nāga* plant with that [substance], they should be dried in the shade;
then, having placed it in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*), it is blown [with a blowpipe] using the juice of *śāka* leaves.
One should sprinkle it and then extract [the essence]; thereafter, one should cause it to melt manifestly again.
It should be sprinkled with the juices of *śāka* leaves, and having melted it once more, one should sprinkle it again.
In this manner, one should divide it into seven parts and then have new leaves made;
having smeared them as before and dried them, they should be sealed and heated as previously described.
One should perform sprinkling and liquefaction seven times;
thus one should perform the sevenfold rite, beginning with the application of ointment and ending with liquefaction.
That divine nāga is born with a luster equal to Jāmbūnada gold;
once burnt, one should place the crushed stone in fermented rice-gruel (āranāla).
Having placed it stirred in an earthen vessel, one should diligently keep it day and night;
once it has become clear, one should take its liquid and use that liquid for the tender shoots of vegetables.
One should grind the powder of lead (nāga) with that paste and knead it;
at the end of a *yāma*, one should dry it in the sun, and after kneading it again, one should dry it once more.
Having thus divided it into ten parts, one should again place that ball inside the core of a fresh vegetable stalk and enclose it with that very [stalk].
Having coated it with clay, one should bake it thoroughly in a gajapuṭa once it has dried;
having extracted it, it becomes yellow, and its application as a stambhana (paralyzer) is now described.
First, one should wash lead and gold with cow urine along with *bhūnāga* and mercury;
having added an equal amount of *sauvīrāñjana* to these, one should grind them together.
One should extract the mass produced from buffalo urine for one day;
from that, the oil should be carefully collected using the pātālayantra apparatus.
Into that oil, one should repeatedly add either *pūrvanāga* or pure *nāgaka*,
melting it each time, twenty-one times in total.
That divine nāga is produced, possessing a luster equal to Jāmbūnada gold;
the powder of pure nāga should be mixed with an equal amount of powdered bhūnāga.
One should extract the juice from *śāka*, *kiṃśuka*, and *koraṇṭa* flowers;
with whatever is available, one should grind it for one day with those fluids.
Having placed it in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*), one should heat it and then reduce it to powder;
having ground it as before, it should be heated again—thus one should repeat this twenty-one times.
Divine gold is produced; that is the *nāga* which is the ornament of the gods.
With one *pala* of pure *nāga*, a well-rounded crucible (*mūṣā*) should be fashioned.
One should place one *pala* of pure mercury and two *palas* of sulfur into that [crucible];
then, one should hold that crucible in a clay vessel under a strong sun.
For one day [it should be processed] with the juice of *jambīra*, for one day with the juices of *kākamācī*,
for one day with the juices of *kāsamarda*, and for one day with the juices produced from *dhattūra*.
One should thus meditate on the heat for four days in succession,
removing everything from the earthen vessel so that nothing whatsoever remains.
Having ground the seeds of *karañja* with the juices produced from *dhattūra*,
one should smear the interior of the crucible to the thickness of a finger with that very [mixture].
One should first cast a *piṇḍa* there weighing one *pala*, and then add one *niṣka* of sulfur;
one should then pour five *niṣkas* of the liquid of *bhūnāgas* into it.
Then, having applied a coating of paste and sealed the crucible,
one should cook it for one day in a fire of dried cow-dung cakes within an earthen furnace.
Having removed it while still warm from its own body heat, one should place it in a crucible as before;
then, having applied a coating of sulphur and realgar, one should roast it in a closed crucible (puṭa) as previously described.
In this manner, having properly prepared twenty times the amount of well-refined fragrance,
one should take two and a half palas of *tāla* and an equal amount of *rasaka*.
Having ground one *pala* of *ṭaṅkaṇa* (borax), one should divide it into two parts and place three [parts] separately;
having cast them into the interior of a glass flask (*kācakūpyā*), one should then add half a part of *tālaka* (mica).
Then one should add *rasaka* and *ṭaṅkaṇa*; thereafter, the previously prepared mercury again;
then *ṭaṅkaṇa*, *rasaka*, and *tāla*—one should add these three in succession once more.
One should wrap the mouth of a glass flask with one's own body heated by a lamp,
or else seal it with a glass peg and a mixture of clay and salt.
Having smeared the small crucible with clay to a thickness of one finger-breadth all over,
and having first placed the lid [into position], one should insert it into the *bhūdhara* furnace once it has dried.
Having applied [the powder], one should coat the joints with clay; then the *gajapuṭa* should be administered again.
Once it has cooled on its own, one should extract [the substance] and perform the offering (*bali*) and worship (*pūjā*).
One should quickly transmute copper with a sixty-fourth part [of the mercury];
it becomes gold, rich in beauty—this is declared to be the perfected yoga.
Ten *pala*s of gold (candrārka), twenty-one *pala*s of mercury (*sūtaka*),
and five *pala*s of oil extracted from the seeds of *mahākāla* should be used.
Having sealed everything inside a smooth jar, one should cook it over a gentle fire,
applying a coating of black gram flour so that the smoke does not escape.
That mercury is indeed born as a *khoṭa*; when the moon and sun are liquefied, one should cast it [into them].
By that very [mercury] in the proportion of a thousandth part, the gold becomes divine.
Equal parts of mercury and sulphur should be ground for one day with the juice of *devadālī*;
with that, one should apply a coating to the leaves of copper.
Having rotated it in the blind crucible and then extracted it from there once more,
one should take the juice of the tender leaves of the Śāka tree.
One should repeatedly cast the previously mentioned *śulba* (copper) into that liquid;
by doing this a hundred times, the gold becomes divine.
Having impregnated yellow sulphur powder with the juice of betel leaf for three days,
one should apply a coating of that [mixture] to copper leaves.
Having dried it and placed it in a closed crucible, one should cook it with auspicious forest stones;
then it should be rubbed with the juices of red *aśvamāraka* and the bark of the *śāka* tree.
One should smear the leaves of previously [purified] copper with this paste, seal them, and smelt them over a fierce fire; when this has been done a hundred times, [the process is complete].
That copper becomes gold, possessing a luster equal to that of Jāmbūnada; likewise,
the powder of the root of *kāñcanī*, yellow orpiment (*haritāla*), and realgar (*manaḥśilā*).
Equal parts of ṭaṅkaṇa and mākṣika, rubbed for three days with the juice of vāsā flowers,
should be used to smear a well-purified copper vessel.
One should heat it slowly with a mild fire and apply a dry coating;
having heated it again, one should apply another coating, repeating this diligently seven times.
Then, being smelted with a fierce fire, it becomes auspicious gold;
[one should smelt] calamine, cinnabar, realgar, and orpiment along with one-and-a-half parts of mercury.
Having placed [the mercury] in a mortar and stirred it for three days with the juice of *kākamācī*,
one should smear a leaf of *ravi* and *śaśi* with that [mixture] and heat it in a crucible over fire.
The gold of Saubala, which surpasses wrought copper for travelers,
is produced by rubbing one *pala* of pure mercury with the juices of *Jvālāmukhī*.
At the end of the day, one should add to it a quarter-part of powdered mica (*abhraka*) and a quarter-part of copper powder,
along with a quarter-part of *phullatorikā*.
One should grind everything with the juices of *Jvālāmukhī* for seven days;
having sealed that ball in a *vajramūṣā* crucible, one should blow it with a fierce fire.
One part of that dross and four parts of pure copper should be placed in a blind crucible (andhamūṣā) and smelted; having extracted [the metal] from there, it should be processed again.
The substance should be melted in an open crucible with oil derived from *putrajīva* seeds;
it should be cast [into the mold] again after being melted, and this process should be repeated twenty-one times.
Divine gold is produced; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
One should process sulfur with the juices of white *pālāśa* fruits.
Having dried it with effort one hundred times and ground it again and again,
one should diligently smear the leaves with that [substance] one hundred times.
Having sealed pure copper and roasted it in a *gajapuṭa* fire, one should extract it,
heat it again, and then fashion it into leaves.
One should repeatedly apply the plaster, repeatedly heat it, and repeatedly turn it back in due order;
by doing this twenty-one times, it becomes divine gold.
Twelve parts of silver and sixteen parts of copper [make] eight-colored gold.
Having turned it over, one should cause the leaf to be prepared; having smeared it and sealed it, one should cook it in a *puṭa*.
In this manner, one should grind mercury and sulphur with sixteen successive applications of the resin of *mahendī* leaves, increasing the quantity of each ingredient in sequence.
Having smeared it with oil from the *maṅkola* plant of the day as before,
and having sealed it in the same sequence, one should heat it intensely and then produce the leaf once again.
It should be smeared again and cooked again until the bronze has been consumed;
the gold will then become of eight-fold purity—of this there is no need for doubt.
The medicinal herb named Karuṇī, which transforms mercury into gold, grows during the rainy season;
it has blue flowers, white leaves, and is extremely slimy and succulent.
One should cast that liquid into purified mercury while it is being smelted within a diamond crucible, continuing for a period of up to seven days.
Divine gold is produced from mercury alone; of this there is no doubt.
(Mercury, lead, gold = gold)
One pala of mercury, one pala of fragrance, and three days with the juices of *kṛṣṇa* and *unmatta*.
Having ground it in a vajra-crucible, sealed the opening, and covered it,
one should extract it at the end of the day, grind it again in the same manner, and cook it.
One should perform this for seven days, and the mercury will indeed become dead;
then one should wrap that mercury, the serpent, and the gold with the moon and the sun in succession.
When equal parts of *andhita* and *dhāmya* are heated, it becomes divine gold.
[In the *cakrayantra*:
a crucible for mercury is placed in the center of a cavity, with fire applied on all sides around the outer cavity.
This wheel-mechanism has been proclaimed by those expert in the meaning of all scriptures:
equal parts of copper (which becomes gold), *mākṣika*, and *rasaka*, with half a part of *saindhava* salt added.
It should be ground with citron fruits for one day and then cooked in an earthen vessel for one day.
One should cook it in the furnace until it takes on the color of saffron;
then, one should grind that paste for a day, combined with sugar and honey.
Furthermore, one should cook it in an earthen pan together with cow's milk, stirring for one day; then, having removed it from the heat, one should apply a coating.
Having enclosed pure copper leaves and blown them with a fierce fire,
one should then apply a coating to those leaves that have been made into plates and blow them likewise with a steady fire.
Furthermore, one should act in this manner so that it becomes yellow in color; for three days, the intensely red realgar should be processed with *munipuṣpa* flowers.
Having first made a leaf from this *śulba* (copper) and smeared it,
one should place it inside a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*), heat it, and then immerse it in *kaṅguṇī* oil.
In this manner, one should perform the process three times; thus the silver becomes divine gold.
By this very method, one should color the impure silver (*tārāriṣṭa*).
Divine gold, possessing a luster equal to that of Jāmbūnada, is produced;
[one] pala of pure mercury and one karṣa of sulfur [are required]. (Rājanighaṇṭu 3.6.83)
Having placed [the mercury] in a smooth mortar and saturated it with the juice of *devadālī*, one should rub it with the fingers of the hand; thus, the fragrant paste (*gandhapiṣṭikā*) is produced.
One part of *dhānyābhraka* (rice-grain mica) and eight parts of purified mercury [yield] mercury (*khoṭa*) and gold (*candrārka*).
Combined with *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, it becomes a paste (*piṣṭikā*) through rubbing.
Having ground these two powders together with the juices of *jambīra* for one day,
one should then grind them with a decoction of *pālāśa* roots for three days.
Having ground together equal parts of *brahmamūla*, jaggery, *guñjā*, wool, and borax,
one should mix them with honey and smear the previous mass.
Having blocked [the crucible] and heated it with a fierce fire, that mercury becomes a *khoṭa*;
it should be cooked in an open crucible, and one should add glass and borax.
In this manner, it should be purified again and again until it becomes stainless;
thereafter, having added lead, it should be smelted repeatedly.
One should thus cause the serpent of the king of mercury to circulate three times;
then, by means of black-cloud-like *puṭa* vessels, one should gradually color that *khoṭa*.
When that [mercury] is repeatedly heated in a crucible a hundred times,
adding black abhraka each time, it certainly becomes colored.
By that very same thousandth part, mercury and lead become gold.
That which is a solidified paste of fragrance, devoid of the process of digesting the fragrance, is called *stambhitā*.
One should grind one *pala* of it for a day with the juices of *jambīra* fruits, and thereafter for three days with decoctions of *brahma*; then add an equal amount of jaggery and *ṭaṅkaṇa*.
One should throw wool and *guñjā* seeds into that [mixture] and grind everything together;
one should make pills that have dried in the shade and blow them into a great fire.
One should subsequently purify that *khoṭa* with white *ṭaṅkaṇa* and glass;
by means of heating alone, the *khoṭa* becomes stainless.
One should apply that solidified, crooked, and fragrant *pratikarṣa* as a coating;
it should be heated within a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*) until only the solidified residue remains.
By this sequential method, having extinguished the tin six times,
one should then process the sulphur and lead six times again.
One *pala* of copper powder combined with *siddhacūrṇa*, having been sealed and heated in a crucible, becomes a *khoṭa*; one should then grind that with sulfur.
Having sealed it in a *gajapuṭa* furnace, one should cook it in this manner fourteen times;
with this, one should slowly join the previously melted *khoṭa*.
One should repeatedly cast [the substance] until it takes on the color of saffron;
thereafter, one should take equal amounts of gold, fragrance, and *khoṭa*, each separately.
Then, having sealed it, one should blow strongly until only the solid residue remains;
in this manner, gold combined with sulfur should be processed three times.
Furthermore, one should have the *samāvarta* performed with an equal amount of gold;
then again with twice that amount of gold, and thereafter again with three times that amount.
When the mercury has been processed in three ways, it pierces copper by a thousandth part;
there is no doubt that the molten copper becomes divine gold.
The previously purified *khoṭa* should be melted down and made equal in weight to gold; [this results in] six-colored gold (*ṣaḍvarṇa*), which is the coloring (*rañjana*) of gold (*sitasvarṇa*).
Then, having made it into a fine powder, [one should place it] into three times the amount of purified mercury.
Having added [the ingredients] and sealed it in a crucible, one should heat it with a mild fire;
one should diligently continue heating until its internal contents melt.
Alternatively, one should heat quick mercury in a *dolikā* apparatus;
with this [mercury] at a hundredth part [of the weight], one should coat white gold.
Having wrapped it with *arka* leaves, one should steam it in a swinging apparatus (*dolikāyantra*) for three days with *kāñjika*;
then, having placed it in a closed crucible (*andhamūṣā*), one should heat it by blowing.
Gold becomes rich in color; it is the supreme excellence of the six colors.
One should take one part of purified mercury-cake (*sūtakhoṭa*).
Gold with a sixteenfold part [of mercury] should be placed in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*) and heated;
then, by means of the sequential application as before, one whose essence is mercury should perform the transmutation (*vedha*).
By that same hundredth part, the six-colored [substance] becomes as before; [lead = copper].
Having ground *dhānyābhra* with the milk of *arka* for one watch (*yāma*), one should likewise coat [silver] with it; [this results in] silver = gold.
One should cook it in a crucible called *kapota*, then grind it again and cook it once more;
thus, after being cooked in twenty crucibles, that mica (*abhra*) is reduced to a sixteenth part [of its original weight].
That [substance] should be placed inside a sealed crucible (*pakvamūṣā*) over pure mercury;
having first been enclosed with the juices of *arka* leaves, it should be subjected to sudation for three days.
Then, having carefully extracted it with the fire of chaff, one should place it there;
having added both the cloud and the liquid, one should cook it in that manner for three days.
In this manner, one should digest the mercury in the presence of the iron filings until it becomes equal in weight to the mica;
then that mercury and the mica [should be processed] again with the juice of *tilaparṇī*.
One should grind it in a heated mortar until it forms a ball;
then, one should prepare a paste of sulfur with an equal amount of mercury.
That fragrant paste which has been solidified and is devoid of the digestion of fragrance—
that paste, as well as the gold-paste, the mercury-mercury (rasābhra), and likewise the globule (golaka).
The three [substances] should be ground in equal parts with cotton-derived liquids for one day;
having formed that into a round ball and bound it in cloth, one should then dry it.
One should cook the fragrant oil until it becomes like the color of saffron;
once it has reached that state, one should remove it and grind it with the juices of *nirguṇḍī*.
With that very same eighth part, one should smear the *nāga* leaves;
having ground cotton leaves, one should smear them with that paste.
Then, having sealed the nāga-leaves within a crucible called a *bhūdhara*, one should cook it;
having removed it, one should indeed smear it again with an eighth part of that [same substance].
Having smeared it with a paste of cotton leaves and sealed it, one should cook it in a *puṭa* (hermetic vessel);
after a day and night, having turned it over from top to bottom, one should extract it.
Having added another eighth part [of mercury] and grinding it with the previous paste,
one should coat the exterior of that ball with the juice of *nirguṇḍī* for one day.
Having sealed it with a paste of cotton leaves, one should cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire;
in this manner, one should repeatedly perform the process of mardana and puṭapācana.
That nāga, which has the luster of saffron, dies after ten cycles of heating;
with one-eighth part of this, one should quickly transfix copper (śulba).
One should pierce silver with that copper by an eighth part; the copper thus produced becomes gold, an excellent ornament for the gods.
This is the Nāgarañjana method, specifically the piercing of copper using mercury and the sun and moon.
May people, who are vessels for the bliss of the Dharma-body, accomplish the protection of the entire world.
The sequence for the stabilization of mineral essences and living beings using a paste, the application of a fetter,

one should grind that ball— wrapped in cloth— firmly in a mortar.

First, one should seal the crucible (*mūṣā*) properly with that paste.
Having placed salt above and below, having sealed it, and having coated it as before, one should heat it until dried in the shade; it becomes a solid mass (*khoṭa*) and attains the state of a *rasa*.
Having repeatedly added *sauvīra*, *ṭaṅkaṇa*, and glass, one should heat it firmly;
that *khoṭa* becomes purified, there is no doubt about this.
In this manner, one should have a paste prepared separately by all the beings;
through the sequential application as before, that mercury becomes a solid bolus (khoṭa).
Two parts of mercury (khoṭa), three parts of gold, and one part of mercury—
one should prepare a paste as before and likewise purify the *khoṭa*.
Having thus prepared the flour-pills (*piṣṭikhoṭa*), one should employ them everywhere.
That pill of *viḍa* salt, equal in weight to gold, should be subjected to repeated smelting (*samāvarta*).
Equal parts of honey, magnetite stone, and realgar; Rrā_3,7.25.
One should grind it with *bhūnāga* for one *yāma*; when formed into pills the size of a chickpea, this is known as *viḍavaṭī*, to be employed everywhere in the process of *jāraṇā*.
One should cause each part to be carried away as the ore is repeatedly smelted;
in this manner, one should digest gold ten times over according to that sequence.
But within the womb of the *prakāśa* crucible, the submarine fire (*vaḍavānala*) devours [the mercury] that pierces a hundredfold (*śatavedhin*).
One should prepare an equal powder of honey-lead ore (mākṣika), vermilion (darada), sulfur (gandha), rājāvarta, coral (pravālaka), realgar (śilā), blue vitriol (tuttha), and kaṅkuṣṭha.
One should repeatedly saturate it for five days with yellow and red powders along with *kaṅguṇī* oil, while heating it again and again in the heat of the sun.
The processed metallic mass (sūtakhoṭa), combined with this medicinal paste,
should be placed within a sand-pan (vālukāhaṇḍi) and enclosed inside a pair of crucibles (śrāvasaṃpuṭa).
One should cook it on the hearth for three days, adding the paste again and again;
thus the mercury becomes colored and attains a penetration of one hundredfold, without a doubt.
One should apply [the mercury] to silver, copper, or a serpent-metal (bhujaṅga), or else to the moon and sun;
thus divine gold is produced, possessing a luster equal to that of Jāmbūnada.
One should cause the paste and bolus of the melted mercury to become a fine powder and then saturate it with women’s menses for three days in the hot sun, or in oxalic acid, or in coconut water.
One should grind together mīnākṣī, the root of the plantain, white and red punarnavā,
bitumen, and rock salt with the menstrual blood of a woman.
One should cast the previously prepared *khoṭa* into that mass;
one should cast the previously prepared *khoṭa* into that mass.
Having sealed the mouth [of the crucible] with that medicinal paste, one should fix the pill;
then, one should cook the birch-bark leaf for three days in a *dolāyantra* (swinging apparatus) with *kāñjika*.
The mercury shall quickly become manifest; then one should again apply the *khoṭa*—previously prepared as before—to that [mercury] foot by foot, repeatedly.
One should place it into the previous *piṇḍa* and cook it likewise for three days;
in this manner, the well-refined paste (*piṣṭi*) and the solid mass (*khoṭa*) should be added again and again.
One should add an equal amount of *āroṭa* until it becomes liquefied (*druta*).
[The resulting] liquid mercury (*drutasūta*) is then combined with ginger, radish, dry ginger, garlic, asafoetida, and honey.
The three alkalis, the five salts, potassium carbonate (kāṅkṣī), iron sulfate (kāsīsa), and sulfur,
combined with the group of acidic substances, should be ground together to form a paste.
In that bolus, one should cause the previously mentioned liquid metal (sūta) to be cast;
[the ingredients are] mārjārī, ceśvarī, guñjā, kukkuṭī, and kṣīrakandaka.
In the midst of these, one should meditate upon the mercury as before;
this is known as "molten mercury" (drutasūta) and should be employed in all ritual activities.
Two parts of quicksilver and one part of the essence of black mica [are to be used] for the gold [produced from] quicksilver.
One part of the essence of *rasaka* [should be processed] for one day with the juices of black datura.
One should cause a ball to be made from the crushed [substances], and having added a quarter-part of the ball and the dead iron (pavi),
one should then grind everything for one yāma with the juice of *unmatta*.
Then, having sealed it within a *bhūdhara* crucible, one should cook it with a single *puṭa* and extract it;
then, having added that previously mentioned portion of molten mercury, one should grind it again.
Likewise, one should cook it for a watch (three hours) with the juices extracted from *dhattūra* on a furnace;
in this manner, having added the mercury again and again, [this is done] seven times.
One should cook it in a *bhūdhara* yantra until that mercury is reduced to ashes;
with that very [ash], one should grind it together with honey in a hundredth part [of the original quantity].
One should blow [the mixture] placed in a blind crucible using leaves produced from the moon and sun;
it becomes gold, rich in beauty and possessing a luster equal to Jāmbūnada.
One should blow [the mixture of] lead and an equal amount of sulfur, which has been reduced to ash, inside a closed crucible (andhamūṣā).
By piercing [the resulting mass] with one hundredth part of that, lead becomes gold.
The essence of mercury and mica, and the essence of gold (candrārka), each being equal and melted together— one *pala* of these three combined with the *siddhacūrṇa*.
One should rub it with the juices of *unmattaka* for one day, blindfold it, and then heat it in a furnace;
that resulting mass (*khoṭa*) should be powdered and rubbed with *mātuluṅga*, sour liquids, and sulfur.
Having sealed it in a *gajapuṭa* vessel, one should cook it in this manner for thirteen times;
having repeatedly ground it, one should cook it while sealing it with wild blue lotuses (*āraṇyotpalaka*) in succession.
Having smeared it with that [substance] mixed with honey, which is a hundredth part of a hundredth of the moon and sun, and having sealed it, one should heat it intensely; it becomes beautiful gold.
The essence of copper and *rasaka* (borax), the essence of *abhraka* (mica), quicksilver, and *ṭaṅkaṇa* (borax)—
all these, taken in equal parts, should be ground for one day with the juices of black *unmatta*.
Having made a pill that has dried in the shade, one should blow it while it is placed in a great fire;
thereafter, one should purify that *khoṭa* with white glass and *ṭaṅkaṇa*.
Then, having processed it with an equal amount of gold, one should digest it;
thereafter, one should administer each of those aforementioned *viḍavaṭīs*.
Once it has been reduced to the state of mercury (sūta) within an open crucible,
one should then perform three purificatory alloyings (sāraṇā) with pure gold.
By that hundredth part [of the mercury], the copper becomes gold.
One part of the quicksilver (sūta) that has been melted should be cast into a *sāraṇā* apparatus.
Therefore, one should take four times that amount of pure lead, melt it separately,
and having cast it into that same crucible, one should collect the resulting *khoṭa*.
Having combined an equal amount of pure honey with that [mercury], one should grind it together;
then, one should cook it in an earthen vessel for a day using the juices of *dhattūra*.
One should extract it from the furnace as long as it remains the color of saffron;
then, one *pala* of this very substance should be combined with the perfected powder (*siddhacūrṇa*).
Having sealed it and blown [into the crucible], the *khoṭa* will be produced; one should then grind it for a day with honey and acidic substances.
Having sealed it again with wild blue lotuses (*āraṇyotpalaka*), one should cook it in honey-sealed packets (*madhupuṭa*).
One should smear the silver leaves with this honey-mixture, seal them, and smelt them; after repeating this process three times, they become gold.
It is born endowed with a divine form; this is the truth spoken by Śaṅkara.
However, in the absence of honey, one should employ vaikrānta here instead.
Melted mercury, cinnabar, kaṅkuṣṭha, sulphur,
and realgar should be taken in quantities of one, two, three, four, and five palas respectively.
Having ground all of that with cow-bile for four watches (yāmas),
one should smear clean silver leaves with an equal measure [of the paste].

Having sealed it in a *gajapuṭa* vessel, one should cook it; then, having removed it, one should grind it with an equal amount of the previous paste, seal it again, and cook it in the same way in a *puṭa*.
Thus, when cooked with a hundred folds [of heat], the serpent [mercury] certainly dies;
by a hundredth part of this, through the piercing of silver, gold is produced.
Alternatively, one should smear a leaf of gold— equal in weight to that mercury (mṛtanāga) ground with acid— with that [mercury]; then, having enclosed it, one should cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire.
Furthermore, the nāga should be given repeatedly; in this manner, three layers (puṭas) should be applied.
With this dead gold, one should then pierce the molten silver.
When perfected by a thousandth part [of that process], it becomes divine gold.

One should saturate *dhānyābhraka* seven times with the juices of *tumbaru-vallī* in the sun, and subsequently process it into a solid mass (*khoṭa*). Then, one should add it to one *karṣa* of molten mercury.
One should add a measure of one *māṣa* of this and grind it in a heated mortar;
having placed it in a crucible shaped like a cow’s teat, one should cook it over a mild fire.
Once it has been processed within a *vālukāyantra*, one should again add a dose of the additive.
In this manner, one should digest [the mercury] in equal measure; thus the mercury becomes bound in a pill (khoṭabaddha).
One *māṣa* of this bound [mercury] which is like gold, half a *māṣa* of pure gold,
and half a *māṣa* of pure mercury— one should grind all of these together in one place.
For three days, one should apply a paste made from this [substance] with the acidic juices of *mātuluṅga*;
likewise, one should apply one *karṣa* of lead leaves along with the juices of *vṛścikālī*.
Having smeared it, one should cook it in a *pātanāyantra* for three days,
grinding it every day.
One should smear one *karṣa* of these with *tārapatrāṇi* (silver leaves) and cook it for three days in the *pātanāyantra* as before.
By means of this very [substance], one should quickly transmute copper with a thousandth part;
divine gold is produced, fit for adorning the ornaments of the gods.
Pure mercury, white in color for the purpose of killing (*māraṇa*), is processed with the milk of *uttaravāruṇī* for three days.
One should grind it in a heated mortar with *auṣadhajha* [... // Rrā_3,7.79 //
One should cook it for three days, day and night, in a fire of dried cow dung or in a fire of husks;
then, having extracted it and ground it again, one should seal it as before and heat it once more.
In that same manner, it should be ground again and cooked; thus the pale liquid (rasa) is killed.
[The ingredients are: gold (*candrārka*), ginger, *tuvarī*, *sindhukaṅguṇī*, oil, and honey.
One should grind that juice with *amlavetasa* for one day,
form it into a ball, bind it in cloth, and cook it in a *dolāyantra* for three days.
When its juice is bound within castor oil,
that juice and an equal amount of gold and lead should be enclosed and strongly heated.

That powder, finely ground, along with a portion of powder equal to the amount of quick mercury, should be rubbed with acidic juices until it forms a ball; one should then heat it in sour gruel for a day.
Take three parts of sulfur, an amount of *suvarcala* equal to the sulfur, and one part of black mica; grind all of this together with breast milk.
One should heat a ball smeared with this, placed inside a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*),
repeatedly until only the mercury remains.
Having added the previous powder again, one should melt it in that same manner gradually;
in this way, once the gold has been melted until it is tripled [in weight], it becomes [pure].

Having processed it with gold and subjected it to three cycles of *sāraṇā*, one should pierce the "moon and sun" (copper and silver) with that; from a hundredth part [of the resulting mass], gold is produced.
Gold equal to the *piṣṭīkhoṭa* [of copper], mercury equal to gold,
*kāntaloha*, and the essence (*sattva*) of *vyoma*— each of these [should be used] at half the amount of the mercury. (Rājanighaṇṭu 3.7.89)
Having combined these, one should blow [the crucible] until only gold remains;
then, having added *viḍavaṭī*, one should perform three *sāraṇā* purifications.
By this very hundredth part, the mercury becomes a golden *śulba* (solidified mass);
[the metals] gold, silver, copper, *kānta*, *tīkṣṇa*, and *mākṣika* [are likewise transformed].
Having sealed an equal amount of the essence of black mica, one should heat it strongly.
Having added a quarter-part of quicksilver to that powder of the refined cinnabar,
one should then grind it with acidic juices until it forms a ball (golaka).
One-fourth part of bola and one part of dead-vajra should be ground for one day in a heated mortar with the juice of kanyākā.
Then, having sealed it within the *bhūdhara* [crucible], one should cook it; at the end of the day, one should extract it.
Within that, the molten mercury should again be ground with a maiden’s [menses].
As before, one should cook it in a crucible (bhūdhara) in this manner seven times; likewise, the molten mercury should undergo sequential rubbing (mardana) and heating in a sealed crucible (puṭa).
One should blow that ash, which is equal in quantity to the fragrance, into a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*);
it becomes fixed as a *khoṭa*, and its coloring process is now described.
One should quickly melt together the essence of black mica, tin, and the pair consisting of *tārāriṣṭa*, *candrārka*, and *mākṣika* [which yields] gold.
When that [substance] is blown in a blind crucible with equal parts [of the flux], it becomes a *khoṭa*.
One *pala* of that powder, combined with *siddhacūrṇa*,
should be rubbed with sulfur and acid, then sealed and cooked in a *gajapuṭa*.
It should be rubbed again and boiled again in this manner for fourteen cycles;
by means of this, one should gradually dye the previously prepared mass once it has been liquefied.
One should dye it a hundred times until it becomes like saffron;
having processed it with gold, one should perform three refinements (*sāraṇā*).
With that very same thousandth part, one should pierce the *tārāriṣṭa*;
having heated mercury, silver, and copper, they become divine gold.
Lead and silver [equal to] gold:
having powdered sharp copper and [the other metals] equally, one should blow [the mixture] while enclosed in a *vajramūṣā* crucible.
That resulting residue (*khoṭa*), weighing one *pala*, should then be combined with the perfected powder (*siddhacūrṇa*).
One should rub it with sulfur and acid, seal it, and cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire;
having rubbed it again, one should cook it again, repeating this process fourteen times.
That should be added to the melted gold a hundred times over again and again;
that becomes "matured seed" (pakvabīja), which remains equal to the liquefied mercury for a day.
One should grind four parts of that [substance] with sour juices;
likewise, one part of *vajra* [should be ground] in a heated mortar for the duration of a day.
One should rub it with the juices of *kanyā* plants, seal it, and cook it in an earthen crucible (*bhūdhara*).
Then, having added an equal amount of liquefied mercury again, one should rub it and subsequently place it in a *puṭa*.
In this manner, the molten mercury should be given [the medicine] seven times until the end of the puṭas;
then one should rub it with acidic liquids, seal the crucible, and likewise subject it to puṭa-firing.
It should be rubbed again and cooked again for three hundred and sixty [applications];
a *puṭa* should be applied with great care, whereby it becomes the color of vermilion.
With a thousandth part of lead, quicksilver, and silver, the impregnation (vedha) should be applied;
thus gold is produced, the most excellent of divine ornaments.
One should carefully saturate finely powdered sulphur with sour chickpea juice a hundred times,
and seven times with the menstrual blood of a woman.
One should add a small amount of sulphur mixed with camphor into the midst of molten mercury,
and then cause it to settle in a copper mortar under the heat of the sun.
Camphor and sulfur should be added repeatedly, little by little, for three weeks; thus, a fragrant paste is produced.
One should grind the seeds of *kaṭukośātakī* together with the root of *cāṇḍālī* in breast milk; having made a paste with these equal parts, one should apply it as an ointment.
On the outside, however, one should apply a coating of clay to the extent of one finger-breadth all around;
once dried, one should cook it in the *bhūdhara* [furnace], turning it over from top to bottom.
Then, having extracted that solidified ball,
one should smear it onto gold of equal proportion within a crucible, close the vessel, and heat it in a closed crucible (*mūṣā*).
By means of this eighth part, one should cause the piercing of the silver;
that silver becomes divine, possessing a luster equal to Jāmbūnada gold.
Alternatively, there is gold that has been solidified into a sphere (*stambhita-gola*) and is free from any crucible casing (*saṃpuṭa-varjita*);
of that, there are four parts, and one part is dead diamond (*mṛta-vajra*).
Then, one should grind it again with the juices of kanyākā for one day; thereafter, having blinded it [with a seal], one should cook it in a *bhūdhara* (earth-pot) for four watches (*yāma*).
Having extracted that again, one should add the previous portion—the prior *sūtaka*—and grind it;
one should seal it (*puṭet*) in the same manner, repeating this twenty-one times.
In that [crucible], one pala of ash, mercury, and sulfur,
placed in an *andhamūṣā* crucible and heated, becomes a *khoṭa* equal to lead (*pannaga*).
One should add three times as much gold as there is of the snake-mercury;
once all that is melted, one should grind it with the group of acidic substances (amlavarga).
At the end of the day, having sealed it in a diamond crucible, one should carefully heat it;
from the three [substances], gold resembling a serpent is produced in due order.
One should refine the gold in three ways and then pierce it with that [mercury] in a thousandth part; by that very means, it becomes divine gold.
Having sealed equal parts of the powder of gold (*hemā*), copper (*arka*), and iron (*tīkṣṇa*), one should heat it strongly;
that resulting *khoṭa* (solidified mass) is one part, while quicksilver (*sūtaka*) is three parts.
One should rub it with acidic *gaṇḍhaka* (vitriol) and, having sealed it properly, bake it in a *puṭa*;
after rubbing again and baking again, this should be done fourteen times.
One should transmute white gold with a hundredth part of this;
by sprinkling it with *kaṅguṇī* oil, divine gold is produced.
When the excellent mercury has been bound and liquefied, and when it has been digested within superior gold, I have observed a tenfold gain that is easily accomplished.
When the diamond is killed and joined with the essence of the sky (space), there truly exists for men a fruit multiplied many times over in that very process.
For purification:

one should repeatedly pour tin—which has been placed in a well-heated crucible—into a liquid made from the roots and fruits of *kārpāsa*, *arka*, *karañja*, *dhūrta*, *muni*, *bhallātaka*, *guñjā*, *agni*, *snug*, *vajrī*, and *sūraṇa*, mixed with buttermilk (*takra*). This should be done for five days until it becomes pure; such purified tin may always be employed in alchemical operations.
Alternatively, tin powder should be ground for one day in a mortar with black gram and *bhallātaka* fruits in equal proportions, combined with *bhallātaka* oil.

Having placed that mass into the horn of a buffalo and sealed it within a large crucible (*mahāpuṭa*), one should cook it; then, having extracted it from there, one should grind it once again in the same manner.
In this manner, one should perform the sevenfold processes of solidification, heating, and rubbing;
that tin, thus freed from impurities, should be employed in the rite of immobilization.
One should quickly cast the essence of sharp stone (*tīkṣṇapāṣāṇasattva*) into molten tin;
by means of a sixty-fourth part [of the additive], it will certainly become immobilized.
Silver, white cloud-mineral (śvetābhra), white glass, borax, conch-flower (śaṅkhapuṣpikā),
and poison— these should be taken in equal parts and their powder should be infused twenty-one times.
One should add a post-casting powder (prativāpa) of tin melted in the juices of *kākamācī*, milk, *snuhī*, and *arka* under a fierce sun,
and one should sprinkle it [with these liquids].
By repeatedly anointing it seven times with oil extracted from *putrajīva*,
that divine syllable *tāra* becomes manifest for as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure.
Tin (which is silver),
white mica, white glass, poison, rock salt,
and borax— having ground these together with the milky sap of *snuhī* for one day, [one should apply it] to the leaf of white *vaṅga*.
One should smelt [the substance] placed in a blind crucible (cāndhamūṣā) after coating it with a paste consisting of one-quarter part of the foot-powder;
having taken it out, one should liquefy it on the ground and sprinkle it with the aforementioned oil.
One should sprinkle the paste upon the leaf and so forth seven times;
that tin then becomes silver, resembling a conch shell, a kunda flower, or the moon.
Having ground equal parts of tin, silver, mercury, and realgar with the juices of *devadālī* for one day,
one should then macerate them for one day with the juices of *īśvaraliṅgī*.

Lead and tin should be melted together in equal proportions; that powder, weighing five palas, should be mixed with an amount equal to the previous paste, stirred well, placed in a sealed vessel, and roasted in a fire-pit.
In this manner, it should be cooked again and again, combined with the previous paste;
when perfected through sixty cycles, it becomes a supreme fixative for tin.
It should be given in a hundredth part; by means of piercing, it makes one fully capable of transmuting.
One part each of tin (or silver), mercury, and talaka, two parts of human skull,
and an amount of poison equal to the sum of all these should be combined with the five parts of red *citraka*.

One should cast the powder, which is equal to poison and has been saturated with the milk of a *vajrī* plant, for a full month day and night; its application should be one-sixteenth part [of the total].
When it is processed three times in mercury (vaṅga), it becomes beautiful silver (tāra).
One should grind the medicinal herb named *gorambhā* with human urine;
having formed two pills from it, one should place [the other] on top of one of them.
Upon that, one should place the powder of the three alkalis and then the powder of tin; having added the three alkalis again, one should cast a lump on top of it.
Having sealed the mouth, one should cook it in a crucible and remove it when it has cooled to the temperature of one's own body;
one should do this three times, and the silver becomes beautiful.
In the spring, that Gorambhā plant with yellow flowers arises;
in the middle portion of its stalk, it becomes like white cotton.
Or, in its absence, one should employ the *vasantapuṣpikā*;
that which is known as *bālā* is likewise like dust upon the hips.
One should powder tin (or silver) and white *pālāśa* flowers dried in the shade;
then one should saturate it twenty-one times with the milk of a ewe.
One should add that powder in a sixteenth part to molten tin;
it becomes silver, rich in beauty, resembling a conch shell, a kunda flower, or the moon.
One should grind tin (or silver), that flower, and yellow orpiment with the milk of a ewe;
one should then apply that addition in a sixteenfold proportion to molten tin.
It becomes bright, rich in color, and resembles a conch shell, jasmine, or the moon;
having infused those flowers with buttermilk twenty-one times, one should use them.
One should smear the leaves of vaṅga with that paste;
placed in a sealed crucible (andhamūṣā), it should be smelted in this manner twenty-one times.
That divine mercury, which bestows the fruits of dharma and desire, becomes purified;
[the substances are] tin, silver, *mūṣakapāṣāṇa*, *phaṭkirī*, sapphire, and collyrium.
Having ground everything with the exudations of *agasti* leaves for the duration of a day,
one should then place it inside a vessel and cook it over a lamp-flame.
One should administer the resin of the Agasti leaf whenever [the previous dose] has been digested;
at the end of the day, having extracted that [resin], one should administer it when the tin (vaṅga) is molten.
With a thirtieth part [of that], it becomes refined silver (*tāra*), the ornament of the gods;
with that silver, one should alloy the *vajra*, just as it is alloyed with gold.
Take two parts of this pair and one-third part of pure mercury;
grind them with acid until a pill-like mass (golaka) is formed.
One should grind the five parts of *meṣaśṛṅgī* with breast milk;
with this, one should envelop the pill (*gola*), and that [envelope] externally with an iron chain (*nigaḍa*).
The process beginning with sweating and ending with sublimation should be performed as in the case of the gold-paste;
one should then smear that *khoṭa* with the milky sap of the *uttarāvāruṇī*.
Then, having placed [the mercury] in the middle of a crucible and added equal amounts of silver and viḍavaṭī,
one should blow the fire until only the mercury remains.
In this manner, having subjected it to heating twenty-one times again and again,
one should melt it evenly and refine it three times with silver.
One should cast this very one-thousandth part into molten tin;
that tin becomes silver, which is called the "stabilization of tin" (vaṅgastambha) by Śiva.
One part of red mercury, one part of conch powder, and two full parts of the essence of white mica; these [are to be combined with tin or silver]. Rrā 3.8.39.
And one part of *ṭaṅkaṇa*—all of this should be rubbed with the milk of a *vajrī* plant for three days; in this manner, for fourteen days.
By means of this one-hundredth part, one should quickly transmute tin;
it will solidify, there is no doubt here, and it becomes beautiful silver.
Just as a beautiful *piṣṭī* or *khoṭa* is produced by means of gold-transformed mercury,
in that very same way, one should prepare a *piṣṭī* or *khoṭa* by means of silver-transformed mercury.
That cinnabar and tāravanga, along with an equal amount of sattva derived from white clouds,
should be processed by adding medicinal fluxes (viḍa) and pills until only the cinnabar residue remains.
Having processed it three times by means of *jāraṇa*, one should apply it to molten copper;
by a hundredth part [of that], that silver is produced, as spoken by Śambhu.
Melted tin and silver, along with an equal portion of powdered *tīkṣṇa* iron,
should be rubbed in a heated mortar with the juice of *ṭeṇṭū* bark until it forms a ball.
One-fourth part of golaka and one part of mṛtavajra should be ground for a day in a heated mortar with fresh juice from the bark of ṭeṇṭū.
One should cook it in a crucible until it is blinded; at the end of the day, one should extract it.
Having added a liquefied mercury equal to the previous amount, it should be rubbed as before.
As before, one should cook it in the *bhūdhara* [furnace] in this manner seven times in succession; then, molten mercury should be added, followed by grinding and heating in a *puṭa* in due order.
By means of this sixteenth part, one should quickly transmute tin;
it becomes silver, rich in divine form, resembling the kunda flower and the moon.
Regarding the tin [or] silver that has been treated with a sixteenth part of lead, there is another method:
having sealed an equal amount of sulfur and heated it, a *khoṭa* (solidified mass) is produced.
One should prepare equal parts of that calx and sharp powder; with an amount of quicksilver equal to those two, one should place all of it in a heated mortar.
One should grind it with the juices of *iṭṭuñjāḍa* until it forms a pill;
having then sealed it, one should cook it in a *bhūdhara* [furnace] and extract it after twenty-four hours.
Having added a previous portion and quick mercury, one should grind it in the same manner;
having sealed that, one should roast it in a *puṭa* in the same way, and thus one should do this twenty-one times.
The mercury, having been heated in a closed crucible (*andhamūṣā*), becomes a *khoṭa* (a solidified mass);
one should then grind it with an equal amount of fine iron powder (*tīkṣṇacūrṇa*), seal it in a closed crucible, and heat it again.
By this sequential method, the sharp [reagent] should be added again and again;
having repeatedly added the sharp [reagent] up to seven times its amount, one should indeed heat it.
One should then cause that calx to flow by means of alkali alone, three times in succession;
with just one-hundred-thousandth part of that very [alkali], one should effect the transmutation of tin.
[The result] becomes beautiful silver, resembling a conch shell, a jasmine flower, or the moon.
Having ground *madhusaṃjīvanī* with the urine of a donkey,
one should then saturate it with that same urine for seven days.
One should grind that very mercury in a heated mortar for three days;
then, having added an equal amount of sulfur, one should heat it in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*).
That divine cinnabar is produced;
its coloring is described as being joined with the union of a pair consisting of tin and the essence of white mica.
One should grind that *khoṭa* (residue) weighing one *pala* in the middle of a crucible,
rub it with sulfur and acid, seal it, and cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire.
It should be rubbed again and boiled again in this manner for fourteen times;
with this, one should color the previous *khoṭa* seven times.
Just as with tin and mica, so too with lead and mica;
one should dye it seven times and then reduce it to a fine powder.
One should liquefy [the mercury] joined with the liquid metal (drutasūta) according to the previous sequence;
then, one should diligently cause the silver to be digested by the liquefied [mercury] using the dolāsveda method.
When the mercury has become aged through three times six qualities,
one should perform three purifications (sāraṇās) and it will pierce with a thousandth part.
The molten copper becomes silver, resembling a conch shell, a kunda flower, or the moon.
Copper is [equal to] silver; likewise, the essence of white mica (śvetābhraka), the essence of magnetite (kāntasattva),
iron, tin, silver, vaikrānta, kadamba, and nāga.

When the equal parts have been heated in a blind crucible, one should grind the resulting mass (khoṭa) into powder; then, having rubbed it with molten mercury, one should form a ball with acid until it reaches the desired consistency.
One-fourth part of golaka and one part of mṛtavajra should be ground for one day in a heated mortar with the juices of kanyā.
Then, having sealed it within an earthen crucible, one should cook it; in this manner, one should perform the process twenty-one times.
Having added an equal amount of sulfur, one should blow upon it while it is contained within a closed crucible (*andhamūṣā*).
Having processed it with silver and refined it through three cycles of *sāraṇā*,
one should apply it over molten copper in a proportion of one-thousandth part.
That divine mercury is born; once placed in the crucible, it does not diminish.
Whatever lead-ash was previously processed with a *vajra*,
by that very substance ground with acid, one should coat a copper leaf four times its weight.
Having smeared [the vessel] and sealed it, one should cook it in a *puṭa*;
then, having extracted it, one should grind it, adding one-fourth part of calcined mercury (*bhasmasūta*), and having sealed it again, one should cook it in a *puṭa*.
Thus, when cooked in four layers, that silver certainly dies [is killed]. With exactly sixteen parts of that, one should transfix molten copper;
or else, tin melted with it becomes beautiful silver.
One should kill tin using mercury in the same manner as silver; with that [mercury], one should transfix copper.
That copper becomes divine silver at a sixteenfold proportion; of this there is no doubt.

One should grind silver leaf, equal in weight to pure mercury, with the juice of kanyākā for three days in a heated mortar (taptakhalva), and then place that mercury inside the interior of a crucible (kharpara).
One should cook it in a small cauldron over a fierce fire, adding the juices of *kanyā* [herbs];
after three days, one should remove it and add four times as much rock salt (*saindhava*).
Having added [the ingredients], one should grind it for one watch (yāma) and cook it in a sublimation apparatus (pātanāyantra).
After four watches have passed, one should remove it and wash it with fermented rice-gruel (āranālaka).
One should collect that which remains at the bottom; thus the mercury (pārada) becomes pure and auspicious.
This [mixture] consists of dead mercury, tin, the essence of white mica, and ṭaṅkaṇa.
Poison and *tālasattva* in equal parts, together with the four-fold compound (*catuḥsama*),
should be ground in a mortar with the juices of *snuhī* and *arka* for three days.
Having placed those pills inside a glass flask, one should coat the flask with clay;
then, one should cook the jar in a sand-bath furnace with a mild fire.
When the liquid has dried, one should seal the mouth [of the crucible] and cook it slowly for eight watches (yāmas).
Once it has cooled to the temperature of one's own body, one should extract it and quickly pierce the copper with a sixty-fourth part [of the mercury]; thus it becomes beautiful silver.
One *pala* of mercury and one *pala* of *tāla*, or else *śilā* in place of *tāla*,
should be rubbed with the juices of black *unmatta* for three days; at the end of those three days, one should extract it.
Having placed it in a diamond crucible and sealed it, one should cook it for a day in a wheel-press (*cakrayantra*).
It should be ground again and cooked again; when this has been done seven times: // Rrā_3,8.84 //
One should wrap that dead [mercury] in turn with equal parts of tin, silver, and copper;
having sealed it and smelted it with a fierce fire, it becomes beautiful silver.
Three parts of pure mercury and one part of copper leaf should be ground for one *yāma* in breast milk; thus, a silver paste (*tārapiṣṭikā*) is produced.
One should grind the seeds of uttaravāruṇī with breast milk;
with that very [mixture], one should smear the crucible (piṣṭī) and seal the vajra-mūṣā.
One should cook it for one day on a furnace, and having smeared it again, cook it once more;
thus, after being cooked seven times, the solidification of the paste becomes firm.
With that very thirty-second part, one should cause the piercing of the copper;
by adding a tenth part of silver, it becomes beautiful silver.
Having ground *śṛṅgāṭī* and conch-shell powder with cow’s urine and *sāranālaka*, one should repeatedly pour molten [copper or silver] into the midst of that paste. (Rājaratnākara 3.8.90)
One should remove that copper leaf once it has become worn out;
then, having placed it inside a crucible along with honey, clarified butter, and *ṭaṅkaṇa*, one should blow upon it [to heat it].
Having combined it with half of the *tāra*, that becomes pure *tāra*.
The alkali of *arka*, *apāmārga*, and plantain, stirred with acid,
should be smeared upon a copper leaf; this [leaf] placed in a crucible (*mūṣā*) is then to be smelted again.
Having made a leaf and smeared it, one should heat it again and again;
thus one should perform this seven times so that it becomes suitable for the *dalas* in the ritual.
Alternatively, one should heat copper plates well and immerse them a hundred times in a mixture of salt and sour gruel, as described previously.
Having smeared copper leaves with alkali produced from the roots of the *palāśa* tree and *phaṭkirī* ground with sour liquid, one should melt them and then re-plate them.
In this manner, one should divide it sevenfold; thus it shall become suitable for the petals.
Equal parts of very pure talaka (orpiment), mercury,
and sea salt should be ground together in a mortar for two *yāmas* and then cooked inside a new vessel.
One should stir it over a mild fire until it becomes thick;
then, one should separately grind sea salt with an equal portion of palmyra juice.
One should collect [the substance] as long as the *ciṭ-ciṭ* sound continues;
once it has been pulverized in an earthen press, one should then add half a portion of salt.
On top of that, having placed the previous triad and half a *lavaṇa* in its center,
one should seal the joint with clay and salt, let it dry, and then pulverize it.
For up to twelve *yāmas*, one should apply a strong fire upon the back of the crucible;
then one should collect that substance, which resembles dead mercury and adheres to the upper surface.
Having bound it with a cloth, one should apply the piercing of the spear-point to the tip of the staff.
When the copper has been melted down to a tenth part, one should cast it into cow-dung and curd.
Having refined it by smelting with half the amount of silver, it becomes like a conch shell, a kunda flower, or the moon.
One should thus grind the nāga together with one-eighth part of kāntaloha; then,
having smeared a crucible with the *dvandva* mixture, one should strongly blow upon all the powders.
When that brass is melted with tin, it attains the state of silver.
Silver, copper, magnetite, and lead, powdered and smelted as before,
should be processed together with half the amount of silver; thus, beautiful silver is produced.
Silver,
tin, and bell-metal, along with an equal amount of borax, should be melted together for the purpose of coloring (optimizing the hue).
One part of this alloy and three parts of pure copper [are to be used].
Having thoroughly stirred the prepared *khoṭa* and mixed it with an equal amount of silver,
that silver becomes pure, resembling snow, the *kunda* flower, and the moon.
One should cause five parts of the powder of muṇḍaloha to be taken for the purpose of coloring (rañjana), which is the optimization of the color.
One should place a single part of the essence of the *tāla* within its interior.
Having added borax and white glass above, one should seal it;
once it has been intensely heated, one should grind it to powder and again cause the essence to be given.
Having added glass and borax, one should blow the crucible while it is sealed;
in this manner, one should perform the process five times, repeatedly adding the essence.
Equal parts of that [mercury], pure silver, and the ash of "raised from death" (mṛtottha) lead ore— having thoroughly mixed this triad, one should melt equal amounts of copper and iron.
One should apply the piercing (vedha) by a tenth part and join the seed-syllable by a quarter;
thus it becomes a divine silver, resembling a conch, a kunda flower, or the moon.
Equal parts of purified mercury, killed tin, white mica, and borax, as well as five parts of each of these and four times the amount of "mouse-stone" (mūṣakapāṣāṇa), [should be taken]. Rrā 3.8.113.
One should firmly combine purified talaka with the milky sap of snuhi and arka;
having ground it all for three days, one should place it inside a glass flask.
Then, once it has been properly smeared with soft cloth and well-dried,
one should cook it by placing it inside a perforated *kūpī* (jar) within a sand-oven (*vālukāyantra*).
When the liquid has dried, seal the opening firmly with salt-earth (loṇamṛttikā),
and then cook it over a fierce fire for sixteen watches (yāmas).
Having removed it once it has cooled to the temperature of one's own body, one should break the glass flask;
having collected the *tāla* essence adhering to the upper part, one should perform the piercing (*vedhana*) with it.
One should melt the copper with a sixteenth part [of silver] in cow dung;
then, having amalgamated it with equal pure silver,
that silver becomes purified, resembling snow, the kunda flower, and the moon.
Having ground talaka equal in measure to soap-nut (sābuṇī), one should roast it in an iron pan.
Stirring it gently over a mild fire until it becomes black,
one should place it inside a glass jar coated with clay and then put [the mixture] back into that [jar].
Having roasted salt and adding one-tenth part of orpiment (*tālaka*),
one should cook it as before in a sand-oven (*vālukāyantra*) and extract the essence (*sattva*).
Having added one-sixteenth part of soap-nut essence (*sābuṇī-sattva*) and ground it,
one should cook it again in a *vālukāyantra* for eight watches (*yāma*), as before, using a small flask (*kūpikā*).
One should cook that *sattva* and sesame oil in equal parts with the flesh,
stirring it in an iron vessel until the oil has been fully absorbed.
In this manner, it should be cooked seven times with oil, repeatedly;
likewise, once prepared, it should be cooked seven times with an equal amount of *kathaka*.
One should quickly pierce the copper with a sixty-fourth part [of the mercury];
one should pierce it by the "spear-piercing" method and melt it in cow-dung and curd.
One should add a quarter-part of the seed; it becomes beautiful silver.
One should apply borax in a tenth part of the amount of purified calamine.
It should be ground in a mortar for three days with the milk of a ewe and likewise with clarified butter.
Having rubbed [the substance] with castor oil for a day, one should place it in a sealed vessel (kūpī);
one should cook it in the apparatus as before, and once the liquid has dried, one should place it back [into the vessel].
At the end of sixteen yāmas, the great being becomes exceedingly subtle;
with that very sixteenth part, one should pierce the gold plate.
And half of tāra should be melted quickly; it becomes pure as before.

Having melted six *niṣkas* of copper with one *niṣka* of *ākhu-pāṣāṇa*, it should be administered by the *kunta-vedha* method; thus the leaf [of the copper] becomes half-seed (*ardha-bīja*). (Rrā 3.8.129)
Tālaka, ṭaṅkaṇa, sarjikṣāra,
and that produced from apāmārga should be ground together with the milky sap of the vajri plant in a mortar for four watches (yāmas).

One should coat copper plates with this half-portion; having been heated in a sealed crucible (*andhamūṣā*), when this is done three times and mixed with an equal amount of silver, it becomes pure silver.
One should take the oil of *guñjā*, cotton, and *śigru* from a single one of these;
into that oil, one should repeatedly immerse molten copper twenty-one times.
One should cause the seed (bīja) to be given as one-sixth part, so that it becomes pure silver;
then, one should melt it in a crucible smeared with the root of the *śigru* tree.
To soften silver and gold, one should stir them with water mixed with the ashes of *arka*, *apāmārga*, and plantain.
That clear water, having dripped from that cloth, should then be collected in the sunlight.
Having diligently extracted the salt from that [solution],
one should add it to melted silver or gold in a proportion of one part per hundred.
One should cause that very [substance] to be soaked and then fried in sesame oil;
by performing this three times in such a manner, it will become extremely soft.
{Softening}:
One should collect the hooves and horns of horses, cows, and buffaloes;
by merely sowing that powder [upon the hair], it will become exceedingly soft.
One should apply either the powder of elephant tusk or dried human excrement to hard [substances] as a seed for soaking; thus they will become exceedingly soft. (Rājanighaṇṭu 3.8.138)
Various types of medicinal preparations and ornaments are indeed made with the leaf;
having ground the white and red roots of the *varṣābhū* plant with *āranālaka* (sour gruel), [one obtains the desired results].
Then, having ground a little salt and thrown it into that very [mixture], one should grind it again;
after half a ghaṭikā, one should extract that which has become somewhat leaf-like.
Rubbing it with salt and sour substances, one should heat it in fire and cook it again;
by performing this process three times, the leaf becomes pure.
Taking the powder of *phaṭkarī* for the purpose of purification (*nirmalīkaraṇa*), one should place it upside down in an earthen pan (*kharpara*),
seal it with a leaf, and cook it properly in a *gajapuṭa* fire.
Having taken [the substance] and bound it with a rope, one should cook it for a day in a swinging apparatus (dolāyantra) within a vessel made of tamarind stalks;
it then becomes as white as a conch shell.

Herein, for the benefit of alchemists (*vārtikānām*), the method of immobilization (*stambhana*) is described— easily accomplished with mercury (*sūta*), copper (*śulba*), and iron (*āra*), which are free from excessive impurities— and which is easy to perform, clear, and proven effective through methods containing sound reasoning when applied to pure *vaṅga* (tin) for the attainment of ever-new bliss.

Having fashioned the peak of the Mountain of Gold with mercury colored by vajra mixed with gold and well-colored by gold through most beautiful applications, one should then perform sacrifices for the sake of attaining the station of Śakra.
{Dvandvamelāpana}:
A crucible-mouth made of magnetite, with *guñjā* and twice that amount of sulfur ground with breast milk,
should be smeared upon the crucible for the *dvandvamelaka* [fusion].
One should grind together in equal proportions *vajra*, *gandha*, rabbit’s teeth, the mouth of the *bhrāmaka* [crucible], *amlavetasa*, and *śilādhātu*.
By that very same application to the crucible, the pair of vajras fully unites.
(3) Vajradvandvamelāpana:
the impurity arising from the ears and eyes of a buffalo, powdered borax,
breast milk, crab shells, and bitumen— all in equal parts.
Having ground [the ingredients], one should apply them as a coating to the crucible for the purpose of merging in the "vajra-couple" (vajradvandva).
{Vajradvandvamelāpana (4)} One should grind together beeswax, human bone, human hair, ṭaṅkaṇa salt, the "face" produced from *kānta* iron, and the dung of a young calf with breast milk.
When smeared with that paste, the pair of diamonds will fully unite within the crucible.
{The Alchemical Union of the Vajra-thread}:

Earth-lead (bhūnāga), loadstone (kāntapāṣāṇa), pyrite (mākṣika), borax (ṭaṅkaṇa), honey, the milky sap of *snuk*, the bones of a crab, glass, and the milky sap of the *arka* plant— [these] in equal parts.
One should grind all [the ingredients] with breast milk and apply them as a coating to the crucible;
when the *vajrasūta* placed therein is heated intensely, it will surely merge [with the crucible].
{The Alchemical Fusion of Gold and Vajra (the Binary Compound):} Four parts of dead vajra, twelve of gold,
three parts of nāga, and six of pure mercury. Rrā_3,9.9.
Having combined these, one should grind them for a day with some kind of acid;
then, having extracted that paste into a heated mortar, one should seal it.
When forcibly blown in a crucible smeared with the two [substances], they thoroughly merge together.
{The Union of Gold and Vajra (2):} One should visualize the vajra as deceased by means of the alkaline substances of the *utpala-sāriṇī* plant;
having been purified for one day and ground into a paste, one should fashion it into individual pills. Rrā_3,9.12.
Take one-third part of mercury and four parts of gold;
one should form a paste with an acid and place that pill within its interior.
Having bound that with birch bark, one should place it within a heap of grain;
after a fortnight has passed, one should extract it and blow upon it while it is in the previous crucible.
It certainly meets [the target] again and again as it is being heated; of this there is no doubt.
{The Union of Gold and Vajra (the Couple-Compound, 2):} One part of dead vajra should be wrapped with a gold leaf;
it should be properly placed in the crucible as before, together with a sixteenth part [of gold]. // Rrā_3,9.16 //
Having powdered glass that resembles gold in color, or white glass, or even a human skull,
one should cast it into that [liquid], seal it, and blow it with a fierce fire.
Having extracted it again, one should place either glass or a human skull [inside];
having smeared the crucible, one should blow upon it, and thus [the process is repeated] in seven crucibles.
Just as that diamond is mixed with gold, one should mix them again in this manner until the dead diamond is merged into the gold in the proportion of one quarter.
Two parts of the alloy of copper and gold, and three parts of molten mercury, should be rubbed together with acidic juices; at the end of the day, that mass should be formed into a ball.
One should grind the five parts of *meṣaśṛṅgī* with breast milk;
with this, one should pierce the pill (*gola*) and its exterior with a binding seal (*nigala*).
One should perform the process from sweating (sveda) up to the stage of amalgamation (melana), like the grinding of gold;
then, one should rub that *khoṭa* for a moment with the alkalis derived from *meṣaśṛṅgī*.
One should smear the interior of the crucible with that [substance] and cast into it an equal amount of gold;
one should blow [the fire] until it is digested, and then add more gold again.
One should digest [the mercury] by means of heating alone, having gradually administered the *viḍavaṭī*;
in this manner, one should digest the gold until it has become twenty times [the original amount].
Having processed it with gold through the application of three *sāraṇās*,
one should transmute copper (*śulba*) with that very [gold] by a thousandth part;
it becomes rich in divine form, possessing a luster equal to *jāmbūnada* gold.
Gold,
having been placed in a diamond crucible (*vajramūṣā*) and heated with a fierce fire, forms a *dvaṃdvakhoṭa* alloy;
or else, one may use the washed essence (*dhautasattva*) from *mākṣika* ore, or the essence produced from *mākṣika*.
One should add it little by little to that [substance] as it is being blown upon, again and again, until it takes on the appearance of saffron; then one should extract the vajra.
By that very same one-hundred-thousandth part, one should transmute white gold;
it becomes divine gold, the most excellent ornament for the gods.
Gold, vaikrānta, mākṣika, tuttha, mercury, añjana,
gairika, vimalā, and vaiḍūrya— one of these [substances] weighing half a pala [should be used].
Take one part of each—nāgabhaṅga and arka—as available, in the amount of half a pala;
having then formed a double-powder (dvaṃdvacūrṇa) and sealed it, one should heat it in a vajra-mūṣā crucible.
As before, having ground it with sulphur and acid, one should seal it and cook it in a *puṭa*;
by fourteen such *puṭas*, it becomes like the rising sun.
With this, one should color the *vajra-khoṭa* as before;
likewise, by adding a hundred-thousandth part of white silver and gold, it becomes pure gold.
Alternatively, one should cause the *khoṭa* of the *dvaṃdva* [compound] to be made into a fine powder;
this pure powder, placed in a closed crucible (*andhamūṣā*), should be heated.
One should grind [the mercury] equal in weight to the juice of *āroṭa* and *jambīra* fruits for one day;
then, having bound it in a cloth, it should be subjected to heat for one day in a *dolāyantra* with *kāñjika*.
Afterwards, one should cook it with the cloth for a period of days in fragrant oil;
then, having removed it from the cloth, one should cook it again in a balance with a chain.

One should subject it to the process beginning with sweating and ending with sublimation (*dhamana*), like gold being ground into a paste; having extracted that residue (*khoṭa*), one should then color it—this is what is described.
Having finely powdered sharp copper and made it into a powder, one should blow it in a blind crucible;
then, that residue, weighing one *pala*, should be combined with the perfected powder (*siddhacūrṇa*).
Having sealed the powder, one should heat it intensely; then that *khoṭa* should be ground again with the acid of sulfur as before, and fourteen *puṭas* should be administered.
By this [process], one should place the previous powder into the middle of the crucible as before,
slowly and repeatedly, until it attains the color of saffron.
Having processed it with gold and subjected it to three cycles of *sāraṇā*,
one should pierce molten copper with one-hundred-thousandth part of this [substance].
Divine gold is produced; this is the truth spoken by Śaṅkara.
One *karṣa* of red mercury-bhasman, eight *guñjās* of gold,
and four *guñjās* of dead diamond [are to be processed] for one day with the juices of *haṃsapādī*.
One should rub it in a heated mortar and cook it sealed in a *vajramūṣā* crucible;
having extracted it after a single *bhūdhara*-named *puṭa*, one should then rub it again.
In this manner, with the juices of *haṃsapādī* in a heated mortar for a full day, one should cook it as before in an earthen vessel; thus one should cook it with a hundred *puṭas*.
The ash shall be red in color; one should employ it in all yogic practices.
Having impregnated *dhānyābhra* seven times with the juices of the *vartulapatrā* plant or with the juices of the *somavallī*, one should then begin the process of *jāraṇa*.
One should place purified mercury into a crucible shaped like a cow’s udder,
along with the previously mentioned abhra in a sixteenth part of the quantity, using chickpea juices as the flux.
One should cook it over a mild fire in a furnace inside a vessel filled with sand; when the mica has been digested, one should add chickpea juice again once it has been digested.
In this manner, one should gradually digest an equal amount of *gagana* (mica) with mercury;
then, having ground *dhānyābhraka* (grain-mica) for one *yāma* with the juice of *somavallī*, [it should be processed].
Having sealed it with forest-lotuses, one should apply [the heat] in this manner for three successive *puṭas*;
one should then saturate it seven times in the sun's heat with the juices of *somavallī* for one day.
Having smeared an earthen vessel with the roots of the *śvetā* and *śarapuṅkhā* plants ground into a paste and rubbed with cow’s milk, one should place abhra (mica) therein.
One should place the mercury (sūta) in the middle of that, and then abhraka on top of it;
first, that vessel should be [drenched] with the juices of somavallī in the hot sun.
If one retains it for a long time while practicing, even the sky becomes a paste;
[copper becomes] gold, with a penetration of ten million (*koṭivedha*).
This previously mentioned "fragrant paste" (*gandhapiṣṭī*) is that which has been solidified without the process of digestion (*jāraṇa*).
For thus: first the powder of mica, second the essence of mica, third the fourth is red ash, which was previously produced by the Vajra.
Take one *pala* of mercury that has been processed through four successive reductions;
all of this should be macerated for one day in a heated mortar with the juices of *haṃsapādī*.
Having crushed it and extracted [the essence], one should cook it in a kacchapa-yantra until only the mercury remains;
indeed, it should be processed with a *puṭa* until that point.
One should add an equal portion of the two types of *vajra* to this mercury and cook it by means of *dolāsveda* until it forms a solid ball (*golaka*).
One should cause [the mercury] to digest [the medicine] in the kacchapa yantra until only the mercury remains;
in this manner, one should diligently cause the pair of diamonds to digest six times their weight.
With that very same pair of vajras, one should perform the three extractions (*sāraṇā*).
By this tenth-millionth part, one should transmute the molten copper;
thus, divine gold is produced, fit for adorning the ornaments of the gods.
Take one part of gold (derived from *candrārka*) and sixteen parts of purified mercury along with dead-vajra;
one should grind them in a heated mortar (*taptakhalva*) with the group of acidic substances (*amlavarga*) for the duration of a day.
One should smear the leaves of the ripened seed with this [mixture] in equal measure;
then, one should wrap the smeared leaves with well-ripened *bhānu* leaves.
Having enclosed it within a pair of earthen saucers, one should bury it in the middle of the hearth;
there, one should kindle a fire for three days, gradually increasing it little by little.
Then, one should seal it in a crucible coated with iron filings and cook it with a fire of dried cow-dung; after a day and night, one should extract it.
One should rub it slightly with honey, and then, having smeared copper and silver leaves with a hundredth part of that [substance], one should heat them in a blind crucible (andhamūṣā).
It becomes gold, rich in beauty; this is the truth spoken by Śaṅkara.
One part of dead-vajra (mṛtavajra), one part of gold (hāṭaka),
and three parts of quicksilver (drutasūta)— one should grind all of this with breast milk.
One should wrap that ball in cloth and cook it for three days in scented oil;
thereafter, one should cause it to be amalgamated with an equal amount of gold.
Having added *viḍavaṭī* twenty-one times,
once it has been digested twenty-one-fold, one should perform three *sāraṇā*s.
By means of that very same thousandth part, one should cause the piercing of the lead;
