divine gold is produced, fit for adorning the ornaments of the gods.

Pure mercury, dead *vajra*, and silver and copper [which become] gold— these should be ground together with an equal amount of the juices of *haṃsapādī* in a heated mortar for three days; at the end of that period, one should extract the mixture.
Having ground the seeds of divine medicinal herbs, one should smear the crucible;
then, having poured the aforementioned liquid into it and sealed it, one should heat it with a fire of dried cow-dung.
Having extracted it again, one should add an equal amount of pure mercury to it;
it should be rubbed with the juices of *haṃsapādī* for three days as before.
Having first sealed that ball in a crucible, one should cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire;
this mercury becomes an ash, which one should employ in all ritual operations.
One should grind an equal amount of pure mercury with one-quarter part of borax using acidic liquids for one day; having done so, one should extract the resulting ball.
Having ground together the seeds of red cotton, black mustard, *yavaciñcikā*,
and *vandhyākarkoṭakī*, one should smear a ball [of clay] with this paste.
Having placed salt above and below and having sealed the crucible, one should dry it;
after cooking it in a fire of dried cow-dung for a day and night, one should extract it.
Having thrown that ball into the previous paste and sealed it as before, one should cook it in the *puṭa* for a day and night; in this manner, one should repeat the process seven times.
Then, having smeared it with that very paste and sealed it, one should let it dry; one should cook it thoroughly in a *gajapuṭa* fire and then blow upon it while it is inside the crucible.
By that very same hundredth part, one should quickly pierce mercury with the moon and sun;
thus there arises divine gold, fit for adorning the ornaments of the gods.
Alternatively, that work may be performed with mercury mixed with ashes and combined with borax;
when heated in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*), it becomes an excellent *khoṭa*.
One should melt together everything—pure gold and [the alloy] equal to the dross—and pierce the moon and sun with it; as before, it becomes gold.
{The hundred-fold piercing paste (śatavedhikalka) for silver and copper}:
One should grind vajra-ash with the milky sap of *snuhī* for one day;
having sealed it, one should cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire, and in this manner, one should cook it for a hundred *puṭas*.
Having added an equal amount of purified mercury and rubbed it for three days with the juices of *devadālī*, one should then seal that ball and place it in a *puṭa* furnace.

Having extracted [the substance] from a fire of dried cow-dung cakes day and night, one should then grind it for three days with the juices of *devadālī*; likewise, having enclosed it, one should cook it in a *puṭa*.
In this manner, it should be cooked ten times until the gold becomes equal to a diamond;
then, having added the juices of *kāñcanaka*, one should grind it for three days.
As before, one should cook it with ten *puṭas* using the *puṭapāka* method;
then, having made a powder of sharp iron equal in weight to the gold, one should employ it.
One should grind all of that with the juices of triphalā for three days;
one should then roast it using the previous method, thus cooking it with ten *puṭa* applications.
Having added dead mercury (nāga) equal in weight to sharp [iron],
one should grind everything together in a mortar for three days with the juices of *vāsā*, *raktāśva*, and *māra*.
Having sealed it in a *gajapuṭa* vessel, one should cook it; then, having ground it again, one should cook it once more.
Thus, having been cooked in ten *puṭas*, one should extract it and then grind it.
All of that should be ground with the group of sour substances for four watches;
having sealed it, one should cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire, and after grinding it again, one should cook it once more.
Thus it should be cooked in ten layers until it becomes like vermilion;
with one hundredth part of this, one should quickly perform the transmutation (*vedha*) of mercury, even that of the sun and moon.
Alternatively, one should then smear the moon and the sun with honey-anointed [substance];
divine gold is produced, and once placed in a crucible, it does not diminish.
Alternatively, one should smear tāra leaves with honey mixed with a sixty-fourth part [of mercury]; it becomes divine gold.
One part of mercury sixty-four times the amount of gold (the *śatavedhī* paste), and one part of dead diamond.
One should grind it with the group of sour substances (amlavarga) in a heated mortar for three days.
One should smear a gold leaf with three parts of this [substance], seal it, and then cook it in a *bhūdhara* (earth-oven); having extracted it, one should then grind it.
Combined with three parts of pure mercury and processed for three days with the group of acidic substances (amlavarga), one should then seal it and roast it in a *bhūdhara* (earth) furnace.
It should be rubbed again and boiled again twenty-one times;
with this [mixture], using one hundredth part [of the mercury], one should combine the "moon and sun" (mercury and sulfur) with honey.
Having smeared and sealed it, one should heat it intensely; it becomes divine gold.
[Silver =] Gold: One should smear [the silver] with the previously mentioned ash-elixir ground with acid.
Having enclosed a gold leaf weighing four times as much, one should cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire.
Furthermore, one should add mercury in the form of ash to that [mercury] by a quarter part.
One should rub it with the group of acidic substances (amlavarga) and likewise cook it, having sealed it in a crucible (puṭa).
Thus, cooked by four such applications of heat, the auspicious gold (hāṭaka) dies.
One should quickly pierce the silver with that very sixteenth part;
or else, by means of a leaf-coating, it becomes divine gold.
{Copper becomes} gold;
[the recipe for] a hundredfold transmuting paste:
one part of dead vajra and sixteen parts of pure mercury.
It should be rubbed with the juices of *devadālī* and *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for three days.
Having sealed it within a *vajramūṣā* crucible, one should cook it for one day in a *bhūdhara* (earth-heater) furnace;
then, having extracted it, one should grind it with its own melts for one day and seal it once more.
One should cook [the mercury] on a furnace for one day, and likewise grind and cook it;
in this manner, one should perform the process seven times, whereby the mercury is reduced to ash.
One should blow upon that ash-mercury, equal [in weight], enclosed within a *vajramūṣā* crucible;
it becomes a divine *khoṭa*, which is said to be used for coloring [the mercury].
Having finely powdered sharp copper and made it into a paste, one should heat it in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*).
That resulting *khoṭa* should then be ground with the "perfected powder" (*siddhacūrṇa*) and sulfur-juice (*gaṃdhakāmla*).
Following the sequence as before, one should apply fourteen *puṭas*;
by this means, the previously mentioned *khoṭa* should be melted again and again.
One should heat that ash together with an equal amount of sulphur, enclosed in a *vajramūṣā* crucible;
after ten cycles of heating, it becomes a solid mass (*khoṭa*) with the luster of saffron.
Having processed it three times with gold, it becomes a hundred-fold pénétration (śatavedhī);
when added to molten copper, it becomes divine gold.
One *pala* of the previously mentioned ash-mercury, combined with an equal amount of mercury (*pannaga*), [is mixed with] *tārāriṣṭa* (gold), which is a paste capable of piercing a thousand times.
It should be rubbed for one day with a lump of iron inside a beautiful vessel.
One should rub that [substance] in its vessel with a mild fire and cook it slowly;
once it has become well-mixed, one should remove it, seal it, and cook it in a *gajapuṭa* (elephant-seal) furnace.
It should be rubbed with the juice of vāsā and cooked in this manner fourteen times;
then it should be rubbed again with cow bile and subjected to fourteen puṭapāka treatments.
Having added an equal amount of gold powder, one should grind it with bile;
at the end of the day, having extracted that [mixture], it should be combined with a *krāmaṇa* agent.
By means of that very same thousandth part, one should pierce the *tārāriṣṭa*;
thus, divine gold arises, the most excellent ornament for the gods.
When mercury is placed in the "Nāga" position according to the previous sequence,
one should apply the process of *vedha* (penetration) to copper combined with silver powder;
by a thousandth part [of the mercury], that copper becomes like the jasmine flower or the moon.
Copper [is transformed into] gold by means of liquefied mercury, by means of *vajra* and *vajras*, or by means of purified mercury;
or by means of dead mercury, *vajra* and *vajras*, or by means of purified mercury.
Whatever various types of *khoṭa* were previously described by means of the most excellent divine yogas— that single *khoṭa* one should cause to melt, just like a *piṣṭi-khoṭa*.
One should quickly [use] divine mercury, which destroys death and poverty;
then, one should cause the ripened seed (pakvabījaka) to be digested by this liquefied mercury.
Gradually, up to six times [the amount], in the vessel called *kacchapa* containing *viḍa*,
the *vyomasattva* should be digested according to the method that will be described.
That [mercury], having been heated and processed three times with ripened seed (*pakvabīja*) in due order,
should then be used to transmute molten copper by this proportion of one ten-millionth part (*koṭimāṃśa*).
Divine gold is produced, serving as an ornament for the jewelry of the gods.
{Vajra:: Melting} Now, there is another procedure for this mercury (*rasendra*) that pierces ten million [times]:
*viṣṇukrāntā*, *cakrāṅkā*, *kaṇṭārī*, and *ciñcikā*. (Rasārṇava 3.9.121)
Having taken the liquid of these [substances], one should apply it as a coating to the crucible;
having poured the previous liquid into it, one should heat it while repeatedly pouring in more liquid.

The *vajra* should be applied to that very [mercury]; it certainly melts, there is no doubt. Then, having extracted it from that, one should cook it for three days in a swinging apparatus (*dolāyantra*).
Having extracted it and placed it in a crucible smeared with cow dung ash, one should blow the fire openly;
when blown strongly with the bellows, it will certainly be consumed—of this there is no doubt.
Having processed either diamond or ruby in a tenfold liquid, one should cause it to be acted upon by the diamond-seed; thus the mercury becomes capable of piercing through sound.
Alternatively, once that sapphire has been killed, one should again perform the process of *jāraṇā* (digestion) using *uccaṭā*,
*mīnanayanā*, *sarpākṣī*, and red *citraka*.
One should pour these fluxes into the molten mercury contained within a crucible;
one should then cast sapphire into it, and it will surely melt—of this there is no doubt.
By means of the *viḍa*-yoga through sweating as before, one should digest the sapphire (*indranīla*); thus, the sapphire should be digested three times in due order. (Rāma-kaṅkāli 3.9.128)
That best of men who places that nectar within his mouth is worthy of worship by the gods of gods, and he rejoices through the state of a sky-walker (khecarī).
From his urine and excrement, all metals and gold are produced, rich in divine form; this is the truth spoken by Śaṅkara.
Thus, when another *khoṭa*—which has been thoroughly processed with impurities (*saṃkara*) and bound into a pill—is melted, it indeed becomes pure once dead, and produces a heap of gold.

Or rather, if that [elixir] swallows the ripened seed and becomes liquefied, it pierces ten million-fold; if the mercury (*rasa*) assimilates diamond, mica, and various gems, it bestows the power of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*).
Having prepared the seed by cooking it with *viḍa* salt using the best great-essences (*mahārasa*) of metals, it should then be properly digested within the excellent mercury.
It should likewise be employed in all processes of *sāraṇā*; that procedure for the various seeds and *viḍas* will now be described.
One should melt equal parts of purified copper and matured seed (*pakvabīja*), then smear it again with a paste of *tāpya* mixed with acid; one should blow the mixture until only gold remains.
In this manner, having heated the external substance ten times— whether it be tuttha, sattvaka, or the like— one should collect the remaining gold, which is known as "ripened seed" (pakvabīja).
Equal parts of *nāgābhra* and matured seed (*pakvabīja*) should be combined and processed into gold sixteen times over;
as before, the remaining gold should be taken as the matured seed.

One should smelt equal parts of *pakvabīja* (matured seed), gold, and yellow mica-essence as a binary compound; by adding *tālaka* (mica) to the *tāpya* (cinnabar), one should recover the residue as gold.
In this way, the external essence consisting of ripened seed-syllables is tenfold.
The essence of mercury and mica, copper, and lead, in increasing order [of their proportions], along with ripened seed. (4) Rrā 3.10.6.
Having ground it and sealed it in a crucible smeared with a pair [of substances], one should blow it while closed.
Then, having ground that residue (khoṭa), along with *mākṣika* and *tuttha*, with acidic liquids, one should cook it in a *puṭa*.
Having extracted it again, one should grind it with sour liquids, seal it, and cook it in a *puṭa*.
Cooked thus by five *puṭas*, one should process it into molten gold;
one should heat it until it has increased tenfold, at which point it becomes "cooked seed" (*pakvabījaka*).
When iron is being beaten and thoroughly heated, its scales indeed fall away; having taken those up, this is known as *lohaparpaṭa* (iron leaf).
Loha-parpaṭa, mākṣika, kaṅkuṣṭha, vimalā, abhraka, dead copper (mṛta-śulba), realgar (śilā), mercury (sūta), vermilion (darada), and the milky sap of the arka and snuhī plants.
One should grind these together with powdered nāga (lead), seal it, and cook it in a *puṭa*;
having ground it again, one should cook it again, repeating this process fourteen times.
Thus, by repeatedly smelting pure gold a hundredfold,
that gold becomes the seed of *nāga*, resembling *gorocana* in appearance.
When lead has been melted in a crucible, one should indeed add the petals of the *brahmabīja* seed, which is ripened and colored.
Having cast the fire, one should kindle it fiercely and stir it with the Brahmadaṇḍa.
After four watches, one should take that ash from the vessel;
having sealed it in a *gajapuṭa* crucible, one should cook it again with a quarter-part of sulfur.
Having added sour gruel and ground it, one should cook it in this manner for fourteen cycles;
the ash will become red in color, and one part of that should be placed in a shallow pan (kharpara).
One should place three parts of powdered stone in a separate vessel,
along with the powder of the five parts of *vāsaka* and the powder of the bark of *arjuna*.
One should gather the flowers of the śāka, kiṃśuka, koraṇṭa, and śigru;
[these are used for] the nāginī, the nāgakanyā, the kumārī, and the ahimāraka.
One should place a single portion of each of these inside a stone vessel and prepare a decoction by boiling everything with goat urine four times the quantity.
One should mix [the substance] placed in a skull-cup with the previously mentioned nāgas and bhūtas;
one should stir and cook it on the hearth for a period of up to seven days.
With effort, a bath should be given to the molten [metal] using a dead serpent;
after three washings with the seeds of the *pakva* plant, it becomes auspiciously colored.
For the stabilization of the paste of leaves and seeds, and especially for the rites of eradication (*uccāṭa*) and transference (*krāmaṇa*),
the previously mentioned "dead lead" (*mṛtanāgaka*) should be employed.
The seed, the ripe [fruit],
and the dye— namely, *mañjiṣṭhā*, the *brahmapuṣpa* flower, and the *karavīra* flower.
One should also gather red flowers from all species of trees,
as well as *khadira*, *devadāru*, the two types of *niśā* (turmeric), and red sandalwood.
Having ground everything with lac juice and added four times as much oil,
one should cook it until only the oil remains; then, having cooked the seed twenty-one times, one should pour it into that oil, and it becomes beautifully dyed.

One should employ the seed that has been ripened and colored by means of internal fluxes (garbhadrāva) in all processes of transmutation (sāraṇa). One should digest the mercury with an equal amount [of the flux], but one should cause it to transmigrate with twice that amount.
Indeed, the rubbing-in (pratisāraṇa) must be performed with this very [substance] three times over;
once it has been rubbed in, one should employ it with the transmuting agent (krāmaṇa) at the time of piercing (vedha).
One should grind together in equal parts the seed derived from silver, vimalā, sharp powder, white mica (sattva), rasaka, silver, and mākṣika.
One should blow upon a mixture of tin four times the weight of the powder until they are fused together;
then, having rubbed it with acidic juices and sealed it, one should cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire.
Having thus cooked it with five layers, one should then process it in silver; one should blow upon it ten times until that silver becomes the seed of silver.
One should kill tin with cinnabar (tāpya) just as [it is killed] by talaka;
then, one should process that thirty-two times in silver by adding talaka.
Copper seed, however, is the best; it is beneficial for both transmutation and coloring.
One should prepare a powder that is curved, stainless, sharp, and even, [derived] from silver as the seed;
it should be blown [into the furnace] after being smeared in pairs, and the pill (khoṭa) should be ground with acid.
Having folded it five times, one should slowly blow upon it while reciting the *tāra* [mantra];
when that becomes tenfold, the *tāra* seed-syllable will become auspicious.
Tin, white mica-essence, and the essence of silver-pyrite—
these three, powdered in equal parts, should be melted together in a crucible using the *dvaṃdvamūṣā* method.
When ten times that amount of base metal is added to the silver through the addition of honey,
that silver becomes the seed capable of accomplishing all tasks.
With white flowers produced from various trees, colored by the seed-syllable *tāra*, as they may be obtained.
One should add four times the amount of juice and sow it with *kaṅguṇī* oil;
one should cook it until only the oil remains, and then one should pour [the medicinal substances] into that oil.
The seed of silver, having been melted twenty-one times, becomes colored;
that indeed is the colorant for the king of mercury.
Taking a single oil produced from *sāraṇā*, *jyotiṣmatī*, *karañja*, and *akṣakaṭutumbī*,
together with an equal amount of frog fat, [one should proceed].
Alternatively, one may take the fat of a tortoise, a boar, a ram, a snake, a leech, or even a fish;
from among these, one should take a single kind of fat and procure the previously mentioned oil.
One should prepare a red group and a yellow group with four times the amount of milk;
from each of the red and yellow flowers, one should take their juice.
This division of pairs consists of the four previously mentioned decoctions,
as well as those derived from *pāṭalī* and *kākatuṇḍī*, and likewise the juice of *mahārāṣṭrī*.
Each individual portion should be combined with one part each of old oil and fat;
furthermore, two parts of *bhūlatā*, *amalaka*, and *tāpya* should be added there.
One should add sixteen parts of oil for each of the two— the *dvandva* and the *melāpa*— to that [mixture], and cook everything together in one vessel.
The remaining oil, which has been strained through cloth, should be carefully preserved;
it is known as *sāraṇā-taila* for the work of the king of mercury (*rasarāja*).
Lead and tin, equal in amount and combined with acid, should be made into pills;
these are to be employed for the purpose of *krāmaṇa* (transference) at the time of the transmutation of mercury.
One should saturate *saurāṣṭrī* three times with the bile of cows in the heat of the sun;
its essence should be extracted like that of *soma*, and one should employ it as a transmuting agent (*krāmaka*) in the mercury.
Realgar, poison, pyrite, the wax from a buffalo's ear,
crow-dung, and donkey-blood— these, combined with the milk of *snuk*, constitute a transmuting agent (*krāmaṇa*).
Human blood, the milky sap of the Arka plant, borax, *bhūlatā*, and realgar—
these should be combined in equal parts as a transmuting agent (*krāmaka*) at the time of the piercing (*vedha*) of mercury.
One should grind together in a single vessel *krāmaṇasattva*, *indragopa*, poison, *kānta* iron, human blood, the milky sap of *snuhī*, *rasaka*, cinnabar, and oil.
One should employ the transmuting agent through both throwing and smearing at the time of penetration.
Equal parts of mercury,
paddy-processed mica, its essence, crow-dung, orpiment,
the eye of *sahadevā* plants, and *bhūnāga* [antimony] should be taken together.
Once it has been consolidated and perfected for the purpose of transference, one should employ it in casting or in anointing.
The transmuting essence (krāmaṇasattva) consists of plantain-root and *sauvīra* salt, saturated with the juice of *kaṇṭakārī*;
it is the transmuter of all metals and the means for blending all dualities.
Without *krāmaṇa*, the mercury (*sūta*) does not permeate the body or metals;
therefore, one should employ it in all the aforementioned places and formulations.
Having burnt *mahāviḍa* and conch shell, one should saturate them a hundred times in the sun with the milk of a *ravikṣīra* plant;
then, having repeatedly sealed it within a crucible, one should cook it in five successive layers of *puṭa*.
Having added an equal amount of borax (ṭaṅkaṇa), one should indeed macerate it with the group of sour substances (amlavarga);
[then add] rājāvarta, coral (pravāla), cinnabar (darada), sulfur (gandhaka), and realgar (śilā).
One should employ an equal powder of the five [ingredients] together with an amount equal to conch-shell;
all of that should be ground with the group of sour substances (amlavarga) for three days.
This is known as the great *viḍa*, beneficial for the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of *khoṭas*;
one should always employ it as a coating for the crucible in all processes of digestion.
At that very moment, the alchemist reduces diamonds and other such substances to ash; of this there is no doubt.
Vidanga, the three alkalis, the five salts, navasāra, the three pungents,
indragopa, ghanasāra, śigru, sūraṇa, and vanasūraṇa.
One should macerate [the mercury] with the group of sour substances for three days in the intense heat of the sun; thus processed by this, the mercury will dissolve the eight metals.
Vidanga, trikaṭu, gandhaka, kāsīsa, svarṇapuṣpī, suvarcala,
sarjī, ṭaṅkaṇa, sauvīra, saindhava, and śigru— [these should be processed] with the juices of śigru.
One should process it for ten days in heat; this is beneficial for the digestion of the *viḍa* salt.
Burnt *viḍa* salt and conch shell, processed a hundred times in the sun with the milk of the *ravikṣīra* plant,
and then cooked in five layers (*pañcapuṭa*), is the supreme *viḍa* for the process of *jāraṇā*.
{Viḍa (5)}:
One should grind mercury with the three alkalis, the five salts, and *amlavetasa*; by this, the essence of mica (*abhrasattva*) will readily dissolve.
One should process vitriol, cow urine, and sulfur one hundred times in the heat;
likewise, one should process burnt conch shell with juices of *śigru* roots.
Equal parts of these— sulfur, conch-shell, poison, and rock salt—
with mercury rubbed together by means of them, swallow all metals.
Vid salt and ṭaṅkaṇa should be saturated one hundred times with the juices of the palāśa tree;
this salt, named Vahnimukha, is beneficial for the digestion of all [substances].
Vida salt,
sulfur, or navasāra, along with the mouth of *kānta* iron, should be processed one hundred times individually with the group of urines while exposed to the sun. Rrā 3.10.67.
{Jvālāmukha} is *viḍa* (9).

One should cook equal parts of the three alkalis (*trikṣāra*), sulfur (*gandhaka*), orpiment (*tāla*), realgar (*bhūkhaga*), borax (*navasāraka*), and rock salt (*saindhava*) with the group of urines for one day.
Jvālāmukha, known as Viḍa, is beneficial in all processes of digestion (jāraṇa).
Vida salt and sulfur should be processed a hundred times with the juice of the roots of *vanaśigru*,
or alternatively, *navasāra* should be processed separately with *jambīra* fruits to become *viḍa*.
Viḍa, vaḍavānala, vāsaka, eraṇḍa, kadalī, devadālī, punarnavā, vāsā, pālāśa, nicula, tila, kāñcana, and mokṣaka.
Having taken these together with their roots while they are not yet completely dried, one should cut them into pieces;
likewise, having burnt the five parts of the radish and an equal amount of sesame stalks.
One should saturate the aforementioned paste with alkaline substances and the group of urines;
then, having filtered it through cloth, one should cook the liquid over a mild fire in an iron vessel.
When there is an abundant emergence of vapors and bubbles,
then one should employ ferrous sulfate (*kāsīsa*), rock salt (*saurāṣṭrī*), the three salts, and the three pungents.
One should place the powder of sulphur, the five salts, ammonium chloride,
and vermilion into that vessel and then stir it.
Having removed the boiled jaggery from the fire, one should place it in an iron casket; then,
after seven days in the interior of the earth and likewise again for seven days in a heap of grain, this perfected *viḍa* is the "Horse-Gut Fire" (*vaḍavānala*).
One should saturate *nicula* alkali twenty-one times with the juice of *devadālī* leaves; this is *biḍa* salt, used for the digestion of the essence (*sattva*).

Take equal parts of *viḍa* salt, *tīvrānala*, the root and seeds of *devadālī*, *guñjā*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*), along with the alkali of *nicula*, and process them seven times with the group of acidic substances (*amlavarga*).
One should saturate it for seven days with the juices of *kośātakī* leaves;
this is the *biḍa* salt named Tīvrānala, prepared for the digestion of gold.
{Viḍa salt for the digestion of gold}:
One should take the alkali of radish, ginger, and saltpetre, stirred with cow’s urine, filtered through cloth, and extract the liquid; with this, one should saturate the sulphur.
This mineral salt, processed a hundred times in a hot crucible, is used for the digestion of gold.
For the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of gold,

one should cook together the three alkalis (*trikṣāra*), the five salts (*pañcalavaṇa*), conch-shell, orpiment (*tāla*), and realgar (*manaḥśilā*) with the group of acidic substances (*amlavarga*) for one day. This [mixture] is used for the digestion of gold.

One should grind sulfur and ammonium chloride with the acidic juice of *jambīra* fruit a hundred times in the intense heat of the sun; this is the *viḍa* salt used for the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of gold.
Gandhaka should be processed a hundred times with the juices of kanyā, hayāri, and dhattūra; this is the viḍa salt used for all processes of digestion (jāraṇa) in a hot oven.
By this, one quickly swallows [the substance] within a shell-cup made from a pearl-oyster.
{Viḍa: for the improvement of grāsa} Equal parts of rock salt (saindhava) and sulfur (gandhaka), saturated with the juice of *tāmravallī*, [are used];
by means of this *viḍa* formulation, mercury (*rasa*) swallows the sky (*gagana*). Rrā 3.10.86.
Take one *pala* each of *siddhaviḍa*, *śilājatu*, *gandhaka*, and *sindhūttha*, and three *palas* of *bhūnāga*; grind them all together as one.
One should dry it again and add three *pala* of *bhūnāga*;
likewise, having ground it and dried it once more, one should cook it over a gentle fire.
Having thus given it eight times [the quantity], one should grind it, cook it, and reduce it to powder;
this is the perfected *viḍa* (alkaline flux), to be employed in the process of digestion (*jāraṇa*) for gold-work.
Having properly processed secondary minerals such as sulphur and the like, and then the essence born of space (mica), followed by the essence of honey and the finest gold, melted within the crucible;

having colored the entire web of seeds with dyes, one should cause all this—which produces external liquefaction and the state of union—to be digested in due order according to the ritual by means of the *biḍa* preparations perfected by the adepts.
The eighteen refinements of mercury:

Having experienced and observed all the various well-established procedures for the work of the best of elixirs through diverse sequences, and having distinguished between what is achievable and what is unachievable,

I shall now set forth for the sake of the skillful this eighteen-fold method according to specific rules— beginning with sudation and ending with transmutation— which is easy to accomplish and brings happiness.
The eighteen *saṃskāras* are:
sweating, rubbing, reviving the fainting state, causing to fall, the threefold suppression, fixing, kindling, and oil enema.
Digestion (jāraṇa), assimilation (cāraṇa), internal and external liquefaction (druti),
coloring (rañjana), amalgamation (sāraṇa), subsequent amalgamation (anusāraṇā), re-amalgamation (pratisāraṇā), and transmutation (krāmaṇa) [are the processes] regarding bodies and metals.
One should fill an earthen vessel with various grains as they are obtained, provided they are husked and mixed with water,
and preserve it until it attains acidity.
In their midst are bhṛṅgarāja, muṇḍī, viṣṇukrāntā, punarnavā, mīnākṣī, sarpākṣī, sahadevī, and śatāvarī.
One should collect triphalā, girikarṇī, haṃsapādī, and citraka,
together with their roots, and cut them into pieces according to what is available.
This *dhānyāmlaka* (fermented rice water) is produced within a previously used sour vessel;
one should employ it everywhere for the sudation and other processes of the king of mercury (*rasarāja*).
In the absence of *kāñjika*, one should employ *āranāla* or very sour *āranāla*.
Sudation [is prepared with]: the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), salt, black cumin (rājī), leadwort (citraka), the three myrobalans (triphalā),
fresh ginger (ārdraka), mahābalā, nāgabalā, meghanāda, and punarnavā.
Equal parts of *meṣaśṛṅgī*, *citraka*, and *navasāra*—
all these together or individually— should be ground with sour gruel (*pūrvāmla*).
One should smear that paste onto a cloth to the thickness of one finger-breadth;
having placed mercury in its center and bound it, one should cook it for three days in a *dolāyantra* combined with acidic liquids. Thus the mercury becomes sweated (*svedita*).
Having washed it with warm *kāñjika* and taken it up, one should rub it;
if that is too sour, one should employ *āranāla* in its place.
House-smoke, brick-powder, burnt wool, salt, jaggery, black mustard,
the three myrobalans, kanyā, citraka, bṛhatī, and kaṇā.
Then, one should boil either *vandhyākarkoṭakī* alone or all [the ingredients] together with fermented rice water (*āranāla*). With that decoction, one should grind the mercury for three days.
Having washed it with sour gruel (*kāñjika*) and taken it up, one should cause it to undergo the process of *vimūrchana*.
The *mūrchanā* consists of Meṣaśṛṅgī, Kṛṣṇadhūrta, Balā, and Śvetāparājitā.
Kanyā, agni, triphalā, sarpākṣī, sūraṇa, vacā, gojihvā, aṅgulī, nīlī, muruṇḍī, and kṣīrakandaka.
One should grind together the juices of black mustard, *kākamācī*, the latex of *ravikṣīra*, and *kāñcana*, either individually or all combined.
One should seal the king of essences (mercury) within a crucible for one watch (*yāma*) and then cook it with a single *puṭa* in a *bhūdhara* furnace, or else grind it.
Having repeatedly sealed it with all the fluxing agents as before, one should cause it to undergo digestion;
in this manner, one should perform the process seven times, whereby the mercury becomes liquefied (mūrchita).
{Raising up}:
By means of water or warm *āranāla* (sour gruel), it becomes raised through agitation;
or else, it becomes raised through heating in a *pātana* apparatus.
Once thus raised, the *sūtra* is to be lowered in three ways in succession.
*Ūrdhvapātanam* [is achieved with]:
*kākamācī*, *jayā*, *brāhmī*, *cāṅgerī*, *raktacitraka*,
*aṅkolī*, *rājavṛkṣa*, *tilaparṇī*, and *kumārikā*.
Maṇḍūkī, citraka, pāṭhā, kākajaṅghā, śatāvarī, bhūpāṭalī, devadālī, nirguṇḍī, and girikarṇikā.
One should [soak the powder] for one day in the juices of all or some of these: śaṇapuṣpī, ginger, śṛṅgī, gojihvā, kṣīrakandaka, and indigo.
One should grind mercury together with copper and sour fruits;
that paste should then be subjected to the upward-descending (ūrdhvapātanaka) apparatus once again.
One should take that [substance] and grind it likewise, combined with copper powder;
having added copper again and again, one should cause it to fall [from the crucible] and grind it.
In this manner, one should perform the grinding and the falling [of the ash] seven times in succession.
Having grasped it at the upper end, one should cause it to fall by letting it drop downward.
{Adhaḥpātanam}:
Triphalā, rājikā, śigru, tryūṣaṇa, salt,
and citraka— all these, equal in quantity to mercury (sūta), should be ground with kāñjika for one day.
With that [substance], one should smear the upper vessel; a light *puṭa* should be applied on its back.
Once it has been processed in the downward-dropping apparatus (*adhaḥpātanayantra*), one should extract it.
{The horizontal casting (*tiryakpātanam*):} One should grind together triphalā, *rājikā*, *śigru*, *tryūṣaṇa*, salt, *citraka*, *dhānyābhraka*, and mercury with *āranālaka* vinegar. Rrā_3,11.28.
That [substance], having been ground into a fine powder, should be cast into a horizontal crucible with a steady fire.
For the cessation [of the flow],
one should cover the liquid inside the vessel with salt ground in water,
then add a little water and seal it with a lid.
The small crucible should be placed above; even if [the mercury] is obtained, the essence (rasa) will remain below.
{The Illumination}:
The three alkalis, the five salts, earth, *bhṛṅgarāja*, the root of *śigru*, *svarṇapuṣpī*, *kāsīsa*, black pepper, *rājikā*, and honey. Rrā_3,11.31.
Kṣīrakanda, jayā, kanyā, vijayā, girikarṇikā,
kākajaṅghā, śoṇapuṣpī, pātālagaruḍī, and kaṇā.
One should grind Vandhyākarkoṭakī and Vahni, either individually or all together,
with the group of sour substances (amlavarga), and then macerate the mercury with those juices.

At the end of the day, one should bind it in a cloth and cook it for three days in a *dolāyantra* (swinging apparatus) within a jar filled with the previously mentioned liquors; thus the mercury becomes eager to consume [the reagents].
The anuvasana [treatment] consists of the ignited mercury (rasarāja) combined with the juice of jambīra;
one should keep it for one day in the heat within an earthen vessel, and it will thus be infused.
When it has been refined by auspicious processes such as sweating and the like, and is freed from the seven coverings,
and only an eighth part remains, then it is called "pure mercury" by the wise.
I shall now describe the feeding of sulphur for the purpose of digestion (*jāraṇa*) using various easily available formulations, both in its direct and indirect forms;

following that, there shall be feeding with iron powder (*ghana-cūrṇa*) which serves as a digestive process (*pācana*), for the sake of the complete mastery of mercury and for the happiness of alchemists.
One should saturate finely powdered sulphur seven times with the juice of *bṛhatī*,
or alternatively, seven times with the juice of *vṛntāka*.
One should place one *pala* of purified mercury inside a glass flask,
along with one *karṣa* of processed sulphur and one *māṣa* of camphor.
Having cast [the ingredients] therein and blocked the opening, one should smear the jar with clay;
one should cook it for a day over a lamp-fire and then open the mouth again.
When [the mercury] has digested [the previous substance], one should likewise digest it with sulphur and camphor;
in this manner, when it has digested [the sulphur] a hundredfold, one should digest sulphur into the mercury.
Having prepared a bolus (*modaka*) consisting of *kāsīsa*, *saurāṣṭrī*,
and *sajjīkṣāra* combined with the juice of *śigru*, it should indeed be processed (*bhāvita*) with this.
Having ground that fragrance for seven days, one should again digest that fragrance;
one should properly cast the purified mercury into the middle of a pit made of bricks.
One should cover its mouth with a clean cloth behind it;
having added one-tenth part of sulfur, the practitioner should cause it to cease.
A small lid should be placed on the back [of the crucible]; once it has been digested, one should again add sulphur.
In this manner, sulphur should be slowly digested into the mercury a hundredfold.
One should place that mercury, filtered through a cloth, into a heated mortar (taptakhalva);
having added one-fourth part of the processed seed (pakvabīja), one should grind it with acidic liquids for a day.
One should place that [mercury] in a *cāraṇa* apparatus combined with the juice of *jaṃbīra*;
one should keep that apparatus in the heat, and the mercury becomes liquefied.
One should place mercury together with viḍ salt in a vessel and cook it for one day in a *puṭa*.
Once it has been processed (*jārita*), one should add the seed (*bīja*) again and process it as before.
And one should digest that [mercury] again in the same manner; thus the substance to be digested is digested gradually in equal measure.
One should cast the processed mercury into a *sāraṇā* apparatus along with oil mixed with fat;
it should be melted in a *nālamūṣā* crucible together with the juice of ripened seeds (*pakvabīja*).
When one maintains it in this manner within the apparatus, the mercury, having been processed (*sārita*), will undergo digestion (*jārayet*).
That processed [mercury] should again be rubbed together with the *viḍa* salt as before.

One should cause [the mercury] to digest within the *kacchapa* apparatus; once it has digested, one should perform the *sāraṇā* (transmutation) upon the seed, using double the amount of seed as before in the *sāraṇā* apparatus.
One should digest that [mercury] again in the same manner and likewise extract it;
then, one should digest it once more with three times the amount of seed (bīja), as before.
Equal parts of mercury (mukha), *tālaka*, and oil derived from *dhattūra*,
along with the liquid extract of the group of divine medicinal herbs (*divyauṣadhīgaṇa*), should all be ground together for the duration of a day.
One should cook [the mercury] sealed in a *vajramūṣā* crucible over a fire of dried cow-dung for a period of one day.
Then, having ground it again with the juices of divine medicinal herbs, it should be cooked for another day.
By performing this process repeatedly in this manner, the mercury becomes "sealed-mouthed" (*baddhamukha*).
{The Binding of Mercury}:
That mercury, washed vitriol, sharp iron, copper, mercury, and lead—these in equal parts should be rubbed for a day with the juices extracted from *devadālī*. Rrā_3,12.19.
Having rubbed it for three days with honey and clarified butter and formed it into a ball,
one should place it inside a *vajramūṣā* crucible, seal it, dry it, and then blow it with a fierce fire.
By means of the application of acacia charcoal, the mercury becomes bound as a *khoṭa* (solid mass).
One should indeed purify that *khoṭa* by repeatedly blowing it in a furnace with *ṭaṃkaṇa* and glass.
A mass of splendor, with its essence bound, becomes like the rising sun.
Having wrapped that mercury in wax, one should worship it;
when the silver is melted, one should add a hundredth part [of the mercury] along with the *krāmaṇa* [transmuting agent].
That gold which is produced becomes like Jāmbūnada in its luster;
it shall consist of ninety-eight parts—thus is the piercing [process] considered.
Now I shall describe, in due order, the "mouth" (mukha) of the perfumed mercury, by which [the mercury], once consecrated,
quickly assimilates [substances] ranging from mica (vyoma) to vaikrānta.
One should grind mercury for three days with amlavetasa, jambīra, bījapūraka,
and bhūkhaga, and for three days with bhūnāga; having ground it for one day in a heated mortar (taptakhalva) in this manner, the mouth of the mercury is formed.
One should cause two bricks to be prepared, joined together at their center;
[using] purified *dhānyābhraka* and *gandhaka*, ten *niṣkas* each.
One should grind [the powder] for one watch (yāma) with the juice of *jambīra* fruits and smear it with that very same [juice].
One should prepare two equal-sized cavities, having thoroughly cleansed the lower cavity.
One should cast twenty niṣkas of the molten metal; thereafter, other bricks should be placed above.
Having sealed the joint with clay and salt, one should ignite a blazing fire beneath it.
Continuously day and night for up to seven days,
having extracted the juice— free from dross and cooled to the temperature of one's own body— one should thus perform this process three times; then the "mouth" (mukha) of the mercury is formed.
Mercury (sūta) placed inside a bamboo tube within a vessel filled with cow urine should be cooked over a stove for twenty-one days; in this way, the mouth of the mercury is opened.
The digestion (*jāraṇa*) of the mercury, which is like a ritual act, will be described in due order for both the manifest (*samukha*) and the unmanifest (*nirmukha*) births.
It is traditionally taught that the mercury, when swallowed by the mortar (*khalva*), undergoes rubbing (*mardana*) and cleansing (*mārjana*).
One should perform a ritual bath with the juices of various medicinal herbs, worship with living beings and seeds,
and present offerings consisting of gold and various kinds of jewels.
The offering of food (naivedya) is the divine coloring; the extraction (sāraṇā) is the dismissal (visarjana);
and the piercing (vedhana) within the metals of the body is the fruit of the rite of perfect worship.
For as many days as the mercury is processed while being held within the fire,
for that many thousands of yugas is one honored in the world of Śiva.
Whatever expenditure may occur for the purpose of preparing the king of elixirs,
the illustrious Bhairavī certainly bestows all of that back multiplied ten millionfold.
Therefore, for wise practitioners in this world and the next, this [teaching],
which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, should be mastered by kings and leaders of scholars.
Having ground *dhānyābhra* with the milk of *arka* for one day and having sealed it,
one should cook it in the crucible called *kapota*; then one should grind it with milks for one watch (*yāma*).
Having blocked the lower opening as before, one should cook it in this manner four times;
likewise three times with the juice of *mūlaka* and three times with the juice of the root of the plantain (*rambhā*).
Apāmārga, kākamācī, mīnākṣī, bhṛṅgarāja, muni, punarnavā, meghanāda, vidārī, and likewise citraka; Rrā 3.12.40.
One should gradually perform the rubbing and the *puṭapācana* (enclosing and heating) with the juices of these [substances] one by one, each time only once, and then process it again.
Śatāvarī, tālamūlī, kadalī, taṇḍulīyaka, arka, punarnavā, śigru, and yavaciñcā, in this sequence.
However, when processed with counter-irritants for one day, it is beneficial for use as a laxative.
Having ground *dhānyābhra* with the milky sap of the *arka* plant for one watch (*yāma*) and having sealed it,
one should cook it in a crucible called *kapota*; thus one should repeat this fourteen times.
Kadalī, musalī, śigru, vandhyā, aṅkola, arka, pīluka, nāgavallī, kuberākṣī, bhūmy-apāmārga, and tumbaru.
One should take these as a single liquid mixture along with *kāñjika* and *vyoma*;
all of this should be placed in a vessel and cooked within it for three days.
Having first extracted the impurities from the dolikāyantra, one should then dry it;
[then add] equal parts of green vitriol (kāsīsa), alum (tuvarī), rock salt (sindhu), and carbonate of soda (ṭaṅkaṇa).
Having added one-tenth of all this to it, one should grind it;
having added it to that heated mortar (*taptakhalva*), one should grind it for one day.
That mica is beneficial for the process of *cāraṇa* (dissolving) when heated in a *taptakhalva* for one day.
One should repeatedly immerse molten lead one hundred times in the juice of *muṇḍī*.
With that juice, *dhānyābhra* should be rubbed and subjected to seven *puṭa* cycles.
Having repeatedly massaged [the area] and then restrained [the breath], one should cook it in the crucible known as the "pigeon" (kapota).
Having added an equal amount of sulphur, [one should process it] with the juices of *muṇḍikā* as previously described.
It should be infused for a period of days with juices extracted from *bījapūra* fruits mixed with honey;
this mineral (abhraka) is supremely beneficial for the digestion of mercury (*sūta*).
*Siddhamūlī*, *vyāghrapādī*, *haṃsapādī*, *kadalī*,
*agnikumārikā*, *bṛhatī*, *lāṅgalī*, *vajrī*, *khaṇḍajārī*, and *indravāruṇī*.
Vandhyākarkoṭakī, mūṣā, sarpākṣī, śaṅkhapuṣpikā,
maṇḍūkī, and agnimathanī are renowned as the Siddhamūlikās.
One should employ all these, either collectively or individually, in the locations previously mentioned.
Now, therefore, regarding mercury with a face (samukha-sūta) in the process of moving through mica (abhra-cāraṇa): first, one-sixteenth part of mica [is to be added] to the mercury with a face.
Having added [the ingredients], one should grind them for a day in a heated mortar with the juices of the *siddhamūlī* plants.
Then, having placed that [substance] in a distillation apparatus together with the juice of *jambīra* fruit, it should be kept in the heat for one day; it will certainly liquefy, there is no doubt.
Mercury, whether it penetrates a *lakṣa* or a *koṭi*, should be processed and bound within a cloth for a period of days using a *dolāyantra*.
Indeed, by means of the juices of *siddhamūlī* combined [with other substances], it is thoroughly digested through the process of *pātana*.
If it is undigested, one should cook it for a day in the apparatus called *kacchapa*, having added one-eighth part of *viḍa* salt; it will certainly become mobile, there is no doubt.
By this sequential method,
having repeatedly refined the mercury until it is a hundred times aged, it properly pierces [the base metal] with a thousandth part of itself.
When it has been digested a thousandfold, the mercury becomes a "piercer of a hundred thousand" (lakṣavedhī);
likewise, when it has been digested a hundred-thousandfold, the mercury becomes a "piercer of ten million" (koṭivedhī).
One should digest either black iron or gold according to one's capacity;
by means of the sequential application as before, the result for both will be equal.
By this very same sequence, one should digest either silver or white mica according to one's capacity; this is recommended for the work of producing silver.
For mercury— [specifically] for *mukhabandhana* and *koṭivedhin*—
the processes beginning with *sāraṇā* are performed in sequence using the matured seed (*pakvabīja*), as previously described.
The transmutation (vedhana) and the permeation (krāmaṇa) of the king of essences (rasarāja) must likewise be performed.
One should digest all of the mercury with copper for the purpose of silver-making;
when it has been thus digested a hundredfold, one should perform the transmutation with a thousandth part [of the resulting substance].
When that has been digested a thousandfold, one should perform the three *sāraṇās* as before;
then, having caused it to be digested again in the same manner, one should cause it to circulate three times once more.
And furthermore, having thus repeatedly purified [the mercury], one should cause it to digest;
one should perform the process from the "binding of the mouth" up to the "piercing," as previously described for the mercury.
By that very same one-hundred-thousandth part, divine gold is produced;
when it has been digested a hundred-thousandfold, one should digest it again after having divided it into three parts.
Thus, having performed the binding in these seven ways, one should then apply the mouth [of the crucible]; and by performing everything up to the *krāmaṇa* as before, that mercury becomes perfected.
One who pierces through the *koṭi* [of the body] reaches the Moon and the Sun; this is the truth spoken by Śaṅkara.
{Mercury:: Nirmukha:: Cāraṇa} Now I shall describe the cāraṇa and jāraṇa of purified mercury (nirmukhasūta). To pure mercury, one should add sixteen parts of killed vaikrānta.
Having cast [the mercury] into a heated mortar and rubbed it for three days with the juices of the *siddhamūlī* plants,
by this very refinement, it certainly moves without a mouth.
Alternatively, mercury combined with *bhūlatā* should be ground in a heated mortar for three days, and thereafter it should be precipitated using a *pātana* apparatus.
For by means of this very refinement, one moves without a face in an instant.
Regarding this very [process] of *jāraṇā* for mercury that is "mouthless" (*nirmukha*), the purification of *vyoma* (mica) suitable for *jāraṇā* is now described:
one should cook *dhānyābhra* with the group of acidic substances (*amlavarga*) in a *dolāyantra* for three days.
Then, having ground it with the milky sap of the Snuhī plant for one watch (yāma), one should heat it in a closed crucible.
Then, having taken that [substance] with a single vessel called *kapota*, one should grind it together with radish,
plantain root, *mīnākṣī*, and *kākamācikā*.
A sage should administer a mild *puṭapāka* (herb-encasement) using the juices of *ārdraka*, *varṣābhū*, *meghanāda*, *apāmārga*, and *eraṇḍa*, each separately.
Then, one should cook it for a period of one day in a swinging vessel (dolāyantra) with the milk of the *vajrī* plant;
[and add] well-powdered *vacā*, *nimba*, *dhūmasāra*, and *kāsīsa*.
Then, one should mix [the substances] individually with a sixteenth part of mica;
subsequently, one should grind them in a copper mortar for a period of one day using tamarind juice.
One should coat an iron vessel with mineral salts (navasāra) and place therein processed mercury,
mica, chickpea-sour, and sour gruel (kāñjika).
One should cook it on a low fire in a pan; the mercury flows at that very moment.
One should digest it by means of the previous method, and then one should digest the noble [mercury] as well.
This process of digestion (*jāraṇā*) starting from the mouth, involving the proper dosage and method as previously described, is the "mouthless digestion" (*nirmukhajāraṇā*);
in the work of gold-making, black mica (*kṛṣṇābhraka*) and gold should be digested.
Either silver or white cloud-like mercury should be used for the process of silvering;
one should digest it through the stages beginning with *sāraṇā* and ending with *krāmaṇā*, exactly as described before.
In the case of the king of elixirs (*sūtarāja*), it likewise becomes gold;
one should cause the white [mercury] to digest the white [substance], for as is the seed, so is the sprout.
As it has been taught, when black sulphur, black mica, gold-dust, silver, and white mica have been easily prepared and rendered yellow,
the best of great alchemists, having mixed them into that excellent mercury, may produce a quantity numbering a thousand great *bhāras* of gold.
This [treatise] certainly bestows the fruit of the yoga of vision and is beneficial for the superior digestion (*jāraṇa*) of mercury;
it contains the precipitation of the essence (*sattvapātana*) through various yogas, the dual fusion (*dvaṃdvamela*), and the noble consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
One should perform the purification of *dhānyābhraka* for seven days by immersing it in a decoction of *mustā*, and then in the juices of one of the tubers: *śigru*, *sūraṇa*, or *rambhā*.
Alternatively, one should soak the abhraka with the juices of peṭārī root and jambīra;
once the abhraka has been thus saturated, one should add a quarter-part of ṭaṅkaṇa.
One should grind it for one day in a mortar combined with some kind of acid.
{The extraction and falling of the essence of kāntaloha, mākṣika, and minor metals (uparasa):} Guñjā, guggulu, lac, wool, sarjī, sarjarasa, and jaggery.
Small fish, barley-alkali, glass, oil-cake, and suraṇa;
Bhūlatā, triphalā, vahnī, kṣīrakanda, punarnavā,
dhattūra, lāṅgalī, pāṭhā, balā, gandhaka, and tiktaka.
Cow’s milk, the five salts, the venom of a snake and a scorpion, honey,
six drops [of water], and the bones of a small snail and a hare.
One should grind together *pārāvata*, *mala*, the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), *indragopa*, *śigruka*, wheat, and mustard in equal parts with goat’s milk.
This [substance], whether taken individually or combined, is condensed in a single watch (yāma);
one part of this compound and two parts of purified abhraka [are used].
One-fifth part of the fifth [ingredient] should be stirred together with everything else;
pills weighing one *karṣa* each should be made and dried slightly in the shade.
Repeatedly casting five pills at a time into a crucible furnace heated by acacia charcoal embers, he should blow upon them with a blowpipe.
Upon completion, one should take the dross and, once it has cooled naturally, break it open;
having extracted the circular essence (sattva), one should pulverize the remaining dross.
Half of the powder is the first lump; likewise, there are five of buffalo [meat].
Having combined these together, one should blow upon them and extract the essence from each accordingly.
And furthermore, one should act in this manner; thus, by means of this sequential yoga, one releases the substance three times, whether it be the lovely *sattva* or honey.
Other ores, such as iron and copper, as well as pure earth and clay, release a mass of sentient beings; one should grasp them individually.
Having taken the essence of mica (*abhra-sattva*) in equal parts with glass (*kāca*) and borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*), one should soften it.
Having added [the ingredients] three times over, one should blow upon it while it is contained within a diamond crucible.
One should grind together the group of sour substances (amlavarga), the leaf of *snuhī*, and the seed of *ciñcā* along with its bark;
one should then pour that essence [of mercury] over it seven times.
The essence (sattva) shall become soft and bright; one should sprinkle it seven times.
Ten parts of purified *dhānyābhra* (rice-iron ore), three parts of pure lead (*nāga*),
and one part each of well-purified *ṭaṅkaṇa*, *mākṣika*, and mercury (*sūta*) [should be taken].

One should mix equal parts of wool-ash (ūrṇā), saltpeter (sarjī), and barley-alkali (yavakṣāra); having obtained whatever is available, they should be ground with the groups of urine and acids for a period of days.
Having prepared the extraction of the essence (*sattvapātana*) as before using the five parts of a goat,
one should take that which is soft and visibly pure and apply it below.
One should steam the essence of *mākṣika* (pyrite) for a day in a *dolāyantra* using *sāranāla*. Then,
having powdered it, one should cook it for a day in an iron vessel with honey and clarified butter.
Having taken it, one should let it steep in cow’s milk for a day in the heat;
then, for a day, one should rub it together with house-soot, clarified butter, and honey.
When the essence is heated in a blind crucible, it becomes like a *guñjā* berry.
Mākṣika-sattva should be precipitated by soaking the mākṣika a hundred times in the juice of plantain roots under the sun;
it should then be cooked for one yāma with ghee and vātāri-tailaka.
Through the upward movement as before, the being becomes like the color of a cochineal insect (indragopa).
For the extraction and precipitation of the essence (*sattva*) of *mākṣika*:
one should grind *mākṣika* with the milky sap of *snuhī* and *arka*, and with breast milk, for one day;
it should be mixed with one-quarter part each of *kaṅkuṣṭha* and *ṭaṅkaṇa*.
When the essence is blown in a sealed crucible, it becomes like a jewel.
One should successively impregnate finely powdered *mākṣika* seven times with the juices of plantain root, *tulasī*, and citron,
using each juice as a solvent in turn.
When [the breath] is obstructed and blown, the auspicious essence, resembling a parrot, falls away.
One should saturate the essence of *mākṣika* with the group of urines and the group of acids for fourteen days;
one should then grind the *mākṣika* with acids under intense heat for several days.
Having prepared pills combined with the five friends (*mitrapañcaka*), one should heat them firmly through a curved tube like the sky; the essence will become like copper.
Mākṣika [sattva] should be processed for seven days with breast milk, kaṅkuṣṭha, and the juice of plantain,
combined with the five "friends" (mitrapañcaka).
One should massage the processed [substance] for one watch (yāma) or a day with oils that ward off wind;
then one should cook it over a mild fire for one watch until it becomes a ball (golaka).
The essence (sattva), having the luster of a *kiṃśuka* flower, becomes like the sky through sublimation (*dhamana*).
And for those who are stainless and pure, the procedure for heating them correctly should be like that [previously described].
The highly purified *mākṣika* essence (*sattva*), namely washed *sattva*, should be ground with some kind of acid.
One should wash it with fermented rice-gruel (āranāla), like gold powder placed at the bottom.
Having extracted that [impurity], it becomes this "washed essence" (dhautasattva);
one should indeed employ it in the sowing of seeds wherever they may be.
Mākṣika ore smeared with the five friends (pañcamitra) and formed into pills at the end of seven days,
when subjected to the aforementioned heating process, its essence becomes like lac.
Realgar (manaḥśilā) should be soaked for three days in water extracted from Agastya and Śigru plants;
through the application of talaka and medicinal herbs, its essence (sattva) becomes gold-colored.
Realgar, which is the *sattva* for causing [metals] to fall,
should be soaked for one day in cow’s urine and the acidic juice of *mātuluṅga*;
it should then be processed with the juices and bile of plants that bear red and yellow flowers.
At the end of the day, one should grind [the ingredients] for one *yāma* combined with the five "friends. Having placed that pill inside a glass flask,
one should coat that glass flask on all sides with a mixture of cloth and clay to the thickness of one finger-breadth.
Once it is dry, one should slowly cook it in a sand-furnace with a mild fire;
when the liquid has dried up, one should then properly seal the opening with clay and salt.
One should cook it over a fierce fire for as long as twelve watches;
once it has cooled to the temperature of one's own body, one should remove it, break the vessel, and collect [the substance].
The essence of the stone is fixed upward, resembling the rays of the rising sun.
For the extraction of the essence (*sattva*) of yellow orpiment (*haritāla*),
one should mix sixteen parts of orpiment with one part each of poison, mercury, borax, and the powder of white mica and *baṅga*.
One should grind everything with the milky sap of *snuhī* and *arka* for three days;
then, like a stone, one should extract the essence from *tālaka*, which resembles crystal.
Haritāla should be saturated twenty-eight times with the juice of snuk and the extract of kaṭutumbī for the purpose of precipitating its essence (sattvapātana).
One should grind sesame, mustard seeds, *śigru*, salt, and the five "friends" (mitrapañcaka) in equal parts with the previously mentioned *tāla* for one day.
When heated in a crucible with a perforated base within a *bhūdhara* furnace, one should extract the essence (*sattva*).
For the extraction of the essence (*sattva*) from yellow orpiment (*haritāla*):
one should grind purified orpiment together with equal parts of lac, *rājī*, jaggery, *śigru*, *ṭaṅkaṇa*, salt, and sesame seeds, using the milky sap of the sun-plant (*arka*).
Alternatively, having smeared the interior of the *chidramūṣā* crucible with a paste made from the milk of *vajriṇī* and the juice of *kuṣmāṇḍa* for a day, one should seal it.
The essence should be extracted from the crucible by means of heating in the *pātālayantra*.
For the precipitation of the essence from *haritāla*: one-eighth part of mercury and *ṭaṅkaṇa* should be added to *tālaka*;
this should be rubbed with the juices of *kuṣmāṇḍa* and the milks of *snuhī* for three days.
That globule should be placed inside a crucible with a hole, and the essence extracted as before.
Tuttha, sattva, and pātana; lac, abhayā, and bhūnāga; house-soot, jaṭā, and kaṇā;
niśā, ṭaṅkaṇa, honey, and clarified butter—with these, tutthaka is to be mixed in equal parts.
All of this should be rubbed with goat's milk and heated in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*);
the essence (*sattva*) will emerge with the luster of *kiṃśuka* flowers—of this there is no doubt.
Tuttha, sattva, and pātana;
haridrā, sūraṇa, aṅkolla, taṇḍulī, gandhaka, and jaggery;
honey, ghee, and ṭaṅkaṇa—these should be equal [in measure], and tuttha should be equal to all of them combined.
One should rub everything with breast milk and smear the crucible;
having sealed it with the *pātālayantra*, when heated, it releases its essence (*sattva*).

One should grind one-quarter part of *ṭaṅkaṇa* with honey and clarified butter; this, mixed with *tuttha*, should be heated with a strong fire in a crucible (*koṣṭhīyantra*). *Tuttha*, *sattva*, and *pātana*.
*Tuttha* [is processed] with *ṭaṅkaṇa* as a quarter-part; one should grind it with honey and clarified butter.
Mixed with *tuttha*, it is blown [into the flame] in a crucible furnace with a steady fire.
He bears and releases his essence, which has a luster like that of a parrot's beak.
One should close a crucible with equal parts of *varanāgasattva*, *sauvīra*, and sharp powder;
when blown with forceful heat, it becomes *sattva*, which is called *varanāga*.
The *rasaka* [calamine] should be processed day by day with alkalis, acids, fats, and bile;
it should then be processed for two days with the juices of red and yellow flowers.
One should then powder the *rasaka*, followed by wool, lac, turmeric, *abhayā*, borax,
the smoke of *śigru*, and *bhūnāga* as the seventh ingredient.
One should grind that powder together with these [ingredients] in goat’s milk for one *yāma*; with this paste, a crucible made of *vārtāka* gourd should be smeared.
When it is dry and half its mouth has been filled with charcoal, one should extract the essence by blowing upon it.
Take one part of *rasaka* (calomel), one part each of the five ingredients of *triphalā*,
and one part each of turmeric and soot (*gṛhadhūma*). Rrā_3,13.61 //
It should be rubbed for a day with goat's milk or some kind of acid;
then, as before, one should extract the essence from the mercury, which has the luster of a conch shell.
One should grind the powder of *vandhyā* and *vaikrānta* together in the shade for one day with goat’s urine; the essence (*sattva*) will then emerge like silver.
The alkali of *mokṣa*, *morata*, and *pālāśa* filtered through cow’s urine,
dried in the sun after being collected, along with *vajrakanda* and *ṭaṅkaṇa*; [these are used for the precipitation of the essence of *vaikrānta*].
Lac, vaikrānta equal to the crest of a peacock's plume, and all [other ingredients] in equal parts—
this entire mixture should be rubbed with the juice of meṣaśṛṅgī for the duration of a day.
Having placed it in a closed crucible and heated it with a fierce fire,
the vaikrānta mineral releases its essence right there, which binds mercury.

One *pala* of *vaikrānta* [minerals] and one *karṣa* of *ṭaṅkaṇa* should be processed for one day with the milky sap of the sun-plant (*arka*), and then for one day with the juice of the *śigru* plant.
One should apply one part each of *guñjā*, oil-cake (*piṇyāka*), and fire-seed (*vahnī*).
Having formed a pill with this, one should heat it strongly in a crucible apparatus (*koṣṭhīyantra*).
The sattva produced from vaikrānta is like a conch shell, a jasmine flower, or the moon.
One should grind together equal parts of *vaikrānta* and *vajrakanda*, along with an equal amount of *snuk* latex,
buffalo butter, and honey, for one day.
By blowing as before, the essence becomes like the color of an indragopa insect.

{Gairika:: sattva:: precipitation} One should grind gairika, which has been impregnated with the red group and the yellow group, for seven days along with the five friends (mitrapañcaka) for one prahara.
That pill releases pure essence within the crucible apparatus.
Saurāṣṭrī is white and white; one should saturate it with cow bile a hundred times with great care,
combined with the five "friends."
One releases the vital essence from the vessels into the digestive tract by means of the ascending movement.
Sasyaka powder should be infused for one day with rabbit blood,
or with women’s urine or cow’s urine; then one should add haridrā (turmeric) in a quarter-part of that amount.
That ball should be rubbed with silver-leaf oil for one watch (yāma).
When placed in a blind crucible and smelted for half a ghaṭikā with a steady fire,
it releases a beautiful essence resembling an indragopaka insect.
Regarding the precipitation of *sattva* from *kāsīsa*: there are four kinds of *kāsīsa*—red, yellow, white, and black.
One should grind it with the group of bitter [herbs] (*pittavarga*) and the juices of bitter *kośātakī*.
And with the juices of *kāsamarda* combined with the five "friends" (*mitrapañcaka*), those pills,
when heated in a crucible furnace, release their essence.
One should cook [the substance] made of rājāvarta in a vessel with buffalo ghee and milk for one day, combined with the five "friends" (mitrapañcaka).
At night, one should cause it to be formed into a pill using the five products of the cow;
through contact with the charcoal of *khadira* wood, the essence is released within the crucible.
That which has the shape of an anthill’s peak, which possesses the luster of a blue lotus when broken,
and the hue of red ochre when rubbed— this is *srotoñjana*.
Sattva is the precipitant for *srotoñjana*; it should be taken from *rājāvartaka* as well as from *srotoñjana*.
{A binary compound of *vyomasattva* and minerals}:
Whatever powder of *vyomasattva* and whatever powder of metal ores there may be—these two, in equal parts, are placed in a crucible smeared with the *dvandvamelāpa* [fusion-paste]. Rrā 3.13.81.
When the host of enemies blows [upon it], it melts instantly when thrown.
Having ground together mercury, borax, *guñjā* seeds, hoof, horn,
and medicinal herbs with the fat of a frog, one should apply it as a coating to the crucible.
In that [mixture], various powders of living beings are combined;
the three alkalis, dhātakī flowers, and guggulu are each taken in equal parts.
A paste ground with the breast milk of a woman is beneficial for the union of couples.
For the "Gathering of All Beings" (*sarvasattvamelāpana*):
one should grind together equal parts of *varṣābhū*, the root of the plantain tree (*kadalīkaṇḍa*), *kākamācī*, *punarnavā*, *guñjā*, human skull (*narakapāla*), and *ṭaṅkaṇa*.
By this, as before, gold-ore is produced from the impurity in an instant.
One should likewise mix silver and *vyomasattva* with this very [substance].
The fruit of the *lāṅgalī* plant is used for making yak-tail hair, hooks, and cotton.
Having ground together earthworms, cochineal insects,
and *pāṣāṇabhedin* with breast milk, one should apply it as a coating to the crucible.
All metals, minerals, and likewise great essences meet together here through the fire of intense smelting; of this there is no doubt.
{The Union of the Couple}:
Having ground together poison, the flesh of a muskrat, and carbonate of potash,
one should apply this very mixture as a coating to the crucible and then cast [the substance] therein.
Whatever pair of opposites there may be, it is entirely resolved through the practice of *dhamana*.
Having ground the ashes of *apāmārga* with *kaṅguṇī* oil, one should forcefully blow upon the crucible after it has been smeared with that [mixture] and the two [substances] have been placed inside.
There is no doubt that they will indeed meet, by being sown in the fields of those very Mārakas.
Gold-mercury-ore (hemābhra), lead-salt-ore (nāgatāpyābhra), copper-ore (śulbābhra),
and sharp-iron-ore (tīkṣṇābhra) become firmly bound by means of sulfur, rock salt, and cinnabar through the process of heating.
Nāgābhra combined with śilā, vaṅgābhra with tālaka, and tārābhra with both vaṅga and tāla;
all these are like tāla for all living beings.
Tin-bearing mica (vaṅgābhra) certainly melts without a doubt in an instant when placed in the aforementioned crucible;
likewise, the essence of white mica and tin powder, taken in equal parts, [behave in the same way].
One should grind together borax with the juice of plantain tubers;
when blown in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*), tin and mica merge in an instant.
Having ground together mercury, mica, *vaṅga*-mica, *guñjā*, human skull, *ṭaṅkaṇa*,
and wild *śigru* with breast milk, one should apply it as a coating to the crucible.
One should add powdered *baṅga* and the essence of white mica (*śvetābhra-sattva*) to it;
having sealed [the crucible] and heated it, they surely melt together, and one should digest them in the process of silver-making (*tārakarma*).
First, having finely powdered the essence of mica (*abhrasattva*)— specifically tin-mica—
one should add one-quarter part of borax (*ṭaṃkaṇa*) and a portion of mercury equal to the borax, and then process them with the juice of *kākamācī* for one day.
Having ground that ball together with portions of mica and lead-leaf, it is to be heated in the previously prepared crucible; then the lead and mica merge in an instant.
One should cast one *pala* of well-fermented *nāga* into *kāñjika*;
when it has reached exactly one hundred *palas*, it should be stirred very rapidly a hundred times.
One should saturate it one hundred times with this very *kāñjika* [fermented gruel];
then, whatever substance is used for the *cāraṇa* process, one should digest that within the mercury.
This is known as *abhiṣeka* (consecration), but another opinion is now stated.
{Consecration (2)}:
The three alkalis, the five salts, potassium carbonate, iron sulfate, and sulfur,
combined with buffalo urine and sour gruel, should be kept in a copper vessel for three days.
When it has cooled again, one should cast the molten nāga back into it;
or, for the purpose of making *tāra* (silver), one should sprinkle tin (*baṅga*) upon it a hundred times.
The wise know that liquid, when placed in a copper vessel, is the consecration;
with this, one should saturate the object of worship one hundred times.
Regarding the *sāraṇā* [practice], the convention is as follows:
one should always cause the coupled sky-being (*vyomasattva*) and various seed-syllables (*bīja*),
as well as the coupled vajra-seed-syllable, to be brought forth through meditative cultivation.
All metals such as gold and others, having been reduced to purified powder, should be added in equal parts to the excellent sattva of *gagana* (mica).
When this pair is combined and the excellent mercury is consecrated, it flows [like] a Brahmin consuming sweet milk-rice with clarified butter.

The wise one who understands this, having processed mercury refined with sattva and well-mixed according to the number of qualities of the seeds known as "matured," becomes a lord among alchemists and produces gold by the method of piercing with the moon and the sun.
Having thoroughly amalgamated lead with gold and rubbed it to the measure of one *māṣa*,
one should then add one *pala* of mercury into that heated mortar (*taptakhalva*).

Having added the juice of *siddhamūlī*, one should grind it with fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*) for a day, either in the sun or in a heated mortar; thereafter, one should administer the "bite" (*grāsa*).
First, sixty-four parts of the previously manifested *dvandva* essence should be given and ground for one day, then placed in a *cāraṇa* machine.
If worn during the daytime heat along with citron fruits, it certainly moves [the poison].
Regarding the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of mercury:
one should cause the three alkalis, the five salts, the group of acids, and the milk of *snuhī* to be stirred together with cow’s urine. With that [mixture], one should smear a thick cloth.
Having bound the mercury (sūta) that has been processed within that [mixture], one should wrap it with birch bark;
then, combined with the juices of the *siddhamūlī* plant, one should cook it for three days in a *dolāyantra* (swinging apparatus).
Having removed [the solidified substance], one should wash it in an iron vessel with warm sour gruel;
then, having filtered it through a cloth, one should macerate it in a warm vessel.
As long as the mercury remains on the hand, one should wash it again with a well-washed cloth four times its size; thus it will become pure.
Furthermore, if it is not digested, one should add sour liquid and grind it again;
by subjecting it to heat in a swinging vessel (dolā) for a period of one day, it will undoubtedly become digested.
{Mercury:: preparation for grāsana} Brick, jaggery-burnt wool, soot from a house, and sarjikā— all these,
combined with rock salt, should be sixteen parts relative to the mercury.
Then, having added the group of acidic substances (*amlavarga*), one should grind it for a day in the heat;
subsequently, one should cook it for a day in a *dolāyantra* (swinging apparatus) with brick-dust and the group of acidic substances.
As each portion is digested, one should repeat this process until the mercury becomes capable of swallowing the "bites" (*grāsa*).
Then, having given a morsel (*grāsa*) of thirty-two parts and performed the *ācārya* [process], one should cause it to digest (*jārayet*).
Having performed everything up to the stage of sweating (*svedana*) as before, one should give the third morsel.
A sixteenth part should be given; when that is digested, an eighth part [should be added].
One should cause it to digest according to the previous method; thus, four "mouthfuls" (grāsa) are completed.
Then one should cause it to digest by means of a tortoise-press; this is what is described:
at each morsel, one should add *biḍa* salt in an amount equal to one-eighth part above and below.

Then, one should give a morsel consisting of a fourth part, and again give morsels of equal size; as each is digested, another of equal size should be given, and in this way it should be digested six times over.
And for the purpose of seizing those possessed by passion, at every morsel [of food] as before;
thus, specifically regarding beings engaged in the union of the pairs.
The digestion (*jāraṇā*) of all metals such as gold and the like, which has been performed upon their seeds (*bīja*), must be carried out;
the dosage and application thereof will be explained there, as before.

In the absence of the essence of *vyoma*, the essence of *kāntapāṣāṇa* (magnetite) or the essence of *tīkṣṇapāṣāṇa* (pyrites) should be used as a *dvaṃdvita* (binary compound), just like the essence of *vyoma*.
One should cause [the substances] to be digested by means of the previous method; thus, for all of them, the result shall be equal.
In this way, whatever pair of sixfold qualities one causes to be digested within the mercury, [that shall be the result].
That which has been incinerated by the seed-syllable of the perfected one (*siddhabīja*) is said to be "extracted" (*sārayet*).
Refined copper, bell-metal, and pure gold are all equal in value when they weigh the same.
Having turned it over and sealed it again in a crucible smeared with *dvaṃdvam*, one should lift it out and blow upon it; then, one should blow openly upon it in the crucible once more.
One should gradually add small amounts of purified essence derived from honey until the remainder is gold; then that [mixture] should be cooked once again.
And as before, one should blow upon it until only gold remains; thus, one should repeatedly perform this process of smelting with copper that has been reduced to its essential essence.
It should be extracted by distillation six times until only gold remains;
this is known as the perfected seed (siddhabīja), and it becomes like the flower of the pomegranate tree.

Having performed the three types of extraction (*sāraṇā*) as before with this perfected seed-syllable (*siddhabīja*), one should then cause [the mercury] to digest; once it has been digested, one should likewise seal its mouth.
The binding, the purification, and the transmutation are to be performed as before;
once the moon and sun have been liquefied, they should be joined with gold in the proportion of one part to a thousand.
Now, therefore, regarding the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of purified mercury: first, one should digest that which was previously prepared;
then, one should digest the previously described essence (*sattva*) of the purified [mercury].
But by means of the *tulāyantra*, it subsequently consumes the sulfur entirely.
One should make [the tube] twelve finger-breadths long, provided with a mouth-tube, facing upwards, firm, and made of iron; another [tube] similar to this should be prepared.
One should place the mercury into one [vessel] and an equal amount of sulfur into the other;
then, one should insert the mouth of the second vessel into the middle of the mouth of the first.
Having smeared the joint with clay and salt, one should apply a mild fire from below the sulphur;
having placed water beneath the mercury, it will thoroughly inhale the fumes of the sulphur.
When the [original] fragrance has been digested, one should remove it and cause a fragrance of equal quality to be applied;
in this manner, the sixteenfold fragrance should be processed again and again.
This king of elixirs, once processed, becomes permeated with latent impressions.
Having melted mercury,
mica, copper ore, and pure copper in equal proportions,
one should smelt them together in a crucible smeared with a mixture of two parts each, and then grind them into a powder.
One should perform the consecration one hundred times as before,
and one should apply this to the mercury that has been made manifest through its latent impressions, just as previously described.
In the same way, one should diligently refine the mercury until it becomes sixfold;
then that refined mercury, when combined with the perfected seed (*siddhabīja*), should be processed as before.
Having formed a seal upon the mouth, one should cause it to reach the end of the piercing;
when joined with the process of transmutation (*krāmaṇa*), the moon and sun become gold. This mercury, which takes any form at will, is truly effective even by a thousandth part. // Rrā_3,14.37 //
As before, one should properly digest six times the amount of previously prepared sulfur with pure mercury using the *tulāyantra*, as described previously.

One should cause the juice of bitter *kośātakī* mixed with the juice of *lāṅgalī* to be administered to the previously mentioned mercury, which should then be ground in a mortar for a period of one day.
