Having caused a quarter-part of the ripened seed to circulate, one should then cause it to digest;
by means of the *biḍa* mixture as before, it should be digested in this manner according to the equal sequence.
Then, having extracted the ripened seed in three ways, one should cause it to digest;
by applying a penetration (vedha) into the silver at a hundredth part, it shall become gold.
The procedure for the hundredfold [alloy]:
ninety-eight parts of silver and one part of gold.
One part of the piercing mercury is to be reckoned as the hundred-fold piercer.
As for the essence (*sattva*) of mercury, whether it be powdered or dissolved,
one should cause it to enter and digest it in the mercury by means of the sequential application as described before.

Subsequently, one should add eight times as much high-quality black mica (*kṛṣṇābhra-sattva*), which is to be processed and refined in due order; likewise, four times as much ripened seed (*pakvabīja*) is to be added.
Furthermore, one should digest [the mercury] again in a crucible called *kacchapa*, combined with *viḍa* salt, until the color is absorbed; then, having performed this, one should wash that mercury.
One should grind equal parts of *unmatta*, *munipatra*, *rajanī*, and *kākamācikā* with fermented grain water (*dhānyāmla*), and then macerate the mercury with that liquid.
One should cook it for seven days in a heated mortar and for one day in a tortoise-shaped vessel;
thereafter, one should grind it with divine herbs for three days.
Having sealed it in a vajra-muṣā crucible and sweated with the fire of chaff for three days,
one should grind it again and likewise seal it and heat it strongly.
It arises bound, resembling a hen’s egg; one should then grind it, rub it with the juice of *brahmapuṣpa* for one day, and again seal it in darkness.
In this manner, four *puṭas* should likewise be administered while it is processed in the "elephant-pot" (*gajapuṭa*);
similarly, four *puṭas* should be given using the juices of *vṛścikālī*.
In the same manner, one should apply four *puṭas* with saffron essence,
and having given one *puṭa* with the juice of *mātuluṅga*, one should collect [the medicine].
With that very same thousandth part,
one should pierce either pure mercury or molten lead; through this process of transmutation (*krāmaṇa*),
all of it becomes gold, the most excellent ornament for the gods.
One should prepare an equal amount of powder from the seed of gold (*svarṇārka*), sharp lead (*tīkṣṇanāga*), realgar (*sasyābhraka*), and the essence (*sattva*) of *vaikrānta*.
One should blow upon the sealed crucible smeared with the *dvandvamelāpa* [mixture];
having extracted that residue (*khoṭa*), one should blow upon it openly in the crucible.
The paste should be given with honey powder little by little, until only gold remains; then one should apply it again to the *arka* plant.
One should blow [the substance] according to the sequence as before until only gold remains;
by doing this again in this manner, the seed of gold (*svarṇabījaka*) is produced.
Having made equal parts of the powder of mica-essence (abhrasattva), iron,
and copper, the powder of purified tāpya should be twice the amount of the copper.
Having sealed [the crucible] in a crucible smeared with a pair [of substances], one should blow it with a fierce fire;
then, having reduced that residue to a fine powder and sealed it again, one should cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire.
Thus, having cooked it with five layers, one should process it into molten gold;
one should blow it in an open crucible slowly until it has increased tenfold.
A small amount of powdered pyrite should be added, and one should sow it little by little;
having extracted the remaining gold, this shall be the "gold-seed."
One should digest the seed of gold (candrārka), equal in weight, just as one digests the essence of mica;
then, with a hundredth part of that [seed], one should apply a coating smeared with honey.
One should wrap equal quantities of *caṃdrārka* leaves with *arkapatra* leaves and cook them slowly for ten days in a *dolāyantra* using the juice of *sāra*.
Having extracted them, one should cause them to revolve; they become divine gold.
Take one part each of mercury, iron, and copper, along with an equal amount of powdered *tāpya* (calamine);
this should be added slowly to molten gold until it has increased tenfold.
Having taken the remaining gold, this shall be the "gold-seed" (svarṇabījaka).
Equal parts of sharp iron (*tīkṣṇa*), magnetite (*kānta*), mercury (*mṛta*), copper (*śulva*), and silver (*tāra*)—
having sealed them in a crucible smeared with a mixture of two [substances]— one should blow it with a fierce fire.
When that dross has been melted into gold, it should be gradually added ten times over;
with the addition of the previously mentioned powder of *tāpya*, this is the supreme seed of gold (*svarṇabīja*).
Just as silver [is transmuted into] gold,
one should digest a single part of a gold seed in the mercury according to one's desire; then,
by means of the *sattva* seed, one should purify it through the sequential application of the previously described method.
One should cause that to be digested by means of the *sārita*; one should cause it to be digested by means of the *anusārya*.
Then, having caused the *jārya* to be drawn back (*pratisārya*), and having bound the mouth, one should bind [it].
By piercing the *tārā* with the tenfold yoga at one-fifth [of its measure],
and combining it with the process of transmutation (*krāmaṇa*), the gold becomes divine.
Silver, *nāga*, *rasaka*, *sattva*, and copper, each increasing by one part in sequence,
should be smelted and then cast into gold; one should gradually add [the mixture] until it is six times the amount.
That gold residue should then be processed with mercury in equal proportions,
and one should perform the sequence of operations starting from "killing" (māraṇa) up to "binding" (bandhana), exactly as before.
By this sixtieth part, as before, gold is produced.
One should kill copper with gold and *tāpya* (calamine), just as [it is killed] by means of *gandha* (sulfur);
then one should process that copper into lead, blowing repeatedly within the crucible.
Gradually, by repeatedly adding copper powder up to a hundredfold,
one should process that copper into gold in a sequence of thirty-two-fold increments.
One should digest that seed, which has gold as its residue, in equal parts within the mercury;
and by means of this very seed, one should again cause it to flow and digest it.
As before, one should perform the process up to the binding by means of the sequential yoga;
joined with the *krāmaṇa* [transference], one should pierce it with a thousandth part.
Thus, the moon and sun become gold, the supreme ornament of the gods.

Having successively placed the essences of mercury and mica, followed by copper powder, into a crucible smeared with a *dvandva* mixture and sealed it, one should extract [the product] when it has been heated. (Rasaratnākara 3.14.77)
Having added an eighth part of that [substance] as a powder of mica (tāpya), one should grind it with acid;
then, having sealed it in a small crucible, one should cook it, and thus one should cook it with five such *puṭas*.
One should gradually introduce that powder into gold being smelted,
until that seed has been assimilated into the mercury a thousandfold.
One should diligently refine it up to a hundredfold by this very means;
the processes of *jāraṇa* (digestion), *sāraṇa* (refining), and ending with *bandhana* (binding) are as before.
Then, by taking one part in a hundred thousand, it becomes gold with silver.
One should grind silver, gold, mica-essence, copper, and lead in increasing proportions;
having sealed them in a crucible smeared with the *dvandva* mixture, one should blow it with a fierce fire.
One should grind that equal amount of powdered *tāpya* with all the acidic liquids, seal it, and cook it with five *puṭas*; then one should quickly cause that powder to flow out.
One should digest gold in proportion to one hundred [parts of mercury],
and having done so by means of skillful application, one should purify it three times until it has become a hundredfold.
Once it has been brought back [to its original state], one should perform the process of digestion (jāraṇa) and the binding (bandhana) as before;
by means of that very [substance] in the proportion of one ten-thousandth part, silver becomes gold.
Alternatively, the aforementioned powder, increased a thousandfold, should be introduced gradually into molten gold;
one should then digest that seed within the mercury.
One should cause it to be transmuted a thousandfold, repeating this process three times;
thereafter, one should digest that which has been transmuted, and having transmuted it again, one should digest it once more.
Through the application of the sevenfold chain (*saptaśṛṅkhalikā-yoga*), the wise one should cause the mercury to flow and digest it;
having bound its mouth and fixed the mercury, the mercury becomes capable of ten million-fold penetration (*koṭivedhī*).
When joined with the *krāmaṇa* agent, even the sun and moon (silver and gold) become gold.
One should grind copper, silver, vimalā, tālaka, and tīkṣṇa in increasing proportions;
then, having smeared a crucible with a *dvandva*-mixture, one should thoroughly grind that resulting mass into a fine powder.
One should rub it with acids and cook it in a *puṭa*; thus one should subject it to *puṭa* treatment five times, repeatedly adding ten parts of *tāla* powder to the silver (*tāra*).
One should cause this seed to produce [the mercury] equally and digest it according to the previous sequence;
thereafter, one should perform three purifications (sāraṇā) by means of the seed-syllable of Tāra.
By means of that very hundredth part, one should quickly transmute copper;
it becomes beautiful silver, resembling a conch shell, a kunda flower, or the moon.
One should prepare a powder consisting of equal parts copper, dead tin (mṛtabaṅga), and the essence of haritāla; then,
blowing it repeatedly, one should process it into silver sixteen times its weight.
One should digest that seed in mercury until it has increased tenfold in sequence;
thereafter, one should perform three *sāraṇā* (purifications) using the seed of silver.
By means of this thousandth part, one should cause the copper to be transmuted;
that copper becomes silver, resembling a conch shell, a kunda flower, or the moon.

One should prepare an equal powder of the essence of mercury (śatavedhin), the essence of white clouds (śvetābhra) and mica (tāla), the essence of calamine (rasaka), and fourthly, the essence of silver pyrite (tāramākṣika). Rājanighaṇṭu 3.14.96.

One should smelt all that together with an equal amount of tin powder in a crucible smeared with *dvaṃdvamelāpa*; once it has formed into a solid mass (*khoṭa*), one should grind it into a fine powder.
One should cook [the substance] ground with sour gruel in a *puṭa* vessel; thus one should apply the *puṭa* treatment five times.
One should then process that powder in silver until it has been smelted ten times over.
That mercury of the king of essences (rasarāja) should indeed be gradually digested with equal amounts of copper;
and as before, it should be processed three times, whereby the mercury becomes a hundred-fold penetrator (śatavedhī).
In this same way, the powder of *sattva* and *abhrasattva*, as well as their binary combination (*dvandva*), should be treated as before;
having added a quarter-part of *tālaka* and ground it with acidic liquids, one should seal it.
One should cook it in this manner with five layers; the external mercury should be twice sixfold [twelvefold].
This seed should be digested equally, ten parts for each.
Ten parts each of tin, white mica essence (śvetābhrasattva), and that which is called silver (tārākhya); five parts each of vimalā and iron (tīkṣṇa).
One should strongly heat that [substance] in a crucible smeared with a mixture of the two [metals];
it should be cooked in a *puṭa* five times, repeatedly ground with acid.
Repeatedly adding the powder of the "star" (tāra) to that external portion of the "star," one should gradually digest that seed of the king of mercury until it has increased a hundredfold.
One should perform the three-fold transmutation (*sāraṇā*) according to the ritual procedure using the *tāra* seed-syllable.
By means of this very [seed-syllable], one should pierce molten copper with a ten-thousandth part [of the mercury];
it becomes divine silver, resembling a conch shell, a *kunda* flower, or the moon.
Thus, having prepared the golden seed within the mercury through infinite yogas, the physician should duly digest that entire mass;
and by means of that very [mercury], having produced an abundance of gold and silver, he should extinguish the fever of poverty among all people.

Now, the seed-attainment (bījasādhana) suitable for the womb, which is beneficial for the process of coloring through various yogas, is being fully described here for the sake of the transmuted mercury (pārada), O King. (Rrā 3.15)
One should powder together equal parts of sulfur, pyrite,
and lead; then, repeatedly blowing upon molten gold, one should process it until it has been tripled [in weight].
This gross, putrid seed dissolves into fluidity within the womb at that very moment.
Having heated equal parts of lead and gold, one should repeatedly add powdered mica;
once the lead is digested, it should be added again, and so on three times slowly.
This seed indeed melts through churning within the womb of mercury.
{The Seed-Practice (3)} One should smelt lead-bearing ore and gold, repeatedly casting the lead into the gold;
in this manner, three parts of the lead-bearing ore are to be introduced into the gold.
That seed of the king of mercury dissolves instantly within the womb.
Then, one should melt equal parts of copper, mercury, and gold; [and] the leaf,
having been pierced through the neck, [is treated] with sulfur and salt.
Having cast it [into the crucible] with sour liquid, one should cook it in a *puṭa* until only gold remains;
this is the seed of the Lord of Mercury (*rasendra*), which dissolves through rubbing within the womb [of the mercury].
{Seed-Practice (5)} One should roast [the substance] with rock salt, grind it with acidic liquids, and cook it in a *puṭa* vessel;
having ground it again, one should cook it again, repeating this process twelve times.
One should grind all this together with an equal amount of dead snake and sour gruel;
having smeared gold leaves with this [mixture] repeatedly, one should heat them strongly.
One should quickly sow that [seed] seven times again and again;
this seed of mercury dissolves through churning within the womb.
{Seed-Practice (6)} One should grind together rock-salt, black salt, iron sulfate, sulfur, copper sulfate,
and borax with the acidic juice of chickpeas for the duration of one day.
Having added this sixteenth part of mercury, one should cause the seed (bīja) to be given;
wherever [the substance] is applied, it melts at that very moment.
One should collect the alkali from the ashes of *apāmārga* and *palāśa*,
as well as borax, nitre, green vitriol, and *suvarcala*. (Rājanighaṇṭu 3.15.13)
Sea salt, rock salt, black salt, honey, fermented salt (navasāra),
camphor, and sour gruel— these in equal parts should be rubbed with the milky sap of *snuhī* and *arka*.
Having applied a coating to the crucible with this very [substance] and with *biḍa* salt, one should apply a coating to the depth of a finger;
this shall be the crucible apparatus (*mūṣāyantra*).
One should then cast the mercury (sūta) into the seed that has been liquefied within the womb;
having sealed it, one should subject it to sudation for one day over a fire of dried cow-dung, and it will readily consume [the ingredients].
One should again melt the combined essence of mercury (or *rañjana*) and the essence of *tāpya* and mica;
then, one should very gradually introduce the powder of dead copper (*mṛtaśulba*) and *tāpya* into it.
When that [intellect] has discarded the three qualities, it is indeed said to have discarded attachment.
Having ground the red group of minerals with cow’s urine, one should saturate [the mercury] with that very [liquid].
Take equal parts of cinnabar, pyrite, sulfur, and powdered realgar. (Rasārṇava 3.15.19)
Having processed [the ingredients] seven times, one should dry and grind them repeatedly;
then, having powdered sharp copper in equal measure, it should be fused as a binary compound (dvaṃdvamela) as before.

Having quickly sown the aforementioned powder into that [substance], one should then sprinkle it with oil derived from *jyotiṣmatī* combined with the group of red substances (*raktavarga*). In this manner, one should perform the process ten times; this shall be the "coloring agent for mercury" (*rasarañjaka*).
(3) For coloring with mercury, one should saturate cinnabar three times with the group of red minerals and cow’s urine;
then, when pure copper of equal weight has been melted, one should cause it to be infused by blowing.
That mercury, when processed seven times with cinnabar, becomes a colorant for mercury.
{The color-enhancer (4):} Equal parts of gold-lead, metallic vapor, realgar, ochre, pyrite, calamine, and the red group [of minerals] are to be fused together in a binary union. Rāra 3.15.23.
One should grind all [the ingredients] into equal parts and indeed add a flux (*vāpa*) by means of this;
repeatedly, to the previously doubled *khoṭa* that has been melted.
When sown ten times, this becomes a colorant for mercury as well.
Manahshila of red color should be processed twenty times with the juices of *yavaciñcā*; one should carefully smear [the lead] with that paste.
One should cook the nāgapatra leaf in a vessel until it has reached the state of powder;
[using] three parts of mercury and one part of cinnabar (darada).
One should grind one part each of realgar, sulphur, and rhinoceros horn with the acidic juice of *mātuluṅga*; one should then apply a paste made from that.
One should cast the previously mentioned naga into the interior of the crucible;
once it has melted, one should extract it, smear the crucible with it, and blow upon it again.
Thus, by smelting seven times in this manner, the naga [lead] becomes gold-like;
[silver, lead, and copper =] gold.
The essence of yellow mica (pītābhra) and the "eastern serpent" (pūrvanāga) are equal to that.
One should cause it to be joined in pairs according to the previous yoga and consecrated;
in the presence of the King of Mercury (sūtarāja), it should be increased sixfold in sequence as before.
Then, one should add a quarter-part of the seed for internal liquefaction (*garbhadrāvaṇabīja*) of that mercury (*rasendra*) into the mortar, together with the juice of *mātuluṅga*.
One should grind it with sour chickpeas or with *garbhadrāvaṇaka* [juice]; thus the embryo indeed dissolves. Then, one should digest it in a crucible-furnace (*mūṣāyantra*).

In this manner, the substance to be processed (jārya), once liquefied, should be brought to the end through the three stages beginning with *sāraṇā*— namely, until it is equal in measure to the seed (*bīja*) within the mercury— following the sequence as previously described.
One should pierce copper with mercury, tāla, ariṣṭa, and mahiṃ, using even a single part as desired;
by that very [mercury] in a thousandth part, it becomes divine gold.
Diamond combined with gold— [the latter being] the [result of the transmutation of] the moon and sun— and consecrated as before,
one should digest it in the presence of the mercury in equal parts, just like the essence of mica.
One should cause that which has been heated to digest itself by means of that gold-vajra in three ways;
having bound the mouth and bound the mercury, one should then apply it with a *krāmaṇa* agent.
When applied to the moon and sun (silver and copper) in a thousandth part, it becomes divine gold.
{The liquefaction of Gandhanāga}:
Having taken the urine of a bull, or of an elephant or a buffalo,
one should repeatedly pour the liquefied *sūtanāga* into its midst seven times.
Then, one should have the leaves of that very [metal] made into pieces thin enough to be pierced by a needle;
pure powdered sulphur, four times the weight of the leaves, [should be applied].
Having soaked it with lac and fashioned it like a cotton leaf,
one should place human hairs upon its back once it has dried.
Upon its back, one should place powdered fragrance, then *nāgadalā* leaves,
sulfur, human hair, and cotton wool on top of that.
One should have a wick made from this and wrap it with an outer thread;
then one should keep it immersed in silver-white oil for ten nights.
Having ignited [the fire] at both ends, one should quickly collect the liquefied oil into a vessel containing sour gruel (*kāñjika*);
having extracted it from there, one should preserve it with care in a glass flask (*kācakūpī*).
This is the liquefaction of *gandhanāga*.
Pure mercury should be firmly rubbed together with a powder of turmeric until it becomes black; then one should wash it with warm *kāñjika* vinegar.
In this manner, one should perform [the process] twenty-one times; thereafter, one should begin the digestion (*jāraṇa*).
Having ground realgar with acidic juices, one should apply a coating with that.
One should pour the previous liquid into this crucible shaped like a cow's udder;
then, the mercury-essence of sulphur (gandhadruti) should be added gradually in sixty-fourth parts of the previous amount.
Having sealed the crucible and dried it, one should then place half of the crucible into a pit filled with cow dung, using a fire of dried cow-dung and husks.
One should apply the *kapota* (pigeon) type of *puṭapāka* and, once it has cooled to the temperature of its own body parts (*svāṅgaśīta*), extract [the medicine].
However, if there is a suspicion of indigestion (*ajīrṇa*), one should administer the juice of *siṃhavallī*.
One should cook it in a crucible within a pit to the measure of four drops;
in this manner, the liquefaction of gandhanāga should be processed again and again in due order.
The mercury, having been processed three times, becomes the color of gold.

One should grind well-ripened seeds into a fine powder, using a one-fourth part of this mercury, and macerate them with sour chickpea water for one *yāma*; thus, it will readily liquefy within the crucible.
Having melted the gold in a crucible apparatus by means of sudation as before,
once it has been digested, one should add the seed (bīja) again, melt it, and then cause it to digest within the womb (garbha).

In this way, having caused the seed to digest equally, or having it ripen, one should gradually cause it to digest either the *rañjana* [dyeing] substance or the *garbha* [womb] or *drāvaṇa* [liquefying] seed— whichever one is desired.
Then, repeatedly blowing upon the outer brass, which consists of three parts of copper, it becomes silver; having prepared a leaf, one should smear it with that [silver].
That [substance] should again be mixed with honey in a thirty-second part according to the previous recipe,
wrapped in *arka* leaves, and cooked in a *dolāyantra* with *kāñjika*.
At the end of ten days, having been extracted, it becomes liquefied gold.
One should cause [the mercury] to digest [the mineral] either in the presence or in the absence of the king of mercury;
one should cause the powder of *vyoma* (mica), processed as before, to digest gradually.
One should cause it to flow and digest it up to sixty-four times;
likewise, one should cause it to circulate and digest it until it has become sixty-fold.
Then, one should cause the essence of honey (*mākṣika-sattva*) to digest therein, in a portion equal to one-quarter [of the previous amount].
One should extract whatever essence (sattva) can be obtained from the great minerals (mahārasa) and secondary minerals (uparasa);
having added a quarter-part of that to mercury, one should grind it together.
In a heated mortar, combined with a flux that causes the melting of the interior, all of those substances indeed liquefy; then, one should digest them in a crucible apparatus (*mūṣāyantra*).
In this manner, one should cause all the essences to dissolve and digest them through the yoga of liquefaction (*drāvaṇa*).
[The result is] the colored, ripened seed, pure copper, and gold.
Equal parts of the seed for causing the dissolution of the embryo and of dead iron (mṛtatīkṣṇa) should all be ground together;
having formed a pill (khoṭa), it should be smelted again and again.
When the sharp [mercury] has been consumed in the copper, one should add powdered honey;
then, having extracted that seed, it should be added as a one-fourth portion to the previously mentioned mercury.
As before, one should cause [the mercury] to liquefy within the crucible (mūṣāyantra) and then digest it;
one should digest the seed (bīja) thirty-two times in this sequence.
When the embryo is digested, the liquefied mercury is colored—this is what is described.
The lead that has been killed by sulphur (gandha) serves as the means for processing the ripened seed;
one should blow upon that lead, equal in weight to gold, once it has been placed inside a blind crucible (andhamūṣā).
One should cause that powder and the consecrated portion to be added to the mercury;
one should then rub it with the group of sour substances (amlavarga) or with a fluxing agent for the internal core (garbhadrāvaṇaka).

One should digest it for four watches in a heated mortar, or then in a crucible apparatus; by this sequential method, one should digest that [mercury] possessing the quality of a sixteenth part (kalā).
Dead copper and dead iron are to be introduced into gold six times over;
this is the seed (bīja), which is then to be digested gradually until it has become four times the original amount.
As before, it is melted in the mortar and in the crucible apparatus as previously described;
then the mercury, having its color fixed, arises with the luster of saffron.
Having thus produced the coloring agent and processed it three times in succession,
one should digest the processed substance in urine within a *mūṣāyantra* by repeatedly applying heat.
One should cause that which has been digested to flow out, and likewise cause that which has flowed out to be digested;
by this sequential application, according to the order of the sevenfold chain.
Then, having bound his mouth as before, one should bind him;
joined with the *krāmaṇa* [transmuting agent], one should pierce it with a ten-millionth part.
That molten copper will undoubtedly become divine gold.

One should grind mercury produced from cinnabar with *bhūnāga* for three days in a heated mortar (*taptakhalva*). Then, having caused it to fall [into a receiver], one should collect that which adheres to the upper surface.
One should digest a quarter-part of that [mercury] with an equal amount (dvaṃdvita) of the essence of *vyoma* (mica);
then, one should digest a quarter-part of the essence of *mākṣika* (pyrite) therein.

As before, by means of the application of binary combinations (*dvaṃdvayoga*), the digestion of the *mātrā* is performed as previously described; and that essence (*sattva*) which was previously precipitated by means of great minerals (*mahārasa*) and secondary minerals (*uparasa*).
One should add that sattva separately as a fourth part and grind it for one day in a heated mortar (taptakhalva),
combined with a fluxing agent (garbhadrāvaṇa).
Then the crucible-mechanism melts the substance to be processed as before;
as it is repeatedly consumed, one should again add an equal amount of the material in due order.
Then, in the same manner, one part in four of the seed for causing the fetus to fall (*garbhadrāvaṇabījaka*) should be melted as before and processed (*jārya*) in this sequence until it is sixfold.
One should cause the piercing (*vedha*) to be applied to the *tāra* (silver) through the process beginning with *sāraṇā* and ending with *krāmaṇā*;
by a thousandth part [of that], the gold will possess the luster of *jāmbūnada*.
One should take the juice of the tender leaves of the *śākavṛkṣa* tree,
as well as the juice of *brahmapuṣpa* flowers and the juice of *viṣṇukrāntā*. (Rasārṇava 3.15.79)
One should saturate pure mercury with these liquids for seven days;
then, one should place the thoroughly purified mercury into the center of a crucible (iṣṭikā).
One should cover his face from behind with a clean cloth;
having applied one-tenth of the previously mentioned fragrance, one should seal it with beeswax.
A small *puṭa* should be applied to the back; once it is digested, one should add more sulfur again.
In that same manner, it should be processed by means of the *puṭa* itself, and sulfur should be added once more.
In this way, one should extract the equalized mercury and the fragrance from the apparatus;
or else, the mercury to be processed should be equal in measure to that fragrance.
One should cause it to be digested by means of the previous method, or even inside a glass flask (kācakūpī).
Copper and lead [become] gold:
one should digest an equal portion of the essence of *vyoma* with this very king of elixirs;
it should be processed in pairs as before, and the application of dosage is as before.
Then, the essence of *rasaka* should be digested eight times in the mercury;
likewise, *tīkṣṇa*, *śulba*, and *uraga* should be added to the mercury in sequence, each eight times.
One should diligently digest each [ingredient] consecrated as before;
then, the ripened seed should be digested in sequence thirty-two times over.

Then, having added an equal amount of the seed for internal liquefaction (*garbhadrāvaṇabīja*) to this king of essences (*rasarāja*) in a heated mortar, together with the liquefier (*garbhadrāvaka*), [one should proceed].
One should rub it for one day, and it will quickly liquefy within the crucible;
thereafter, it should indeed be processed by means of sudation (*svedana*) in a *mūṣāyantra* as previously described.
When that has been digested, one should add an equal amount of coloring seed (rañjakabīja) as before;
then, within the liquid matrix, it should be melted and likewise processed through the stages of digestion in due order.
Then, having melted it with effort up to four times its weight, one should digest it within the womb;
by this sequential method, the mercury becomes like the color of lac.
Then, one should digest that [mercury] which has been processed with the ripened seed (pakvabīja) in due order;
one should perform the process of re-integration (pratisāraṇaka), digest it, and then cause it to flow.
Having bound the mouth by means of the sevenfold chain-yoga, one should then apply the piercing (*vedha*) to the copper, conjoined with the *krāmaṇa* [transference]. Rrā 3.15.93.
Or, by a ten-millionth part of a naga, it becomes divine gold.
One should grind *dhānyābhraka* with the juices of *rasabīja*, *tintiṇī*, *brahma*, and *māṇḍūkī* in succession for three days, and then saturate it with the juice of *tintiṇī*.
For three days, it should be dried in the heat and ground again and again;
having placed purified mercury in an earthen pan, one should cause it to become warm.

Having added sulphur in the measure of a *truṭi* and previously prepared mica in the measure of a *truṭi*, one should cook it over a gentle fire repeatedly; thus the mica-paste (*abhrapiṣṭikā*) is produced.
One should process the sulphur with the juices of *ekavīrā* twenty-one times by means of heat;
having melted that sulphur in a greased vessel over a mild fire, one should pour it [into the mercury].
In the midst of that, one should cook the previously prepared powder in a swinging apparatus (*dolāyantra*) according to the prescribed method;
in this way, one should digest six times the amount of sulfur using a gentle fire.
One part of its juice, sixteen parts of ripened seed,
and the same amount of well-refined mercury, having been powdered, should then be mixed together in pairs.
As before, by blowing [into] a crucible smeared with a pair [of substances],
one should sprinkle this celebrated seed of mercury once it has been powdered.
Now, therefore, [the process of] *jāraṇa* (digestion) of mercury with *rasabīja* (seed-mercury), when the purified mercury has been placed inside a glass flask (*kācakūpī*).
As before, one should refine the cultivated fragrance; that very [fragrance] is increased sixfold.
One should indeed cause it to be digested in a *tulāyantra* according to the procedure of the *gaurīyantra*;
[one should add] a quarter-part of the seed-mercury (*rasabīja*) of that very king of mercury.
As before, one should cause it to liquefy within the crucible-apparatus (*mūṣāyantra*) and then digest it;
by this sequential method, the mercury-seed (*rasabīja*) of the mercury itself should indeed be liquefied and digested again and again until it has been multiplied sixteen times.
Having processed two parts of pure silver and one part of pure gold together,
one should indeed make a leaf from that [alloy] using the previously mentioned liquid.
Then, one should again smear it with honey mixed with a thousandth part [of the aforementioned substance] and wrap it with *arka* leaves in a *dolāyantra* (swinging apparatus) over *kañjika*.
When processed and melted for ten days, it becomes divine gold.
One should digest well-purified lead powder, consecrated as before,
within the presence of the sovereign mercury, just like the essence of mica.
One should indeed refine [the mercury] by thirty-six times the same amount in due order;
and the seed for the liquefaction of the embryo is likewise liquefied in sequence as before.
One should digest its seed, which is the colorant, three times over;
then it should be digested an equal amount again, gradually by means of the ripened seed.
Then, having blocked the mouth by means of the sevenfold chain-union (saptaśṛṅkhalikā-yoga), one should bind it;
when joined with the process of transmutation (krāmaṇa), the mercury becomes capable of piercing ten million [atoms] (koṭivedhī).
One should digest tin thirty-six times in succession using copper as the *nāgavajra* (mercury-copper compound); then,
having melted it as before, one should digest the seed of silver (*tārabīja*) within its core.
It should be tripled; then, by means of that very [mantra], one should cause it to flow.
Having bound the mouth through the application of the sevenfold chain (saptaśṛṅkhalikā), one should then bind [it].
One should cause the transmutation (*vedha*) of copper using [the mercury] conjoined with *krāmaṇa*;
by means of a ten-millionth part [of the mercury], it becomes silver resembling the jasmine flower or the moon.
One should cause silver,
copper,
and lead to be digested within the king of elixirs (sūtarāja), whether it is present in its manifest form or otherwise.
The dualized being of space (vyomasattva), however, extends up to eightfold in that same manner.
Then, one should likewise digest eight times the amount of mercury-satva;
and having digested the ripened seed in equal proportions, one should digest it just as with the satva of mica.
One should digest diamond (vajra) combined with gold in equal proportions,
using the *biḍa* formulation in the tortoise apparatus (*kacchapa-yantra*) as previously described.

One should grind the seed for causing the melting of the womb (*garbhadrāvaṇabīja*) in a quantity of one-quarter part within a heated mortar with the acidic juice of *mātuliṅga*; it melts in the womb at that very moment.
Or, by administering a formula for causing the embryo to flow out, it liquefies through friction;
one should then cook that mercury in a crucible apparatus using a fire of dried cow-dung.
Once [the mercury] has been digested, the seed should be melted again; one should digest it and melt it again.
In this manner, the seed for melting within the womb should be digested four times over.
Then, having similarly purified that coloring seed in equal measure,
one should perform the process in sequence from *sāraṇā* up to *krāmaṇā*, just as before.
One should add a ten-millionth part of either mercury, copper, or lead;
it produces divine gold, the most excellent ornament for the gods.
One should digest mercury—the king of alchemists—directly like the essence of mica. Mercury is the "smoke-piercer" (*dhūmavedhin*); [it transforms] copper into gold.
From gold up to muṇḍa, these are the eight metals in their respective order.
Each [element] is multiplied by eight, and the consecration is as before;
all that pertains to the beings beginning with the clouds is each multiplied by three in sequence.
In the tortoise apparatus (*kūrmayantra*), one should separately place the noble [substance] according to the previous method using the *biḍa* mixture;
thereafter, one should add a quarter-part of the seed for internal liquefaction (*garbhadrāvaṇabījaka*).

When the mercury, having been liquefied as before, becomes threefold in weight, one should then cause it to assimilate by means of the ripened seed (*pakvabīja*); thus, one should digest it three times.
Thus, having performed [the purification] sevenfold, one should bind the mouth and then apply the seal;
by this, there shall be piercing through smoke and vision, and copper becomes gold.

Having thus performed the various processes of *cāraṇa* (moving) and *jāraṇa* (digestion) upon the mercury, one should, according to the prescribed method, effect the *garbhadruti* (melting within the womb), which is the seed for liquefaction in the *garbha*.

Once it has been digested (*jīrṇa*), one should then perform the stages of *rañjana* (coloring) and *sāraṇā* (spreading), and having bound the mercury, one should make it into gold as majestic as Mount Meru for the sake of giving and enjoyment.

Those creepers from which blood flows constantly upon being cut, mostly on a ground of blood—those "earth-creepers" (*bhūlatā*) should be gathered; they bestow the power to remove poison and grant wealth.

If mercury (*pāradendra*) moves in conjunction with them through the application of the process of *sāraṇā*, it becomes bound; this [mercury] pierces ten million times (*koṭivedhī*) and shines brilliantly in battle. One should employ it in the sun (*bhāskara*).
Having ground the *bhūnāgasattva*, the earth-vine, and the *kāntapāṣāṇa* into equal parts,
that *sattva* should be extracted like mica together with the local medicinal herbs.
One should prepare an equal amount of *bhūnāga* powder together with *sauvīra*, *kāntapāṣāṇa*, *tīkṣṇa*, and powdered stone in a single place.
One should cause the being to grasp it like a cloud by blowing with the medicinal herbs found there.
The powder of *bhūnāga* and *sattva*, along with *kāntapāṣāṇa* and *sauvīra*, should be equal in measure to *bhūlatā*.
Like mica, it causes the *sattva* to be grasped, acting as a binder for the king of mercury (*rasarāja*).
One should take a powder of *bhūnāga* (antimony), *sattva* (mercury), *sauvīraka* (borax), and *tīkṣṇa* (iron), equal in measure to the *mṛd* (clay) of *bhūnāga*.
This should be kept in a vessel, and then one should throw living *bhūlatā* (earth-creeper) into it.
One should constantly sprinkle it with water until they indeed consume it;
having bound that being into a cloud-like mass, one should extract the essence.
Take the powder of *kāntapāṣāṇa* (magnetite) combined with the powder of *bhūlatā* (earth-creeper);
one should saturate it with goat’s urine for twenty-one days in the intense heat of the sun.
One should hold that mass within the stomach, grasping the most beautiful essence.
(6) One should grind together equal parts of *bhūnāgasattva*, cow’s urine, turmeric, *rājī*, and salt;
one should then sprinkle that mixture upon the *bhūnāga*, and it will readily liquefy under a hot sun.
Having made equal parts of kaṅkuṣṭha and its liquid, one should extract the essence;
through the sequential application [of this process], it becomes a binder of mercury, like the sky.
Having powdered earth-born sattva, sulphur, and *rasaka* in equal parts with the powder of *bhūlatā*,
and having sealed it in a *vajramūṣā* crucible and heated it, a beautiful *sattva* is produced.
Then, having pulverized this sattva and consecrated it as before, [one should proceed].
One should grind *sauvīra* collyrium for a day with an equal amount of *bhūnāga* oil;
then, having mixed it with the five products of the buffalo (*pañcamāhiṣa*), it should be formed into pills.
Therefore, oil should indeed be extracted by means of the pātālayantra using a *puṭa*.
One should wash *bhūlatā* with cow urine and extract the oil from it using a *pātālayantra*;
that oil is beneficial for the process of *jāraṇā*.
O Guhyasūta,
one should grind purified mercury together with *jīva* (organic matter) and *bhūnāga* (orpiment) for three days in a heated mortar; having thoroughly rubbed it, one should extract that entire mass.
One should place [the substance] in a crucible mixed with powdered *bhūnāga*;
having added powdered *bhūlatā* on top of that and sealed it, one should then dry it.
Having thrown cow dung together with [the mercury] into the interior of the pit, one should place the crucible therein;
then, one should fill the pit up to the level of the foot with dried cow-dung and ignite it with a fire of husks.
One should cook it in a *puṭa* for one day;
then, having removed it, one should apply the powder of *bhūlatā* above and below, and cook it again in a *puṭa* in the same manner.
If one performs this for only a month, the mercury becomes fire-resistant;
for that which is bound in form, there arises the "Rākṣasa" or "Vaḍavāmukha" [state].
It swallows all metals and various living beings;
it consumes all metals such as diamond (vajra), whether they have been offered or are already dead.
This is known as the secret elixir (guhyasūta), and its digestion (jāraṇa) will now be described.
Having added sixteen parts of this very [substance]— gold— to the essence of *bhūnāga*,
it should be ground for one day in a heated mortar, then combined with the perfected *viḍa* salt.

One should place that [substance] in a crucible smeared with *bhūnāga* oil, seal it, and subject it to heating in a fire of dried cow-dung; once the essence is digested, it should be treated as before.
Having added [the mercury] and rubbed it in a heated mortar, one should add *viḍa* salt in a tenth part;
then, having smeared it as before inside a crucible, one should indeed digest it by means of sweating (*svedana*).
In this way, having processed the mercury equally as before with a tortoise or by means of *garbhadrāva*, one should slowly apply the seed [of the medicine] six times over.
One should cause it to digest the liquefied [metal] in a crucible within a *mūṣāyantra* as before;
thereafter, the coloring seed (*rañjakabīja*) itself should be digested six times its weight.
Then, by means of the ripened seed according to the sequence of the seven chains, one should perform *sāraṇa* and *jāraṇa*; having bound the mouth [of the crucible], one should effect the binding.
And by this ten-millionth part, gold becomes like the moon and sun.
One should grind equal parts of copper-gold (*guhyasūta*) and gold with sour gruel until it forms a ball; then, one should place it in the middle of the *sāraṇā* process.

When the essence of the earth-naga (bhūnāga) from two [substances] of equal measure has been melted in a crucible, one should pour that [melted substance] into that essence; thus, it all becomes a *khoṭa*.

One should seal the crucible, which has been smeared with *bhūnāga* oil, and roast it in a *puṭa* fire until only the mercury remains; one should cook it with gentle *puṭas* until that point is reached.
One should perform this process again and again, having smeared the crucible and placed it in a *puṭa*;
or else, one should seal and roast it in a crucible smeared with *biḍa* salt.
One should cook it in small crucibles until only the essence remains;
then one should extract an equal amount of the seed for internal liquefaction from that very substance.
Then, one should cause [the mercury] to digest within the *sāraṇā* apparatus as before;
thereafter, indeed, equal amounts of the essences (*sattva*) of space (*vyoman*) and the other elements [should be added].
One should cause them to be killed separately again and then caused to be digested;
thereafter, one should digest the processed seed of the colorant with that [elixir].
One should roast it four times as before, placed inside a smeared crucible;
then it should be mixed with the cooked seed, indeed in the same sequence as previously described.
Then, having bound the mouth by means of the sevenfold chain-union (saptaśṛṅkhalikāyoga), one should bind it;
by that very [process], copper becomes gold through the part of a crore.
One should grind the secret mercury (guhyasūta), which is equal in quality to *bhūnāga* and *satva*,
along with gold (*candrārka*) in a heated mortar (*taptakhalva*) for three days, rubbing it with the juices of divine medicinal herbs.
Having sealed all of that within a vajra-musha crucible and dried the joint,
one should heat it for three hundred days and nights in a fire of dried cow-dung or in a fire of chaff.
One should cook it with gentle heat, then remove it and grind it for the duration of a day in a heated mortar using the juices of divine medicinal herbs alone.
Then, having sealed it, one should heat it intensely; that becomes the *khoṭa* (solidified mass) of the mercury.
Having added an equal amount of secret mercury (*guhyasūta*) to it again, [one should heat it] for three days.
One should massage it and likewise foment it; one should apply a seal as before.
Then, one should indeed dissolve it with an equal amount of sour gruel (kāñjika), and then certainly pierce it with a hundredth part [of mercury]; thus, "moon-and-sun" (candrārka) becomes gold.
Moon and sun, copper and lead [combine to become] gold;
likewise, one *pala* of pure red *vaikrānta* [is transformed].
One should cook it in the interior of a tiger-cub's belly within a swinging vessel (dolā) using horse urine.

Having extracted it for half a watch (yāma), one should then saturate it seven times with the juice of *vyāghrī* tubers under the heat of the sun; thereafter, [one should place] that equal amount in gold.
One *pala* of pure mercury, together with three [other ingredients],
should be ground together for four *yāmas* with the juice of *vyāghrī* tubers and horse urine.
One should cook that ball in a *haṇḍikā* vessel for one *yāma* over a mild fire;
having removed it, one should grind it for one *yāma* with the previous juices along with urine.
One hundred palas of gold leaf should be smeared with this very [substance];
having sealed it, one should cook it in small crucibles twenty times, repeatedly.
One should rub this gold with the juices of *vyāghrī* and *kanda*, as well as with horse urine; thus consecrated, it [acts] like a *sattva* within the mouth of mercury.
One should circulate and digest it in this manner gradually until it is a hundredfold;
that mercury [should be processed] with horse urine and the juice of the *vyāghrī* root.

One should grind it with the seeds of divine medicinal herbs in a heated mortar for three days; then, having extracted it at the end of those three days, one should roast it sealed within a *vajramūṣā* crucible.

Day and night one should perform the rubbing and the *puṭapāka* (sealed baking) three times over a fire of dried cow-dung and for three nights over a fire of husks; thus one should repeat the process again and again.
By exerting effort in these seven ways, that mercury will certainly die;
by this very method, ending with the process of *krāmaṇa*, one should perform the piercing (*vedhana*) even in ten-thousandth part.
Whether it be mercury, copper, lead, or gold,
once it has been processed by means of the previously mentioned elixir (*sūta*), it becomes [the desired metal] even without the application of *māraṇa*.
One should kill the ripened seeds and then digest that [substance] three times in succession;
having performed the binding as before, one should indeed proceed with the transmutation (*krāmaṇa*).
When that [substance] has been liquefied within the moon and sun, one should join it in the proportion of one part in a hundred thousand;
it becomes gold of exquisite beauty, as proclaimed by Śambhu.
One should purify the yellow-colored *vaikrānta* known as *koṭivedhin* mercury for a number of days;
then, having placed it inside the root-tuber (*kaṇḍa*) of *vyāghrī*, one should cook it with the juices of *vyāghrī* and horse urine.
Having extracted [the substance] day and night using a swinging apparatus (*dolāyantra*), one should then powder it;
one *pala* of this powder should be thrown into ten times its weight of mercury.
Having rubbed [the mercury] for a full day with the juice of *vyāghrī* tubers and horse urine,
one should then smear a gold leaf weighing one hundred *palas* with this.
Having placed it in a diamond crucible and sealed it, one should subject it to sudation for three days with a fire of chaff, or day and night over a fire of dried cow-dung; then one should remove it.
One should grind it with the root of *vyāghrī* and horse urine, and likewise cook it in a *puṭa*;
having thus been cooked in a hundred *puṭas*, one should cause it to be consecrated (*abhiṣikta*).
And one should cause this to be digested in the presence of the sovereign lord of mercury (rasarājendra),
gradually increasing it by a hundredfold according to the procedure for the celestial essence (vyomasattva).
Alternatively, it should be digested in a crucible-melting apparatus according to the previous sequence;
therein lies the seed for the internal liquefaction of the lord of mercury (rasendra).
As before, having melted [the substance] and gradually digested it four times its weight in the crucible,
one should digest what is situated therein with the ripened seed through seven chains.
Having bound the mouth and bound the mercury, the mercury becomes capable of piercing through a crore [of obstacles].
One should place black-colored *vaikrānta*, which is equal in weight to silver, inside the bulb of a *vyāghrī* plant;
it should be steamed with horse urine for one day, and then one part of it should be ground into powder.
One part of pure mercury should be ground for a day in a heated mortar with the juice of *vyāghrī* roots and horse urine.
Having added silver (tāra) in a sixteenth part, one should again grind it in the same manner;
then, having added mercury equal to the total amount, one should grind it right there.
Having extracted the produced globule, one should smear it with a binding agent (nigala);
having placed it inside a diamond crucible and sealed it, one should heat it for three days with a fire of chaff.
Or one should cause it to sweat day and night in a windless place by means of a fire of cow-dung;
then, having extracted it, one should grind it with seeds and the juices of divine medicinal herbs.
For three days, it should be processed in a heated mortar combined with horse urine;
having applied a coating as before and sealed it, it should likewise be cooked by means of a *puṭa* (herbivore) fire.
By this sequential method, one should cook it seven times with *puṭas*.
By means of this, one should transmute molten copper by a hundredth part.
Having applied the *krāmaṇa* as before, it becomes beautiful silver.
Vaikrānta that is white in color and well-purified should be treated in the same sequence as before; by means of its union with red vaikrānta, one should "kill" the silver with that very substance.
One should slowly digest that copper in mercury by means of a hundredfold [repetition];
likewise, having killed it with a *puṭa* [furnace], it becomes capable of ten thousandfold transmutation (*ayutavedhaka*).
In that same way, one should cause the mercury to digest [the impurities] gradually by means of the *tāra* seed-syllable;
having bound its mouth and bound the mercury, the mercury shall become capable of piercing a hundred thousand [leaves].
It should be added to molten copper; that [copper] becomes auspicious silver.
One should grind copper-colored *vaikrānta* combined with pure *hiṅgula* in a heated mortar (*taptakhalva*) with the group of acidic substances (*amlavarga*) for three days.
With this, the gold leaves should be smeared and cooked in a closed crucible (*puṭapāka*);
having removed them, they should again be ground together with the group of sour substances (*amlavarga*).
One should cook that ash in seven layers in this manner until it measures one *pala*;
then, for three days, one should process one *pala* of purified mercury with the juices of divine medicinal herbs.
One should cause it to be kneaded into a ball and smear it with pure [substance];
having sealed it, it should be heated for three days by a fire of dried cow-dung and chaff.
Then, having rubbed it with the juices of divine herbs and having enclosed it in a crucible, one should coat it and heat it intensely; it will certainly attain a firm bond.
By this hundredth part, silver becomes gold.
One should grind the essence of red vaikrānta together with gold; having smeared it inside a crucible for double-melting (*dvaṃdvamelāpa*) and sealed it, one should heat it in a closed furnace.
Or that same pill, once consecrated, should be made to digest [the mercury] in the presence of the mercury;
one should cause the mercury to digest it in the manner of the essence of mica (*abhrasattva*), part for part.
One should cause that mercury to digest with the ripened seed three times as before;
likewise, the process of digestion (jāraṇā) should be performed, and then, having bound the mouth [of the vessel], one should seal it.
By that very same thousandth part, it becomes gold with the color of a star.
Equal parts of the essence of red vaikrānta and pure mercury [are combined with] silver, copper, and lead [to become] gold.
It should be ground for three days in a heated mortar with the juices of divine medicinal herbs.
Then, having sealed it in a crucible smeared with lead,
one should perform a *puṭa* roast for three days in a fire of dried cow-dung by day and in a fire of chaff by night.

Having extracted it again and applied a coating, one should place that ball along with its binding within the crucible; having added salt to the interior of the crucible and sealed the joint, one should let it dry thoroughly.
Furthermore, having added salt and sealed the joint, one should dry it thoroughly;
one should smear that crucible on all sides with conch-shell powder to the thickness of one finger.
It should be heated forcefully in a *koṣṭhīyantra* furnace, and then that mercury becomes bound.
One should pierce it with a thousandth part [of the agent] in silver, copper, or bell-metal;
it becomes divine gold, the most excellent ornament for the gods.
The varieties of *capalā*: red, yellow, white, and black—*capalā* is thus fourfold.
By means of the method for *vaikrānta*, these should be purified as binders of mercury.
For the *capalā* piercing, one should grind lāṅgalī, karavīra, agni, girikarṇī,
and ṭaṅkaṇa in equal parts with women’s breast milk.
One should smear the interior of a diamond crucible all over with that [substance] to the thickness of one finger-breadth;
then, one part of mercury (capalā), whether red or yellow, should be finely powdered.
Four parts of gold and two parts of pure mercury should be rubbed with the juices of divine medicinal herbs for all three days.
Having first sealed the crucible and then dried it in the shade, one should heat it intensely;
all that becomes a *khoṭa*, and indeed by means of that, [the result] is increased a hundredfold.
One should purify the *nāga* [mercury] thoroughly; it should then become like a *guñjā* berry in color.
With this *nāga*, one should transmute copper (*śulba*) by means of exactly one hundredth part.
Copper should have the luster of dawn; with that copper, one should pierce pure silver by means of a hundredth part [of it], and that silver shall become gold.
In the same manner, the process of digestion (jāraṇā) should be performed; having bound the mouth, one should then apply the seal.
By that very [substance] in a thousandth part, silver becomes gold.
One should purify the *nāga* [mercury] thoroughly; it should become like a *guñjā* berry in color.
Then, one should purify copper (*śulba*) with this *nāga* by means of exactly one hundredth part.
Lead = copper = silver = gold;
one-sixth part of calamine powder and seven parts of silver [should be used].
Eight parts of gold and nine parts of mercury.
One should grind everything with the juices of divine medicinal herbs for three days;
then, one should thoroughly coat that ball on all sides with a thick layer of sealing wax.
One should grind equal parts of lāṅgalī, karavīra, agni, and vulture dung together with the acidic juice of mātuluṅga; with this, one should coat the crucible.
Having sealed that [crucible] as before, one should heat the *gola* (ball); it shall become *khoṭa*.
With exactly one hundredth part of that, one should administer the *vedha* (transmutation) to lead (*nāga*).
With that mercury, one should pierce copper with a hundredth part;
by piercing silver with copper as before, it becomes gold.
One should place one *pala* of silver, [equal to] gold, and pure mercury into a glass vessel;
then, as before, one should add three *pala* of sublimed sulphur (*gandha*) to it.
Having added the juice of *jaṃbīra* fruits equal in weight to the sulphur,
one should cook it slowly inside a sand-vessel (*vālukābhāṇḍa*) until the sulphur is fully digested.
Having added one *pala* of previously processed *dhānyābhra* to that,
one should cook it after adding *jaṃbīra* juice and *biḍa* salt.
While it is being digested, one should continue adding acid until it is exhausted;
then, one *pala* of powdered gold, having been consecrated, should be cast into that [mixture].
Then one should cast feces into that, and add it together with jambīra juice;
one should cook it over a gentle fire until it becomes well-digested.

While it is still digesting, one should add fermented gruel (biḍa) and sour substances; once it has digested, one should remove it and grind it for three days in a heated mortar (taptakhalva), combined with the juices of divine herbs.
One should grind the root of *mūleśvaraliṅgin* and the root of *śigru*;
having smeared the *vajramūṣā* crucible with this very [paste], one should place the previously mentioned liquid inside it.
Having sealed it and subjected it to sweating over a fire of dried cow-dung for a day and night, one should extract it;
then, having ground it as before and sealed it again, one should heat it in a crucible, whereby the mercury becomes bound.
When mercury is given with sixty-fourth part of this [substance],
one should indeed transmute and dissolve it into divine gold, as approved by the Siddhas.
One hundred *niṣkas* of pure mercury and ten *niṣkas* of sulfur,
having been ground for a moment with the juices of a virgin (*kanyā*), should be cooked in a *pātana* apparatus.
Having taken ten niṣkas of sulphur and placed it upon the upper part [of the apparatus],
one should grind it again in the same manner and cook it in the vessel, then remove it.
One should repeat this process twenty-one times;
having placed that mercury into the Gaurīyantra, one should then add sulfur.

Having processed it according to the previous method and reduced it to powder in a twentieth part, one should seal it in a small crucible and cook it; once it is digested, one should add the fragrance.
In this manner, one should digest it again and again according to one's capacity in due order;
when the odor has been digested a hundredfold, the mercury becomes a "hundred-penetration" (śatavedhī) substance.
When it has been digested for a thousandfold [duration], one should pierce with a thousandth part;
when digested for a hundred-thousandfold, it becomes a piercer of a hundred-thousand; the mercury shall become a piercer of ten-million.
When the odor has been digested, it becomes ten million times stronger; in this same way, it should proceed further and further.
One should refine it with the ripened seed and digest it gradually as before.
Having bound the mouth and bound the rasa, one should cause the piercing to be applied in the *tāra*;
divine gold is produced, fit for adorning the ornaments of the gods.

Having observed and experienced everything through the most supremely secret *bhūsattva* minerals, along with *sūta*, *vaikrāntaka*, *capala*, *rasa*, and *gandhaka*, this method of properly producing gold by means of easily accomplished formulations has been declared for the wise.
One should prepare a mass of vajra, mica, sattva, and excellent gold, which, once melted into a liquid state, is indeed fit for binding.
This will be explained through various easily understood and refined *yogarājas*, which bring about supreme accomplishment for human beings.
{Abhrakadruti (1)} One should smear pure black mica-plates with *pīlu* oil;
having smeared them again and again, they should be dried in the heat for seven days.
Likewise, for three days, they should be dried with sour substances;
then one should collect [the juices] from *snuhī*, *arka*, *arjuna*, *vajrī*, and *kaṭutumbī*.
This alkali and the three types of alkali— these eight substances ground together in equal parts—
along with *vajrakanda*, *kṣīrakanda*, *bṛhatī*, and *kaṇṭakārikā*.
These should be processed with the juices of forest eggplants for three days;
with this alkaline paste, one should smear the previous leaves.
Having placed the material to be smeared in a bell-metal vessel, one should repeatedly expose it to the sun;
by doing this for three days, a pure liquefaction occurs.
{Abhrakadruti (2)} One should soak the leaves in the group of sour substances for three days in the heat;
likewise, one should wash other abhra leaves with milk-yielding tubers.

Having made a paste with alkaline substances until it reaches the consistency of a kalka, one should repeatedly smear the previous leaf with that paste, place it in the heat, and dry it in a bronze vessel.
Within seven days, there is no doubt that a liquefaction in the form of mercury will occur.
(3) For the liquefaction of mica (*abhrakadruti*): the powder of *kākāṇḍā* fruit, combined with the five "friends" (*mitrapañcaka*),
should be ground for a period of days with sour liquids together with an equal amount of *dhānyābhra*.
When placed in a blind crucible and heated, it becomes a pure liquefaction.
{Abhrakadruti (4)}:

One should grind grain-processed mica (*dhānyābhraka*) with beef, mica-dust (*abhrapāda*), and rock salt (*saindhava*) with the milks of *snuhi* and *arka* and their decoctions for three days by the sages.
Having placed that ball inside the root of a plantain tree and smeared the exterior with clay, one should cook it in a fire of dried cow dung for three days; then a pure liquefaction occurs.
Having ground *dhānyābhraka* for one day with the resin of *agastya* leaves, one should place that ball inside a tuber of *sūraṇa* and seal it shut. (5) *Abhrakadruti* (The liquefaction of mica).
One should bury that bulb in the ground of a cow-pen and extract it after one month;
from the interior of the bulb, a pure liquid should be taken, which is equal to mercury.
{Abhrakadruti (6)}:
Grind grain-processed mica for one day with the juices of *ajamārī* for another day;
place it in an earthen vessel and leave it in the heat for three days—it will then be thoroughly liquefied.
{Abhrakadruti (7)}:

For seven days, one should grind *dhānyābhra*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and realgar (*śilā*) with the urine of a sage (*munitoya*); then, having processed them in the sun, one should add *dārvī* and *suvarcala*.
One should grind long pepper with a one-fourth portion of mica for one day using the juice of *mūrvā* leaves,
and it should be processed for a full day with the liquid extracted from *vajravallī*.
Having enclosed it within a pair of earthenware bowls and heated them, it will become liquefied.
Regarding the liquefaction of mica (abhrakadruti): one should employ grain-mica (*dhānyābhraka*) in an amount equal to the seed of the *kākinī*;
having heated it for seven days in the sun with the milk of *snuhī*, liquefaction will occur.
Having ground *dhānyābhra* together with *suvarcala* and the juices of *vajravallī*,
one should process it for three days with an equal amount [of the juices]; thereafter, place it within a sealed crucible (*śarāvasampuṭa*).
When obstructed and blown upon, it surely melts into the form of mercury;
thus, it undoubtedly arises in the form of mercury—of this there is no doubt.
{Abhrakadruti (10)}:
One should cook the mica leaves in milks produced from the *udumbara* tree, or one may cook them in a pot; they become like butter.
Then, having made that into a pill and having sealed the perforated crucible, one should heat it intensely for three watches; the liquefied substance will fall into the lower vessel.
{Abhrakadruti (11)}:
Grind *dhānyābhraka* for one day with the milky juices of *kākoduṃbarī*;
then add the seeds of the forest mouse (*vanamūṣaka*), excluding the bark, in equal measure to the *abhraka*.
Having crushed it for half a watch, one should liquefy it using Pātāla yantras; a *puṭa* should be applied for a day and night, and a pure liquefaction (*druti*) will occur.
One should grind *dhānyābhraka* firmly together with the fruits produced from *kapittha* for one day, and then place it inside a glass flask (*kācakūpī*). (Abhrakadruti 12)
Having blocked the mouth with "hell-hairs" (narakeśa) and smeared the crucible with clay, one should perform puṭapāka using the pātālayantra; at the end of the day, it will attain liquefaction.
{Abhrakadruti (13)}:
A powder of *dhānyābhraka* and *guñjā* fruit in equal parts,
processed for seven days with the milky sap of *snuhī*, becomes [liquefied] through heating.
{Abhrakadruti (14)}:
One should grind *dhānyābhraka* with the juices extracted from red and blue lotuses for three days;
having sealed it, one should heat it, and then heat it while placed inside a *vajramūṣā* crucible.

Pulverized *dhānyābhraka* equal in weight to the powder of *veṅgīphala* should be infused for three days with the milky sap of *snuhī* in the heat; when heated and placed in a crucible (*saṃpuṭa*), it will liquefy.
Alternatively, one should saturate the powder of *kapitinduka* fruit with goat’s urine; once that is dried, one should cast it into the liquefied essence (*satva*). (Abhrakadruti 15)
Through practice for two or three times, the melting becomes stainless.
(2) For the liquefaction of the essence of mica (*abhrakasattvadruti*): one should sprinkle the essence of mica with oils produced from human hair;
having smeared that ball with cow-dung, one should place it inside a *vajramūṣā* crucible.
When blown with force, it indeed melts and remains like the king of mercury (rasarāja).
One should impregnate the essence-extract of mica with the powder of *kṣīrakanda* using human urine;
it should be dried and ground again and again with effort ten times over.
Therefore, one should repeatedly add the *āvāpa* into the molten metal and blow the furnace;
as long as it remains in a liquid state, it should be added again and again.
By this means, the metal will undoubtedly melt even when blown with force.
(4) The essence-extract of mica (*abhrakasattvadruti*):
one should take the powder of the five parts of *devadālī*, saturate it with its own juices,
dry it, grind it, and then saturate it again with effort one hundred times.
One should heat that powder with a tenth part [of its weight] while the essence is in a molten state;
it will be bound again, and the process of pouring (vāpa) should be repeated again and again.
The essence of mica should be processed with the juices of *kṣīrakanda* a hundred times; by sowing that [essence],
the essence as well as all metals will liquefy.
(6) Regarding the liquefaction of the essence of mica (*abhrakasattvadruti*): the essence of mica should be processed with all types of fermented grain-liquor (*dhānyāmla*).
When combined with the alkali of *nicula* wood and heated in a furnace, it remains [in a liquid state] like mercury.
Powdered *indragopaka* seeds, processed for twenty-one days with the juices of *devadālī* fruit, should be cast into molten gold.
As long as it remains even slightly level, it stays like a thread.
One should saturate *devadālī* a hundred times with human urine and the liquefied forms of gold and silver;
by merely sowing its powder [into them], there shall be liquefaction and the state of gold and silver.
The liquefaction of sharp iron [is achieved as follows]: ash derived from *suradālī* (gallnut), processed twenty-one times with human urine, should be sown into that alkaline solution;
thus, the liquefaction of sharp iron occurs.
One should sow sharp iron flux, *meṣaśṛṅgī*, tortoise bone, and *śilājatu* [into the crucible];
it will truly become a refined flux. One should apply this at the beginning of the melting process.
Having powdered sulfur and magnetite in equal parts,
it should be added as a flux to molten iron; thus the eight types of metal will flow.
One should process sulphur for seven days with the juices of *devadālī*, which causes the melting of all metals;
by merely adding that [sulphur], the metal remains like liquid mercury.
{Gold-melting (3)}:
One should remove the entrails of an extremely large frog,
fill its belly with *ṭaṅkaṇa* salt, and preserve it within a vessel.
Therefore, one should cause the oil to be extracted from [the plant] eight days later using a *pātālayantra* (underground apparatus).
When that oil is poured into molten gold, it will attain the state of fusion.
Having ground together liquid gold, cochineal insects, horse saliva, the fat of a hare and a frog, and bones, one should cast it into molten gold.
It arises in the form of rasa and remains for a long time.
{Suvarṇadruti (5)}:
One should powder indragopa, crab bone, and the seed of *devadālī*,
and then macerate it for one day with the juices extracted from *devadālī*.
When the gold has been liquefied by this [process], the seed (vapa) should be added again and again;
that which remains in the form of mercury will endure for a long time, as declared by Śiva.
(3) Melted sharp iron and its powder should be stirred for seven days with the juice of ripe *dhātrī* fruits,
and then further processed in the heat with the juice of milk-tuberous roots (*kṣīrakanda*).
One should likewise meditate correctly for seven days upon the vessel of the flow;
thus it becomes liquefied when heated and remains for a long time like mercury.
Melted iron, jackal, sheep, tortoise, snake, and porcupine [gallstones], and *śilājatu*— having powdered all of these into the thoroughly heated iron powder, [one should apply it].
One should cause it to be sown so that the mercury certainly attains a state of fluidity.

{The Dissolution of All Metals (3):} One should impregnate iron powder with the juice of *panasa* fruit as desired for seven days in the heat, and then grind it with the group of acidic substances (*amlavarga*).
By means of smelting alone, it melts and becomes fit for writing; of this there is no doubt.
(4) For the liquefaction of all metals:
an equal amount of sulfur and red salt should be added repeatedly;
this is the supreme method for melting all [metals] that have been heated and powdered.
{The liquefaction of all metals (5):} One should throw powdered borax into the interior of a yellow frog;
having sealed it in a vessel, one should bury it in the ground and extract it after twenty-one days. Rrā_3,17.58.
Then, having pulverized all of that together, one should cause it to be absorbed into molten iron;
in this way, all metals remain in the form of mercury, and not otherwise.
By sowing [the seed] of *guñjā*, honey, and *ṭaṅkaṇa* ground together with castor oil, the essence (*sattva*) derived from *mākṣika* ore will liquefy. (Rā 3.17.60)
The liquefaction of all gems and all metals [is achieved by] the three alkalis, asafoetida, chickpea sour, and amlavetasa.
Having finely ground *jvālāmukhī*, *ikṣuraka*, and the fruits of *sthalakumbhī* with the milky sap of *snuhī* and *arka*, one should insert that ball [into the ear].

Having tied superior gems such as diamonds in a cloth, one should cook them forcefully in grain-vinegar using a swinging apparatus (dolāyantra) for eight watches; thus they will quickly become liquefied.
Vajra, abhraka, blue flower, pearl, coral,
honey, pauṇḍra, vaiḍūrya, ruby, rājāvarta, and sapphire.
Vaikrānta and crystal indeed melt like liquids;
by means of these very medicinal herbs, the entire range of metals melts through the process of sowing.
Having placed [the substance] inside a *vajravallī* vessel and sealed it with a *vajra*,
it should be heated while contained in a water-pot; after seven days, it will attain a state of liquefaction.

One should place fine powder of *vajradruti* in the acid of cane (*vetasāmle*) for seven days; having extracted it after seven days and sealed it within a crucible (*puṭa*), it becomes a liquefied substance (*druti*).
Regarding the liquefaction of *vaikrānta* (1):
White-colored *vaikrānta* that has been saturated with *amlavetasa* for seven days will, without doubt, melt sufficiently under intense heat.
One should take the fresh juice of the *ketakī*, rock salt (*saindhava*), *svarṇapuṣpikā*,
and *indragopaka*; all of these should be placed together in a vessel.
One should subject vaikrānta to sweating within that [mixture] for seven days; by the power of this yoga, it attains a liquid state, as do the eight metals and the gems.
This king of formulations brings about the supreme liquefaction of gems.
{The support for stabilizing all liquefactions}: The liquefactions should be placed individually in the midst of safflower oil;
they will remain stable for a long time, and one should employ them when the occasion arises.

Thus, having prepared this accumulation of mercury with well-selected, most excellent essences according to the established doctrines, the preeminent among commentators should constantly mix it with the venerable *pārada* (mercury).
Having thereby rendered the wonderful elixir into fine gold, O best of the wise, it should be given to the poor; thus one should make the entire world free from suffering.

In this process, the flux (druti) is to be matured; one should digest the mercury (pāradendra) calculated according to the number of sages (seven). Then, once it has been processed (sārita), it possesses a penetration of ten million (koṭivedhī).
Furthermore, if the lord of mercury (rasendra) moves into the molten seed containing jewels that has been purified, then it becomes a "sound-penetrator" (śabdavedhī).
(1) The alchemical fusion (*melāpana*) of the fluxes (*druti*) with the mercury:
*pāṭhā*, *vaṃdhyā*, *tālamūlī*, *nīlī*, vermilion (*sindūra*), *citraka*, the root of the lotus (*padmakanda*), the milk-lily root (*kṣīrakanda*), and likewise *nāgabalā* in equal parts.
One should cause these to take up their clear essence, filtered through a cloth,
as well as the liquefaction of mercury (sūta) facing [the crucible], and likewise the liquid of medicinal herbs.
Having thrown everything into a metal vessel, one should dry it in the hot sun;
liquid should be added again and again until three watches have passed.
All fluxes merge into the mercury; of this there is no doubt.
Having ground together *vajrakanda*, *amṛtā*, and *guñjā* with their juices as before,
all the liquefied substances (*druti*) will undoubtedly merge into the king of essences (*rasarāja*).

{The Melting of All [Metals] (3):} One should add an equal amount of powdered black agallochum, white asafoetida, musk, and *brahmabījaka*, along with one-tenth part of mercury, to the molten metal. Rrā 3.18.7.
All the swift flows meet by this very means; of this there is no doubt.
(4) *Sarvadrutimelāpana*:
Black agallochum, white asafoetida, sugar, garlic, and navel [of the earth]—
by rubbing these together as before, the liquefactions merge within the mercury.
(5) *Sarvadrutimelāpana*:
Horse-urine, fresh ginger, neem leaves, and garlic in equal parts,
combined with borax, effect the fusion of all liquefied metals as previously described.
(6) For the melting and unification of all [metals]: grind together equal parts of honey, poison, *guñjā*, borax, and female menstrual blood, along with breast milk;
using this mixture, one should coat the crucible.
Having cast the flux (druti) mixed with mercury into that [crucible] and sealed it, one should subject it to heat for a period of days—
either three days in a fire of dried cow-dung or in a fire of husks;
then all the fluxes will unite, and once united, one should digest them.
One should smear the crucible with that very same flux which has been melted;
likewise, by means of the "living" (jīva) mixture, this is known as the *liptamūṣikā* crucible.
One should mix an equal amount of the liquefied essence of copper-gold (*hemakāntadruti*) with the mercury in its presence;
having smeared everything with a sixteenth part of the mercury, one should seal it in a closed crucible (*liptamūṣā*) and heat it in a *puṭa* fire.
Then, one should roast it in a fire of dried cow-dung until only the essence remains;
thereafter, one should mix it again in that same manner and digest all the vajras.
In this way, it produces an even liquefaction; one should digest [the mercury] through the sequential application of the process.
Then, one should cause that [liquefied mercury] to flow by means of the "cooked seed" (*pakvabīja*) through the three types of digestion (*jāraṇā*).
Having bound the mouth [of the crucible] and then sealed it, one should digest that [substance] in a mūṣāyantra;
then, one should apply it at a hundredth part [of the weight] to silver combined with copper.
When joined with the process of transmutation (*krāmaṇa*), the gold becomes divine.

One should digest twice the amount of copper, gold, mica, and copper-mercury (śulba-druti) in the mercury by means of the sequential application as before; thereafter, the coloring seed (rañjaka-bījaka).
Having processed [the mercury] equally in a crucible (mūṣāyantra), one should perform three transmutations (sāraṇā).
Having fixed the mouth [of the vessel] and bound the mercury, one should pierce [it] with a thousandth part [of the seed].
When combined with copper, the silver-essence becomes divine gold.
One should digest the fluxes of gold, copper, and refined gold in the presence of the mercury, using the previously mentioned method, each in double the amount in successive order.
Then one should cause the dyes' seeds to digest that [mercury] twice its weight;
thereafter, having caused it to be processed three times with the seeds, one should cause it to digest and process it again.
Then, having melted it and sealed the mouth, one should bind the mercury and perform the transmutation;
by that very [substance] in the proportion of one part in ten thousand, it becomes gold as before.
The mercury that pierces a hundred thousand [leaves] (through the process of *druti-jāraṇa*) should gradually digest copper,
gold, and the liquefactions of mica up to five times their weight according to the previous method; thereafter, one should digest the coloring seed (*rañjaka-bījaka*).
One should diligently digest the fivefold [mercury] in that crucible-apparatus (*mūṣāyantra*);
one should then refine it with the ripened seed (*pakvabīja*) and digest it again three times.
