Having again caused it to flow and again caused it to digest, when this has been done three times, having bound the mouth and bound the mercury, the mercury becomes capable of piercing a *lakṣa*.
{The mercury that pierces ten lakhs}:
until the liquefactions of jewels and gold are digested sixfold within the mercury,
one should then digest the coloring seed (bīja) of that very [mercury] sixfold.
Having purified it three times and then subjected it to the process of digestion (jāraṇa) again, one should do this four times;
having sealed the opening and bound the mercury, one should cause it to penetrate with nāga-oil.
By means of a ten-millionth part [of the additive], it becomes divine gold.
For each [of the substances] from mercury (vedhin) up to koṭi— each being an equal portion of mercury— one should melt two types of fluxes from mica and gold;
having mixed them with the previous formulation, one should indeed digest that in due order.

The mercury becomes a hundredfold-penetrating (śatavedhī) [mercury] when doubled; it becomes thousandfold-penetrating (sahasravedhaka) when tripled; it would be ten-thousandfold-penetrating (ayutavedhī) when quadrupled, and hundred-thousandfold-penetrating (lakṣavedhī) when fivefold.
When the five qualities have been properly digested, the mercury pierces ten lakhs;
likewise, when the quality of the *rasa* has been digested, the mercury becomes a "crore-piercer" (*koṭivedhī*).
Then, one should process seven times as much dyeing seed (rañjakabīja) for that [substance];
thereafter, one should extract it three times with the ripened seed (*pakvabīja*) according to the previous sequence.
The processes of *jāraṇā* (digestion) and *sāraṇā* (assimilation) should be performed, followed again by *sāraṇā* and *jāraṇā*;
by this sequential application, according to the order of the sevenfold chain (*saptaśṛṅkhalikā*).
Having bound the mouth and bound the *rasa*, he shall become a piercer of ten million;
one should apply it to silver (*tāra*) combined with copper until the process of transmutation (*krāmaṇa*) is complete.
Mercury, bound by means of white clouds, star-noise, and quicksilver, should be digested in the presence of the mercury;
it should be processed equally as before, and one should purify it with the seed of silver.
Having purified that [channel] three times as before, one should then bind the mouth and perform the binding.

Tin, silver, copper, brass, tin, and lead— these, doubled in quantity, should be digested in the presence of mercury; or alternatively, they should be digested three times over using a matured seed (pakvabīja).
One should perform the processes of *sārita* and *jārita*, and fashion three chains as before;
having bound the mouth and bound the mercury, one should effect penetration by means of a ten-thousandth part (*ayutāṃśa*).
When mercury is processed with vaṅga, it becomes as white as a kunda flower or the moon.

The fluxes produced from tin, copper, and sharp-sounding [iron] should be applied to the mercury in the crucible; one should refine it with the seed of copper until the mercury has increased fourfold.
Having bound four chains up to the mouth, one should then bind them;
by this application of a hundred thousand parts, the pillar of mercury becomes firm.
Mercury (koṭivedhī), silver,
and tin are to be melted together seven times in the mercury;
that [mixture] is to be processed with the seed of silver through a sequence of seven linkages (saptaśṛṅkhalikā).
Having bound the mouth and bound the mercury, the mercury becomes capable of piercing through a koti.

One should cause the previously prepared *dhānyābhraka* to be consumed by mercury (*rasendra*) that has seven chains (*saptaśṛṅkhalā*) and faces [the fire]; likewise, one should cause it to digest [the *abhraka*] in equal proportions. Rrā 3.18.87.
When the [substance] has been doubled in the crucible, everything should be processed six times as before;
then, one-quarter part of the essence of *mākṣika* (pyrite) should be added from its interior.
In the same manner, one should melt and digest the *rasaka* and the *satva*;
it should be melted and digested as before, sequentially in the *mūṣāyantra*.
One should again digest the liquefied seed that causes the dissolution of the embryo;
this should continue until it becomes four times the quantity of the mica and gold.
Having caused it to liquefy equally, one should then cause it to digest by means of the dualization process;
furthermore, the liquefaction of the beloved gold occurs again through the sequential application as before.
One should digest each [of these] in equal measure, as well as gold and the flux of *tīkṣṇa* (steel);
then one should digest an equal amount of the combined pair, followed by the coloring seed (*rañjakabīja*).
When that has been processed according to the sequence as before, it becomes fourfold;
then one should perform three *sāraṇās* with that using a ripened seed (*pakvabīja*).
One should heat that very same [substance] in a mūṣāyantra as before;
thus, after being processed seven times, it should be refined three times over.
The process of *jāraṇā* (assimilation) should be performed as before; this is known as the "Sevenfold Chain.
Furthermore, wherever *sāraṇā* (extraction) is mentioned, it should be understood by the commentators (*vārttikas*) in that same manner.
By binding the mouth and binding the mercury, the mercury becomes capable of piercing through a crore [of atoms];
when joined with *krāmaṇa*, it turns the sun and moon into gold.

The piercing [of the channels] is revealed to occur through eighteen actions in due order; likewise, it is taught as being with face (*samukha*), without face (*nirmukha*), binding (*bandha*), and the binding of mercury (*rasabandha*).
Kept secret by Śambhu and indicated but not revealed by the Siddhas,
that [teaching] has been made manifest by me for the benefit of those who compose Vārttikas.
Vajra-seed, vajra-ash, purified gold, and mercury from the essence of space— these four in equal parts, together with an equal amount of powdered *nāga*. Rrā 3.18.99.
One should blow upon the sealed crucible smeared with the union of the two [substances];
once they have become one, having removed it from the crucible, one should blow upon it openly.
One should gradually add small amounts of purified essence derived from honey until only gold and vajra remain; then, one should extract it from there.

Into that crucible, which has been smeared with a mixture of two substances and sealed, one should place mercury, a sky-born being (mica), and iron powder as before, and then heat it in a closed furnace.
Having extracted the mixture, one should blow it openly in a crucible;
when that which remains is gold and diamond, one should extract it as soon as it has been produced.
In this manner, having repeatedly digested the "sky-beings" (space-elements) and iron,
the serpent [mercury] should again digest them sixfold through the sequential application of the previous method.
Having repeatedly cast the washed essence of honey [into the crucible], one should blow the bellows;
thus, the external [mass] becomes sixfold.
This is known as the vajra-seed, which is supremely beneficial for the process of digestion (jāraṇa).

Through the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of the vajra-seed, there arises the piercing by touch and the piercing by sound; when the mercury has been awakened by its latent impressions (*vāsanā*), one should again digest the doubled celestial essence (*vyomasattva*) sixfold, following the sequence as before.
In that [state], the seed of the vajra is indeed digested by means of the sequence of the space-being;
it is consumed within the tortoise-machine, and the fruit is exactly as when it has been fully digested.
When it is doubled, one becomes a piercer of ten thousand; when tripled, a piercer of a hundred thousand;
and when it has been processed fourfold, one pierces ten million.
In the fifth stage, it pierces the *koṭi*; in the sixth, ten *koṭis*;
in the seventh, from the portion of an *arbuda*; and in the eighth stage, it pierces the *śaṅkha*.
In the ninth stage it becomes a piercer of iron; in the tenth, a piercer of lotuses;
and when matured through thirteen qualities, the mercury becomes a piercer by touch.
When it has been digested for fourteen qualities, it becomes a piercer of stone;
when digested for fifteen qualities, [it can pierce] the earth along with its mountains, forests, and groves.

It would pierce the entire earth, and that mercury (rasa) becomes a "walker on the earth" (bhūcara); when its qualities have thus matured through the [proper] application of the arts, it becomes pervasive throughout the three worlds.
The sovereign lord of mercury, when held in the mouth as a *khecara*, bestows the power of movement through the sky;
once it has arisen according to its capacity, it should indeed be gradually expelled.
The first drawing forth (*sāraṇā*) should be performed with [the mantra] equal to the Vajra-seed;
the digestion (*jāraṇā*) should be done as before, and one should perform the subsequent drawing forth (*anusāraṇā*) with double [the number].
In that very same manner, one should cause it to digest further; a counter-application (pratisāraṇā) must be performed.
Then, having bound the opening with three times that same [substance], one should fasten it.
This same procedure applies even for piercing up to two thousand or a hundred thousand [units];
and in this manner, one should again perform the sāraṇā for piercing ten million units.
When the penetrating mercury has been processed from ten koṭis up to one arbuda,
the sāraṇā should be performed in three ways, each in three varieties.
In piercing a conch shell, it is fourfold; above that, it becomes fivefold;
in piercing a lotus, it is sixfold; but in piercing the root, it is sevenfold.
In the piercing of touch, it is eightfold; in the piercing of sound, tenfold;
thereafter, the qualities of the *kalās* are thirteenfold, [and] the qualities of the *kalās* [are further increased].
Gradually, sāraṇā should be performed according to one's capacity;
having bound the mouth and bound the mercury, one should thereafter apply the piercing (*vedha*).
Whether in the moon or the sun, or in a serpent, when combined with the process of transmutation (*krāmaṇa*),
that mercury which results from piercing [the metals] up to the number of petals of a lotus— thus [is it described].
When that [iron] is wrapped in beeswax and subjected to the *kuntavedha* process, it all becomes divine gold; this was spoken by Śambhu.
Regarding the procedure for the piercing by smoke (*dhūmavedha*):
having ground the mercury for the smoke-piercing, one should smear a cloth with it;
then, having placed it in *jyotiṣmatī* oil, one should prepare a wick.
When that [substance] has turned into leaf-form, one should apply it to a mass of copper while it is blazing;
by the mere scent of its smoke, everything becomes gold.
Regarding the procedure for penetration by touch (*sparśavedha*):
one should prepare a pill with that mercury which possesses the power of penetration by touch;
having cast it into the midst of the eight liquefied metals, one should extract [the metal] from within.
That would become divine gold, beyond measure; of this there is no doubt.
Regarding the method of piercing by sound:
one should prepare a pill with that mercury which pierces by sound;
one should hold it within the mouth and thereby pierce metals.
All that becomes gold when the sound is heard; of this there is no doubt.
Regarding the method of piercing stone:
by means of that very [method], one indeed pierces mountains;
when heated by fire, everything becomes gold.
The Procedure for Piercing the Earth:
That which pierces the earth is a measure of half of half a mustard seed;
with that very [measure], one should pierce everything—the mountains, forests, and groves.
That earth shall truly become made of gold; this is the truth spoken by Śiva.
Regarding the *Trailokyavyāpaka-vidhi*:
whoever holds in his hand that which pervades the three worlds shall become a divine sky-walker (*khecara*), possessing a great body and great strength.
Acting according to his own will, that great hero shall become equal to Śiva;
from his urine and feces, all metals and gold shall arise.
They are born from this, there is no doubt in this; even by the touch of its sweat, one becomes a great siddha with a body of mercury, worshipped in all worlds.
Invulnerable to gods and daityas as long as the moon, sun, and earth endure,
he enjoys divine pleasures and sports like Bhairava.
Take three parts of mercury that has been processed with a hundredfold penetration (*śatavedhī*), one part of purified mercury, and one part of dead diamond (*mṛtavajra*);
these should be ground for a full day in a heated mortar (*taptakhalva*) with the powder of *kākinī*.
With that same one-quarter portion, one should smear gold leaves with *kānta*,
*ṭaṅkaṇa*, and *tālaka* ground together with the juices of *vyomavallī*.
With this eighth part, one should smear the previously smeared [substance];
having sealed it, one should then subject it to sweating for a day and night in a fire of dried cow-dung.
Having ground equal parts of plantain root, *sauvīra* salt,
and *ṭaṅkaṇa* together with the juices of *kaṇṭakārī*, one should indeed smear the crucible (*mūṣā*) with this.
In the midst of that, whatever has been previously cooked should be sealed and heated with a steady fire;
all of that becomes *khoṭa*, *sauvīra*, glass, and *ṭaṅkaṇa*.
By repeatedly adding the *khoṭa*, it becomes like the sun;
this is known as the seed of mercury (*rasabīja*), beneficial for the processes of piercing (*vedha*) and assimilation (*jāraṇa*).
It performs a hundredfold piercing on moon and sun [metals], producing auspicious gold.

{The taste that pierces sound} Now I shall describe the consumption of mercury (rasendra) in equal proportions; one should cause the previously mentioned seed of mercury to enter into the mouth of the mercury. Rrā_3,18.140.
One should indeed digest that [mercury] gradually by means of the various types of mica-essence;
when the mercury swallows [the essence] multiplied five times fivefold, [it is successful].
Then, by means of that very seed, one should perform the three processes of *sāraṇā* and *ākrāmaṇā*;
thereafter, having bound the mouth, one should cause it to be digested (*jārita*) and then fix it.
For that mercury indeed becomes a "piercer by sound" (*śabdavedhī*), as spoken by Śaṅkara.
One should digest the hundred-fold-piercing mercury-seed (*rasabīja*) with an equal portion of the ripened seed of *samukha* mercury,
having indeed consecrated it according to the procedure for the essence of mica (*abhrasattva*).
One should cast dead-vajra (mṛtavajra) in the proportion of one-sixteenth part into that elixir;
likewise, orpiment, borax, and magnetite—the third—each in the proportion of one-eighth part.
Having added that [substance] to it at that time, one should grind everything for a day with the juices of the *vyomavallī* plant, and then dry it carefully in the shade.
One should blow upon the sealed crucible smeared with the mixture of the two [substances] while it is closed;
when blown day and night over a fire of dried cow-dung, that becomes a *khoṭa*.
One should purify it by repeatedly blowing [into the furnace] with glass, borax, and *sauvīra* salt;
this is known as the "seed of mercury" (*rasabīja*), which, as previously described, possesses a hundredfold piercing power (*śatavedhaka*).
This king of mercury is produced and brings about auspicious gold.
Alternatively, when mercury is in front of it, one should cause it to digest for a day as before;
when the mercury swallows [the substance] multiplied by five times five parts, [the process is complete].

Having processed it in three ways sequentially with another *rasabīja*, once it has been processed (*sārita*), one should perform digestion (*jāraṇā*); then, having bound the mouth [of the crucible], one should effect the binding.
It becomes a direct "piercer by sound" (*śabdavedhī*) and indeed turns copper into gold.
The seed of mercury is the powder of the ripened seed, consecrated as before;
one should cause it to be consumed by the "facing" mercury in a proportion of one-sixteenth.
By massaging with two fingers alone, that seed instantly moves in the heat;
one should digest it for him through sudations, like the essence of mica.
By this sequential method, one should extract the seed-syllable evenly;
likewise, its ripened seed-syllable indeed consists of twelve parts.
One should cause it to circulate while rubbing it;
then, one should digest it by means of the method for the essence of mica (*abhrasattva*), and continue the digestion until it is equal [in quantity].
Then, one should cause the ripened seed to be given in an eighth part of that;
one should rub it in a heated mortar, for it indeed flows [as a liquid] at that very moment.
Having placed that mercury inside a *sūraṇa* tuber, having sealed it within its core,
and having smeared the tuber, one should cook it in a closed crucible (*puṭa*) so that the tuber is not burnt.
In that very state, the alchemist swallows it; once it is digested, he should cause another morsel to be given.
By this sequential method, the seed becomes equal and even again.
Having added a quarter-part of the ripened seed and the *ārya*, one should grind it;
then it should be subjected to digestion in a crucible apparatus (*mūṣāyantra*) by means of sweating again and again.
By this sequential method, one should digest the equal seed;
when the mercury has thus digested the seed fourfold and it is matured, the lord of mercury (rasendra) arises, possessing the luster of saffron and being exceedingly powerful.
The mercury that pierces with smoke, pierces with sound, and pierces with stone;
mica, *bhrāmaka*, *brāhmī*, and likewise the eight types of dead metals;
the great minerals (*mahārasa*), the secondary minerals (*uparasa*), and the seeds of the bitter gourd (*kaṭutumbī*).
Conch-navel, *meṣaśṛṅgī*, and *vajrakanda* in equal parts should all be cooked for the duration of a day with the blood of a peacock.
Then one should grind that *khoṭa* for two days with fire-blood;
thereafter, one should cause a dead-vajra (*mṛtavajra*) to be smeared with this.
One should have a crucible made in the shape of an *āmra* fruit, coated twice;
into its center, one should place the previously mentioned mercury, a quarter-part in measure, together with the smeared diamond.
Alternatively, a vajra-seed smeared with the aforementioned paste;
or else, a vajra alloyed with an equal amount of gold that has been prepared.
Having smeared it with the previous paste, one should place a quarter-part [of the substance] therein;
covered, one should gently blow upon it with air from below the crucible.
Having added a small amount of *viḍa* salt, once that has been digested, one should extract it; then,
having placed it back into the crucible smeared with that same substance and combined with *vajra*,
one should extract it once the *vajra* has been digested according to the previous sequence of procedure.
By this sequential yoga, one should [visualize] either the vajra or the seed-syllable of the vajra.
One should repeatedly digest either gold-coupled vajra or [other minerals] within the mercury (rasendra) until it has been increased elevenfold.
One should grind well-burnt conch-shell navel with the juice of *mātuliṅga* for a day;
with that, one should stir and mix very beautiful pearl powder.
Alternatively, one should melt pearl and digest it by heating as before,
bit by bit, very slowly, in a crucible smeared with *viḍa* salt.
That [gold] should be refined by the kacchapa method up to eleven times.
One should rub together peacock bile equal in measure to indigo extract;
having smeared [the substance] with that, one should then digest both sapphire and blue [gems].
By means of the sequential method as before, through blowing or heating,
[the substance] within a crucible smeared with *viḍa* increases elevenfold in succession.

Either melted sapphire or melted blue [gem] should be combined with the king of mercury (rasarāja) in sequence for the purpose of digestion (*jāraṇa*), just as the liquefaction of mica (*abhradruti*) occurs;
in this manner, one should digest the blue [gem], whether it has been melted or remains solid.
A ruby smeared with peacock bile and human blood should gradually digest the king of mercury eleven times over;
or else it should be digested after being liquefied, just as was previously described for the liquefaction of mica.
One should macerate equal parts of *rajanī* and *kaṅkuṣṭha* for one day with the juices of *brahmapuṣpa*;
then, smeared with that, one should digest the *puṣparāga*.
Whether solid or liquefied, by means of the sequence of the Rudra numbers,
the mighty king of essences (mercury) becomes thus satisfied by the jewels.
One should smear pure gold leaves with beeswax using exactly one-hundredth part of this [quantity], enclose them, and cook them in a *gajapuṭa* fire.
That gold becomes auspicious, appearing like a *iṃdragopa* insect;
with this very gold, one should perform three *sāraṇā* processes.
One should place the king of elixirs, satisfied with the [other] jewels, into a crucible apparatus (*mūṣāyantra*) and blow it gently and gradually until only the elixir remains.
By binding the mouth and binding the *rasa*, it becomes a penetrator by means of smoke;
through this sequential application, there occurs again the processes of *sāraṇā* and *jāraṇā*.
Indeed, three types [of seals] should be made; then, having bound the mouth, one should apply the seal.
This mercury, which pierces sound, becomes a bestower of movement through the sky.
Furthermore, one should perform three types of processing—sāraṇā and jāraṇā—in successive order;
and for that very mercury (rasendra), one should effect the sealing of its mouth.
By that very [means], one should pierce everything— the mountains, stones, and the ground—
and divine gold arises, possessing a luster equal to that of Jāmbūnada.

The Siddhas, both those who move on earth and those who move in the sky, obtained from the mouth of Śiva this great *mahājāraṇā*; having performed it with mercury, this entire subterranean realm was filled with gold.
Having reflected upon their entire essential practice, I have made it clear; it shall be effective only for one who is devoted to the Guru, the Tantras, and the Mantras.

That wealth which is the very essence of saṃsāra, which brings about all happiness, and which is truly abundant, is indeed to be accomplished by the best of practitioners through the method taught from the mouth of the Guru; for the sake of its accomplishment, the auspicious preparation of gems and other substances will be described here in their entirety, along with the discourse on perfumes—each of these being well-proven, accessible to the path of experience, and purifying for the wise.
{The preparation of ruby (padmarāga):} Having ground lac with four times its weight of water,
one should take a hundred palas of that liquid, strain it through cloth, place it in an earthen vessel, and cook it.
When it has been reduced to one-quarter by a mild fire,
one should add one *pala* at a time of the powder consisting of *sarja*, *ṭaṅkaṇa*, and *lodhra*.
Once it has been cooked slightly, one should keep it cool and well-protected in a glass flask;
then, one should cook the skin of a large fish with that [liquid] and water for a day and night.
Having removed it once it has become solidified, this is known as *matsyakajjala*.
One should place two *karṣas* of this into that glass jar.
Having nourished rain-stones with that very [substance] until they are well-ripened,
one should cook them for a moment in honey-wood oil and then extract them;
they become rubies (*padmarāga*) consisting of divine splendor.
{The process of making indranīla}:
Take one *pala* of indigo powder and its liquid from a previous fermentation;
having added two *palas* of that liquid to the powder, one should stir everything together.
Having cast *varṣotpala* flowers into it, one should cook them with the aforementioned oil;
they will undoubtedly become sapphire (*indranīla*) gems.
{The Preparation of the Emerald Gem}: One should prepare an equal powder of madder, yellow orpiment, and indigo;
all of this should be thoroughly stirred with liquids contained within a glass flask.
Having sprinkled *varṣotpala* flowers with that very same [liquid], one should cook them as before;
by that means, all emeralds indeed become of excellent quality.
{The preparation of gomedaka gems}: One should grind fish-ink with a decoction of *mañjiṣṭhā*;
having sprinkled *varṣotpalas* with that very [liquid], one should cook them as before.
Those very [stones] indeed function as gomedas; of this there is no doubt.

{The preparation of *puṣparāga*:} Having ground together mercury, saffron, and *tālaka* in equal parts with water, one should add an eighth part of collyrium derived from fish into that mixture. Rrā_3,19.13 //
One should cook all of that for one watch (yāma) and, having removed it from the fire, keep it well-guarded.
By sprinkling hailstones with that very [liquid], one should cook them as before;
they become like topazes (puṣparāga) as if they had been extracted from a mine.

{The preparation of blue rubies}: One should add an equal portion of indigo powder, fish-derived collyrium, and an equal portion of *bījakāṣṭha* wood, and let it stand in water for the duration of a day. Rā_3,19.15.
One should cook all of that for one watch (yāma) after removing it from the fire, and keep it well-protected.
Then, having sprinkled hailstones with that very [liquid], one should cook them as before;
they will undoubtedly become like sapphires and rubies.
The coloring substances mentioned for the production of pearls should be kept separately in glass vials,
preserving them with great care, and employed when the occasion arises.
One should make a perfectly circular cavity in the middle of one sun-crystal (sūryakānta),
and likewise prepare another sun-crystal to serve as a cover.
First, one should liquefy fine pearls according to the previously mentioned method;
that liquid should then be carefully poured into a cavity in a sun-crystal (sūryakānta).
When covered by another [gem] called sūryakānta while being heated,
it becomes fixed as pearl within a single watch (yāma), and it is exceedingly beautiful.
Having made a hole and tied it with a very bright piece of cloth,
one should then pound it together with very white rice-grains in that mortar.
Then, having extracted [the pulp] with a light hand for one watch (yāma), one should wash it;
however, one should grind the bark of the Ariṣṭa fruit together with water. By that very [liquid], once washed, the pearl becomes beautiful.
{The preparation of pearls (2):} One should cast very fine powdered pearls into the milk of a woman who has just given birth for a period of one moment. Rrā_3,19.23.
Then, one should have pills made from that very [substance] in a spherical shape;
they should be kept in a glass vessel and dried for the duration of a day in the shade.
One should weave the rosary using horse-hair, then dry it in the shade;
it should be left suspended until it has become firm.
Having removed the intestines from the belly of a large black fish with a single gill, one should first place the rosary right there within it.
One should sew the belly with thread itself, having enclosed it within a vessel;
after a month has passed, one should remove it and dry it again in the shade.
One should perform the rubbing and washing slowly, as before;
thus they indeed become perfectly bright pearls.
{The Making of Pearls (3)} Having taken a pearl-oyster shell or even a water-oyster shell, one should rub its back surface in order to remove its blackness. Rrā_3,19.29.
One should grind those bright [pearls] finely as before with milk from the *īḍā* cow and other substances;
by performing the process up to the final washing, they indeed become pearls.
{The making of pearls (4):} Having immediately extracted the eyes of a large fish, one should take them,
tie each one individually in cloth, and cook them for a day in the milk of the *īḍā* plant.
Afterwards, one should dry it in the shade; then, one should perform the threshing and washing as before, and they indeed become pearls.
{The preparation of coral (1):} One should prepare an equal powder of burnt conch-shell and cinnabar;
on the fifth day after a buffalo has given birth, one should take [this mixture]. Rrā_3,19.33.
That same milk should be used to grind that previous powder for one watch (yāma);
having formed it into round pills, one should thread them onto a copper string.
Having encircled the middle finger, the thumb, and the index finger with a petal from the interior of a *rambhā* plant, those pills should be grasped individually with them.
Having repeatedly rolled them and carefully fixed them with *raṃbhā* leaves,
they should be dried in the shade until auspicious, and then strung together with a copper thread.
One should slowly fume *madhuka* soaked in heated oil with smoke;
coral will arise with the luster of a ruby—of this there is no doubt.
{The Preparation of Coral (2):} One should then powder burnt conch shell together with vermilion in equal parts;
this should then be thoroughly rubbed with the milk of a ewe that has recently given birth.
One should fill it with [water] in a vessel made of grass, or one produced from bamboo and the like,
or in a well-baked earthenware food-vessel, provided it is devoid of gruel.
Having covered the crucibles and cooked them over a mild fire, one should remove them at the end of one *ghaṭikā*;
coral-like [substances] will arise within the interior of the tubes like rubies.
{The preparation of vermilion}: Take one part of impure mercury and four parts of borax;
having placed both in an iron vessel, cook them for a moment over a gentle fire.
Having added powdered realgar to that [mixture] in a tenth part of the quantity of mercury,
one should stir it with an iron ladle and then remove it from the heat once it has become thoroughly cooled.
Then, having cut it into pieces and placed them inside a glass flask,
and having sealed it properly with cloth and clay, one should thoroughly coat the glass flask.
One should cause it to dry in the shade until it measures one finger-breadth on all sides,
and then place it inside a sand-encased apparatus for two days over a mild fire.
Thereafter, one should cook it for five days with a gradually increasing fire;
after seven days, having extracted that, it shall become beautiful cinnabar (hiṅgula).
(1) The process of making sindūra:
One should throw one-quarter part of the ash of tamarind bark into molten lead;
it should be cooked in an iron vessel and rubbed with an iron ladle.
When heated by a fierce fire for a single day, it becomes auspicious vermilion.
{The preparation of vermilion (2)}: Having added one-fourth part of the ash of red *śākhinī*, *apāmārga*, and *kuṭaja* to molten lead, it should be rubbed for two days. Rrā_3,19.47.
As before, however, auspicious vermilion is produced in an iron vessel.
{The Preparation of Vermilion (3)}:
By means of ash, as before, using either *nāga* or aquatic *śāka*, divine vermilion is produced; it arises according to one's desire—of this there is no doubt.
{The preparation of vermilion (4):} One should melt two hundred *palas* of lead in an iron vessel;
one-fourth part of the ash of *vāsaka* with its roots should be added therein.
One should cook and stir it until it becomes yellow in color;
then, having made it thoroughly cool, one should stir it again with water.
Having made pills of one *pala* each, one should place them upon the ashes of *vāsā*;
once dried in the shade, they should be collected and placed in a new earthen vessel.
Having cast [the ingredients] in and sealed [the vessel], one should cook it on a hearth in a windless place with a fierce fire;
one should make a hole in the mouth of the vessel and insert an iron rod.
When it becomes red in color, one should cook it and examine it;
divine vermilion (sindūra) is produced—this is declared as the perfected yoga (siddhayoga).
{The preparation of saindhava}:
One should place one hundred palas of sea salt in a new vessel;
having added one niṣka each of mercury and sulphur, one should cook it with a fierce fire.
If one should cast an iron arrow into that [fire] at the end of two watches (six hours),
and it becomes red in color, then one should extinguish the fire.
The substance produced from the ocean (sindhūttha) should be taken as naturally cool in its inherent nature.
{The preparation of *suvarcala*:} Having ground one *pala* of *āranāla*, two *niṣkas* of *suvarcala*,
and one *māṣa* of sulphur (*gandhaka*), one should place the whole mixture in a vessel.
Having heated one *pala* of *saindhava* salt, one should pour [the liquid] over it;
having heated it again, it should be poured over again, until the liquid has completely dried up.
At that point, it becomes *suvarcala*; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
The preparation of *hiṅgu*: one part each of asafoetida and ginger, two *palas* of garlic,
four *palas* of nimba seeds, and eight *palas* of powdered black gram (*māṣa*).
One should grind equal parts of the pulp of the *bilva* fruit with goat’s milk;
all of this should be bound tightly inside a fresh cow-hide.
One should then place it in a heap of grain for three fortnights, after which it becomes *hiṅgu*.
{The preparation of asafoetida (2):} One should grind together the resin of the *babbūla* tree, sea salt,
and *kaṇā* (long pepper) without its bark, in equal parts, with the milk of a ewe.
One should add a quarter-part of pure asafoetida to this bolus;
all of that should be bound with leather as before for three days.
One should preserve it suspended in a windless place; hiṅgu is to be treated like pure hiṅgu.
{The preparation of asafoetida (3):} One *pala* each of jaggery and ginger, two *palas* of borax and guggulu,
and two *palas* of castor seed kernel, free from husks. Rrā_3,19.65.
One should grind two *pala* of skinless black gram together;
having added three *karṣa* of asafoetida into that mixture, one should stir it with water.
Having bound all that as before, one shall indeed attain the state of a *hiṅgu* within seven days.
{The Preparation of Hingu (4)}:
Two palas of pure asafoetida, twenty palas of ewe’s milk, and four palas each of the flour of wheat and black gram. Rājanighaṇṭu 3.19.68.
One should stir and pour all that [mixture] situated within a gourd-vessel;
it should be dried in the shade until the asafoetida becomes auspiciously prepared.
{The process of making it malleable (1):} One should saturate the powder of *dhattūra* seeds with the milk of a *vajrī* cow;
having dried it and ground it again, one should saturate it in this manner in the sun's heat twenty-one times.
One should cause that lead (drutanāga) to be treated with a tenth part of that [mercury];
one should melt it in the midst of *snuk* juice, and thus auspicious tin (*vaṅga*) is produced.
One should steep it in the midst of turmeric (*rajanī*), and thus auspicious tin is produced.
One should saturate the powder of *rajanī* seven times with the milk of a *vajrī* plant.
One should then apply that infusion in a quantity equal to one-tenth [of the mercury] to molten lead.
One should cause that powder of quicksilver to be cast with a tenth part [of the usual amount];
it should be melted in a decoction of the three myrobalans (triphalā), and then one should cast it again in the same manner.
Having added borax and navasāra, it should be sprinkled with human urine;
once melted, it should be poured back again into human urine, and it will turn into tin.
{The preparation of amlavetasa}:

Having boiled tamarind fruit stripped of its skin and seeds together with sour gruel (kāñjika), one should strain it through a cloth; this is amlavetasa, and [sour] citron juice is prepared in the same manner.
One should collect as available sour *cāṅgerī*, *mātuliṅga*, and *amlavetasa*;
having strained all of that through a cloth, one should boil it down until only a quarter remains.
One should add equal parts of *saurāṣṭrī*, *tuttha*, *kāsīsa*, the three alkalis (*trikṣāra*), the five salts (*paṭupañcaka*), and *mūlasāra*, and then pour in the entire powder.
When it is half-cooked, one should cook it again over a mild fire, adding a quarter-part [of the ingredients];
one should stir it with a ladle until it becomes thickened. This is called *amlavetasa*, which arises as something most excellent.
{Sāhīkaraṇam}:
Equal parts of triphalā, bhṛṅga, koraṇṭa, bhallātaka, karavīraka, and mango seeds, together with an equal amount of bola and kajjala; Rrā 3.19.79.
Having cast it into a copper vessel and rubbed it, ink is produced within five days;
it can then be written with on palm leaves or birch bark, being most excellent and durable.
{The preparation of ghee}: Four parts of the juice from coconut fruit should be taken;
having added one part of ghee into the middle of that, one should stir it in a vessel.
One should add the root of *raktaśākinī* to that [mixture] in a hundredth part;
one should cook it slightly over a gentle fire, and all of that becomes clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
{The Preparation of Ghee (2)} Having made the ghee and water equal in measure, and having added powdered *cunnaka* in the twentieth part [of the total],
one should place it all in an earthen vessel and rub it with the hand for a moment.
All that becomes clarified butter (ghṛta), yet it never withstands the fire.
{The preparation of ghee (3):} Five palas of ewe’s fat and an equal amount of sesame oil should be cooked over a gentle fire until the froth subsides.
Having added two niṣkas of sour gruel (kāñjika) to it, one should stir it with a cloth;
then, by adding a quarter-part of ghee to it, the entire mixture becomes ghee.
{The preparation of clarified butter (4):} One should first cook sesame oil until the froth subsides;
then one should add guggulu to it to slightly eliminate the odor. Rrā_3,19.86.
Having added powder equal to one-twentieth part of the water, one should stir it;
then, one should mix in the previously prepared oil, which has been cooled well, in an amount equal to the water.
One should rub it with the hand for just a moment in an earthen vessel;
when it has become solid, by adding half as much ghee, it will all turn into ghee.
Having cut down a nimba tree, one should leave one cubit of it intact at the bottom;
one should make a cavity in its top and place fresh guggulu right there.
One should fill [the vessel] with that wood, seal the opening, and then plaster the joint with clay and salt; once dry, one should cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire.
That which is to be grasped as naturally cool would have sandalwood as its root.
{The preparation of camphor}: One should cook three *pala* of rice using high-quality *rājānna* rice grains.
Having carefully cooled that rice with cow’s milk, [one should proceed].
Having added one *niṣka* of camphor, one should grind it with that [mixture] and smear the interior of a thick,
dried bamboo tube with it.
One should have it plastered with a thickness of one finger-breadth and allow it to dry in the shade;
then, having cut off a plantain flower, one should fill [the cavity] with its resin.
Then, having enclosed the bamboo tube within a piece of cloth and sealed its opening,
one should dry it in the sun for three days and subsequently bury it in the ground.
Having extracted it after three weeks and dried it, one should collect it;
the camphor situated within its interior should be preserved in a camphor vessel.
Thus, divine camphor is produced from the seed, of this there is no doubt.
{The preparation of javādīyāṅkastūrī}:
One should cut the seeds from half of a ripe jackfruit;
having placed them in a new vessel, along with one *niṣka* of ginger and one *pala* [of other ingredients].
Having powdered it, one should throw it into that [mixture], and all of it will turn into a liquid.
Having rubbed [the powder] with that, one should throw four *niṣkas* of sandalwood into it.
One should cook it over a mild fire until it has turned a reddish color;
then, having placed that [substance] in a glass vessel while it is cool, one should pour [the liquid] upon it.
Furthermore, having tied campaka, ketakī, mallī, and jātī flowers to a white cloth during the day, one should protect the face of that very [cloth].
Then, having removed the flowers, one should place one *māṣa* of musk and one *māṣa* of pure camphor into that very [incense].
One should also properly deposit even the *jāva* and other items with a twentieth part;
all that has been previously churned [is placed] into the vessel for the *jāva* and other substances.
One should wrap that vessel with jasmine flowers for three days; then it becomes perfectly endowed with the qualities of fragrance and color.
{The preparation of musk}:
One should combine five palas of either Madhūka oil or sesame oil with ten palas of the juice of Muṇḍī, mixing everything together in one vessel.
One should place there the *mallikā*, *mālatī*, *jātī*, *ketakī*, and *śatapattrikā*,
as well as other fragrant flowers.
One should preserve the flower, sealed for one day, and then discard it after squeezing it out;
having added twenty *niṣkas* of beeswax to it, one should cook it slowly.
When only the oil remains, one should add half a *niṣka* of camphor,
one *niṣka* of cat’s hair, goat’s hair, and so forth, and then remove it from the heat.
Having poured it into another vessel, one should cook it again once it has become cool;
after removing it for just a moment, one should pour it into a container made of jāvā or similar materials.
All that becomes dense, just like a seed; there is no doubt, as with the flowers of the *bakula* tree or a string of jewels, each one equal to the next.
Having placed that powder inside the hollowed-out core of a sugarcane stalk,
one should seal its opening with clay mixed with its marrow.
One should roast it with a grass fire until the fragrance is no longer burnt;
those flowers will melt, and having pierced the opening, one should extract the liquid.
One should powder hairless musk-skin equal in weight to musta;
one should then properly add musk equal to one-tenth part of that powder.
All that should be ground with the previously mentioned liquid and formed into a ball;
with effort, it should be fashioned slightly into the shape of musk and madana.
All that should be dried in the shade; one should preserve the *madanā* fruits separately.
Having cut the pills into pieces, one should mix them with *madanā* fruits.
Bound with musk-deer skin, it becomes perfectly pure musk.
{The preparation of saffron} (1):
One should prepare it with water using either coconut shell, or rubbed neem wood, or any other white wood. Rrā_3,19.115.
Then one should place that powder and turmeric in the middle of it;
or, by adding half as much turmeric to realgar, all of it shall become saffron.
{The preparation of saffron (2)}:
One should keep a decoction made from *pālāśa* flowers in a shallow pan in the heat;
then, one should add to it twenty parts of ground white rice.

Likewise, one should stir all the powder and half a portion of rice with a wooden stick until it becomes solid; one should keep it moving in the heat until that point. Then, having formed pills from that very mixture, they shall become like saffron in color.
{The preparation of saffron (3):} Having ground one-quarter part of *pālāśa* flowers together with perfectly pure rice,
pills should be made and dried until they resemble saffron in color. Rrā_3,19.119.
One should gradually prepare divine incense (*divyadhūpa*) with these ingredients: musk, camphor, saffron,
claw-wood (*nakha*), spikenard (*māṃsī*), resin of the *sarja* tree, musta-grass, black aloe-wood, and white aloe-wood.
One should mix these ten, including sandalwood, after they have been powdered;
one should grind everything together as one with guggulu equal in weight to the powder.
One should drop oil little by little onto a stone with an iron fist for one day with diligence, and with that [oil], one should prepare a wick.
One should cause its tip to blaze up, immediately extinguishing the flame;
this is the divine incense of the gods, beneficial for the accomplishment of mantras.
Divine incense (2):
one *pala* each of powdered *pāṣāṇabheda*,
*guggulu*, *māṃsī*, *mustā*, *nakha*, *bola*, *candana*, *aguru*, and *vālaka*.
Having powdered two niṣkas each of lac, jaggery, resin (sarjarasa), sugar, and camphor, as well as musk and saffron, [one should mix them].
One should drop each individual bean into it, crushing everything in the mortar;
one should then add a little sesame oil and strike it firmly with an iron rod.
A perfected one should grind [the ingredients] for one watch (three hours); this is the divine incense proclaimed by Śiva.
It should be offered as the "maker of gods beyond gods," prepared as a wick as previously described.
It generates all good fortune and leads away all mantras and sins.
One should repeatedly soak pure cloth with *vajrīkṣīra* mixed with *puṣpadruti* and dry it in the sun; in this manner, one should do so for seven days.
One *niṣka* of jasmine (*jātī*) flowers, one *niṣka* of powdered borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*), and three *niṣkas* of honey should be combined; all of this should be stirred together into a single mixture.
One should keep it in an earthen vessel or, if pleasant, in a glass container;
one should cover it immediately with a cloth moistened with water.
Those flowers should be liquefied; one should employ that liquid in the various yogas.
In this very manner, the liquefaction of each individual fragrant flower should be performed, and it should be applied in the discourse on perfumes.
{The Method for Increasing Grain (1)}:
On the lunar mansion of Ārdrā or Bharaṇī, one should carefully collect Kuśa grass grown at the root of a Mandāra tree,
and place it within a garland of Dhava flowers.
One should collect wood that has been blown toward by the wind and place it within a heap of grain; this is the supreme method for increasing the quantity of grain.
{The Method for Increasing Grain (2)}:
Having wrapped the left eye of a chameleon with gold and consecrated it with mantras, one should cast it into a heap of grain; this is the supreme means for increasing grain.
{The Method for Increasing Wealth and Grain} (3):
Having wrapped its right eye with gold, one should then cast it [into the fire].
This brings about an increase in whatever object or grain one desires.

{The Method for Increasing Substances and Other Wealth}: Whatever excellent object the root of *kṛṣṇacitraka* is cast upon, all of that becomes eternal and inexhaustible; even when spent, it is not diminished.
Wealth, grain, ghee, oil, gold, and the nine precious gems—
whatever kind of material object there may be, that remains certainly inexhaustible.
{The Method for Increasing Grain} (4):
One should cast the root of white *guñjā* into water;
then, having thrown that root into a heap of grain according to the ritual procedure of the mantra, [the grain will increase]. Rrā_3,19.138.
That grain increases constantly even as it is consumed by the thousands;
the practice for the root of the *guñjā* plant should be performed here exactly as it was taught in the section on mantras, for success occurs only in this way and not otherwise.
Having first traveled through all directions, one receives from the presence of the Guru, by the power of devotion and according to the method of yoga, that great essence of essences;
all of that is declared to be the increase of wealth, most abundant on the path, and in some cases, through the protection of kings, it may become the possession of learned men of great intelligence.

I shall now briefly explain all that I have seen—the quintessential and most excellent essence extracted from the multitude of various yogas along with their limbs and sub-limbs, which involves the gentle and forceful binding of mercury; this has come down through the lineage of perfected masters (*siddhas*), is easily accessible, and bestows sovereignty; let it be observed through direct experience by those groups of commentators.
{Mercury-binding (1)}: Take one part of pure mercury and an equal amount of *ṭaṅkaṇa* (borax);
then grind them together with decoctions of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) combined with human urine.
Having made pills weighing one *karṣa* by coating them with black gram (*māṣa*) powder mixed with water in a quantity eight times that of the mercury,
and having dried them in the shade, one should heat them strongly.
Having broken through the dross in the crucible-furnace and the curved tube, one should collect it; this mercury becomes perfectly spherical and firmly bound like a ball.
The binding of mercury (2):
[one should bind] mercury with the juices of wild jasmine (*āraṇyamallikā*) or with the juices of *kanyā*,
or with the juices of *hariṇakhurī* mixed with human urine.
One should grind it in a mortar for three days, repeatedly adding urine;
then, having coated that pill with black gram flour, it should be heated as before.
In that same way, mercury becomes bound; it should be purified with glass and borax.
{The Binding of Mercury (3):} One should grind mercury for one day with the juice of the roots of *markaṭī*; then,
one should place that ground mercury into a bolus made from the roots of *markaṭī*.
Having sealed that mass in a diamond crucible, one should blow it with a fierce fire;
this becomes bound as a *khoṭa*, capable of performing all functions.
{The Binding of Mercury (4):} Having ground the root of *arka* with the milky sap of *arka*, one should place it as a thick layer inside a crucible;
having cast the melted mercury into its midst, one should seal it and then cause it to solidify. Rrā_3,20.10 //
One should confine it within an earthen crucible and then within an iron crucible;
thereafter, one should cook it in a "gaja-puṭa" fire, whereby the mercury attains fixation (bandha).
{The Binding of Mercury (5):} One should grind mercury for three days with the juices of the *jalakumbhī* plant;
having fashioned a crucible from the leaves of the *jalakumbhī*, one should place that [mercury] therein.
Having sealed it in a vajra crucible and dried it in the shade, one should roast it gently;
one should cook it with twenty rounds of roasting, increasing the dose by one *utpala* at each stage.
Then the "elephant-bowl" (gajapuṭa) should be applied, so that the mercury becomes properly bound.
(6) For the binding of mercury: pure mercury should be rubbed with the juices of *ekavīrā* for three days. One should then coat a *vajramūṣā* crucible with a paste made from the tubers of *ekavīrā*.
Having confined the previous mercury within it, when it is heated, the mercury becomes bound.
{The Binding of Mercury (7):} One should rub mercury for three days with the juices extracted from the *ārakta* and *kṣīrakanda* plants mixed with breast milk,
and for another three days with the juices of the *vajrakanda*.
One should smear a *vajramūṣā* crucible with a paste of *kṣīrakanda*;
having sealed the mercury within it, when heated, the mercury becomes bound.
Having performed the binding with mercury, one should fashion a copper wheel that is broad, four finger-breadths [in diameter],
raised by one finger-breadth, very firm, circular, and even.
One should prepare a kajjali paste from sulphur, mercury, and copper sulfate using a mortar and pestle; that kajjali, equal in quantity to copper, should be placed inside a crucible.
Having placed that wheel into the mouth of a rat and sealed it, one should then dry it;
one should cook it in a *ghaṇḍikā* apparatus for two watches (*yāma*) over a mild fire.
Having extracted it from the wheel, one should cause the king of essences (rasarāja) to be taken up again and again;
one should then apply an equal amount of ṭaṅkaṇa and glass (kāca) above and below it.
When it has been placed in a blind crucible and heated in this manner three times, the mercury becomes bound; it is indeed undiminished—of this there is no doubt.
{The Binding of Mercury (9):} Pure mercury, an equal amount of sulphur, and an amount of orpiment equal to the sum of those two,
should be ground in a mortar with the juices of the *unmattaka* plant for four watches.
One should cause it to fall in a *pātana* apparatus for one day with a mild fire;
then, having collected all of that which is attached to the upper part and situated at the bottom, one should gather it together.
It should be thoroughly ground with the juices of *unmattaka* for four watches;
that ball should be cooked as before, and having removed it, one should grind it again.
It should be cooked again and ground again with effort, placed above and below, until all of it remains at the bottom of the vessel; that is the limit.
All of that should be crushed as before; then, having formed it into a ball, one should dry it.
One should thoroughly grind nalikā and kuṣṭha with acidic liquids.
Having ground yellow collyrium, one should smear a ball with it;
then, inside the interior of a vajra-crucible, one should indeed smear it with that paste.
One should heat the *golaka* there, blowing it with a curved tube;
by means of the intensely radiant fire, it shall truly become bound as a *khoṭa*.
(10) For the binding of mercury: one *pala* of quicksilver (*sūta*) and one *pala* of lead (*nāga*), with realgar (*manaḥśilā*) equal in weight to both;
by means of the sequential application as before, the mercury becomes bound in a solid pill (*khoṭabaddha*).
Having melted lead,
mercury, and silver in equal proportions, one *pala* of that powder,
one *pala* of pure mercury, and realgar (*manaḥśilā*) equal in weight to all [the other ingredients] [should be combined].
By means of the sequential application as before, the mercury shall become bound in pill-form.
One *pala* of mercury and one *pala* of silver should be ground with some kind of acid;
an equal amount of *śilā* (realgar) should be added to these two, and it should be cooked according to the previously mentioned procedure.
The binding of mercury is like that of silver; and the gold-powder [is bound] with sulphur as previously described.
One should finely powder together equal parts of the essence of black mica, *tīkṣṇa* iron, *kānta* iron, gold, copper, silver, and *mākṣika* ore for the binding (*bandhana*) of mercury.
Having placed it within a vajra crucible and sealed it, when it is blown with a blowpipe, it becomes *khoṭa*.

The essence of white mica, silver, steel, and pyrite—having powdered these in equal parts, one should prepare a *khoṭa*; then, an amount of pure mercury equal to the portion of the *khoṭa* [is added]. (Rasārṇava 3.20.35)
Equal parts of the two types of yellow orpiment should be finely ground as before;
when heated intensely in fire, it becomes a solid mass (khoṭa), which is that mercury.
For the binding (*bandhana*) of mercury:
one part mercury and one part sulfur should be ground together with the juice of *kanyā* for a day.
Then, having added double the amount of sulfur, it should be placed within a crucible consisting of an upper and lower chamber (*mūṣā*).

Having sealed the joint and dried it, then having strongly heated it in a crucible apparatus (koṣṭhīyantra), that mercury becomes a solid bolus (khoṭa); this is known as "bound by sulphur" (gandhabaddha).
Having prepared a decoction of the five parts of the *rājavṛkṣa* tree reduced to one-eighth,
one should cast that liquid into the mercury and cook it auspiciously for two watches (yāmas).
Bound by the syllable *co*, this very *khoṭa* indeed accomplishes all tasks.
Pure mercury should be rubbed for three days with the juices of *candravallī*;
then, having combined it with *ṭaṅkaṇa* (borax), the wise one should form it into pills.
The mercury, blown [into the fire] while contained within a crucible apparatus, becomes bound as a solid bolus (khoṭabaddha).
For the binding (*bandhana*) of mercury, one should add one *pala* of the juice of *bhallātaka* into sesame oil;
one should continue adding the juice of *ravikṣīra* (sun-milk) while cooking the oil until it is fully processed.
One should strike it with an iron rod, and the mercury will become fixed as a solid bolus (khoṭa).
{... Mercury-binding (20):} One should grind equal parts of mercury with the juices of *kārpāsī* together with its roots for three days;
then, one should prepare small pills with a quarter-part of *ṭaṅkaṇa*. Rrā_3,20.44.
One should grind together equal parts of anthill clay, black gram, and wheat into a powder, and with that very mixture, kneaded with water, one should fashion the crucible.
Having placed that mercury, which has been rubbed inside it, into a pill, one should heat it strongly;
thus that mercury, having entered the blind crucible (andhamūṣā), becomes bound as a solid bolus (khoṭa).
{The binding of mercury (21):} Take mercury with five times its weight, twice that amount of white *ṭaṅkaṇa*,
and the tender marrow of a horse from white *vātārita* oil.
The practitioner should grind it in a mortar with human urine for three days;
then, having added wheat flour, he should form auspicious pills.
Then, having dried it, one should subsequently blow upon it through the application of glass and borax;
thus the mercury becomes bound as a *khoṭa*, radiant and capable of performing all tasks.
Having ground mercury ash (1) with the juices of *karkoṭī* and the root of *lāṅgalī*, one should place that mercury for three days inside the bulb of *vaṃdhyākarkoṭakī*.
Outside the bulb, one should apply a coating of clay all around to the thickness of one finger-breadth;
once dry, one should bake it in a husk-fire for three days, turning it over.
Having extracted it again and crushed it for three days with the previous juices of *kanda*,
mercury becomes dead (*mṛta*) through the same process of *puṭapāka* as before.
Pure mercury should be rubbed with the juices of *haṃsapādī* for seven days; then,
having placed it inside the cavity of a milk-yielding tuber (*kṣīrakanda*), one should coat the tuber with clay.
One should cook it for a day in a fire of dried cow dung, then grind it again as before;
having placed it inside a tuber, one should cook it in the same manner, and then grind it once more as previously described.
Having sealed it inside a milk-tuber (kṣīrakanda) and coated it with clay, one should let it dry;
then one should cook it properly in a gajapuṭa fire, and it will certainly become dead (reduced to ash).
Having ground mercury ash (3) with the juice of *haṃsapādī* and the tuber of *kṣīrakanda* for three days,
one should place that mercury inside the foot of a *krauñca* bird and coat the foot with clay.
One should cook it for one day in a fire of dried cow-dung and grind it with the previous juices for three days;
likewise, one should cook it in a *puṭa* for one day, and after grinding it again, one should cook it once more.
This becomes a "ash-mercury" (*bhasmasūta*), capable of performing all tasks.
The process of refining [base metals] into gold:
silver, copper, and lead [are transmuted into] gold.
The preparation of the faces for those aforementioned [substances] bound in pills is now described:
vacā, the bulb of caṇḍālinī, and the root of brahmadaṇḍī.
One should grind equal parts of sulfur and borax with the milk of the sun-plant (*bhānu*);
having made pills the size of a chickpea, one should cast them into the previously melted mercury.
Blowing [the bellows] one by one, he gradually swallows seven pills;
there is no doubt that he consumes all metals as he desires.
A morsel of food should be given according to one's ability; then, as before, one should cause [the snake] to die.
Having bound its mouth, one should place the serpent within a copper *tāra* vessel.
All that becomes gold; this transmutation is considered tenfold.
This perfected yoga has been fully explained after observing it correctly from the mouth of the Guru.
Copper, mercury, lead, mica, purified sulfur, *tṛṇajyotis*, and *mūlaka*—
all these in equal parts [should be processed] for one day with the acidic juice of *mātuluṅga*.
One should smear pure copper plates with that paste, seal them, and cook them in a *gajapuṭa* fire; then, having removed them, one should smear them again.
Thus, that copper, having been cooked in three layers, becomes gold.
One should smear copper leaves with the milky sap of red *snuhī* and,
having heated them in fire, immerse them in that milk.
In this manner, one should perform the smearing, heating, and sprinkling seven times;
having thus refined that copper, it becomes divine gold.
Copper, lead,
and silver [become] gold when combined with equal parts of *rasaka*, *darada*, sulphur, *gagana*, and *kunaṭī*.
One should rub that for three days with the slightly reddish milk of the *snuk* plant.
By that [process], copper or lead, or even silver, should be quickly melted;
by adding one-thousandth part of that [elixir], it certainly becomes divine gold.
One should grind turmeric for three days with the milky sap derived from red *snuhī* plants;
with that, one should smear the leaves of the *nāga* plant and cook them in a *puṭa*.
By being smeared again and heated again seven times, it becomes gold.
One should recognize that the *sthalapadminī* (land-lotus), which resembles copper or lead and has the luster and flowers of a lotus leaf,
is to be extracted after knowing that it exudes red milk when broken.
Mercury, sulfur, orpiment, and buffalo-horn manaḥśilā in equal parts,
combined with the previously mentioned *padminī*, should be ground for seven days.
By means of this, copper becomes gold when pierced by one-thousandth part [of the elixir].

Take the paste of the seed-syllable *tāra*, along with lead (*nāga*), tin (*vaṅga*), the essence of steel (*tīkṣṇasāra*), and silver (*tāra*), each increasing in quantity by one step respectively; then add copper equal in measure to all five of these, place everything in a crucible, and blow it [into a flame].
Once it has become visible through the curved tube until only the essence remains, that essence becomes like a ruby; one should then melt it again.
By carefully piercing [the base metal] with a fifth part of the essence of *rasaka*, it becomes divine gold; this is declared to be a perfected yoga (*siddhayoga*).
One should powder the five parts of red *citraka* after drying them in the shade; having repeatedly sealed molten tin with that powder three times, [one should proceed].
That which is given becomes radiant, resembling a conch shell, a jasmine flower, or the moon.
One should apply a paste consisting of the root of *raktacitraka*, fermented rice water (*kāñjika*), purified mercury, and *kaṅguṇī* oil, all combined together, to copper [to turn it into] gold.
One should pour that [liquid] onto heated copper leaves twenty-one times.
This copper constitutes sixteen parts, and silver sixteen parts.
Having combined and thoroughly mixed these,
one should have leaves prepared from the roots of red *citraka*, ground with *bhallātaka* oil.
One should smear the previous leaves with this and cook them in a closed vessel;
by doing this twenty-one times, it becomes divine gold.
Having ground together *nāginī* root, mercury, red *citraka*, and *mūlaka*,
one should smear the previously mentioned leaves with that very mixture.
In this same way, by means of *puṭa* applications, it is cooked until it becomes divine gold.
One should fill a copper vessel with oils produced from *jyotiṣmatī* plants that have turned into gold;
having sealed its mouth, one should bury it in the ground, always placing a layer of husks over it.
In this manner, one should seal and extract [the substance] in sequence for a period of six months;
then, one should cook it externally in a husk-seal for three days and nights.
One should cause that copper and gold, equal in measure, to be melted together;
when cast into jyotiṣmatī oil, it all becomes gold.
One should carefully pour molten copper into milk produced from the *kṣīrakanda* plant a hundred times; that copper will then become gold.
Silver, gold,
sulphur, green vitriol, pyrite, mercury,
and red sandalwood should be ground continuously for three days with the juice of *rudantī*.
Having smeared the leaves of *tāra* with that [substance] and enclosed them in a *puṭa*, one should cook them;
thus one should do this seven times, and the gold becomes divine.
Having made an equal amount of the juice of the fruit of *devadālī*— whether black or yellow— and the juice of *viṣṇukrāntā*, one should rub [the copper] with that very mixture.
One should smear purified mercury for seven days with copper,
then seal it and cook it in a *gajapuṭa* furnace, after which one should blow it with a fierce fire.
By adding one-tenth part of that mercury, it becomes divine gold.
Then, one should sprinkle the well-heated [substance] three times with the juice of *vasubhaṭṭa*; the mineral,
having cracked like salt, will become soft like beeswax.
Having ground the fruit and root of *devadālī* with the juice of *īśvarī* fruit,
by sowing that paste, molten tin or silver will become solid.
Furthermore, this [arrangement] becomes increasingly beautiful as it is spread out.
On the fourteenth or eighth day of the dark fortnight, or during an eclipse,
one should sow white guñjā seeds in a human skull upon pure ground.
One should constantly water it until it becomes fruitful;
then, having performed mantra-recitation and worship, one should indeed gather the fruits during the Puṣya constellation.
Having properly weighed one pure pala of white copper and one hundred and twenty of each of the aforementioned seeds, one should heat them thoroughly.
That copper becomes silver, resembling a conch shell, a kunda flower, or the moon;
that silver becomes gold when pure rītikā is bound [to it].
One should grind purified *tāla* with the juices of *bhūnāgas* for as many days as there are [parts] of copper [in the alloy];
that mass should be sealed within a crucible with a portion of *tāla*.
Thereafter, having sealed the copper plates with *ḍhaṅkaṇa*,
one should fill the crucible with ashes, seal it, and cook it over a fierce fire.
Having extracted [the substance] from the five-fold crucible and joined it with *niṣkaṭaṅkaṇa*,
one should smelt it while it is in a sealed crucible (*mūkamūṣā*) and then extract that pill.
Having collected [the substance] while it is still cool to the touch, one should blow it openly in a crucible;
one should throw the piercing pill into it three times.
Its mouth becomes intense; pure lead melts completely.
When it does not swallow [the mercury], then the pill (vaṭī) should be administered again and again.
When the tin has been processed a hundredfold, one should add copper to it;
by adding a hundredth part of molten silver, that silver becomes auspicious.
{The preparation of the Nāgamukha}:
Take equal parts of sulphur, the essence of soot, *phaṭkarī*, and borax;
the pulp of castor seeds should be twice the amount of all these combined.
The earth-snakes (bhūnāgas) should all be equal; one should grind everything together in a single place. Pills the size of a chickpea should be made; this is known as Vaḍavāmukhā.
Pure lead should be melted and cast into castor oil;
it should be melted again and cast [back] repeatedly until it has been thoroughly boiled.
Furthermore, when that has melted, one should carefully administer the Vaḍavāmukhā pill two or three times; in this way, the mouth of the serpent [the mercury] will be opened.
It swallows all metals and various living beings;
therefore, when it does not swallow, the pill (vaṭī) should be administered again and again.
{Softening the hard element}:
Madhūkapuṣpī, yaṣṭīka, raṃbhā-kanda, ghee, jaggery, sesame oil, goat’s milk, and honey, each taken in equal parts. Rrā 3.20.110.
In the midst of that, one should pour three times over the hardened substance when it has been well-heated;
it will undoubtedly attain softness, becoming fit for drawing threads, as is well known.
(2) Then, having heated it well and sprinkled it three times with the essence of Vasubhadra, the mineral element, which had previously been as hard as salt, becomes soft like beeswax. Rrā 3.20.112.

{3} Softening the hard element: Having removed the intestines from an excessively large frog, one should place powdered borax (*ṭaṃkaṇa*) into it, put it in a vessel, and bury that vessel in the ground. Rrā 3.20.113.
Having extracted [the essence] for three weeks, its application will result in softness;
whether it be gold or silver, it shall become pliable and suitable for leaf-work.
The mercury that devours clouds should be rubbed for three days with the root of *tṛṇajyotis* and the juice of *mātuluṅga*; it then swallows the sky (copper) in an instant.
{The Nāga-penetration according to the Guhyākhya-sūtra}: Fine powder of *bhūnāga* (earth-nāga) should be equal in measure to *ṭaṅkaṇa* (borax).
That powder should be blown into molten *nāga* while heating it a hundred times.
That which is called the "Secret" becomes perfected; its method of consumption will now be described:
[the mercury] should be ground with *śilājatu*, sulfur, and *mākṣika* using the liquid of *bhūnāga*.
One should smear the interior of the crucible with that [substance] and place the material called "guhya" therein;
having placed gold into it, one should blow upon it repeatedly, adding small amounts at a time.
The crucible, however, which is weighed by its capacity, must be smeared again and again;
it releases [the substance] when the mercury is molten. This secret of secrets has been revealed.
{The transmutation of tin by means of the secret elixir}: One should prepare fine powders of equal parts of *bhūnāga* and *ṭaṅkaṇa*.
One should cause that to be blown into molten tin, smelting it until it has increased a hundredfold.
Then one should cause tin, a hundred times [the amount of the previous], to flow over that very [substance];
blowing gently, little by little, it will swallow it—of this there is no doubt.

The secret method for making *vaṅga* (tin): by means of that, piercing occurs. Equal parts of *tālaka* (realgar) and *saindhava* (rock salt), ground with the juice of *bhūnāga*, should be smeared inside the crucible; one should then place that *vaṅga* therein.
Adding a little bit at a time and blowing with the bellows while applying *biḍa* salt, it swallows a weight measured in *bhāra*s; this is known as the secret *vaṅga*.
When it is cast into molten mercury for as many times as [prescribed], there is no doubt;
for that many times in the molten state, there is no uncertainty—this is declared to be the perfected yoga (siddhayoga).
Then, having cast it into the horn of a buffalo, one should cook it while crushing it with fire;
it should be crushed again and again until it becomes one *niṣka* in weight.
Taking that [substance] equal in measure to the mercury, one should then take an amount equal to that.
{The Secret Yoga}: Mercury, pure gold, and the essence (*sattva*) derived from *bhūnāga*—
forty parts of these metals should be ground with the juice of *jaṃbīra* fruit.
Then, having dried that globule, one should first smear it with a paste made from *bhūnāga* inside the interior of a crucible,
and within that, one should seal the globule.
One should blow with a fierce fire until nothing remains there;
then, having offered [the oblation], one swallows it all—this is the supreme yoga called "The Secret."

{The Wish-Fulfilling Cow (1)} Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme method of binding the pill: one should digest the mercury until it is completely assimilated, using space (*vyoma*) which has been made equal [to the other ingredients]. Rrā_3,20.130.
Having added one-twelfth part of copper, one should prepare a paste;
then, having thrown sulphur equal in weight to the grain-sized mica into the copper, one should thoroughly rub it together.
Having fashioned the shape of a crucible for those two, one should place them within the middle of a dough-mixture;
likewise, one should wrap them with human flesh and with a paste of black gram (*māṣa*).
By using castor oil for exactly one month,
the practitioner [attains] an inexhaustible wish-fulfilling cow that causes the immobilization of mercury.

If black mica, eight times the weight of mercury, is processed with gold and colored with *gandharāga*, and then wrapped in human flesh, it becomes a "wish-fulfilling cow" (*kāmadhenu*). (Rājaratnākara 3.20.134)
Having smeared it with a paste of black gram (*māṣa*), one should then cook it in linseed oil (*atasī-taila*).
This is known as the "Wish-Fulfilling Cow" (*kāmadhenu*); it causes the immobilization of *nāgas*.
One should prepare a beautiful golden paste by taking a quarter-part of mercury;
having smeared the *Kāmadhenu* [mercury] with this, one should apply it to the flux of *nāga*.
That *nāga* makes one’s gold yield the fulfillment of all desired objects;
one should wear that wish-fulfilling pill (*guṭikā*) in the mouth every day.
One shall not be pierced by weapons or missiles and will attain a divine body.
The nāga [mercury], killed by the stone and joined with the king of elixirs (sūtarāja),
is colored by gandharāga; together with equal gold, one should cause it to flow.
The piercing with the star [method] should be performed; the gold becomes divine.
One should smear lead with stone and the milk of the sun (sūryakṣīra) upon the leaves of nāga;
by means of the puṭa-yoga, it is killed and becomes divine gold.
Cinnabar,
processed with sheep’s milk and the group of acidic substances,
should be saturated a hundred times with liquid gold and then dried and ground in the hot sun.
Having repeatedly smeared the leaves of white gold and cooked them in a crucible, one should perform this twenty-one times; thus it becomes divine gold.
One should grind mercury for three days with the root of the *tṛṇajāti* plant and the juice of *mātuluṅga*; it swallows the sky (copper) in an instant.
It was bound by hosts of Siddhas and the best of gods who desired the perfection of mercury (rasasiddhi) through the power of supreme mantras with great force;
therefore, the younger brothers, having performed the recitation of mantras, must effect the excellent binding of the superior mercury.
